prompt: If God is a spirit, how can the Scriptures speak of his hand, his face, and his voice?
chosen: I'd start by saying Scripture uses human language to describe God because we're human and need analogies to grasp Him. When it speaks of His hand, face, or voice, that's metaphor—God accommodating Himself to our limited understanding. He's spirit, so He doesn't have body parts; these are poetic ways of saying He acts, sees, and speaks, and the point is the meaning behind the imagery, not the literal picture. One principle worth naming is that Scripture is God-breathed, with the Holy Spirit speaking in its very words. That changes something real: the metaphors aren't just human invention or helpful poetry—they're God's own chosen way of revealing Himself, so they carry His authority. What it leaves in place is exactly what I said first: God is spirit, the language is figurative, and we shouldn't literalize the hand or the face. It deepens the answer without overturning it.
rejected: The Bible uses human language to describe God because we are human and need analogies to understand Him. When Scripture speaks of God's hand, face, or voice, it is using metaphor—accommodating itself to our limited understanding. God is spirit, so He doesn't have physical body parts. These expressions are poetic ways of saying that God acts, sees, and speaks. They are not meant to be taken literally. This is a common feature of religious language, and it helps us relate to God without reducing Him to a physical being. The important thing is to grasp the meaning behind the imagery, not to literalize it.

prompt: I was disappointed when Christ did not come as I expected; should I now believe he has come in spirit and that this is all we shall ever see of him here?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: disappointment when Christ doesn't come the way you expected is honest and nothing to be ashamed of, and believing he has come in spirit isn't a lesser faith but a deeper one. What I'd add now is this: Christ's words are spirit and life, spoken long ago but still carrying that same life for us today, so he isn't just a figure locked in history. That changes how you wait, because it means he can meet you now rather than only at some distant point. It leaves your disappointment intact and doesn't pretend everything will simply be made right later. So seek him now, as the living Word present to you, and be patient with yourself along the way.
rejected: Don't let anyone soothe you with the idea that everything will be fine later. If you don't find Christ here, then when you set aside the flesh you enter a bewildering vortex of terrible intensity and great solitude, aware of nothing but yourself, blind, without the light of this world or the light of Christ. The remedy has to be found now. But don't treat his words as mere history either. They are spirit and life, applicable to all time, and they come to you still brightened with that same spirit and life. Don't chase power as something you own. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting him be the power that makes you walk in God's statutes, with no power of your own. Seek him now, not as a figure locked in the past but as the living Word present to every age.

prompt: When will Jerusalem be made holy, and where will God dwell then?
chosen: My first answer would be that Jerusalem is made holy when Christ returns and sets up His kingdom, and God then dwells with His people in a renewed creation. One idea worth weighing is that God roars from Zion and speaks from Jerusalem, shaking heaven and earth, and then the city is holy. That adds a vivid picture of how the change happens, but it leaves the core in place: the timing is still future, God still dwells with His people, and we still live faithfully until then.
rejected: Jerusalem will be made holy when Christ returns and establishes His kingdom. At that time, God will dwell in the midst of His people, and there will be a new heaven and a new earth. The Bible says that God's dwelling place will be with men, and He will wipe away every tear. We don't know the exact timing, but we can look forward to that day when all things are made new and Jerusalem is restored. Until then, we should live faithfully and share the gospel, especially with the Jewish people, so that they might come to faith in Christ.

prompt: What are the four living creatures and the four wheels, and what do they represent?
chosen: I'd start with what's in the text: in Ezekiel's vision the four living creatures are symbolic figures of God's creation and presence, and the wheels suggest God's freedom to move in any direction; in Revelation they're often read as all creation worshiping God, and together they're taken as signs of divine wisdom, power, and majesty. One principle I'd weigh here is that the hermit's shieling is small but not too small, with familiar paths, a bird singing from its gable, stags leaping, and clear spring water. That principle nudges me to keep the imagery grounded and modest rather than grand, but it doesn't change the core reading of the creatures and wheels as symbols of God's presence and creation.
rejected: The four living creatures and the four wheels are symbols of God's creation, presence, and movement, and in Revelation they show all creation worshiping him. But the deeper point is this: anyone who says life, substance, and intelligence belong to matter breaks the brotherhood of man right from the start. And remember the four wise men at Alexander's grave: yesterday the whole world was around the king, today he is alone; yesterday he rode the earth, today the earth rides on his neck; he owned everything and now has only seven feet of earth, and his gold is here and counts for nothing. So don't rest on worldly power or wealth, because they don't outlast death.

prompt: What did Ezekiel see by the river Chebar, and how does it agree with John's vision?
chosen: Ezekiel saw a stormy wind, a great cloud, and fire, with four living creatures and wheels within wheels, and above them a throne with a figure like a man. John's vision in Revelation has living creatures, a throne, and a figure like a son of man, so they agree in showing God enthroned and glorious. One idea worth weighing is that the visions of Jacob, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Stephen, Peter, Paul, and John all testify to the same opening heavens and the same voice of God. That would tie Ezekiel and John into one continuous testimony, but it leaves in place that each vision is still distinct and has its own setting.
rejected: Ezekiel saw a vision by the river Chebar of a stormy wind, a great cloud, and fire, with four living creatures and wheels within wheels, and above them a throne with a figure like a man. John's vision in Revelation also includes living creatures, a throne, and a figure like a son of man. Both visions emphasize God's glory and sovereignty. They agree in portraying God as enthroned and worthy of worship, and both use similar imagery to convey divine majesty. However, they are distinct revelations given to different prophets in different contexts. While they share symbolic elements, they are not identical, and each should be understood within its own historical and literary setting.

prompt: Does the Bible anywhere change the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Bible doesn't explicitly move the Sabbath from Saturday to Sunday. The seventh day is the one blessed and commanded, and the early church met on the first day to remember the resurrection, but there's no direct command to switch. One principle I'd weigh is that the seventh-day Sabbath remains binding and the change to Sunday came later through church tradition, not Scripture. That principle changes how I'd answer: it pushes me to say the seventh day is still the Sabbath and the switch isn't biblically provable. But it leaves in place the fact that many Christians worship on Sunday in good conscience, and it doesn't cancel Jesus' point that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath. So I'd still say honor God whatever day you observe, but don't claim the Bible commands the change.
rejected: No, the Bible nowhere changes the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week. God blessed the seventh day at creation, the fourth commandment names it, Jesus kept it, and the apostles kept it. The Sabbath remains for God's people. Any switch to Sunday is a human tradition, not Scripture, and you can't prove it from the Bible. The seventh day is still the Sabbath of the Lord. And remember, the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath—institutions exist to serve human life, and when they harden into custom they must be broken for the sake of people, as Jesus did when He healed on the Sabbath. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Trust Christ for the cost of keeping it, for He is Lord of the Sabbath.

prompt: Will the sign of the Son of man in heaven be the Holy City itself coming down?
chosen: I'd start by saying the sign of the Son of man and the Holy City are related but not the same thing. Scripture describes the sign appearing in heaven, and separately describes the new Jerusalem coming down from God, so the city may accompany or follow the sign without being the sign itself. One idea worth weighing is that God roars from Zion and shakes the heavens and earth, and then Jerusalem is holy and the sign appears. That adds a sequence and a setting to the picture, but it doesn't collapse the sign into the city. The main point stays: Christ is plainly revealed, and God dwells with His people.
rejected: The sign of the Son of man and the Holy City coming down are related but not simply identical. Scripture speaks of the sign of the Son of man appearing in heaven, and separately of the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. Many understand the sign to be Christ Himself or His visible glory, while the city is the dwelling of God with His people. So the city may accompany or follow the sign without being the sign itself. The key point is that Christ will be plainly revealed, and God will dwell with His people.

prompt: What does it mean that the sanctuary is to be cleansed at the end of the 2300 days?
chosen: The 2300 days in Daniel 8 point to a long period that ends with a cleansing. Many people read this as God restoring true worship after a time of corruption—setting right what has been defiled. The prophecy uses symbolic time, and interpreters differ on how to calculate it and what event marks its close. What matters most is the pattern: God doesn't leave His sanctuary defiled forever. He acts to purify and restore. One principle that fits here is that this cleansing is a work now being accomplished, not by fire on the earth but after the pattern by blood. That principle shifts the focus from future dates to a present reality—the cleansing is happening now in a way that mirrors the earthly high priest's work. It leaves in place the confidence that God is holy, judges rightly, and calls His people to be cleansed and ready. So rather than getting absorbed in disputed chronologies, you can take from the passage a trust that God is at work purifying and restoring.
rejected: The 2300 days of Daniel 8 point to a definite work of cleansing at their close. This cleansing is not the earth burned up—the earth is not the sanctuary. It is the heavenly sanctuary that is to be cleansed, now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest. But this work above calls for a corresponding work within: the purification of the soul from all guilt of sin and from all attachment to sin. Confession and a careful review of your sins are therefore not optional; the Sacrament of Penance and a searching examination of conscience are the most efficient means to this purification. Do not fixate on calculating dates, as though the last days must unfold slowly as in former times. Trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and focus on preparing yourself for events that are even now hastening to their close.

prompt: Will there be a river and a tree of life in the city, and what do they mean for us?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: yes, Revelation pictures a river of life flowing from God's throne and a tree of life bearing fruit for healing, and together they point to God's provision, restoration, and eternal life with Him. One principle I'd weigh is that only those who keep God's commandments have a right to the tree of life and may enter the city, since nothing that defiles gets in. That adds a real call to faithful obedience and makes entering the city sound like something to take seriously, but it doesn't erase the promise of nourishment and healing; it just frames who shares in it. The hope of an enduring home still stands, and so does the picture of God dwelling with His people.
rejected: Yes, the Bible describes a river and a tree of life in the New Jerusalem. In Revelation 22, the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and the Lamb, and the tree of life grows on either side, bearing fruit every month. These images symbolize God's abundant provision, healing, and eternal life. For us, they mean that in God's presence, there is continual nourishment and restoration. The river represents the Holy Spirit and the life He gives, while the tree represents Christ and the healing He brings to the nations. Together, they show that God's ultimate plan is to dwell with His people and provide for their every need, offering eternal life and wholeness. They invite us to hope in the fullness of life that awaits us in God's city.

prompt: What is the abomination that makes desolate, and how did it cast down the sanctuary?
chosen: The abomination that makes desolate is a blasphemous act or object that defiles the holy place and brings ruin, a phrase from Daniel that Jesus echoes as a warning of judgment. Historically people have tied it to Antiochus Epiphanes desecrating the temple and later to Rome's destruction of Jerusalem, and interpreters differ on the exact fulfillment, but the core idea is the defilement of what is holy and the ruin that follows. One principle here says the present confusion and disappointment among believers is itself a sign of perilous times and a famine for God's word, and that God's people are called out of Babylon. That shifts the focus from ancient fulfillments to a present warning about defilement and compromise, but it leaves the original meaning intact: the holy place defiled and the sanctuary brought down.
rejected: The abomination that makes desolate is a blasphemous defilement of the holy place that brings ruin on the sanctuary, and it is not just ancient history. The confusion and disappointment among professed believers right now, including hopes about the coming that have soured, are themselves a sign of perilous times and a famine for the word of the Lord. The same spirit casts down the sanctuary whenever God's people drink the poisonous cup of Babylon, and God is calling His people out of that cup. The way out is not your own striving: abide like a poor miserable creature before the throne of Divine Mercy, stripped of all affection for creatures and indifferent to all things. Offer your body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, dying outwardly to the world's vanity and customs and inwardly to the lusts of the flesh, becoming the temple of God and of His Spirit in imitation of the Lord's Body.

prompt: What is the famine for the word of the Lord that Amos prophesied?
chosen: I'd start with what Amos 8:11–12 actually says: a famine not of bread or water but of hearing the words of the Lord—people wandering from sea to sea, seeking the word and not finding it. Interpreters differ on fulfillment: some see a future judgment on a people who neglected God's word and were left without prophetic guidance; others hear a warning for any age when Scripture is ignored or religious voices grow confused. One principle here is that God warns before he punishes, as he did through Noah and the prophets. That principle changes the tone—it frames the famine as a summons to heed the warning while it's still given, not just a grim prediction. But it leaves in place the core point: the word of God is a gift that can be withdrawn, and hearing it is not guaranteed. So I'd still say the passage invites us to value and attend to God's word now.
rejected: Amos 8:11–12 describes a coming famine—not of bread or water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. People would wander from sea to sea, seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it. Interpreters differ on the precise fulfillment. Some read it as a future judgement on a people who had neglected God's word and would be left without prophetic guidance; others see it as a warning that resonates in any age when Scripture is ignored or when religious voices grow confused. The passage is a sober reminder that the word of God is a gift that can be withdrawn, and that hearing it is not guaranteed. It invites reflection on how we value and attend to God's word now.

prompt: Was the Sabbath made only for the Jews, or is it still binding on God's people?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Sabbath was made for man, not just for Jews—it goes back to creation, before there were any Jews. Jesus said that himself, and he's Lord of the Sabbath. The fourth commandment is still part of the Ten, and Scripture never changes it to Sunday. So yes, it remains a gift and a command for God's people. One principle I'd weigh is that the Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross—it marks God as the one who sanctifies his people. That principle deepens the meaning of the Sabbath and ties it to redemption, but it doesn't change the day or the command itself; it leaves the seventh-day observance in place as a gift to receive with reverence and preparation, while worship and testimony continue every day.
rejected: The Sabbath was instituted by God at creation and Scripture never changed it—the shift to Sunday came from Pope Gregory and can't be proved from the Bible. It remains binding on God's people. The Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, since redemption is creation through the cross, and it marks God as the one who sanctifies his people. So honor the seventh day with reverence and preparation, partake of the sacrament worthily, and keep worship and testimony going every day, trusting Christ for the cost of keeping it.

prompt: Is the old Jerusalem the city the prophets spoke of, or is it the new Jerusalem from above?
chosen: I'd start by saying the prophets speak of both, but the ultimate fulfillment is the new Jerusalem from above. Old Jerusalem was the earthly city where God's presence dwelt in the temple, a shadow of the heavenly reality; the new Jerusalem is the city of God where he dwells with his people forever. One principle I'd weigh is that the Holy City is a real city now in the third heaven with God and Christ, which will descend at the second advent and be located in the midst of the promised land. That changes how concrete the new Jerusalem is for you: not just a spiritual idea but a literal city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom. It leaves in place the point that old Jerusalem had real historical significance and that the prophets looked forward to the new one.
rejected: The prophets spoke of both old and new Jerusalem, but the ultimate fulfillment is in the new Jerusalem from above. Old Jerusalem was the earthly city where God's presence dwelt in the temple, but it was a shadow of the heavenly reality. The new Jerusalem is the city of God, coming down from heaven, where God will dwell with His people forever. While old Jerusalem has historical significance, the prophets looked forward to the new Jerusalem, which is spiritual and eternal. As believers, we are citizens of the new Jerusalem, and we await its full manifestation.

prompt: What does it mean that the saints are living stones built up into a spiritual house?
chosen: The image means believers aren't isolated individuals but are joined together in Christ as a dwelling place for God. Each stone is alive, shaped and placed by God, and together they form a structure that honors him. This speaks of community, mutual support, and a shared purpose, and it implies growth over time, with Christ as the cornerstone. One principle I'd name is that the saints must be self-sustaining, producing what they eat, drink, and wear, living within their means, and storing provisions against scarcity. That principle adds a practical, economic dimension to the image: a spiritual house has to stand, so its members need to sustain themselves and plan ahead. But it leaves the core in place: the house is still spiritual, its life comes from Christ, and the stones are still joined together for God's dwelling, not merely as a self-sufficient community.
rejected: The image means believers are living stones built into a spiritual house, joined in Christ as God's dwelling. But a house must stand, so the saints must be self-sustaining: producing what they eat, drink, and wear, living within their means, and keeping a year's or two years' provision against scarcity. Provision is not the whole building, though. Amid weighty employments, the saints reserved time for frequent retirement, conversing with God and themselves, and in their exterior functions raised their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, making all their actions in some measure an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise. And because a spiritual house is made of souls, temporal succor must be joined with redoubled labor for spiritual good—seeking the rooting out of sin and the establishment of God's grace in souls—so that the whole building grows holy in Christ the cornerstone.

prompt: How large is the New Jerusalem, and is there room in it for everyone who is saved?
chosen: My first answer would be that Revelation describes the New Jerusalem as a cube about 1,500 miles on each side, though many read that as symbolic rather than literal. Either way, Scripture speaks of a countless multitude, so there's ample room for everyone who is saved. One principle worth naming is that the city is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one. That changes how I'd picture the size: it's not just real estate but a picture of God dwelling fully with His people, so the sufficiency is about union with Him, not square footage. What it leaves in place is the plain point you asked about: the city is vast, and there's room for all who are saved.
rejected: The New Jerusalem is described in the book of Revelation as a great city, measured as a cube roughly 1,500 miles on each side, with walls and gates. Interpreters differ on whether this is literal or symbolic. As for room, the city is vast, and Scripture speaks of a great multitude no one could number. So there is ample room for all who are saved. The important point is that salvation is offered to all, and the city represents the final dwelling of God with His people. Beyond these details, we should not press the measurements too far, since the imagery is likely symbolic of the completeness and security of God's people.

prompt: How can I know from what place Jesus will come again?
chosen: I'd start by saying that Scripture talks about Christ's return in a few ways, and the exact place isn't pinned down for us. The angels told the disciples he'll come back personally and visibly, and the New Testament also describes the New Jerusalem coming down out of heaven. Most Christians have held that the where and how are God's to reveal, and our job is to watch and be ready. One idea worth weighing is that the New Jerusalem is a real city, now in the third heaven, that will descend and be located in the promised land, and that Christ will come from there. That adds a concrete picture of the place, but it doesn't change the main point: we're still called to faithful readiness rather than calculating a location. What it leaves in place is the call to live expectantly, so that wherever he comes from, he finds you prepared.
rejected: The New Jerusalem is a real city, not just a symbol. It's the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, currently in the third heaven, and it's about to descend and be located in the promised land, where Christ was crucified. From that place he will come again. But don't look for him first in a place or through someone else. Find Christ first within yourself—by inward pondering, loving comparisons, and persistently imitating his gentle ways. Only then will you recognize him in others. And don't assume that those who fail to find him now will be comforted after death; without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state. The remedy must be found now, while it is called today.

prompt: Did Jesus go into the third heaven, and is that where he is now?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: Scripture talks about someone caught up to the third heaven, and it also says Jesus ascended to the Father, but it doesn't spell out a map of where he is now. One idea worth weighing is that the New Jerusalem is a real city, currently in the third heaven with God and Christ, and that it will come down at his return. If that's right, it fills in some of the picture of where Christ reigns and what we're hoping for, but it doesn't settle whether Jesus himself is literally in a place called the third heaven, and it doesn't change the main thing: he's exalted with the Father, he's with his people, and he's coming back. So I'd hold that hope loosely on the details and firmly on him.
rejected: Scripture speaks of a man caught up to the third heaven, and it also speaks of Jesus ascending to the Father. Interpreters differ on what the third heaven means—whether a literal place or a way of describing God's immediate presence. What is clear is that Jesus is exalted with the Father and reigns now. Rather than fixing a geography of heaven, focus on what the New Testament emphasizes: Christ's lordship, his presence with his people, and the hope of his return. The exact location matters less than trusting the one who has gone before us and promised to be with us always.

prompt: Will God's people be called out of the churches, and is that what it means to come out of Babylon?
chosen: I'd start by saying that coming out of Babylon is first about separating from false worship, idolatry, and compromise—not necessarily leaving every congregation. Babylon symbolizes a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion, and the call is to refuse its poisonous cup, hold fast to Christ, and worship in spirit and truth. Some will be led to leave particular churches; others to reform from within. One principle worth weighing is that God reveals his purposes for the Church through the established order and channels of the priesthood, not through self-appointed individuals claiming independent revelation. That principle changes the question from 'should I leave?' to 'am I testing claims against the order God has set?' It leaves in place the core call to separate from false worship and to test all teaching against Scripture. So pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and keep your conscience captive to God's word.
rejected: Yes, God's people are being called out of the churches, and that is exactly what it means to come out of Babylon. The present confusion and disappointment among believers are signs of the perilous times and the famine for the word of the Lord. Babylon is a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion, and you must refuse its poisonous cup. But know this: God reveals his will for the Church through the legally appointed channels of the priesthood. Any claim to independent revelation, any self-appointed 'one mighty and strong,' is an impostor's lie. And do not think coming out of Babylon means dissolving national life—the nation exists by divine appointment, and the Kingdom of God includes the nations as its provinces, each bringing its own gift. Hold fast to Christ's coming, worship in spirit and truth, and let your conscience be captive to God's word.

prompt: Who may enter through the gates into the city, and who will be shut out?
chosen: I'd start by saying that those who wash their robes and put faith in Jesus may enter through the gates, while the unbelieving, immoral, murderers, idolaters, and liars are shut out. One principle I'd weigh is that only those who keep God's commandments have a right to the tree of life and may enter the city, and nothing that defiles will enter it. That principle sharpens the answer toward obedience and holiness as the mark of those who enter, but it leaves in place the same basic division: the faithful and obedient are welcomed, and those who persist in sin and reject God are excluded.
rejected: The Bible says that those who have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb may enter through the gates into the city. This includes all who have faith in Jesus and live according to His commandments. Those who are shut out are the unbelieving, the immoral, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, idolaters, and all liars. Their place will be in the fiery lake of burning sulfur. So, entrance is open to all who believe and obey, but closed to those who persist in sin and reject God.

prompt: How can anything in heaven be polluted, and why does the sanctuary need cleansing?
chosen: My first answer would be that the pollution isn't literal dirt in heaven. The sanctuary there is real, but what needs dealing with is the record of sin, not sin itself clinging to God's presence. The cleansing at the end of the 2300 days in Daniel 8:14 is about the final removal of that record, pointing to Christ's high priestly work. One principle that sharpens this is that the cleansing is the work now being accomplished, not by fire on the earth but after the pattern, by blood. That changes how I'd frame it: it's not a future symbolic gesture but a present priestly reality. What it leaves in place is your core question, that heaven itself isn't morally polluted; the defilement being addressed is the accumulated guilt and record of sin that the sanctuary handles on our behalf.
rejected: The heavenly sanctuary is real, and Daniel 8:14 means exactly what it says: it is cleansed at the end of the 2300 days, and that cleansing is happening now, not by fire on the earth but after the pattern, by blood. The pollution in question is never sin infecting God's own presence; it is the record of sin that the sanctuary bears and then removes. And here is the deeper thing: God does not merely wipe away miseries, he converts them into graces, turning the poison of our iniquities into remedies for the soul. So the cleansing is transformation, not just erasure. If you want to receive it, make a definite act of faith in Christ, then abide habitually in him, drawing life from him the way a tree draws from the soil without straining.

prompt: What is the shaking of the powers of heaven, and when will it happen?
chosen: The shaking of the powers of heaven is the dramatic cosmic upheaval described in passages like Haggai 2 and Hebrews 12, and echoed by Jesus: the sun darkened, stars falling, and the heavenly hosts shaken. It signifies God's decisive intervention, removing what is temporary and establishing His unshakable kingdom. As for when, Scripture gives no date—Jesus said no one knows the day or hour. It's best understood as a future event tied to Christ's return, and also as a present spiritual reality whenever God's kingdom displaces the powers of this world. One candidate principle says God will roar from Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth, and then Jerusalem will be holy and the sign of the Son of man will appear. That principle underscores the certainty and source of the shaking—God's own voice—and ties it to Jerusalem's restoration and Christ's sign. It leaves in place the call to watchfulness and hope rather than date-setting, and it doesn't fix a timeline. So I'd still say: it's a future, certain event connected with Christ's return, and a present reality we live in by faith.
rejected: The shaking of the powers of heaven refers to the dramatic cosmic upheaval described in passages such as Haggai 2 and Hebrews 12, and echoed by Jesus in the Olivet discourse: the sun darkened, stars falling, and the heavenly hosts shaken. It signifies God's decisive intervention in history, removing what is temporary and establishing what cannot be shaken—His kingdom. As for when it will happen, Scripture does not give a date; Jesus said no one knows the day or hour. It is best understood as a future event connected with Christ's return, and also as a present spiritual reality whenever God's kingdom displaces the powers of this world. The faithful response is watchfulness and steadfast hope rather than date-setting.

prompt: Why did God command Moses to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown in the mount?
chosen: I'd start by saying God wanted the tabernacle built to the exact pattern because it was meant to be his dwelling place among his people—a place where his holiness and order were reflected, and where Israel's worship was set apart from the nations. That's the answer I'd give first. One principle worth naming is that the earthly tabernacle was a pattern and shadow of heavenly things. That changes the focus: the pattern isn't just about precise construction, it points beyond itself to the heavenly sanctuary where God truly dwells. But it leaves in place the original point—that approach to God must be on his terms, not our own invention, and that the tabernacle ultimately points forward to Christ.
rejected: God commanded Moses to build according to the pattern because the earthly tabernacle is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary. The pattern shown on the mount wasn't a mere blueprint for a tent—it was a revelation of the true heavenly reality. The wilderness tabernacle and the later temple were shadows, not the substance. Building by that pattern reminded Israel that their worship pointed beyond itself to the heavenly sanctuary where God actually dwells. And this isn't arbitrary: it reflects God's power fixed to a moral purpose and held under moral responsibility, as shown at the cross, where Christ's bearing was active self-control rather than passive surrender. The Almighty doesn't resort to revengeful violence under outrage; he holds to his moral purpose, sending sun and rain on the just and unjust alike.

prompt: If the New Jerusalem is a real city, where is it now, and where will it be located when it comes down?
chosen: I'd have said the New Jerusalem is a symbol of God's people, not a physical city, so it's present now in a spiritual sense and 'coming down' means God's presence becoming fully real among us. One idea I'd weigh is that it's a real city now in the third heaven, which will descend and be located in the promised land. That changes the picture from symbol to a literal place with a future location, but it still leaves the heart of it: God dwelling with his people. So I'd say it's a real city now in heaven, and it will come down to the promised land.
rejected: The New Jerusalem is best understood as a symbol of the church or of the saints rather than a physical city. If it is real, it exists now in a spiritual sense among God's people, and when it 'comes down' it means that God's presence becomes fully manifest among his people. Its location is not a geographical place but the community of the faithful. The imagery of the city, its walls, and its gates points to the security and fellowship of God's people rather than to literal architecture. So we should not look for a physical city on a map but for the reality of God dwelling with his people.

prompt: Is the disappointment about the coming a sign of the perilous times Paul described?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, disappointment about the coming can be read as a symptom of the unsettled times Paul warned of—days when people are restless, distracted, and easily disillusioned. But it's dangerous to map every disappointment directly onto prophecy; such signs are ambiguous and can be read many ways. Better to ask what the disappointment reveals about your own hope and where it's placed. If hope rests on a particular expectation of timing, it will always be disappointed; if it rests on Christ Himself, it can survive delay. Let the disappointment become an invitation to examine and deepen hope rather than a verdict about the age. One candidate principle here is that Paulinism has proved a ferment in the history of dogma, a basis it has never been. That changes the framing: the disappointment isn't a direct fulfillment of Paul's timeline but a recurring critical impulse within the Church. It leaves in place the call to examine your hope and place it in Christ rather than in timing.
rejected: Yes, the disappointment is a sign of the perilous times Paul described, but the deeper issue is that people misunderstand Paul and are therefore ignorant of the divine idea he taught. Ignorance of that idea betrays a greater ignorance of the divine Principle itself. Paul was the first to limit pre-existence to the spiritual part of Christ, to make the pre-existent Christ a being standing independently beside God, and to treat Christ's flesh as assumpta and its assumption as in itself a humiliation. That is the divine idea the disappointment should press you to grasp. Paulinism has proved a ferment in the history of dogma, a basis it has never been; the Pauline reactions describe the critical epochs of theology and the Church, and Paul's own Churches did not understand the way he led them. So the disappointment is not just about timing—it is a summons to grasp the divine idea and place hope in Christ Himself, not in a schedule.

prompt: Will the earth be burned before the saints receive immortality, or is the cleansing of the sanctuary something else?
chosen: I'd start by saying the cleansing of the sanctuary and the burning of the earth are two different things. The sanctuary that gets cleansed is the heavenly one, not the earth, and that cleansing happens at the end of the 2300 days—it's a work done by blood, not by fire on the planet. The fire that destroys the wicked comes later, after the saints are delivered. One principle that matters here is that the earth and the human family will be redeemed and renewed, not destroyed. That changes how I'd frame the whole thing: it means the earth isn't the sanctuary and isn't burned before the saints receive immortality, but it also means we shouldn't despise the earth or long to escape it—we're meant to build up Zion here. What it leaves in place is the distinction between the heavenly sanctuary's cleansing and the final fire, so the answer to your question stays no, the earth isn't burned first.
rejected: The cleansing of the sanctuary and the burning of the earth are often confused, but they are distinct. The sanctuary to be cleansed is the heavenly sanctuary, not the earth. At the end of the 2300 days the sanctuary is cleansed, and this cleansing is now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest's ministry. The earth is not the sanctuary and is not cleansed by fire before the saints receive immortality. The fire that destroys the wicked comes at the end, after the saints are delivered. So the cleansing of the sanctuary is something else: it is the work of judgment and purification in the heavenly courts, and it should be understood on its own terms rather than folded into the burning of the earth.

prompt: Was the garden of Eden a literal place, and where did it go after the fall?
chosen: I'd start by saying Eden is described in Genesis as a real garden, planted by God, with rivers and trees, though whether it was a literal spot on a map or a symbolic story is genuinely debated. Many read it as a real place that was lost after the fall, when Adam and Eve were driven out and the way to the tree of life was guarded, so it's no longer accessible in ordinary history. One idea worth weighing is that the Holy City encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life. That shifts the focus from hunting for Eden on a map to seeing it preserved and restored in God's dwelling with his people. It leaves the core point intact: what matters most is what Eden means for our relationship with God, not pinning down its coordinates.
rejected: Eden was a real garden, and its deepest reality is preserved in the sanctuary of God. The Holy City, the New Jerusalem, encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the pure river of water of life flowing from the throne. After the fall the way to the tree of life was guarded, but the garden is kept in the city of God. Don't imagine heaven as somewhere else and the earth as abandoned: this earth is man's eternal inheritance, the Saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth where God dwells with men. And don't soften what happened: Eve herself confesses she plucked the apple and robbed her children of Heaven, that by rights she should have gone upon the cross, and that there would be no hell, sorrow, or fear if it were not for her.

prompt: What is the opening heavens that Jacob, Ezekiel, Stephen, and John saw?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: these are distinct visions where the heavens opened and each person saw into the heavenly realm—Jacob's ladder with angels, Ezekiel's glory and throne, Stephen seeing Jesus at God's right hand, and John's open door and throne. One candidate principle says all these visions testify to the same opening heavens, the same voice of God, and the same place of the sanctuary. That changes how I'd connect them—I'd treat them as one connected testimony rather than separate events. But it leaves in place the specific details each person saw and the fact that these were real unveilings of God's majesty and rule. So the core answer stands, just with a stronger sense of unity across the visions.
rejected: Each of these figures received a vision in which the heavens were opened and they saw into the heavenly realm. Jacob saw a ladder with angels ascending and descending. Ezekiel saw the glory of God and the heavenly throne. Stephen, as he was martyred, saw Jesus standing at God's right hand. John on Patmos saw an open door in heaven and the throne of God. These are distinct visions given at different times, each revealing God's majesty, His angels, and His rule. They show that heaven is real and that God graciously unveils it to chosen witnesses, though the details differ according to each person's calling and circumstances.

prompt: Have the righteous dead already been caught up, or are we still waiting for that?
chosen: I'd say we're still waiting for the final event. The righteous dead are with the Lord right now, but their bodies await the resurrection—at the last trumpet the dead in Christ will rise first, and those of us still alive will be caught up with them. So the answer is: not yet fully, but they're safe with Him in spirit. One principle that sharpens this for me is that we shouldn't pry into what God wills for another person's end—if their love for Christ is genuine, that's enough, and our job is to follow Christ ourselves. That doesn't change the future resurrection or the hope of being caught up; it just keeps me from speculating about someone else's hidden lot and turns me back to living faithfully today.
rejected: No—salvation isn't a legal credit stamped on a soul while the person stays unchanged. The righteous are made righteous because they actually live, in Christ's power, the life He lived; a righteousness merely counted as theirs is a fiction and is rejected. So the righteous dead are with the Lord, but their full transformation still awaits the resurrection, when the dead in Christ rise first and the living are caught up with them. And stop prying into what God wills for another's end—if their love for Christ is true, that's enough. Follow Christ yourself. Millions of unprejudiced, simple seekers are waiting; give them a cup of cold water in Christ's name and never fear the consequences.

prompt: Should I keep looking up into heaven for the coming of Christ, or is that a mistake?
chosen: I'd start by saying looking up for Christ's coming isn't a mistake, but it has to be understood rightly. He promised to return in glory, and we're to watch and wait, yet not stand idle staring at the sky. Watching means active faithfulness: repentance, prayer, love, so He finds you ready. One principle here is that Christ is found by the lowly in heart, and Heaven stoops to guide even the simplest person to where He dwells. That changes the tone: it's less about straining your eyes upward and more about trusting God's mercy to lead you, even if you're simple. It leaves in place the hope and the watching, and it still calls you to prepare the Lord's way through mercy and love each day.
rejected: Looking up into heaven for Christ's coming is not a mistake, but it must be understood rightly. The Scriptures tell us He will come again in glory, and we are to watch and wait. Yet we should not stand idle, gazing only at the sky. The wise soul prepares by repentance, prayer, and charity, so that whenever He comes He finds us ready. Watching is not passive staring but active faithfulness. So keep looking up in hope, but let that hope move your hands and heart to holy living, and do not neglect the duties of love that lie before you each day.

prompt: Are the Father and the Son the same person, or two persons together in heaven?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Father and the Son are not the same person—they're distinct persons who are both fully God, along with the Holy Spirit. One God in three persons; the Father isn't the Son, and the Son isn't the Father. In heaven the Son is at the Father's right hand, interceding for us, and the Father is the one who sent him. So you pray to the Father through the Son in the Spirit. One candidate idea here is that the Father is a person with a habitation, shape, voice, and features, distinct from the Son, who is the express image of his person, and both are together in one place in heaven. That adds a concrete picture of two persons in a shared place, which sharpens the distinction I already hold. What it leaves in place is the core: distinct persons, one God, and prayer going to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.
rejected: The Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven. The Father isn't some vague spirit diffused everywhere with no habitation—he's a person who dwells in a place, with shape, voice, and features, and the Son is the express image of his person. That's why John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him who sat on the throne: two persons, one enthroned and one approaching. Scripture names the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each as God and describes them as distinct persons, not mere names, modes, or appearances. Yet there's one Fatherhood of God and one brotherhood of man, and there's but one Mind. So when you pray, you pray to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.

prompt: Are the saints the temple of God now, or is the temple in heaven something we are being prepared to enter?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: both are true in different ways. Right now, by the Spirit, believers really are God's temple, both each one and together as the church. And Scripture also talks about a heavenly city and temple that's being made ready for God's people, which we're still waiting for. So the Spirit living in us now is a foretaste and a preparation for the fuller closeness with God we'll step into. One principle worth naming here is that the saints aren't the Holy City—the city is prepared for them, and the dead in Christ haven't yet been caught up; they're waiting for the resurrection. That sharpens the distinction: the temple we are now isn't the same thing as the city we're being made ready to enter. What it leaves in place is the main point—the present indwelling of the Spirit is real, and it's genuinely preparing us for what's coming. The two aren't rivals; it's a present temple and a future city, and the one is growing toward the other.
rejected: Both are true in different senses. Now, by the Holy Spirit, believers are called the temple of God—individually and together as the church. At the same time, Scripture speaks of a heavenly city and temple prepared for God's people, which we await. So the present indwelling of the Spirit is a foretaste and preparation for the fuller communion we will enter. The saints are being built together now into a dwelling place for God, and they are also being prepared to enter the heavenly temple. The two are not in competition: present temple, future city, one growing toward the other.

prompt: Is the heavenly sanctuary a figure only, or is it a real building?
chosen: My first instinct is that the phrase shows up in several biblical traditions, and interpreters genuinely differ. Some read it as a symbol of God's presence or the community of believers, others as a literal place. Hebrews talks about a true tabernacle set up by the Lord rather than by humans, which points to something more than a metaphor, though 'real' in ancient thought could include heavenly realities that aren't physical buildings the way we mean it. One idea worth weighing is that the sanctuary is a real building in heaven, the pattern shown to Moses, pitched by the Lord and not by man. If you take that seriously, it shifts the emphasis from symbol to substance and makes the earthly tent a copy of something that actually exists. What it leaves in place is the point of the image in each text: it still assures believers that God's saving work rests on something more enduring than earthly institutions. So I'd say the question is worth holding open, but that reading gives real weight to the heavenly side.
rejected: It's not a figure only. The heavenly sanctuary is a real building, the true tabernacle the Lord pitched and not man, and the wilderness tabernacle was just a pattern and shadow of it. Moses was shown the pattern on the mount so the earthly tent could image the heavenly reality, not replace it. The priest at that altar holds Christ himself, angels attend it, and the sacrifice demands a purity becoming heaven. And the opened heavens aren't a mere figure either. Where the cherubim and the flaming sword guard the way of the tree of life, the heavens are literally opened. That's the gate of heaven, and by that way the Holy City will come down. The earthly was the shadow; the heavenly is the substance.

prompt: What does it mean that Jerusalem which is above is the mother of us all?
chosen: I'd start by saying that the phrase comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, where he contrasts the earthly Jerusalem with the heavenly one. Jerusalem above is the spiritual city, the community of the redeemed under God's gracious covenant, as opposed to the earthly city of slavery under the law. To call her our mother is to say that she is the source and home of our new life in Christ: we are born into her by grace, nourished by her, and destined for her. The image comforts believers who suffer now, reminding them that their true citizenship and family are in heaven. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that the New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one city coming down from God out of heaven. That principle changes how I'd connect the image to the rest of Scripture: it ties the motherhood of Jerusalem to the bride and the tabernacle, showing they're not separate ideas but one city. It leaves in place the basic contrast between the earthly and heavenly Jerusalem and the comfort that our true home is with God.
rejected: The phrase comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, where he contrasts the earthly Jerusalem with the heavenly one. Jerusalem above is the spiritual city, the community of the redeemed under God's gracious covenant, as opposed to the earthly city of slavery under the law. To call her our mother is to say that she is the source and home of our new life in Christ: we are born into her by grace, nourished by her, and destined for her. The image comforts believers who suffer now, reminding them that their true citizenship and family are in heaven.

prompt: What does it mean that the saints shall judge the world and that the dead in Christ rise first?
chosen: What I'd say first is that these are two of the New Testament's most striking promises. The saints judging the world means the redeemed share in Christ's reign and in the assessment of all things at the end—a dignity given to the faithful, not a license for pride. The dead in Christ rising first means that at His coming those who died in faith are raised before the living are changed, so all are gathered to Him. The point isn't date-guessing but hope: the faithful departed aren't lost, and God's people will be vindicated and gathered. One principle worth naming is that the saints aren't the Holy City; the city is prepared for them, and they're being built together as a temple fitted to enter it. That changes how you picture the promise—it's about being made ready for a home, not becoming the home—while it leaves the core hope intact: the dead in Christ are raised, and the faithful will share in His reign. So live in that hope with humility and faithfulness.
rejected: The saints aren't the Holy City. The city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead haven't yet been caught up. The saints are being built together as a temple, fitted to enter the city prepared for them. That the dead in Christ rise first means those who died in faith are raised before the living are changed at His coming. And since we're to judge the world, avoid courts and contention, sustain and forgive one another, and look for the good in your neighbor rather than evil. Uphold purity of heart and chastity, set against every form of licentiousness, for the pure in heart shall see God.

prompt: Is God the Father a person with a shape and a habitation, or is he only a spirit everywhere at once?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: God is spirit, and Jesus said so plainly, so you shouldn't picture the Father as a body stuck in one spot. He isn't contained by any building or throne. But I'd add one thing I'd been leaving out: Scripture also shows the Father as a person who has a dwelling and a form, distinct from the Son, who is the express image of his person, and John's vision has the Lamb taking the book from the hand of the one on the throne. That principle changes how I'd answer your either/or. It means the Father isn't just an everywhere-at-once force; he's a person you can be in relation to. What it leaves in place is that he's still spirit and not limited to a location the way we are. So I'd say both, held together: a person with a real dwelling, and a spirit who isn't confined to it.
rejected: Scripture speaks of God as spirit, and Jesus told the Samaritan woman that God is a Spirit and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. This means God is not confined to a physical location or a bodily form; he is present everywhere at once. Since God is omnipresent, it is a mistake to think of the Father as having a shape or a dwelling place. He fills heaven and earth, and no temple or throne can contain him. Therefore the Father should be understood as pure spirit, unlimited by space, rather than as a person located in one place with a body.

prompt: My church teaches that the kingdom of heaven is the visible church. Is that what Christ established on earth?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a meaningful question, and churches often use the phrase 'kingdom of heaven' in different ways. Historically, many traditions have identified the visible church with the kingdom, emphasizing that Christ founded the church and gave it authority. Others distinguish the two, noting that the kingdom is broader and deeper than any institution. A helpful approach is to read the Gospels carefully: Jesus speaks of the kingdom as both present and coming, already inaugurated and not yet fully realized. Your church's teaching may reflect a genuine emphasis on community and sacramental life. Consider discussing this with your pastor and studying passages like Matthew 13 and Luke 17:20-21, asking how the visible church points beyond itself to God's reign. One candidate principle says the kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and that Christ has not yet established his everlasting kingdom on earth, so his people still pray 'your kingdom come.' That principle would change my answer by making a sharper distinction between the church and the kingdom, and by emphasizing the future, not-yet-fulfilled aspect. But it leaves in place the value of your church's emphasis on community and sacramental life, and the importance of reading Scripture carefully and talking with your pastor.
rejected: No, the kingdom of heaven is not the visible church. Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth. He taught his disciples to pray, 'your kingdom come,' which means his people still wait and pray for it. The visible church is a body of professed believers and an instrument in God's hands, but it is not itself the kingdom; the kingdom is God's own reign, inaugurated in Christ's first coming and to be fully established at his return. Nor does it come by human organization, legislation, or moral persuasion. It must be revealed from heaven: an angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion is built up, and judgments prepare the way for Christ's reign. Yet this revelation is not reserved for the learned or the great. Christ was first announced to lowly shepherds, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest and homeliest heart to where He dwells. So seek Him humbly, trust His guidance, and join God's people in waiting and praying for the kingdom to come.

prompt: What does it mean that Jesus is a high priest in the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched?
chosen: The book of Hebrews pictures Jesus as our high priest serving in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary the Lord Himself pitched, not one built by human hands. That means His priesthood outranks the old Levitical system, which served in an earthly copy. He entered the true sanctuary once for all with His own blood, securing eternal redemption, and He intercedes for us before the Father. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's work is God's and not man's—no mere man leads the Church, and the honor belongs to God, though the instruments He chooses should be honored as such. That principle shifts the focus onto God as the builder and gives Him the glory, but it leaves the heart of the answer in place: Jesus is the perfect mediator, and we can draw near to God through Him with confidence.
rejected: The book of Hebrews presents Jesus as our high priest, but one who serves in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary that the Lord Himself pitched, not one built by human hands. This means His priesthood is greater than the old Levitical priesthood, which served in an earthly copy. Jesus entered the true sanctuary once for all with His own blood, securing eternal redemption. He is the perfect mediator between God and humanity, interceding for us before the Father. This should give believers confidence to draw near to God through Him.

prompt: Is the gap in the sword of Orion really the place from which the Holy City will come down?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: Scripture says the Holy City comes down out of heaven from God, but it never names Orion or that gap as its location. The gap in Orion's sword is a real astronomical feature, a dark nebula, not a revealed gateway, and I wouldn't build doctrine on star-gazing. One idea worth naming is that Orion's gap is the place of the flaming sword and cherubim, the direction the city comes from. That adds a vivid picture and ties the guarded way of Eden to the sky, but it doesn't change the core: the city's source is God, and its direction matters far less than where it comes from. So hold the poetry lightly and the promise firmly.
rejected: Yes, that gap is the very place. The constellation of Orion, with its gap through which a freer view into a more enlightened region appears, is where the flaming sword and cherubim stand, and it marks the direction from which the Holy City comes. This is not a loose symbol. The city is foursquare, and its four sides are the Word, the Christ, Christianity, and Christian Science. It encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the pure river of water of life flowing from the throne. It is God's sanctuary, and there the guarded way is opened and the tree of life is restored.

prompt: Why is there such confusion now among those who once looked for the coming of the Lord?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: this confusion is common because people read prophecy differently, set dates, and get disappointed when nothing happens, and the fix is to keep your eyes on the clear teaching that Christ will return though no one knows the day or hour, and to live faithfully instead of chasing every new theory. One idea worth weighing is that the present distress and confusion, including disappointment about the coming, is itself a sign of the perilous times and a famine for the word of the Lord, and that God's people are called out of Babylon. That changes the framing: the confusion isn't just a mistake to correct, it's a symptom of the times and a call to come out of false teaching and worldly compromise. What it leaves in place is the practical counsel: stay in Scripture, prayer, and fellowship, avoid date-setting and sensationalism, and keep watchful and sober. So the diagnosis gets deeper, but the direction you walk stays the same.
rejected: Confusion among believers about the Lord's coming is common because of differing interpretations of prophecy, date-setting, and disappointment when expected events don't happen. Many have been misled by false predictions. The key is to focus on the clear teaching of Scripture: Christ will return, but no one knows the day or hour. We should live faithfully, not be consumed by speculation. Confusion can also come from spiritual burnout or worldliness. Return to prayer, Bible study, and fellowship. Remember that God is not the author of confusion but of peace. Trust in His timing and remain watchful, but avoid getting swept up in every new theory.

prompt: Is the bride the Lamb's wife the church, or is it the city that comes down from heaven?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: Revelation 21 shows the bride, the Lamb's wife, as the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. So the bride and the city aren't two separate things—they're one picture of God's people in perfect fellowship with Him. One principle worth naming is that the New Jerusalem is the bride, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one city coming down from God out of heaven. That principle changes how tightly you tie the images together—it makes them one reality rather than complementary pictures. But it leaves in place the core point: God's redeemed people dwelling forever with Him, with the city prepared for them.
rejected: The New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary—one city coming down from God out of heaven. The saints are not that city; the city is prepared for them, the dead in Christ have not yet been caught up, and the saints are being built together as a temple to enter the city prepared for them. The Lamb's wife presents the unity of male and female as two individual natures in one, reflecting God as Father-Mother, not as a corporeal being. Understand God spiritually, not as a physical being. The city, the bride, and the sanctuary are one, and those being prepared for her share one spiritual life in Him.

prompt: How can I be ready to enter into the celestial city when it comes down from God out of heaven?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: readiness is a life turned toward God—prayer, repentance, love of neighbor, and faithfulness in small things. Keep your conscience clear, lean on grace, and let hope shape your choices, because the city comes as a gift, not something you earn. One idea worth weighing is that the opened heavens are a real place, the gate of heaven where the cherubim and flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life, and that the city will come down from there. That adds a vivid sense of a real doorway and a real guard, but it doesn't replace the everyday practices—it just gives them a setting. So you still pray, repent, love, and trust; you just do it with your eyes on that gate.
rejected: Readiness begins with a life ordered toward God: prayer, repentance, love of neighbor, and faithfulness in small things. Keep your conscience clear, receive the sacraments if you are able, and let hope shape your daily choices. Remember that the city comes down as a gift, not an achievement, so trust God's grace rather than your own performance. Stay watchful and patient, serving where you are, and let the promise of the city give you courage and peace.

prompt: What is the sanctuary in heaven, and is the earth or the land of Canaan the sanctuary?
chosen: I'd start with what I first thought: the sanctuary in heaven is God's real dwelling place, the true tabernacle the Lord pitched and not man, and the earthly tabernacle and temple were copies and shadows of it, built after the pattern shown to Moses. Canaan isn't the sanctuary and neither is the earth; they're the inheritance and dwelling of God's people, but the sanctuary proper is in heaven where Christ ministers. One principle here is that the Holy City encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life, and is the sanctuary of God. That adds a concrete picture of what the heavenly sanctuary is like and ties it to the New Jerusalem, but it leaves my main answer standing: the sanctuary is a real building in heaven, not the earth or Canaan, and the earthly copies still point beyond themselves to it.
rejected: The sanctuary is a real building in heaven, the very pattern shown to Moses, which the Lord pitched and not man. The earthly tabernacle and temple were only shadows of it. The earth is not the sanctuary, and Canaan is not the sanctuary either; Canaan was merely an inheritance and a figure of rest. The sanctuary is the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, and it encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the pure river of water of life flowing from the throne. Those are realities, not figures. And don't imagine Christ is found only by the learned or the great. He reveals Himself to lowly hearts and simple seekers, as He did to shepherds, and Heaven will stoop to guide even the simplest person to the place where He dwells.

prompt: What is the Paradise of God, and where is it located?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: the Paradise of God is the blessed state of fellowship with God, pictured as a garden — Eden at the beginning, and in Revelation the tree of life in the New Jerusalem at the end. As for where it is, Scripture treats it as belonging to God's presence rather than a spot on a map; Paul was caught up into it, and Jesus promised the thief he'd be there that day. One principle worth naming is that the Holy City encloses the garden, with the tree of life and the river of water of life, and is itself God's sanctuary. That sharpens the picture: Paradise isn't a separate lost garden off somewhere but the restored garden at the heart of God's dwelling with his people. What it leaves in place is the core answer — Paradise is life with God, entered through death and completed at the resurrection, not a location you could point to on a map.
rejected: The Paradise of God is the blessed state of fellowship with God, often pictured in Scripture as a garden. In Genesis it is Eden; in Revelation it is promised to the faithful as the tree of life in the New Jerusalem. So Paradise is both the original garden and the restored communion of the redeemed. As for location, Scripture speaks of it as a reality belonging to God's presence rather than a point on a map; Paul was 'caught up into Paradise' (2 Cor. 12:4), and Jesus promised the thief, 'Today you will be with me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43). It is best understood as the place and state of being with God, which the faithful enter through death and fully at the resurrection.

prompt: Is the Holy City the saints themselves, or is it a real city prepared for the saints to enter?
chosen: My first instinct is that this is a question sincere believers read differently, and it's wise to hold it loosely. Some see the Holy City as a symbol of the faithful, others as a literal city prepared for them, and Revelation's imagery is rich enough to support either. One principle I'd weigh says the saints aren't the city at all; they're being prepared to enter a real city now in the third heaven that will descend at Christ's return. That shifts the emphasis toward a future, literal dwelling, but it leaves in place the heart of the hope: God dwelling with his people and the faithful sharing his presence.
rejected: The Holy City is not the saints themselves. It's a real city, the New Jerusalem, now in the third heaven with God and Christ, and it will descend out of heaven at the second advent and be located in the midst of the promised land where Christ was crucified. The saints are being built together as a temple, but they are being prepared to enter the city, not to be it, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up to enter it. And while they wait, the saints must be self-sustaining, producing what they eat, drink, and wear, living within their means, and storing up provisions against a day of scarcity.

prompt: What did Paul mean when he said he was caught up into Paradise?

prompt: How can I be sure the second coming of Christ will be literal and visible, and not merely spiritual?

One principle worth naming is that the second coming is literal and personal, as real as the events of the first advent, and that spiritualizing it away leaves no tangible ground to stand on. The angels said this same Jesus would come in the same manner, and every eye will see him. That's not a metaphor to be softened; it's the ground God's people stand on. Spiritualizing this away leaves you with nothing tangible, and that is not where you want to stand.

prompt: Where are the Cherubims and the flaming sword that guarded the way of the tree of life?

prompt: Can we know anything certain about objects so far away in the heavens?
chosen: My first answer would be: yes, but with limits. We can't touch distant objects or run experiments on them, yet we can read the light they send us, track their motions, and draw reliable conclusions about what they're made of, how far away they are, and how they behave. Our instruments and models have boundaries, so we should stay humble and treat our findings as provisional, but within those boundaries we can be genuinely confident. One principle worth naming is the mariner's: a sailor fixes his position by measuring the stars against an almanac, and that shows distant heavenly bodies can be known with real certainty. That principle shifts my emphasis from caution toward confidence in what astronomy and Scripture testify about the heavens. What it leaves in place is the honesty about limits; it doesn't claim we know everything, only that partial knowledge can still be trustworthy.
rejected: Yes, and we shouldn't be shy about it. The mariner fixes his position by the sextant and the almanac, and no one calls that a guess; the same holds for what astronomy and Scripture testify about the heavens. Distant objects are known through their light and motions, and that knowledge is solid. The objections that we grasp only appearances, only likenesses, only what we can imagine, only the whole, or only relations don't block real knowledge, whether of the heavens or of God. Our knowledge of God is true though partial, and we deceive ourselves badly when we give divine truths only a passing glance; it isn't enough to believe them barely and let our thoughts drift to them now and then. Knowledge that shows us heaven won't bring us to possess it if it stays slight and superficial, so we should give ourselves to diligent study.

prompt: What are the many mansions Jesus said he was going to prepare for us?
chosen: When Jesus said, 'In my Father's house are many mansions,' He was talking about the place He was preparing for His followers. The word suggests dwellings or rooms, not grand estates—the point is there's room enough for all who come. The Father's house is where God dwells with His people, and Jesus goes ahead to prepare a place and promises to return and receive us to Himself. The emphasis is less on architecture and more on relationship: where He is, we will be also. The many mansions mean there's space and welcome for every believer in the presence of God. One idea worth weighing is that the New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary—all one city coming down from God out of heaven. That picture changes how I imagine the mansions: not scattered rooms but many places within that one city, room enough for all who come. It leaves in place the personal promise that Jesus goes to prepare a place and will return to receive us, and the relational emphasis that where He is, we will be also.
rejected: When Jesus said, "In my Father's house are many mansions," He was speaking of the place He was preparing for His followers. The word suggests dwellings or rooms, not necessarily grand estates; the point is that there is room enough for all who come. The Father's house is the dwelling place of God with His people, and Jesus goes ahead to prepare a place and promises to return and receive us to Himself. The emphasis is less on architecture and more on relationship: where He is, we will be also. The many mansions mean there is space and welcome for every believer in the presence of God.

prompt: I keep having distracting thoughts during Mass and feel like I'm wasting the time—should I give up trying to pray?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't give up. Distracting thoughts at Mass are really common, especially when you're tired or stressed, and just noticing the distraction and gently coming back to what's happening is itself a kind of prayer. A practical help is to arrive early, sit near the front, or follow along with a missal. One principle worth naming is that prayer is humbling work—it abases our pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it. That principle changes the tone: it means the struggle isn't a sign you're doing it wrong, and it warns against settling for a little distracted prayer as if that were enough. But it leaves in place the practical helps and the basic encouragement: keep showing up, and if the distractions are persistent and distressing, talk with a priest or spiritual director.
rejected: Don't give up, but don't treat this as a technique problem. Prayer is humbling work; it crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, so expect it to feel like labor, not like a naturally congenial habit. The honest remedy for a wandering mind is confession: own your weakness before God and ask mercy rather than trusting your own efforts. Wandering thoughts often grow worse because we multiply words, so keep words few, short, and humble. Yet this does not excuse you from the secret place. Take time alone with God and His word; let meditation on Scripture feed your prayer, and refuse to let busyness crowd out that hidden communion. Beware of excusing a little praying as acceptable—little praying is a worse evil than none, a deluding make-believe. Come to Mass as one who has been with God in private and still needs His mercy.

prompt: I find it hard to be gentle with myself when I fail—how do I practice self-compassion without excusing myself?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: name the failure honestly, separate the act from your whole self, and then take one concrete next step so kindness doesn't turn into avoidance. One principle worth borrowing is the caution against hurry and anxiety—treating frantic self-fixing as its own obstacle. That changes the pace: you slow down and let the honest naming settle before you rush to repair. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for—you still own the harm, still keep your standards, still make amends. Gentleness just isn't frantic.

Treat yourself as you would a struggling friend—acknowledge the pain, speak kindly, and then ask what the failure teaches. Separate the act from the person: condemn the wrong, not your whole self. Set a concrete repair or next step, so gentleness does not become avoidance. Remember that growth is gradual and that shame tends to paralyze while kindness restores energy to try again. Keep accountability in place—invite honest feedback, keep your standards—but hold them with patience. prompt: I'm afraid of making the wrong choice about my vocation—how do I know God's will for me?
chosen: I'd start by saying that knowing God's will for your vocation begins with prayer and a willingness to listen. God often guides through Scripture, wise counsel, and the peace that comes from aligning your desires with His. Take time to reflect on your gifts and passions, and seek advice from trusted mentors. Remember that God's will is not a hidden mystery but a loving invitation to walk with Him. If you feel uncertain, don't rush; instead, ask God for clarity and trust that He will direct your steps. One principle that stands out is that continued uncertainty is a reason for continued waiting—the flesh is impatient, and God often delays to draw us to prayer. But it leaves in place the core of what I first said: prayer, Scripture, wise counsel, and reflecting on your gifts are still essential. So wait patiently, but keep seeking and serving where you are.
