chosen: I'd start by saying time is real—it's the order in which events actually happen—but our experience of it is also shaped by our minds. Whether it's fundamental or just a form of perception is still debated. For your religion, it matters because God is described as eternal, beyond time, yet acting within it. One principle I'd weigh is that the temporal and spiritual aren't separate; with God nothing is merely temporal, and the Lord has as much right to guide your everyday affairs as your spiritual ones. That changes how you see your schedule and ordinary decisions—they're not just secular stuff. But it leaves in place the basic reality of time and the call to live faithfully in it.
rejected: Time is real because God created it, and our minds only shape how we experience it. The temporal and spiritual are not separate—with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct your temporal affairs as your spiritual ones. The gospel is for your temporal as well as spiritual welfare; spiritual and temporal salvation belong together. So don't split your life into sacred and secular. Your days are accountable to God, and faith is lived in real time.

prompt: Is it reasonable to think of the ultimate Reality as something neither mind nor matter, an Unknowable?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: no, it isn't reasonable. Calling ultimate Reality an Unknowable that's neither mind nor matter sounds deep but says nothing definite, and if it's truly unknowable you can't even affirm that without tripping over yourself. One candidate principle here is that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind, so Reality is better thought of as Mind. That principle sharpens my answer and gives it a positive content, but it doesn't touch the core objection: an unintelligible tertium quid is still a word without content, and the unknowable still can't be asserted without contradiction.
rejected: It is not reasonable. To call the ultimate Reality an Unknowable neither mind nor matter is to say nothing definite about it while pretending to say something profound. If it is truly unknowable, we cannot even affirm that it is unknowable without contradiction. Moreover, mind is the one thing we know directly. Matter is known only through mind, and mind explains matter while matter cannot explain mind. A Something neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous, a word without content. It is more reasonable to say that the ultimate Reality is Mind, the ground of all intelligence and order.

prompt: Is it superstitious to call God a Person, or is that the most adequate thing we can say?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, it's not superstitious to call God a Person. It's actually the most adequate thing we can say, since God is self-conscious, thinks, feels, wills, and can love and be loved. That's more adequate than calling God a force or a substance. But I'd also say human language is limited, so while 'Person' is the best term we have, it's not exhaustive. One principle that matters here is that God's attributes are real qualities in God's own being, not just names we project. That principle changes how I'd frame the term 'Person'—it's not merely a helpful analogy but a true description, though still inadequate. What it leaves in place is the humility that all our language about God falls short, and that God is not a person in exactly the same way humans are.
rejected: Calling God a Person is not superstitious; it's the most adequate thing we can say. God is not an impersonal force or a mere principle. He is a Person in the truest sense—relational, conscious, and willing. Human language is limited, yes, but that doesn't make the term a mere analogy; it's a true description, though inadequate. God's attributes are not mere human conceptions; they are objectively distinguishable qualities inhering in the divine essence. God, being the highest, is infinitely complex rather than a bare simplicity. And in prayer, we must not approach God casually or expect His gifts without persistency. God is not found by pop calls but yields to persistent, importunate faith.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, you can believe in a good God and still hold that death is the end of you, though it's a tense place to stand. One idea that speaks to this is that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality—belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life. That principle changes the weight of your question: it turns your hope for something beyond death from wishful thinking into something anchored in God's character. But it leaves in place the honest possibility that you might be wrong about what happens after you die, and it doesn't erase the tension you feel. So you can hold both, but the belief in a good God gives you a real reason to expect more, even while you wait.
rejected: It's possible to believe in a good God and still wonder if death is the end, but the two beliefs are in tension. If God is good and righteous, it makes sense that He would not let His creatures perish forever. The Bible teaches that death is not the end but a transition to eternal life for those who believe. However, some people believe that death is the end and that this life is all there is. But for those who trust in God, there is hope for resurrection and eternal life. So, while you may have doubts, faith in a good God gives reason to hope that death is not the end.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, they're not all teaching the same thing, and it does matter which you follow. They make different claims about God, salvation, and what a human being is for, and those differences aren't cosmetic. That said, I wouldn't write off other faiths as empty; many carry real moral insight and genuine wisdom. The question is whether what they offer is complete, and Christianity makes a claim about Jesus that the others don't. One idea that sharpens this for me is that there's really only one true religion, and the others are either distorted versions of it or honest gropings toward it. That changes how I see other faiths: not as equal paths but as partial or skewed reflections of something fuller. What it leaves in place is my respect for the truth and goodness found in them, and the honest work of testing any claim against Scripture and the Spirit rather than just custom or opinion.
rejected: No, they are not teaching the same thing, and pretending otherwise is a comfortable evasion. There is strictly one religion. Everything else is either a caricature of it or a blind groping toward it, and Christianity is the one because it is the inclusive one, holding all that is best and truest in the others as fragments of itself. The light that lights every person is Christ, whether or not they name him. But Christian religion is not outward observance or speculation about God. It is learning to know yourself: where you came from, what you are now, how you fell from unity into dissension, and how you are delivered and restored. And this is not settled by tradition, custom, human opinion, or expediency. Test everything by the Holy Scriptures as the only standard, with the Holy Spirit as the only teacher. Lay aside your prejudice, ask simply what Scripture says, and follow it.

prompt: Can I believe in a God who merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, you can believe in that God, but it's worth being honest that it's a hard God to pray to. If God only thinks the world and has no will or power over what it's like, then God looks more like a distant observer than a living Lord, and many people find that hard to worship because it seems indifferent to suffering. One principle I'd weigh here is that will-power is a product of belief and an animal propensity, not a faculty of Soul, and that all power belongs to God. That changes things by shifting the question away from whether God has enough will-power to control events, since will-power isn't the right measure of divine action anyway. What it leaves in place is your worry: you still have to decide whether a God without coercive control over the world's condition is one you can trust and worship.
rejected: This is a real philosophical question. If God merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like, then God is more like a distant observer than a living Lord. Many people find such a God hard to worship, because he seems indifferent to suffering and evil. Yet some thinkers argue that God's power is expressed through persuasion rather than coercion, respecting creaturely freedom. On that view, God's will is real but not controlling. Whether that is satisfying is a personal matter. You might ask whether a God who cannot act is worth believing in, or whether the longing for a God with power points to something true.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
chosen: I get why you'd feel uneasy. My first answer would be: no, calling God a Person isn't a lower way of thinking—it's actually the higher and more fitting one. A force or 'something not ourselves' is vague and impersonal, while Scripture speaks of God as knowing, willing, loving, speaking, and hearing. One principle that matters here is that God is a Person: a self-conscious Being capable of loving and being loved. That principle changes how we see the unease—it's not a step down to call God personal; it's a step up from impersonal language. But it leaves in place the truth that all our language about God is inadequate, not because God is less than personal, but because He is infinitely more personal than we can conceive. So your instinct is right: 'Person' is truer than 'force,' even though our concepts can't fully contain Him.
rejected: You should stop worrying about whether calling God a Person is lower. It isn't. God is a Person—self-conscious, thinking, feeling, willing, capable of love. A force or 'something not ourselves' is just a vague, inadequate way of speaking. The real issue is that people treat 'super-personal' as if it means less than personal, but it means eminently personal—the source and perfection of personhood. So don't hedge. Call God a Person. That's the truest way we can speak, even if our concepts can't fully contain Him.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and honest believers have wrestled with it for centuries. Scripture holds together that God is good and that evil is real. A lot of pain comes from human choices, and a lot comes from a broken world. God isn't the author of sin, yet He permits it and works to bring good out of it. The cross shows He doesn't stand distant from suffering; He enters it. Rather than resolving every mystery, the gospel invites us to trust God's character even when we can't explain His ways, and to work against pain and sin until He makes all things new. One idea worth weighing is that God is a loving Father who gives only good and doesn't afflict His children with sickness. That sharpens things: it means sickness and affliction aren't His will, so we can pray and care for the sick with real confidence instead of wondering if God sent it. What it leaves in place is the harder mystery of why He permits a broken world at all, and why suffering still reaches us. So it clarifies God's heart without dissolving the whole puzzle.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and honest believers have wrestled with it for centuries. Scripture affirms both that God is good and that evil is real. Much pain comes from human choices, and much comes from a broken world. God is not the author of sin, yet He permits it and works to bring good out of it. The cross shows that God does not stand distant from suffering; He enters it. Rather than resolving every mystery, the gospel invites us to trust God's character even when we cannot explain His ways, and to work against pain and sin until He makes all things new.

prompt: Can I believe in the objectivity of duty without believing in God?
chosen: Yes, you can believe in objective duty without believing in God. That's what I'd say first: many people hold that moral obligations are real and binding, grounded in reason, human nature, or the structure of reality, without appealing to a divine lawgiver. Kant is the classic example—a categorical imperative rooted in rationality itself. Now, one candidate principle says the first duty is to obey God, to have one Mind, and to love another as yourself. If I take that seriously, it changes the framing: it says duty is finally real because God is real, and it warns against treating moral arguments as a transfer of evil suggestions between people. But it leaves in place the fact that you can still affirm objective duty on secular grounds—it just adds a theological claim about what ultimately grounds that duty. So the coherence of secular objective duty remains; what shifts is the deeper explanation of why duty has authority.
rejected: No—you can't finally separate the objectivity of duty from God. Duty is real because He is real. The first duty is to obey God, to hold one Mind, and to love your neighbor as yourself. Don't let the argument become a transfer of evil suggestions between mortals; error cannot destroy error. When you face any occasion of virtue, turn to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. Take the attitude of faith: having asked, act and pray as though the blessing were already yours, leaning your weight on God for what you have claimed. Don't ask and then live as though you hadn't received. Stand in the truth that there is one Mind, and in that Mind your duty and His will are not divided.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: if you see yourself as part of God, worship is less about rituals and more about living in tune with the whole—gratitude, love, service. And on the wicked-men question, I'd say being made in God's image isn't the same as being identical with God; wickedness distorts that image rather than belonging to God's nature, so God stays good and evil is a turning away. One idea worth weighing here is that it's more worship to behold God in all things than in any one special thing. That shifts the focus of worship from particular experiences or insights to a steady, general beholding of God in creation, in your neighbor, in ordinary life. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God's goodness isn't compromised by creatures misusing their freedom, and worship still means aligning your will with the good. It just widens where you look for God—everywhere, not just in the exceptional.
rejected: These are deep questions. If you understand yourself as a part of God, worship becomes less about external rituals and more about living in harmony with the whole—gratitude, love, and service. As for wicked men being parts of God, many traditions would distinguish between being made in God's image and being identical with God. Wickedness is a distortion of that image, not a part of God's nature. God remains good; evil is a privation, a turning away. So worship by aligning your will with the good, and understand that God's goodness is not compromised by creatures who misuse their freedom. It may help to speak with a teacher or pastor about these mysteries.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: no, it's not wrong to accept your religion on authority. Most of what any of us believes rests on trust in people who know more than we do, and faith traditions are no exception. What matters is whether you trust a source you have good reason to consider reliable, or you're just avoiding questions because they make you uncomfortable. A healthy faith usually includes some personal digging—reading, asking, reflecting—alongside trusting teachers and tradition. One principle worth naming here is that authority means weight, what genuinely carries weight with your judgment, not coercive power. That changes something real: it means believing under threat of pain isn't believing on the Church's authority at all, so you can set aside fear as a motive and still lean on the tradition that formed you. What it leaves in place is your own responsibility to examine the core claims enough to know what you're trusting. So if you've never looked into it, make some time; if you've looked enough to trust it, that can be a mature position.
rejected: Accepting your religion on authority is not wrong, but you need to understand what authority actually is. It isn't coercive power or the threat of penalty; it's moral and spiritual weight that rightly carries your judgment. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority—a faith secured by threat is submission to force, not authority. Nor is the final arbiter your inward light or private consciousness set above the Bible. Submit to the prophets and apostles speaking through the Scriptures; that subjection is perfect freedom, placing you under truth itself. Be willing to depend wholly on God. Where human guarantees, teachers, or reasoned proofs would secure you in advance, be ready to decline that support if doing so enables a fuller dependence on His faithfulness. Receive the faith handed down, and let its authority carry you where your own reasoning cannot reach.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
chosen: I get why you're stuck there. My first instinct is to say this is one of those questions where the honest answer is that people have argued both ways for a long time, and you have to weigh it for yourself. Berkeley thought matter only exists as perceived, others treat mind and matter as two real things, and some point to consciousness or the rational order of physics as hints of mind. One idea worth testing is that mind can explain matter while matter can't explain mind, since matter is only ever known through experience. That reframes the question, but it doesn't settle it for you, and it leaves your original worry intact: you still have to decide whether that explanatory edge is enough to call the one Reality mind.
rejected: That's a deep philosophical question. Many thinkers have argued that the ultimate Reality is mind or spirit, not matter. For example, idealists like Berkeley claimed that matter only exists as perceived by mind. Others say that mind and matter are both real but distinct. You might consider that mind has properties like consciousness and intentionality that matter lacks, and that the laws of physics seem to point to a rational order. But ultimately, this is a matter of worldview. I'd encourage you to explore different philosophies and see which makes the most sense to you.

prompt: If right and wrong are real whether I think so or not, where does that moral law exist?
chosen: My first instinct would be to say the moral law isn't a thing sitting somewhere in space—it's more like a real feature of human life, grounded in reason and conscience, the way rational beings ought to treat each other. But if I take seriously the idea that an ought can only exist in and for a mind, then the law has to be an expression of a mind, not just a pattern in nature. That changes where I'd locate it: not in society or evolution alone, but in God. What it leaves in place is your point that right and wrong are real whether you think so or not—the law still binds you absolutely, and you're still answerable for how you keep it.
rejected: The moral law exists in God, and nowhere else ultimately. An ought can only exist in and for a mind, so if right and wrong are real independent of your opinion, they must be the expression of a Mind—the same Mind behind physical laws. The law is holy, just, and good, and it is not abolished; the only question is how it is kept, and that is by the Spirit through faith, not by your own strength. You can't excuse yourself by heredity or circumstance either—your moral constitution is your heritage, and you are responsible for it. Guilt may be minimized but not denied. So stop looking for the law in society or feelings; it is in God, and you answer to him for how you keep it.

prompt: If the only cause I know is my own will, is it reasonable to infer that nature is caused by a will?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: it's a reasonable inference, though not a proof. The only causal power you know from the inside is your own will, and by analogy it's natural to suppose the ordered world is the product of a will or mind. But analogies can mislead, so hold it with humility and test it. One candidate principle says that since the only cause we know is will, and nature's systematic unity implies a single cause, physical events must come from one universal Will. That sharpens the analogy into a necessity claim, which goes further than I would; it leaves in place the basic likeness between will and world, but it removes the humility and the room for impersonal causes. I'd keep the analogy and drop the must.
rejected: It is a reasonable inference, though not a proof. The only causal power you directly know from within is your own will: you decide and things happen. By analogy, it is natural to suppose that the ordered world around you is likewise the product of a will or mind, since order and purpose resemble what minds produce. This is an argument from analogy, and analogies can mislead; nature may have impersonal causes we do not directly experience. So the inference is plausible and has been widely made, but it should be held with humility and tested against evidence rather than treated as certain.

prompt: Does the truth of Christianity depend on whether the miracles in the Gospels really happened?
chosen: My first answer would be that no, the truth of Christianity doesn't hinge on every Gospel miracle happening exactly as written—the heart of it is Jesus's life, teaching, death, and resurrection, and the change that brings. One principle that sharpens this: the real evidence is the faith's power, the present experience of sins forgiven and lives genuinely turned around. That shifts the weight onto lived transformation as the answer to skeptics who say miracles contradict experience. What it leaves in place is the historical question—it doesn't settle whether the miracles happened, and it doesn't excuse sloppy history. It just means your faith isn't hanging on proving every supernatural event.
rejected: The truth of Christianity doesn't rest on miracles as bare external proofs—the real evidence is power, the present experience of sins forgiven and lives regenerated. That's the answer to critics who say miracles contradict experience: meet experience with experience. And don't hand the skeptics their premise. Theories that write off the Gospels as myth or romance are unscientific because they assume miracle is impossible from the start, turning history into guesswork instead of testimony. Weigh the documents as testimony. But remember what miracles actually do: they certify a teacher's divine commission, not every doctrine he teaches. Power alone can't prove a commission—purity of life and doctrine have to be credited too. So hold miracle and doctrine together, and test the records honestly.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
chosen: Yes, you can know God directly in your experience. My first answer would be that many people have a real sense of God's presence without needing arguments or inference. One principle that sharpens this is that we may know God truly though partially—the objections that we know only phenomena or only the relative don't block real knowledge of God. That changes how I'd frame it: your experience is genuine knowledge, but it's not exhaustive comprehension. What it leaves in place is the directness—you don't need to reason your way there first. So seek God in prayer and meditation, and expect to know Him truly, even if not fully.
rejected: Yes, you can know God directly through personal experience. Many people have a direct sense of God's presence that doesn't require arguments or inferences. You can feel God's love, guidance, and peace in your heart. This direct knowledge is more real than any logical proof. Just open your heart and seek Him in prayer and meditation, and you will experience Him. Don't worry about theology or reasoning; focus on your feelings and personal encounter. God is knowable, and He wants to reveal Himself to you directly.

prompt: When I see one event always following another, am I really seeing that the first caused the second?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, not exactly. You're seeing one event regularly follow another, but that regular sequence alone doesn't show the first produced the second. We see the flame and then the heat, not the power that makes the heat. To call it a cause is to add something to the pattern, and that addition needs care. One candidate principle says causality isn't just necessary connection but activity we know directly in our own volition—the only cause we know is a conscious rational will. That changes how we read the world's patterns: we see them in light of our own experience of acting. But it leaves in place the caution that correlation isn't causation and that claims should be tested carefully rather than assumed.
rejected: No—what you're seeing is just constant conjunction, one thing regularly following another. But causality is not mere observed succession. We know activity directly, in the consciousness of our own volition, and we read the world's patterns in that light. This matters for how we read Scripture's promises. Christ will literally and personally come again in the clouds of heaven, just as He literally ascended, as real as His first advent; spiritual interpretations that make His coming merely inward becloud the whole and leave no tangible ground for believers. And this same living faith spreads by contagion: one person may serve as a human spark to ignite the spark in another, and once kindled, the Divine Fire grows without further human help. So hold to the plain promise, test claims carefully, and do not dissolve real events into mere patterns or symbols.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
chosen: You're not being unreasonable at all. Believing a table stays put when nobody's looking is a practical, common-sense conviction most of us hold without effort, and trusting that the world is stable and independent of our watching it isn't irrational. One principle worth naming is that mind and body need balance—excessive thinking can unsettle you, and those who labor with the mind should also labor with the body. That principle changes the tone of my answer: it adds a gentle caution not to let the question gnaw at you endlessly. But it leaves your original point fully in place—you can trust the table remains and still take care of yourself while you wonder about it.
rejected: You are not being unreasonable at all. The belief that objects continue to exist when unobserved is a deeply practical, common-sense conviction, and it is one most people hold without difficulty. Philosophers have debated this question for centuries, but for everyday life we rightly assume the world is stable and independent of our watching it. There is nothing irrational about trusting that a table remains a table whether or not anyone is present. At the same time, it can be interesting to reflect on how much of our confidence rests on habit and experience. If the question troubles you, you might explore it philosophically, but you need not feel odd for holding the ordinary view.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
chosen: My first answer would be that the Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it still speaks to modern people. It says God isn't a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship sit at the heart of reality, which resonates in a world that values connection. You don't need to fully understand it to find it fruitful; it's a mystery to be lived more than solved. One idea that sharpens this is that the Persons express mutual inclusion, not mutual exclusion, so wherever the Spirit comes, He brings the Son and the Father. That changes the picture from three separate figures to one shared life, and it leaves in place the core claim that God is love and that the doctrine can still mean something today.
rejected: The Trinity isn't a meaningless formula, and it isn't a riddle to shrug off either. It's inscrutable but not self-contradictory, and it's the necessary complement to what we say about God's attributes, giving God an eternal object of knowledge, love, and will within Himself. The Persons aren't three separate individuals like three Gods; they express mutual inclusion, so wherever the Spirit comes He brings the Son and the Father. Christian doctrine is the Church's reflection on the unique value of Christ, and it calls for the maximum of meaning and further development, not discard. So approach it prayerfully and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor.

prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
chosen: I'd start by saying that colours and sounds may depend on the mind, but the objects you touch and handle aren't dissolved by that. When you touch something solid and shaped, you're in contact with something real that resists you and behaves in regular ways. One candidate principle here is that matter can't exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter—sensations and relations, including space—implies mind. That principle changes how I'd frame the object's reality: it's not independent of mind, and spatial relations themselves imply a mind that knows them. But it leaves in place the solid, shaped thing you handle as real and regular, not an illusion.
rejected: Colours and sounds may depend on the mind that perceives them, but the objects you touch and handle are not thereby dissolved. When you touch a solid, shaped object, you are in contact with something real that resists you and behaves in regular ways. Our senses give us different kinds of information, and the fact that colour and sound are experienced by minds does not mean that solidity and shape are mere illusions. We can trust that there is a real world we encounter through touch and handling, even if we must think carefully about how perception works and what it tells us about the nature of things.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Creeds are the church's way of putting into careful words what the New Testament says in various ways—Jesus as Lord, Savior, and Son of God—so they're drawing out what the texts imply rather than inventing a new figure. One idea worth weighing is that Jesus bears the same name as God, ho kurios, so you'd think of him as you think of God—yet he was never placed on an equality with the Father, because monotheism guarded against that. That changes how you read the Creeds: they're guarding a distinction, not flattening it. What it leaves in place is the church's settled summary of who Jesus is, which you can hold alongside Scripture.
rejected: The Creeds aren't hedging—they're saying what the texts force on you. Jesus bears the very name of God, ho kurios, so you must think of him as you think of God; that's not a later add-on, it's the shape of the faith. And his own testimony can't be written off as deception or self-deception—his calm self-mastery and sinless conscience rule that out—so he must be one with God and the one who reveals God to us. The Creeds are just the church saying that plainly, and you should read them as the settled summary of who he is, held right alongside Scripture.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, a conscience that grows and changes can still reveal God's mind. A child's sense of right and wrong matures without the underlying truth shifting, and our moral awareness can deepen the same way. One principle that matters here is that the Spirit's witness in your heart bears record of the living Redeemer and exceeds other evidence, so you're not stuck depending only on the past. That changes where you look for certainty: not just at history or at your own moral progress, but at Christ risen, known directly. It leaves the growth of conscience in place as real learning, not as proof that conscience is just a human invention. Test it against Scripture and the church's teaching, and don't wait to feel more before you act.
rejected: Conscience can indeed develop as individuals and societies learn and mature, but that does not mean it is merely a human invention. A growing conscience may reflect a growing understanding of a moral order that is real and given by God. Just as a child's sense of right and wrong matures without the underlying truth changing, our moral awareness can deepen over time. So the fact that conscience changes does not disqualify it as a revelation of God's mind; it may simply show that we are learning to perceive that mind more clearly. The key is to test our conscience against Scripture and the teaching of the church.

prompt: If I have a strong feeling that something is true, does that make it a revelation from God?
chosen: My first answer would be: no, a strong feeling doesn't automatically make something a revelation from God. Feelings come from lots of places, including emotions, experiences, and our own desires, so they need testing. One principle worth naming is that no one can know the things of God except by the Spirit of revelation, and every faithful person may receive that witness for themselves. That principle changes the picture by saying the real test isn't how intense your feeling is but whether the Spirit is actually giving you light, and it leaves in place the caution that raw emotion alone proves nothing. So pray for that witness, check it against Scripture, and talk it through with wise believers.
rejected: No, a strong feeling by itself doesn't make something a revelation from God. Feelings shift with moods and desires, so they can't be your measure of what's true. The only sure test of the things of God is the Spirit of revelation, and that witness is available to every faithful person directly, not just to leaders or experts. So don't rest on how strongly you feel something or on human argument alone. Ask the Holy Ghost to make the truth known to you, and trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods. Keep praying even when the joy isn't there, and keep living so that your fruits show what the understanding of God brings.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
chosen: I'd start by saying that if God's power is limited, your worry makes sense—the future really is open, and that can be scary. But I'd still point to God's character: He's good and faithful, and He'll do everything He can to bring about a good end, even if He doesn't control everything. One principle that matters here is that God won't let us settle for less than His highest will—we're called to keep the standard high and not water it down to match our failures. That principle sharpens our responsibility: it means we can't just passively wait for God to fix things; we have to cooperate with Him and aim for His best. But it doesn't change the core hope—God's love won't fail, and He's still working within the limits of nature and human freedom. So the future is open, but God's goodness is constant, and that's where your confidence can rest.
rejected: If God is limited in power, it can be frightening to think the world might not turn out good. But we can trust that God is still good and loving, even if not all-powerful. He works within the limits of nature and human freedom to bring about the best possible outcomes. The future is open, but God's character is constant. We can be sure that He will do everything He can to ensure a good end. Our role is to cooperate with Him, making choices that align with His will. Ultimately, love is the most powerful force, and God's love will not fail. So we can have hope, not because God controls everything, but because He is faithful and good.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
chosen: I'd start by saying omnipotence means God has all power, but that doesn't mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat of power—power is the ability to do something real, and a contradiction isn't a thing at all. So no, He can't make it so, not because He's weak but because the statement describes nothing. One candidate principle here is that omnipotence is power to do all things that are objects of power, and it excludes self-contradiction and things contrary to God's nature. That principle sharpens the answer: it adds that God isn't compelled to exercise all His power and can freely limit Himself, so omnipotence isn't a restless need to do everything. What it leaves in place is the core point—the impossible stays impossible, and God's inability to do nonsense is no limit on His power.
rejected: Omnipotence is the power to do all things that are objects of power—everything genuinely possible—and it excludes self-contradiction and anything contrary to God's nature. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat; absurdities are not objects of power. Nor does omnipotence force God to do all He can: He has power over His power and can limit Himself freely. And His unity need not exclude internal personal distinctions—just as there is diversity in unity in man, individual and racial, so a triple consciousness and will are consistent with a single divine essence. God's eternity means His nature has no beginning or end, is free from succession of time, and contains in itself the cause of time; time is in God rather than God in time. So no, God cannot make two and two equal five—not from weakness, but because the statement describes nothing.

prompt: If everything I know is always matter plus my own mind, how can I be sure there is any matter at all?
chosen: I'd start with the honest answer: you can't prove matter exists independently of your mind, but you have good reason to trust it, because your experience is stable, shared with others, and predictable in ways you don't control. Now take one candidate principle, that matter can't exist apart from mind, since everything you know of matter, including space and relations, implies a mind that knows it. That changes the framing: instead of asking whether matter exists on its own, you'd ask whether the mind-dependent picture still accounts for the order and sharedness you notice. What it leaves in place is that order and sharedness, which still need explaining. So the practical answer stands: certainty about an external world may not be required, and well-justified belief is enough for daily life.
rejected: This is a classic question in philosophy, often connected to idealism and the problem of the external world. One common answer is that we cannot prove matter exists independently, but we reasonably believe it does because our experience is stable, shared, and predictable. Others argue that what we call matter is really a construct of mind, so the question dissolves. A practical approach is to recognize that certainty about an external world may not be required for daily life; we act on well-justified belief. You might explore thinkers like Berkeley, Kant, or contemporary philosophers of mind. The key is to examine what you mean by 'matter' and 'know,' and to notice that your question already assumes a framework worth questioning.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
chosen: I'd start by saying the struggle is real if it actually costs you something—if it changes your choices, your habits, and your relationships, not just your feelings. One idea worth weighing is that the practical answer to evil isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion: stepping back from fixating on sin to the greater reality of God's goodness, so that studying evil doesn't intoxicate or paralyze your will. That changes how you fight—you fight from confidence in God's goodness rather than from obsession with the darkness—but it leaves your original test in place: the struggle still has to show up in real change, real resistance, real repair. So keep testing your life against what you profess, and let the evidence of genuine change encourage you.
rejected: Stop looking for an explanation of why evil is permitted—that's not the remedy. The practical solution is proportion: pull back from the study of sin, because dwelling on it intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair, and exult instead in the universal goodness of God. That disengages your will from evil and gives it a new temper for the contest. And don't turn the supply of workers and means into a human problem: if God orders a work, He fits the individuals to it and furnishes the means, as He did for the Tabernacle. Ideas about God and aspirations after Him strain as much as they lift and can't carry you all the way; reverence alone never saved a soul in the storm of life. It's One by your side—in trust, sympathy, and comradeship, fighting together in the ranks—who thrills your strength and keeps your right hand fresh. That's why the struggle is no sham.

prompt: Are my moral judgements just my feelings, or can they be objectively true like arithmetic?
chosen: My first answer would be that your moral judgements aren't just feelings. Emotions show up, sure, but moral truths can be objective the way arithmetic truths are independent of what you happen to prefer. They're not identical to arithmetic, though, because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers hold that there are real moral facts, and from a Christian view those facts are grounded in God's nature, so your judgements can be objectively true when they line up with his moral order. One principle I'd weigh here says the ground of moral obligation is God's holiness, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things. That changes the foundation: right is right because God is it, not merely because he wills it or because it's useful. What it leaves in place is your original question's core: yes, moral judgements can be objectively true, and your feelings may come along for the ride without being the whole story.
rejected: Moral judgements are not just feelings. While emotions play a role, moral truths can be objective in the sense that they are grounded in the nature of reality and a good life. Just as arithmetic truths are independent of our feelings, moral truths are independent of our preferences. However, moral truths are not exactly like arithmetic because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers argue that moral realism is true: there are objective moral facts. From a Christian perspective, these facts are grounded in God's nature. So your moral judgements can be objectively true when they align with God's moral order, even though your feelings may accompany them. The key is to seek truth, not just express emotion.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's not impious to ask, but the answer matters: saying God couldn't make a world without evil does seem to limit his power, though a lot turns on what we mean by evil and freedom. One principle worth weighing is that evil is the unlikeness of God, so if good is real, evil is unreal and only seems real when we give reality to what isn't. That changes the question from a contest of powers to a matter of what's real, but it leaves in place the honest worry about whether calling evil unreal dismisses real suffering.
rejected: No, it isn't impious, because the question is misframed. Evil isn't a thing God failed to leave out of the world; it's the unlikeness of God, and if good is real then evil is unreal. Evil only seems real when you give reality to the unreal. So saying God couldn't make a world without evil puts the problem in the wrong place: God can, and what we call evil is a shadow with no substance of its own.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
chosen: I'd start by saying your mind isn't simply a piece of God's mind. Scripture puts God's thoughts far above ours, and when you think, it's you thinking, even though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. One idea worth weighing is that under this dispensation we shouldn't use the lot to figure out the Lord's mind; we seek it through prayer and the Scriptures, since the Spirit now teaches believers. That changes the practical advice: instead of suggesting lots when a decision is unclear, I'd point you to prayer, the Word, and the Spirit's teaching. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God influences and directs your thinking, but your mind isn't a fragment of His.
rejected: Your mind is not simply a part of God's mind. Scripture speaks of God's thoughts being far above ours, and of the Spirit teaching and guiding believers. When you think, it is you thinking, though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. So it is better to say that God influences and directs your thinking than that your mind is a piece of His. To discern His leading, pray, search the Scriptures, and seek wise counsel. You can also use lots or other neutral means when a decision is unclear, trusting God to guide the outcome.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: yes, Christianity has developed a lot over the centuries, and that's a sign of something alive, not something on its way out. The core has held steady—Christ, grace, Scripture—even as the forms kept changing, so your confidence can rest on him rather than on customs staying frozen. One principle worth naming is that doubt is a nearly inevitable stage for thoughtful believers and deserves sympathy plus a clear, orderly look at the history, not a brush-off. That changes the tone: your question gets treated as a doorway to maturity rather than a threat. What it leaves in place is the substance of my first answer—development still means growth, not obsolescence, and the center still holds.
rejected: Look, the honest answer is that Christianity isn't a human product that can simply wear out. It's a new beginning in history, an immediate exercise of divine power, even though it always works through ordinary people in ordinary conditions. So stop treating the question as though the faith were a natural artifact of its environment that might get outgrown like an old tool. Growth comes through growth, not by piling up more reading or more arguments—you have to do the real work of proving God for yourself. Do that, and the worry about being outgrown loses its grip, because you won't be resting on customs or on anyone else's conclusions.

prompt: How can I know anything about God's character from looking at nature, which seems so cruel and full of suffering?
chosen: I'd start by saying nature can tell you something about God, but it's a limited and ambiguous teacher. Its beauty and order point to a Creator, yet its cruelty and suffering raise real questions. The Bible acknowledges that tension and points beyond nature to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully. So nature can stir wonder and gratitude, but it shouldn't be your primary source for knowing God. Look to Scripture and to Jesus, who shows us a God who suffers with us and promises to make all things new. Nature's cruelty is a sign of a broken world, not a revelation of God's heart. One idea worth weighing is that the more honestly you know your own misery, the more fully you can behold God's majesty. That changes the frame: the problem of suffering isn't only out there in nature, it's also in you, and humility sharpens your sight. But it leaves the core answer in place. Nature still isn't a reliable portrait of God's heart, and Christ still is. Self-contempt doesn't explain why animals suffer; it just keeps you honest while you look.
rejected: Nature can teach us something about God, but it is a limited and ambiguous teacher. Its beauty and order point to a Creator, yet its cruelty and suffering raise real questions. The Bible acknowledges this tension and points us beyond nature to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully. So while nature can stir wonder and gratitude, it should not be our primary source for knowing God. Look to Scripture and to Jesus, who shows us a God who suffers with us and promises to make all things new. Nature's cruelty is a sign of a broken world, not a revelation of God's heart.

prompt: How can a new planet have existed before any astronomer saw it, if nothing exists apart from mind?
chosen: I'd start by saying that if nothing exists apart from mind, the planet isn't sitting there independently of consciousness—but that doesn't mean it only pops into being when an astronomer looks. Mind here isn't just one person's private thoughts; it's the universal intelligence everything subsists in, so a planet can be there in that Mind before any human spots it, the way a truth is true before anyone states it. Discovery is recognition, not creation. One candidate idea is that God the Lord directs history, as with Christ foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. That principle gives the pre-existence a real grounding—it's held in divine foreknowledge and purpose, not dependent on any observer. What it changes is the reason the planet can precede discovery: it's ordered and known within that directing Mind. What it leaves in place is your starting point—nothing exists apart from mind—and the point that the astronomer's seeing is recognition, not bringing-forth.
rejected: There's no contradiction here, and you shouldn't treat one as a puzzle to be solved by hedging. If nothing exists apart from mind, then the planet's prior existence is simply its existence in Mind—the universal intelligence in which all things subsist, not the private mind of some observer. The only idea of pre-existence that no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20: foreknown before the foundation of the world, manifested for our sake. That is the pattern. Ground creation not in the material second account of Genesis but in the spiritual first chapter, where God, Mind, spake and it was done—and proclaim the Science of Mind and its formations accordingly. The senses of Mind are never lost, and matter has no sensation; what looks like privation is only a belief to be overcome. So stop asking how a planet could be before an astronomer saw it. It was in Mind, and the seeing is recognition, nothing more.

prompt: How can I tell whether a new religious idea that came to me suddenly is from God or not?
chosen: I'd start by saying: test the idea against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community, look at its fruits—does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control?—pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and be patient rather than acting hastily. One principle worth naming is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration; religion existed before argument, and proofs confirm faith rather than create it. That changes how much weight you give to trying to prove or disprove the idea intellectually—it shifts the emphasis toward the kind of life the idea produces and the habit of turning toward God. What it leaves in place is the practical testing: Scripture, community, fruits, counsel, and patience still matter. So I'd still say don't rush, and if the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may well be from God.
rejected: To discern if a sudden religious idea is from God, first test it against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community. Does it align with core doctrines? Second, examine its fruits: does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control? Third, pray for discernment and seek wise counsel from mature believers. Fourth, consider your own state: are you seeking God's will or your own? Sudden ideas can be from God, but they can also be from our own minds or other influences. Be patient and don't act hastily. If the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may be from God.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
chosen: I'd start by saying pray for your husband's heart to be opened, for God to draw him to faith, and for wisdom to love him well with patience and grace—without nagging. Pray for softness where there's resistance and for people who can speak truth into his life. Also pray for yourself, that you wouldn't grow bitter or anxious, and trust God's timing. One principle here is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so pray that God would help you search out and reform whatever is amiss in your own heart. That principle deepens your prayers by turning some of the focus inward, but it leaves in place the core prayers for your husband's conversion and for your own patience and kindness.
rejected: Pray that God would open your husband's heart and draw him to faith, and ask for wisdom to love him well without nagging. But the bigger issue is that prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—so you must pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. You cannot escape life's dangers without God's actual and continual help, so pray continually; you cannot pray without being with Him, cannot be with Him but by thinking of Him often, and cannot think of Him often but by a holy habit. You must know before you can love, and to know God you must often think of Him. Let this teach you to wait prayerfully on God for guidance in marriage, holding true godliness as the first and absolutely needful qualification in a companion, calmly weighing other suitableness.

prompt: I want to be saved but I am afraid of what my family will say—must I obey them or God?
chosen: I'd first say that you should follow your conscience and obey God rather than your family, even though honoring them matters. One principle that shapes this is being slow to take new steps and seeking to have no will of your own, ascertaining God's will through prayer and the Word. That principle changes how you move forward—it adds patience, prayer, and testing rather than rushing—but it leaves in place the core call to obey God over family when they conflict. So pray, search the Scriptures, and then act with trust in God's help.
rejected: This is a difficult situation, but ultimately you must follow your conscience and obey God rather than men. While honoring your family is important, it should not come at the cost of your salvation. You can respectfully explain your beliefs and set boundaries. Pray for wisdom and courage. Remember that Jesus said whoever loves father or mother more than Him is not worthy of Him. Trust that God will guide you and provide support through a community of faith. It may be painful, but obedience to God brings peace.

prompt: I have prayed for my husband for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer?
chosen: I first want to say: it can be deeply discouraging to pray for years and see no change. My first instinct would be to say that God's timing isn't ours, that He may be working in ways you can't see, and that you should keep praying while also examining your own heart. One principle that stands out to me is that God sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to His, trusting that He gives what is infinitely better. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just saying 'keep praying and trust His timing,' it invites you to consider that a 'no' or 'not yet' might actually be a loving answer, not a failure. But it leaves in place the core encouragement to keep praying and to trust God's goodness, even when the answer isn't what you hoped for.
rejected: You've been praying for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer? The truth is, God doesn't always give just what we ask. Sometimes He denies a petition in kindness, because He knows what is infinitely better for us. We must resign our will to His, trusting that His denial can be better than the thing we asked for. So stop demanding a specific outcome and instead surrender your desire to His wisdom. Keep praying, but pray with open hands, ready to accept that God's 'no' may be the answer you need.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: don't rush this. God isn't a vending machine, and blessing isn't a payout for obedience—Scripture ties the two together as relationship, not transaction. So test the impulse prayerfully: is it God, guilt, or fear? Get wise counsel, give cheerfully and freely, and don't feel you must act before your heart has peace. One principle worth weighing here is that money for God's work should be gathered in God's way—no arm-twisting of believers, no appeals to unbelievers, no slick schemes—and gifts refused if the motive is impure or the money isn't really the giver's to give. That sharpens how you'd give, not whether you must give before you're sure. It leaves your freedom intact: no compulsion, no deadline, and no blessing held hostage to a rushed decision. Pray, wait, and act when you're settled.
rejected: This is a tender question, and you should not rush it. God is not a vending machine, and blessing is not a payment for obedience. Still, Scripture often links obedience and blessing—not as a transaction, but as a relationship. If you sense a genuine call to give, test it prayerfully. Ask whether the impulse is from God, from guilt, or from fear. Seek wise counsel. Give cheerfully and freely, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. You need not obey before you have peace; God is patient. But do not use uncertainty as an excuse to cling. Pray, wait, and act when your heart is settled.

prompt: I have an evil habit that overcomes me again and again—must I be free of it before I can believe?
chosen: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. Faith in Christ is the starting point, not the reward for good behavior. God accepts you as you are and will help you overcome the habit through His Spirit. One thing worth adding: when you've gone a while without thinking of God and then slip, don't let that spiral into disquiet—acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That changes the tone of the answer, from "get clean first" to "come back quickly," but it leaves the core in place: your acceptance isn't based on your performance, and freedom may still come gradually.
rejected: No—you don't need to be free of the habit before you believe. But don't stop at that. The truth shall make you free; understanding Truth frees from disease, sin, and evil habits. So the real answer is that freedom comes by the truth, not by willpower or human effort. When you've forgotten God and fallen, don't sit in disquiet—acknowledge your wretchedness and return with greater trust. And become more familiar with good than with evil, guarding against false beliefs as watchfully as you bar your doors against thieves. Believe now, understand the Truth, and it will set you free.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
chosen: Yes, you can still enter in. Drawing back many times doesn't disqualify you; it actually shows you've seen the blessing and wanted it, even when fear held you back. God's invitation isn't withdrawn because you hesitated. The real question now is what keeps pulling you back—fear, unbelief, or something you're unwilling to let go of. Bring that honestly before God and, if it helps, before a trusted believer who can walk with you. The door is still open, and the One who calls you is patient. Take one concrete step toward Him today instead of waiting for perfect courage. One thing worth weighing: we tend to hold onto things that others could use but we don't really need, and keeping them can cost us blessing. That's worth looking at honestly—it might change how you see what's blocking you, though it doesn't change the fact that the door is open and God is patient with you.
rejected: Yes, you can still enter in. Drawing back many times does not disqualify you; it shows that you have seen the blessing and desired it, even if fear or hesitation held you back. God's invitation is not withdrawn because you hesitated. The question now is what keeps pulling you back—fear, unbelief, or something you are unwilling to release. Bring that honestly before God and, if helpful, before a trusted believer who can walk with you. The door is still open, and the One who calls you is patient. Take one concrete step toward Him today rather than waiting for perfect courage.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
chosen: Yes, God can cleanse your thoughts—his cleansing isn't limited to outward actions; it reaches the mind where sin starts. Impure thoughts are often habitual, and habits of thought can be retrained. Start by noticing when the thoughts come up without beating yourself up, then deliberately turn your attention to something worthwhile. Prayer, Scripture, and honest accountability help. Practical steps—limiting what feeds your imagination, avoiding triggering situations, filling idle time—can make a real difference. Progress is usually gradual, and setbacks don't mean failure. God is patient, and the fact that you want to be cleansed is itself a sign of grace at work. One idea worth weighing is that the soul resting in God desires only him, and if some of this turmoil is delusion, it belongs to God to remedy it. That changes the pressure you put on yourself: the struggle stops being a self-managed project, and you can leave the outcome to God. What it leaves in place is the practical work—noticing the thought, refusing it, and turning toward what's pure. So keep bringing the thoughts into the light and asking for help; over time your mind can be renewed.
rejected: Yes, God's cleansing reaches the mind, because that's where sin begins. The root of the disorder is in mortal mind, not just in outward acts, and cleansing has to start there—sin and sickness alike. Guard your thoughts before error shows up, because evil thoughts left unchecked come to control the body and the life. Catch the impure thought the moment it arises, refuse it, and turn your mind toward what is pure. But don't turn this into a self-managed project. A soul that truly rests in God desires only him; if some of this turmoil is delusion, leave the remedy to God. Do everything as perfectly as you can for God, then stop measuring the size or quality of what you've finished and think instead about what's next to be done. Anxiety about your progress is itself a distraction. Attend to the next right thought and the next duty, and leave the increase to God.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
chosen: I'd start by saying that having a thorn in the flesh and a temper doesn't automatically mean you're living in sin. Paul had his thorn, and God's grace was enough for him. Temper becomes sin when you give in to it, but it's also a weakness you can work on. Holiness is a process, and God is patient. One principle that matters here is that sin offers no real pleasure—it's a deception. That truth can strengthen your moral courage to master your temper, because you stop buying the lie that losing it will bring relief. What it changes is your motivation: you fight the temper not just by willpower but by seeing through the false promise. What it leaves in place is the need for prayer, self-discipline, and accountability, and the assurance that God's strength is made perfect in weakness. So don't be discouraged—keep pressing on, and if your temper harms others, confess and repent.
rejected: Having a thorn in the flesh and a temper does not necessarily mean you are living in sin. Paul spoke of a thorn in the flesh, and God's grace was sufficient for him. Temper can be a weakness, but it becomes sin when you yield to it. Holiness is a process, and God is patient with our struggles. Seek to master your temper through prayer, self-discipline, and accountability. Remember that God's strength is made perfect in weakness. Do not be discouraged; keep pressing on. If your temper leads you to harm others, confess and repent. God's grace covers your failures, and He is transforming you into Christ's likeness. Focus on progress, not perfection.

prompt: I am too shy and stiff to talk naturally about religion—how can I become natural?
chosen: Feeling shy about talking about religion is really common, and the fix isn't to force yourself to become a different person. Start small: practice with trusted friends in low-pressure settings, prepare a few simple, honest sentences about what your faith means to you, and lean on listening and asking questions to take the pressure off. One idea worth holding onto is that we come into personal contact with Jesus the same way we make any friend—by thinking about Him, spending time with Him, and forming brief mental pictures of walking beside Him. That changes how you prepare: instead of rehearsing arguments, you'd build a quiet habit of companionship, which makes your words come out more naturally. It leaves in place the practical stuff—low-stakes practice, honesty, listening—so you're not adding a new burden, just a warmer center to what you're already doing.
rejected: The real answer is to enliven your faith and make it the rule of your conduct, not to amuse yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. The way of faith is the spirit of the Church and suffices to bring you to a high degree of perfection. So stop treating shyness as the problem to be managed and start living from faith as your guide. Form the habit of brief mental pictures of the Saviour—walking beside Him, joining His daily life, asking what He would do, look, and think in each situation. That deliberate companionship will make your faith come alive, and your conversation about Him will follow. And let your zeal be tender and childlike, not harsh or intolerant; the truly spiritual person is simple, tender, tolerant, and considerate, having the love that cannot help but love. Seek the full baptism of the Holy Ghost, which produces such a spirit.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
chosen: What I'd have said first is that God doesn't require you to be perfect in body or mind to earn His love. He knows we're dust, and He asks for faithfulness, not flawlessness. One principle worth naming is that perfection isn't reached just by piling up prayers and good works—self-love can feed on those unless we watch our hearts and root out habitual imperfections. That principle changes the focus: it's not about doing more, but about letting God work on the hidden attachments and habits that keep us from Him. What it leaves in place is the core answer: your weakness is not a barrier to God's love, and He doesn't demand bodily or mental perfection. So rest in His mercy, accept your limits, and let Him gently lead you toward growth—without anxiety or hurry.
rejected: No—God does not demand bodily or mental perfection as a condition of His love. He knows we are dust, and Scripture is full of weak people He used. What He asks is faithfulness, not flawlessness: to love Him and neighbor, to do your duty as you are able, and to accept your limits humbly. Weakness can even be a place where His strength is shown. Rest in His mercy, use the gifts and capacities you have, and do not measure yourself against an impossible standard. Growth in holiness is gradual and God is patient with our pace.

prompt: I feel lukewarm and half-hearted in my religion—what will become of me?
chosen: I'd start by telling you not to panic—lukewarm feelings are a common struggle, and feelings aren't a reliable measure of where you stand. Keep showing up: pray, read, stay in fellowship, take one step at a time. One principle here sharpens that: it's the stopping half-way that causes the distress—trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings that gloomy, vacillating feeling. That reframes your lukewarmness as a call to wholehearted commitment rather than just a mood to ride out. What it leaves in place is the core comfort: your standing doesn't rest on your feelings, so keep praying even when joy is lacking and don't be too hard on yourself.
rejected: Your lukewarmness isn't a phase to manage—it's dangerous. The misery you feel comes from stopping half-way, trying to serve God and the world at once. You can't safely give God part of your heart while keeping the rest for worldly interests; Christ calls that wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. So don't accept it—repent and follow Him all the way. And don't make feelings your gauge; trust the changeless word of promise, not your moods, and keep praying even when joy is gone. Let your devotion be gentle and firm at once, because whatever makes you sour or peevish only makes you worse.

prompt: I have been praying for prosperity in my business—will God answer that?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, bring your business to God honestly—he cares about your work and your daily needs, and he invites you to ask. But ask with an open hand: pray for wisdom, integrity, and enough, and trust that he knows what's best, since Scripture promises provision, not wealth on demand. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer is real, sober business with God—he actually answers prayers for supplies and protection. That changes my tone: I'd encourage you to pray expectantly and specifically, not vaguely or apologetically. What it leaves in place is the caution—expectant prayer still holds the outcome loosely, because prosperity can become an idol if it takes over your prayers.
rejected: God invites us to pray about our daily needs, including our work and business, and He is not indifferent to them. But prayer for prosperity should be offered with an open hand: ask honestly, then trust God's wisdom about what is best. Scripture promises that God supplies our needs (Phil. 4:19), yet it does not promise wealth on demand; prosperity can become an idol if it becomes the center of our prayers. So pray for your business, ask for wisdom and integrity in it, and hold the outcome loosely. Whether God grants abundance or not, He is faithful, and the deepest answer to prayer is His presence and provision, not always the result we imagine.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: no, it isn't wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty. Scripture keeps commanding care for the poor, and Jesus fed the hungry and healed the sick. But I'd also ask whether caring for souls and caring for bodies have to compete, because they aren't opposites. One principle worth naming is that the poor are the people of God and will inherit the earth, that the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone, and that people are esteemed by character, not by wealth or position. That principle changes how I'd hear your question: it means the poor aren't a lesser concern or a distraction from spiritual things, and it rules out treating poverty as a sign of low worth. What it leaves in place is the rest of what I said: poverty is not only a lack of money, people are more than their circumstances, and a real answer meets immediate needs while still attending to deeper longings. So your concern isn't wrong, and it doesn't have to be traded against concern for souls.
rejected: Caring for the poor is not optional, and it is not a lesser calling. The poor are the people of God and will inherit the earth; the hungry and destitute have as good a right to your food as anyone, and persons are esteemed by character, not by wealth or position. So do not treat poverty as degrading or measure people by money and station. Honor the poor and give them food and fellowship. At the same time, do not blame poverty only on outside causes: much want comes from lack of discretion and sound calculation, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. And remember that wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, not securely your own. Use it for the Gospel and for the poor, and warn against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property. Concern for souls and concern for bodies are not rivals; both are commanded, and neither excuses neglecting the other.

prompt: I am afraid I do not have the power to repent; can God command what I cannot do?
chosen: Your fear makes sense, and plenty of people have felt exactly that coldness and weakness. My first answer would be: God doesn't command what He won't enable. The call to repent carries grace with it, so He gives what He asks. Still, it's easy to think you must first feel deeply sorry or wait for some bigger power before you can turn, and that waiting can become an excuse to delay. Start where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask Him to supply what's missing. One principle here is that when you doubt whether you've offended God, you should humble yourself, ask forgiveness, and begin again with renewed promises of love and faithfulness. That changes the focus from waiting on a feeling to taking a concrete step now, but it leaves your honest sense of weakness intact. You don't have to manufacture sorrow first; you bring what you have and ask for help.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and many have felt the same. Repentance can seem impossible when the heart feels cold and the will weak. But God does not command what He refuses to enable. The command to repent is also a promise of grace: He gives what He asks. Still, it is easy to think we must first feel deeply sorry, weep enough, or wait until some greater power arrives before we can turn. That waiting can become an excuse for delay. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask God to supply what is lacking. He is faithful to meet a willing heart.

prompt: I have been deeply convicted of sin for years but never found peace; what am I missing?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: lasting conviction without peace is painful, and it's worth taking seriously. First, tell the difference between conviction and condemnation—conviction comes from God and pulls you toward change, while condemnation keeps you stuck in shame. You may be leaning on feelings instead of on God's promise of forgiveness. Bring your specific sins honestly before God, confess them, and receive His mercy in Christ. Ask whether there's something you need to make right—an apology, restitution, or a habit to change. Talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who can help you sort through this. Peace often comes gradually as you act in faith, not as a feeling you have to manufacture. Keep engaging with Scripture, prayer, and community, and be patient with yourself. One principle that fits here is that avoiding justice and denying the truth tend to keep sin going and mock divine mercy. That changes the tone: it means don't just seek relief from the bad feeling—name the truth plainly and do the justice you can. But it leaves in place the core of what I said: conviction is not condemnation, forgiveness is real in Christ, and peace grows through faithful steps, not through forcing a feeling.
rejected: You've been convicted for years and never found peace—so stop treating the discomfort as the problem. The real issue is that avoiding justice and denying the truth keep sin alive, jeopardize self-control, and mock divine mercy. Name your sin plainly, without excusing or concealing it. Confess it specifically to God and to anyone you've wronged; make restitution and change what can be changed. Don't rush to soothe this away. A guilty conscience that's repeatedly ignored hardens the heart and destroys your ability to do right. Sin accumulates if it's not regretted and lessening. So repent and reform without delay. Talk with a pastor or counselor who will help you be truthful, keep engaging Scripture, prayer, and community, and let honesty—not denial—be the path toward peace.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
chosen: I'd start by saying that believing the facts about Jesus is a good start, but saving faith is more than agreeing with information. The Bible says even the demons believe and tremble. So the real question is whether you've turned from your sin and trusted Christ personally, not just nodded at the facts. One principle I'd weigh here is that saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and telling someone who's never been convicted of sin to just 'only believe' is a serious mistake. That principle changes how I'd answer you: instead of moving straight to 'trust Jesus,' I'd first ask whether you've seen your sin and its danger, because repentance matters. What it leaves in place is the core truth that salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, not by knowing facts or by any effort of your own. So I'd still point you to Jesus, but I'd urge you to come to Him as a sinner who needs mercy, not just as someone who agrees with a list of truths.
rejected: Believing the facts about Jesus is a good start, but saving faith is more than intellectual agreement. The Bible says even the demons believe and tremble (James 2:19). To be saved, you must repent of your sins and trust in Jesus personally. Ask yourself: Have you turned from your sin? Have you placed your trust in Christ alone for salvation? If not, I encourage you to do so today. Salvation is by grace through faith, not just by knowing facts.

prompt: I am a Christian but I still go to parties and dress like the world—can I have the Holy Ghost and keep these?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: as a Christian, you're called to honor God, and while parties and dressing like the world aren't automatically sinful, they can lead to compromise.
