The Holy Ghost is given to those who obey and seek holiness, so ask whether these things draw you closer to God or away. One principle that matters here is that missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually and return as pure as white paper. That principle changes the tone: it makes holiness a daily pursuit, not a later cleanup. But it leaves in place your freedom to examine your motives and the wisdom of mature believers—so you still get to decide, with the Spirit's guidance, what honors God in your actual life.
rejected: You ask if you can have the Holy Ghost while keeping your parties and worldly dress. The answer is no—not if you want the Holy Ghost continually. You must start with clean hands and pure hearts, live so as to enjoy the Holy Ghost every day, and return as pure as white paper. Do not think you can begin pure only later. Remain in a holy nudity of spirit, assuming no care, desire, affection, or pretension, resting on no breast but God's. The Holy Ghost is the special gift of the Father, given according to God's discretion and your faithfulness. Going to parties and dressing like the world may not be inherently sinful, but they clutter your spirit and lead to compromise. Seek the Spirit continually and surround yourself with mature believers who can advise you.

prompt: How do I believe when I have tried and failed so many times?
chosen: What I'd say first is that failure doesn't disqualify you—it's part of learning to believe. Start small: keep honest practices like prayer, reading, and reflection, and treat each setback as information rather than a verdict. Notice what triggered it, adjust, and begin again. One day at a time, with people around you for encouragement, belief grows through repeated attempts, not through never falling. One principle here that sharpens this is that fidelity is yours while failure comes from infirmity—so be faithful in your exercises but don't be troubled or astonished when you sometimes fail. That changes the tone: it takes the sting and panic out of falling and keeps the focus on steady practice. What it leaves in place is the practical core—start small, learn from setbacks, lean on community, be patient with yourself. It doesn't excuse giving up; it just means a stumble isn't a verdict on you.
rejected: Failure is part of learning to believe, and it does not mean you are disqualified. Start small: keep honest practices—prayer, reading, reflection—and treat each failure as information rather than verdict. Notice what triggered the setback, adjust, and begin again. Many people find it helps to lower the stakes, focus on one day at a time, and lean on community for encouragement. Belief grows through repeated attempts, not through never falling. Be patient with yourself, forgive the past failures, and let each new morning be a fresh start. Over time these small faithful steps build a habit, and the habit carries you when motivation fades.

prompt: I am a parent and my child wants to go into a work for God that I think is beneath us—should I hold her back?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I thought before: talk with her openly about her motives and the work itself, check whether your hesitation is real concern or pride about status, and ask a trusted mentor for perspective. A calling to serve God isn't beneath anyone, so encourage her while helping her prepare wisely. One principle that matters here is that the will is a divine endowment to be guided, not broken. That changes how you hold your concerns: instead of just managing your own feelings, you guide her will toward what's right rather than crushing it. What it leaves in place is everything you already said—the open conversation, the honest look at your own motives, the mentors, and the encouragement.
rejected: Don't assume the work is beneath her. Children's complaints and difficulties disappear through understanding God as ever-present and omnipotent—that's what the testimonies describe. Bring your fears to that understanding instead of managing them only with material planning. God has placed a will within us; it should be indomitable for right and controlled by the will of the Almighty. Guide her will rather than break it, because breaking it reduces the child's God-like powers to imbecility. Commend her spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint of indulgence, so she grows in the understanding of man's higher nature. A calling to serve God is not beneath anyone; encourage her and trust divine help.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you don't have to sober up before you come to God. Come to Christ just as you are and believe. One principle worth naming is that the believer should cultivate obedience and gratitude, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized. What that changes is the tone of the practical side—instead of just 'get help and try harder,' it adds grateful, prompt turning from sin, even small ones, as part of walking with God. What it leaves in place is the core answer: you are not saved by cleaning yourself up first, and you still should seek real help for the drinking—counseling, a support group, medical care—while trusting God to change you over time.
rejected: The good news is that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you do not have to clean yourself up before coming to God. Come to Christ just as you are, and believe. At the same time, genuine faith produces change, so you should seek help for your drinking—counseling, a support group, medical care—and lean on God's strength. Do not wait until you are perfect to come to God, but do not treat grace as permission to continue in destructive habits either. Take practical steps and trust God to work in you over time.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, holiness is possible on earth, but not as a badge you wear. My first instinct would be to say it's about love—loving God and neighbor—and that the warning against claiming holiness is just a guard against pride. So stay humble, love generously, and you're on the right track. But one idea that sharpens this is that holiness is fundamentally about being set apart for God, not just about being morally good or loving. That changes things: it means holiness starts with belonging to God, not with your performance or your feelings. What it leaves in place is the importance of love and humility—those still matter—but it reframes them as fruit of being God's own, not the root. So you can pursue holiness by yielding your heart—your mind, emotions, and will—to God, and letting that belonging shape your life, without ever needing to claim the word for yourself.
rejected: Holiness is not only possible—it's demanded, and it begins with God's own character. God is holy before He is loving in any way we can measure; His love is governed by His holiness, and His law flows from His righteous nature. So sin isn't merely a failure to love; it's guilt before a holy God, and that guilt is dealt with only through Christ's sacrifice. Holiness means being set apart—consecrated, belonging entirely to God. It's not about becoming nice or purified by your own effort; it's about being possessed by God. And that separation must start in the heart—the core of your intellect, emotions, and will—so that every thought, affection, and choice is yielded to Him. Anyone who claims to have achieved holiness is deceived, because belonging is God's act, not your boast. But real holiness on earth is a life lived as God's own possession, resting on Christ's work, transformed at the center, and expressed in dedicated obedience—not a claim to have arrived.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: be honest about the drift, confess it, and turn back toward God without waiting to feel worthy. Remember what you first received, and renew the small practices—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, obedience—even before affection returns. One principle worth naming is rejoicing evermore: keep on with the medicine of rejoicing even when it seems ineffectual, and trust God to make your reckoning good. That changes the tone—it adds a call to keep rejoicing through the coldness—but it leaves in place the core path of honesty, confession, returning, and faithful small practices. It doesn't replace them; it steadies you while you walk them out.
rejected: Returning to your first love begins with honesty: name the drift, confess it, and turn back toward God without waiting to feel worthy. Remember what you first received and the joy of your early devotion. Renew the small practices that once fed you—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience—even before affection returns, because love often follows faithful action. Do not be discouraged by coldness of feeling; feelings lag behind commitment. Draw near to God and he will draw near to you. Expect gradual renewal rather than instant warmth, and let others walk with you in the process.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
chosen: Feeling like your prayers aren't heard is really common, and I'd start by saying God isn't distant or indifferent—He invites you to come to Him. Assurance usually grows through practice: pray regularly, even briefly, reflect on Scripture's promises, maybe keep a journal of prayers and answers so you can see His faithfulness over time, and talk with a pastor or trusted friend. Confidence isn't a feeling you have to manufacture; it's trust built on God's character. One principle that fits here is that God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul—like human invention lets us communicate across great distances, so much more does God understand your innermost thoughts, so pray in faith without wavering. What that adds is a real basis for confidence even when feelings lag: God's understanding of you is deeper than any signal can carry. What it leaves in place is everything else—regular prayer, Scripture, honest confession, and community still matter, and confidence is still trust rather than a feeling you force.
rejected: Don't be discouraged by your sins—pray for grace with complete confidence, leaning on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from His presence or forget to ask. So stay faithfully in His presence, calm and attentive, and set aside hurry and anxiety, because those are the greatest obstacles to progress. Bring your sins to God, ask for the grace He's already offering, and rest your confidence on His merits, not on your feelings. God hears the earnest prayer of the soul; as human invention lets people communicate across great distances, so much more does God understand your innermost thoughts. Pray in faith, nothing wavering.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: look at your motives, whether you give cheerfully or to be seen, whether it's consistent and sacrificial, and whether it draws you closer to God or feeds pride. One principle worth naming is that charity is the light—God's own love, our soul held in God, and the virtue it becomes. That deepens the picture: your giving isn't just a moral habit to inspect, it's a share in God's own love that keeps you in faith and hope. What it changes is the focus, from mostly checking your intentions to asking whether your giving keeps you rooted in God and leads you further into love. What it leaves in place is the practical self-examination—motives, consistency, humility—and the call to keep giving and ask God to purify your heart.
rejected: It's wonderful that you give to the poor. To discern if your charity is from God, examine your motives: are you giving to be seen by others, or out of genuine love? Do you give grudgingly or cheerfully? God loves a cheerful giver. Also, consider whether your giving is consistent and sacrificial, not just from surplus. Pray for discernment and ask God to purify your intentions. Remember that even imperfect charity can be used by God. Look for fruits: does your giving bring you closer to God and to others? Does it foster humility or pride? Ultimately, charity is a virtue that grows with practice. Keep giving, and ask God to make it truly His.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your friends are right to be cautious, but caution shouldn't become a cage. New work isn't wrong just because it's unfamiliar; the real question is whether it's faithful to Scripture and fruitful for the gospel. One principle worth weighing here is that you should hold fast to old friends and not let them go unless wicked conduct breaks the thread of fellowship. That changes the tone of how you take their counsel—it makes it a matter of loyalty and relationship, not just a review of pros and cons. What it leaves in place is the actual test: is this work sound in doctrine and motive, does it honor Christ and serve people? So I'd say keep faith with your friends, weigh their counsel seriously, and don't hold back merely because the work is different.
rejected: Hold fast to your old friends and don't let them go—only wicked conduct breaks that thread of fellowship. But don't confuse loyalty to friends with loyalty to God. This work, if it's truly of God, isn't your achievement; it's God's own work through His servant, done in obedience to Him and for the glory of His Name. Stop trying to prepare your own good works or lean on your own strength. You are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works He prepared beforehand; receive them by faith and go forward in His all-sufficiency, even when you feel weak and helpless. Test everything by Scripture, keep faith with your friends, and trust the One who began a good work in you to finish it.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
chosen: Your sense that your life has been one huge error is already a kind of conviction, and it may be enough to start with. Not everyone feels dramatic agony over sin; some are led to repentance through a quieter recognition that things have gone wrong. What matters is whether that recognition turns you toward God and a changed life. Agony isn't the measure of sincerity—honesty is. One principle worth weighing here is that sin is a kind of insanity, and sickness is error, a loss of harmony, so the senses' testimony can't be true of man or his Maker. That reframes your question: conviction isn't about how much you suffer but about whether you stop believing the error. What it changes is the pressure to manufacture agony; what it leaves in place is the real need for honesty and a turned life. Bring your sense of error to God, ask for clearer light on what needs to change, and let that awareness grow into repentance and trust in his mercy.
rejected: Your sense that your life has been one huge error is already a form of conviction, and it may be enough to begin with. Not everyone experiences dramatic anguish over sin; some are led to repentance through a quieter recognition that things have gone wrong. What matters is whether that recognition turns you toward God and a changed life. Agony is not the measure of sincerity—honesty is. Bring your sense of error to God, ask for a clearer light on what needs to change, and let that awareness grow into repentance and trust in his mercy. Conviction deepens over time, and a quiet beginning can lead to real transformation.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this is a hard spot, and kindness matters. Before you say anything, ask whether it's clearly sin or just a personal preference, and whether you're the right person to bring it up. If you do speak, do it privately and gently, with humility, making it about your care for her rather than about being right. Invite her to talk instead of issuing a correction, and be open to correction yourself. Sometimes the wisest thing is to pray and wait. One idea worth weighing is that there's no real pleasure in sin, that what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives. That can give you courage to speak rather than stay silent out of fear of hurting her feelings. What it changes is your resolve to say something loving instead of nothing. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: privacy, gentleness, humility, and not wanting to wound her.
rejected: Silence isn't the safe choice you think it is. Sin offers no real pleasure; what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs far more than it gives, and once you see that clearly, you'll have the courage to help her escape it. So speak, and speak plainly. If she's swearing, treat it as a serious habit to break and put a penance on every oath. Don't settle for gentle hints; severity is what actually breaks a habit like that. And know your limits: it isn't your place to point out the supposed faults of church leaders. God will judge them. Correct what's yours to correct, and don't give the world a reason to speak evil because of careless words.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
chosen: I hear you. You're asking if you can keep that one thing and still be filled. My first answer would be: God's holiness is a gift, not something you earn by giving things up, so don't turn this into a transaction. But if you know something stands between you and God, look at it honestly. One principle worth weighing is that we can hold onto things that are useful to others but not needed by us, and that keeping them costs us blessing. That principle shifts the focus from 'Can I keep this?' to 'Is this something I'm hoarding that could serve someone else?' It doesn't settle whether every attachment must go, and it leaves room for patience and growth. So examine that thing with a trusted friend or pastor, pray for wisdom, and be honest about whether it's a hindrance or just a preference. You don't have to be perfect overnight.
rejected: It is understandable to hesitate when holiness seems to require giving something up. The good news is that God does not ask us to earn His blessing by our own sacrifices; holiness is His gift. At the same time, if you know something stands between you and God, it is worth examining honestly. You may not need to give up everything at once, but consider whether this thing is truly a hindrance or merely a preference. Talk with a trusted pastor or friend, pray for wisdom, and be patient with yourself. God is gracious, and He meets you where you are. The goal is growth, not instant perfection.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
chosen: I'd start by saying your doubt is understandable and many sincere people feel the same. Growth in Christlikeness is a lifelong process, not a single decision. Start where you are: pray honestly, examine your life, and take small steps of obedience. Don't wait until you feel strong or worthy; God meets us in our weakness. Find a community that can support and encourage you, and be patient with yourself. Restoration is God's work, and He is faithful to complete what He begins. One principle that speaks to your doubt is that God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and since He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available right now—the feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. That changes the timing: you don't have to wait for a better feeling or greater strength before you act. But it leaves in place the lifelong process and the need for patience and community; it doesn't promise instant perfection or remove the slow work of growth.
rejected: Your doubt is misplaced. God commands you to repent now, and because He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available this very moment. Stop waiting for a better feeling or greater strength. The feeling follows the surrender, not the other way around. Do not languish over the number and magnitude of your sins. All is possible to God, and it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of yourself you cannot even think what is right; all comes to you from God. With Jesus, affirm that God is the Life of man: individualized existence is restored, not lost in death, which is only a seeming vanishing that Truth restores. So pray, obey, and trust that He will complete what He begins. Your doubt is not humility—it is a refusal to accept the power God offers you right now.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: your fear is worth listening to, and holiness usually means reordering your relationships, not cutting everyone off. Before you leave your whole circle, ask whether you're running from temptation or from the discomfort of being known and challenged. If some ties really do pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically, and get counsel from someone mature in the faith. What I'd add is this: any self-denial you take on has to come from real joy in God and the Spirit's work in you, not just from custom or wanting to look holy. That changes the motive and the staying power of what you do, but it leaves the practical advice in place: stay where you can, set boundaries, and don't act out of fear.
rejected: Your fear is a signal worth listening to. Holiness rarely requires severing every relationship; it requires reordering them. Before cutting loose, ask whether you are fleeing temptation or fleeing the discomfort of being known and challenged. Often the holiest path is to stay, set clearer boundaries, and let your circle see a changed life. If some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Seek counsel from a mature believer or pastor, be patient, and let your choices be shaped by love rather than fear. Holiness grows in community, not in isolation.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
chosen: I'd first say: it's good that you see the habit needs to go—that's where repentance starts. But promising yourself 'next month' over and over is a warning sign. Real repentance means actually turning, not just a good intention for later. That said, change is often gradual, and God is patient with slow progress. You're not automatically unrepentant just because you struggle. Ask yourself honestly why you keep delaying—fear, comfort, lack of trust? Bring that to God and think about one small step you could take today instead of next month. Talk to someone who can support you, and be honest about the delay. One principle here says repentance means ceasing the wrong as soon as you know it—ignorance is overlooked, but once you learn something is wrong you must stop right away. That principle sharpens the point: your 'next month' is disobedience postponed, not just a weak plan. It leaves in place the encouragement that God is patient and change can be gradual—so you don't need to despair, but you do need to act now rather than later.
rejected: Recognizing the habit is wrong is good, but 'next month' again and again is not repentance—it's delay dressed up as intention. Once you know something is wrong, you must stop immediately and for good. Ignorance is winked at, but knowledge makes delay disobedience. Don't despair—it's not desperate to have been wounded, but to neglect the cure. Repent now and take up the cure. Confess your faults and humble yourself before God; humility and confession help still wandering thoughts, while many words in prayer often make the mind wander. Keep your prayer simple and your confession honest. Someone who has fallen can rise again, like wrestlers and soldiers after a fall—so rise today, not next month.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
chosen: I'd start by saying that if your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you can't separate the profit from the harm—the money is the fruit of the injury, and keeping it means consenting to it. So ask whether the harm is essential or incidental. If it's essential, you must leave it, even at a cost. If it's incidental, you can reform the business so it no longer harms. One principle that matters here is that blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive you to prayer and action rather than let you rest in personal security. That changes the focus: it's not just about your own soul being safe, but about letting that burden push you to pray and act. What it leaves in place is the basic moral logic—if the harm is essential, leaving is still required. It doesn't soften that; it just adds a call to prayer and action alongside it.
rejected: This is a serious question, and it deserves a serious answer. If your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you cannot separate the profit from the harm. The money is the fruit of the injury, and to keep it is to consent to it. You should ask whether the harm is essential to the business or incidental. If essential, you must leave it, even at cost. If incidental, you may reform the business so that it no longer harms. Do not rationalize. Personal security is not a sufficient reason to continue in a trade that damages others. Seek counsel, plan carefully, and trust that God will provide as you obey.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
chosen: Yes, you can be saved, and your grief over this coldness is itself a sign that something in you still turns toward God. Feeling hard and cold doesn't mean you've been cut off for good—feelings rise and fall, and they aren't the measure of where you stand. What matters is that you turn toward God again, not that you feel deeply right now. One idea worth weighing is that a real relapse can't actually happen, because there is only one Mind; you meet the cause mentally and courageously, and you face down your own fears. That changes how you see this numbness—it's not a final fall, just a false belief to confront. But it leaves in place the plain call to turn back to God, to bring your hardness honestly to him, to read Scripture even when it feels dull, and to stay among his people. Don't wait to feel convicted before you act; act, and the feeling may follow. Your question itself shows you haven't stopped wanting him.
rejected: You can be saved, but stop treating this coldness as a real relapse. In Truth there is no relapse—only the belief in one, and a belief is not a fact. Meet its cause mentally and courageously: ask what fear or false belief has made you feel separated from God, and face it head-on. Yet know this too—there is no salvation except in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life except through obedience to the law set by the Father of life. And even if you were lifted high into contemplation, don't imagine you've outgrown the need to see your own sin and feebleness; without that sight there is no true meekness, and without meekness no salvation. So turn again toward God, not waiting for warmth, and walk in humble obedience.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
chosen: I get why that fear shows up—going all in with God can feel like handing over the keys without knowing the destination. My first answer would be: don't be afraid, because God is good and wants what's best for you, even when following him is hard and asks for sacrifice. One principle I'd lean on here is that God doesn't will harm toward you; he wants to do you great good, so love him fervently rather than fear him as if he were out to get you. That changes the picture of what you're walking into—it's not a trap—but it leaves in place the honest truth that commitment can still cost you something and feel scary along the way.
rejected: It's understandable to fear that going all the way with God might lead to something terrible, but God is good and loving. He doesn't want to harm you; He wants what's best for you. However, following God can be challenging and may involve sacrifices. But remember that God promises to be with you and to work all things for your good. So, while it's natural to have some fear, you can trust that God's plans are for your welfare and not for harm, to give you a future and a hope. Don't let fear hold you back from fully committing to God.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your tears show a conscience that's still awake, and that's a good thing. Salvation isn't about getting every attachment perfectly sorted out before you come to God—it's about trusting Christ, who takes sinners as they are. Bring this thing you love to him honestly and ask him to change your heart over time. Here's a principle worth weighing: unrepented sin is serious enough to call for a real fear of losing your soul, so that fear can hold you back where love feels too weak. That principle adds weight and urgency to what I said—it means don't treat this attachment lightly or assume time will fix it on its own. But it doesn't overturn the core: grace is patient, God doesn't demand you fix yourself first, and you keep coming to Christ while he loosens your grip. So keep confessing, keep praying, and don't despair.
rejected: Your weeping is a start, but don't let it lull you: one unrepented sin is enough to damn a soul forever. Scripture warns that those who love a lie have their part in the lake of fire. So cultivate an intense, abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss—if love of God is too weak to keep you from this thing, fear of hell must restrain you. I don't say this from above you: I too must confess my own faults, for we are all sinners, and Christ took our sins and made them his own. Acknowledge your sin and your weakness plainly, then trust God's gentle mercy toward the contrite. Bring this loved thing to him honestly, confess it, and let holy fear guard you until love grows strong enough to let it go.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
chosen: I'd start where I said before: that fear is common, and it usually matters less than it feels. You're not responsible for the labels people put on you, only for speaking with kindness and honesty. Look for natural openings, speak gently, and let small faithful steps shrink the fear over time. One principle worth weighing here is committing yourself and everything you care about to God's providence in silence and peace, accepting what comes as from a father's hand rather than churning over what people think of you. That changes the inner ground you stand on: the fear of being called a fanatic loses some of its grip because your reputation is no longer the thing you're guarding. What it leaves in place is the practical side, which still matters: you still choose your moments, still speak with gentleness, and still don't force conversations. The principle steadies your heart; it doesn't excuse you from reading the room.
rejected: Fear of being called a fanatic is common, but it usually matters less than it feels. Start by remembering that you are not responsible for how people label you, only for speaking with kindness and honesty. Pray for courage and for the right moments. You do not need to force conversations; look for natural openings and speak gently. Over time, small faithful steps will make the fear smaller. Also ask yourself whose approval you are really seeking. When concern for God's view outweighs concern for others' opinions, the fear of labels loses its grip.

prompt: I was told to just believe I am saved—but I don't feel saved; what should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying that being told to 'just believe' can feel hollow when your feelings don't line up, and that's worth taking seriously rather than shoving down. Feelings aren't the measure of your salvation; God's promise is. So examine yourself: do you see your sin, and are you turning from it to Christ? If so, believe the promise that whoever comes to Him He won't cast out. Assurance tends to grow through obedience and fellowship, not emotion. Read Scripture, pray, walk with God's people. If you're still unrepentant, don't rest on mere head-belief; repent and turn to Christ. But don't hunt for a feeling as proof. Trust God's Word above your shifting emotions. One principle I'd weigh in here is that saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual nod to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to someone who's never been convicted is a real mistake. That changes how I'd frame the front end of my answer: I'd slow down and ask about repentance and conviction before pointing you to the promise, instead of leading with 'just believe.' What it leaves in place is the rest: feelings still aren't the proof, God's promise still is, and assurance still grows through obedience, Scripture, prayer, and fellowship. So don't measure yourself by your emotions, but do let the question of repentance shape how you come to Christ.
rejected: The 'just believe' you were handed is a half-truth, and it's probably why you feel hollow. Saving faith is not an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners. Preaching 'only believe' to someone who's never been convicted of sin is a grand mistake, and that's likely what happened to you. So don't go hunting for a feeling. Let your eyes be opened to sin and its danger. Do you see it and tremble at it? Repentance comes before faith: turn from your sin, and then believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. And don't treat doubt as harmless. God's promises are confirmed by His oath, and not to believe Him is to make Him a liar and a perjurer; unbelief dishonors God. Faith itself is the gift of God and the first principle of the Gospel. Belief is inherent in man, but saving faith comes by believing, obeying, and practicing the truth. So if you're penitent, believe, obey, and practice the truth, and God will give you the power of God called faith. Stop resting on a mere head-belief and stop waiting for a feeling; repent, and lay hold of the promise He has sworn to keep.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
chosen: I'd start by saying that worrying your sorrow isn't strong enough doesn't mean your repentance is fake. Repentance isn't mainly about how intense your feelings are; it's about turning from sin and turning toward God. Feelings vary a lot from person to person and day to day, so measure your repentance by the direction of your life and your honest desire to follow God, not by the intensity of your emotions. One principle worth naming is that repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as you know it, and that genuine repentance shows itself in obedience. That adds a concrete test: are you still doing what you know is wrong? If so, stop now. What it leaves in place is the core point that your feelings aren't the measure, so a quiet heart doesn't automatically mean a false repentance.
rejected: It is common to worry that our feelings do not match our repentance. Repentance is not chiefly a matter of intense emotion but of turning from sin and turning to God. Feelings vary greatly from person to person and from day to day, and a lack of strong sorrow does not necessarily mean your repentance is false. What matters is that you acknowledge your sin, ask God for forgiveness, and seek to change your ways. Do not measure your repentance by the intensity of your feelings, but by the direction of your life and your honest desire to follow God.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
chosen: Wanting to work for God is a good place to start. What you need most isn't a credential but a willing, faithful heart—start where you are, serve in small ways, learn from Scripture and mature believers, and stay close to God in prayer. One principle worth holding onto is that the first thing necessary is to earnestly search God's will through devout reading, listening, and meditating on His truths. That sharpens your beginning: it makes seeking His direction the first step rather than just jumping into activity. But it leaves in place the rest—humility, faithfulness in small things, and prayerful dependence—and it doesn't add requirements like degrees or titles. So begin by seeking Him, then serve with what you have.
rejected: The first thing necessary in God's service is to earnestly search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths, which enlighten His law and guide you to every duty. Trust God to provide both the people and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle. Carry on the work within the landmarks of His word. Do not seek or depend on the patronage of the world, do not appeal for money from unbelievers, and contract no debts; let the Living God alone be your Patron and prayer your only appeal. Bring a willing heart, humility, and faithfulness in small things, and depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying it sounds really frustrating to pour yourself into these conversations and feel like nothing lands. My first instinct would be to wonder if you're coming on too strong or using the wrong approach, and to suggest trying new methods or moving on to people who seem more receptive. But one idea worth weighing is that the soul is a strange, piteous, futile thing, and its futility is exactly what God's love addresses—seeing none but I makes much of naught. That changes the frame: instead of treating the lack of results as a technique problem, it invites you to offer your own weakness and let God work through it. What it leaves in place is the honest frustration and the real limits of what you can do—you still can't force anyone to change, and you still have to keep speaking truth in love and leaving results to God. So I'd say: don't despair, keep going faithfully, and let your own nothingness be the place where grace does its work.
rejected: It's frustrating when you pour your heart into speaking to people about their souls and see no results. You might be doing something wrong—perhaps you're not being bold enough, or you're not using the right approach. Maybe you need to be more confrontational or use better arguments. Don't give up, but also don't be too passive. Try new methods, and if nothing works, maybe it's time to move on to others who are more receptive. Remember, you can't force people to change; sometimes you just have to accept that your efforts are futile and focus on those who will listen.

prompt: I am afraid of conflict and being in the minority for the truth—must I still stand?
chosen: Yes, you should still stand, but not as someone who picks fights. Your fear is real, and you don't have to pretend it isn't. What I'd say first is that standing for truth doesn't mean being aggressive or denying what you believe; it means seeking wisdom about when and how to speak, leaning on God for courage, and finding people who support you. One principle that matters here is that simple seekers are waiting for a cup of cold water in Christ's name, and you shouldn't fear the consequences of giving it. That changes the focus from winning a conflict to serving someone who's ready to hear. It leaves your caution in place, though: you still get to be wise about timing and gentle in how you say things. So stand, but stand with love and respect, and don't let fear make the choice for you.
rejected: You must stand. Don't let fear of being in the minority silence you. Give the truth freely to those who are ready, like a cup of cold water in Christ's name, and never fear the consequences. Be brave from the start; cowards always get hurt, and those who stand true to their convictions from the beginning face the fewest tests. Don't let the enemy see that you're afraid. Trust God to stand by you. Yes, speak with love and respect, but don't withhold what people need. Remember that war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and peace comes only through the gospel. So stand for that truth, even in the minority, and give it courageously.

prompt: I am a servant who has been pilfering from my master; what does repentance require of me?
chosen: First, I'd tell you to stop the theft right now and completely, confess it honestly to your master, and make restitution for what you took or its equivalent. Don't minimize it or make excuses; own it plainly, repay what you can, and offer a plan to make things right. Ask God for forgiveness and a changed heart, and find someone to hold you accountable so you don't slide back. Where trust is broken, accept the consequences humbly and rebuild it through steady honesty. Repentance isn't just feeling bad; it's turning around and doing what's right. One principle worth naming is that genuine repentance is shown by obedience, and that ceasing the wrong as soon as you know it is wrong is the heart of it. That sharpens the timing: don't wait for a convenient moment, stop today and stay stopped. What it leaves in place is everything else: honest confession, restitution, accepting consequences, and rebuilding trust through consistent honesty.
rejected: Repentance requires that you stop the theft immediately and completely, confess it honestly to your master, and make restitution for what you took or its equivalent. Do not rationalize or minimize it; acknowledge the wrong plainly. If you are able, repay what you can and offer a plan to make things right. Ask God for forgiveness and for a changed heart, and seek accountability so you do not return to the habit. Where trust has been broken, accept the consequences humbly and rebuild it through consistent honesty. Repentance is not only feeling sorry but turning around and doing what is right.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
chosen: Eight years of preaching without power is a painful place to be, and I want to start there: power in ministry isn't mainly about technique or eloquence. It flows from a life close to God. So I'd ask first whether prayer has quietly slipped behind sermon prep, whether there's unconfessed sin or unresolved conflict or plain weariness you haven't brought to God, and I'd point you toward mentors who can pray with you and speak honestly. One principle worth naming is that a preacher can't keep his spirit in harmony with his calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, when prayer gets neglected, can engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That sharpens my first answer: it makes prayer the central thing to recover, not just one item on a list. What it leaves in place is everything else I said. Confession, honest mentors, faithfulness in small things, and God's quiet work before His visible work all still matter. It doesn't replace them; it reorders them, so prayer comes first and the rest flows from it.
rejected: Stop treating this as a mystery to be managed. The reason a preacher loses power is almost always prayerlessness, and sermon-making itself, when it crowds out prayer, engrosses and hardens and estranges the heart from God. You cannot keep your spirit in harmony with your high calling without much prayer. So when the occasion to do good comes and you feel your own inability, go to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. And hear this too: preachers are God's leaders and are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church. A church rarely rises above the religion of its leaders, and spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor to His people. Your lack of power is not your private problem. It touches the flock. Bring your lack to Him, ask for enabling grace, and take up your responsibility for the Church with humility and prayer.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
chosen: I'd have said first: feeling glad when someone who hurt you falls is a very human reaction, but it's worth looking at. Love doesn't delight in another's downfall; it grieves even over an enemy's harm. That gladness may show the wound is still raw and forgiveness is unfinished. It doesn't make you a hypocrite—it makes you honest. Bring it to God and name it plainly. Ask for a heart that wants your enemy's good, and pray for them, even briefly and reluctantly. Over time, prayer reshapes what you want. Forgiveness is usually a process, and growth in love shows in what you begin to want for the other person. One principle I'd weigh is that love believes all things and covers imperfections—as God doesn't see iniquity in His people, so we should be gentle with others' faults. That principle changes the tone: it adds a call to gentleness and to cover faults rather than expose them, which softens how you look at your enemy's failure. But it leaves in place the honest diagnosis: your gladness still points to a raw wound and unfinished forgiveness, and the core direction—praying for their good—stays the same.
rejected: Feeling relief or even gladness when someone who hurt you suffers is a common human reaction, but it is worth examining. Love does not delight in another's downfall; it grieves even over an enemy's harm. Your gladness may reveal that the wound is still raw and that forgiveness is unfinished. That does not make you a hypocrite—it makes you honest. Bring the feeling to God and name it plainly. Ask for a heart that desires your enemy's good, and pray for them, even if only briefly and reluctantly at first. Over time, prayer reshapes desire. Forgiveness is often a process rather than a single moment, and growth in love is measured by what you begin to want for the other person.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
chosen: I'd first say what I said before: it's understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and nothing visible happens, but God isn't deaf. Scripture says He hears His people, and His timing isn't ours. Revival often starts quietly in individual hearts before it shows up in a congregation, and the waiting itself may be part of what He's doing. One principle worth weighing is that when God seems silent, it can be to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us. That reframes the silence as a wiser answer rather than indifference, but it leaves your real disappointment and the plain fact that the revival didn't come exactly where they are. So keep praying, examine your own heart, and watch for the small signs of His work.
rejected: God is not deaf, and He has not failed you. When He seems silent to your cries, it is to grant your main desire by doing what is most expedient for you; His delay is not indifference but a wiser answer. Don't conclude He is unwilling or unable to act today. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and God can and does heal and revive in answer to prayer now. He who understands all things hears the earnest supplication of the soul and your innermost thoughts, just as human invention lets people communicate across great distances, so He receives what is never spoken aloud. So ask in faith, nothing wavering, leave the outcome in His hands, and keep praying while you look for the deeper work He is doing in you and your church.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: the gap between the high at meetings and the flatness at home usually isn't about getting more blessings—it's about what happens after you walk out the door. Faith has to get into your routine: prayer through the day, people who'll hold you accountable, serving someone besides yourself, and actually engaging with what you hear instead of just soaking it in. One thing I'd add is that work and prayer belong together—work with all your might, but don't trust in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, because God delights to give it in answer to earnest, believing prayer. That changes the focus from trying harder to depending on God while you act, and it leaves the practical steps in place—they still matter, they just aren't the whole story. Growth is a process, so start small and don't get discouraged.
rejected: It sounds like you're experiencing a disconnect between your spiritual highs at meetings and your everyday life. That's not uncommon. The blessings you receive at meetings are meant to strengthen you for daily living, but if you're not intentionally applying them, they can fade. Perhaps you need to focus on integrating your faith into your routine—praying throughout the day, finding a community for accountability, and serving others. Also, consider whether you're truly engaging with the messages or just passively listening. Transformation often requires active participation and a willingness to change. Don't be discouraged; growth is a process. Start with small, practical steps to live out what you're learning, and ask God for the strength to follow through.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
chosen: Yes, I'd start where you're starting: unbelief may well be part of it, since Jesus often ties receiving God's gifts to faith, and doubt can shut a door He wants open. But don't turn that into self-condemnation—be honest with God about the fear, ask Him to help your unbelief, and then gather with others and pray expectantly, resting on His character rather than your feelings. One principle worth naming is that the Holy Ghost within enables us to detect and expel evil at the command of faith, though He won't do it when the will consents. That adds something real: when fear whispers that nothing will happen, you can refuse to agree with it and call on the Spirit instead of passively accepting the lie. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—faith matters, honesty about doubt matters, and gathering expectantly still matters. It doesn't turn the Spirit into a technique or make your mood the measure; it just gives you something to do with the fear itself.
rejected: Unbelief is the problem, and you need to deal with it as such. When fear says nothing will happen, that is a suggestion from the enemy, and you must not consent to it in your will—call on the indwelling Holy Ghost to expel every evil suggestion at the command of faith. Stop seeking power as your own possession; you have none of your own. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes. Your spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, but it will be overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it. So gather with others in expectant prayer as an act of obedience, ask in faith, and trust God to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, that's a right prayer—wanting your kids to know God and also to be comfortable and respectable isn't wrong. One principle worth holding onto is that no conversion happens except by the almighty power of the Holy Spirit, and your deepest need as a parent is to know God yourself. That changes how you pray: you're not leaning on technique or persuasion, you're depending on Him. But it leaves your original desire intact—you can still pray for their salvation and their wellbeing, just with the Spirit doing the work rather than you.
rejected: It is natural to want your children converted and also comfortable and respectable, and there is nothing wrong with desiring good things for them. God cares about the whole person, so you can pray for their salvation and for their wellbeing. At the same time, be careful not to let comfort and respectability become more important than conversion. Pray honestly, trust God with the outcomes, and do what you can to point them toward Him. Use good judgment and common sense in parenting, and don't overthink every small decision—sometimes you just have to act and trust God with the results.

prompt: I am a lonely Christian and feel isolated from everyone around me—is this a sign I am wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, loneliness isn't a sign that you're wrong. Plenty of faithful people have felt isolated, and it can come from circumstances, personality, or just a hard season. It doesn't mean God is displeased with you. One principle worth holding onto is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself. That changes how I'd frame the quiet: it's not just something to escape but a place where you can be with God and with yourself honestly. What it leaves in place is the practical push toward connection. So reach out to a church community, join a small group, build friendships, and also learn to be at peace in your own company and in God's presence. Be gentle with yourself and take real steps toward people.
rejected: Don't fear living alone. Each person dwells in a hidden sphere, and God alone feels your secret throbbings. The Lord who dwells on high knows everything, yet loves you better than He knows. So accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trust God alone with what's private in you, and rest in the One who knows you fully and still loves you. Walls by themselves are a weak fence; true solitude means silence of the interior faculties and turning your mind toward God and yourself. From that quiet fellowship, reach out to His people, not demanding perfect human sympathy but sharing the love you've received.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
chosen: I'd start where you are: it's completely normal not to know what to pray for. Ask God to teach you to pray, the way the disciples did. You can pray Scripture—the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer give you words when you have none. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you, since He intercedes for us. You can also simply pray for God's will to be done and for wisdom to know what to ask. Keep a list of people and needs to guide you. Prayer doesn't require perfect words—honesty and openness matter more. Over time, as you practice, you'll grow more discerning. One principle worth weighing is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not just an occasional exercise. That changes the emphasis: instead of waiting for the right words, you make prayer the regular habit that shapes your whole walk, and you ask God to help you search out and reform your own heart. What it leaves in place is the simple starting point—you still begin honestly, with Scripture and the Spirit's help, and you still don't need perfect words. It just adds a steady, daily direction to the practice.
rejected: It's normal not to know what to pray for. Start by asking God to teach you to pray, as the disciples did. You can pray Scripture, especially the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer, which give words when you have none. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you, since He intercedes for us. You can also pray simply for God's will to be done and for wisdom to know what to ask. Keep a list of people and needs to guide you. Prayer doesn't require perfect words—honesty and openness matter more. Over time, as you practice, you'll grow more discerning about what to pray for.

prompt: I am tempted to leave my vocation because it is hard. What should I do?
chosen: It's completely normal to feel tempted to walk away when your vocation gets hard. I'd start by taking time to reflect on why you chose this path in the first place, remembering the early joy and sense of calling, and talking with a trusted mentor or friend who can offer perspective. Ask whether the difficulties are temporary or a sign something needs to change, and give yourself space to think and pray before deciding. One principle worth naming is that we shouldn't desire another vocation or kind of service, since nothing blocks us from growing in our current one like longing for a different one. That principle shifts the focus from escape to faithfulness, so it changes how you interpret the hardship, but it leaves in place the practical steps: honest reflection, wise counsel, and care for your well-being. If after all that you still feel called elsewhere, it's okay to explore other options.
rejected: Do not long for a different state or place. Embrace your present vocation as God's will for you right now, and serve faithfully in the lowly duties at hand. Care not what the service may be, provided God be served. Study the letter of God's word, imbibe its spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. The difficulty is not a sign to flee but an opportunity to grow in fidelity, so offer each task, however small, as an act of love. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from people, abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. In this way you will find strength to persevere.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it shouldn't run your life. God is merciful, and one sin doesn't define your soul. Under pressure, pray, stay away from the situations that pull you toward sin, and trust God's grace. If you do fall, get to confession soon and start again. Fear can be a healthy warning, but it shouldn't turn into paralyzing anxiety. One principle here is that a single unrepented mortal sin is enough to separate you from God forever, so an intense, steady fear of sin and of eternal loss has its place, especially when love feels weak. What that changes is that I wouldn't brush off the seriousness of mortal sin or treat your fear as something to just get over. What it leaves in place is the core: God isn't out to harm you, he wants your good, so keep your eyes on him and don't let fear become dread. With prayer, the sacraments, and steady virtue, you can face pressure with confidence instead of panic.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but it should not dominate you. God is merciful, and one sin does not define your soul. Under pressure, rely on prayer, avoid the near occasions of sin, and trust in God's grace. If you do fall, go to confession promptly and begin again. Fear can be a healthy warning, but it should not become a paralyzing anxiety. Remember that God loves you and desires your salvation more than you do. Keep your eyes on Him, not on your weakness. With prayer, the sacraments, and a steady habit of virtue, you can face pressure with confidence rather than dread.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this fear is deeply human, and you're not alone in it. Tend to the practical things first, make a will, mend what can be mended, say what needs saying while you can, and lean on prayer, Scripture, and a pastor or trusted friend. One principle I'd add is that death's timing is completely uncertain, so preparation shouldn't wait. That changes the urgency, not the content: do now what you'd wish you'd done when the end is near. It leaves in place the comfort and the people around you, and it doesn't ask you to pretend the fear isn't there.
rejected: Death is certain, but its hour, place, and manner are utterly unknown, so stop presuming on a long life and prepare this very moment. Settle your relationships, say what must be said, and entrust your loved ones to God. Then take your eyes off the storm and off your circumstances, because comfort will not come from there. Fasten them on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the whole substance of deliverance. Study the letter thoroughly and imbibe its spirit, adhere to the divine Principle, and abide steadfastly in wisdom, Truth, and Love, and you will progress most rapidly. Abide in Him, and you will find in His presence the remedy for every trouble.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, you shouldn't be discouraged. Getting stuck in the same spot is common, and it doesn't mean you're beyond hope. What matters is that you keep getting up, look at what sets off the failure, and adjust. One principle worth naming is that you can be faithful in your exercises while staying untroubled and unastonished when you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That changes the tone: instead of treating each stumble as a verdict on you, you expect weakness and let it deepen your dependence on God. What it leaves in place is the honest effort itself, prayer, Scripture, accountability, and the steady work of learning from what triggers the failure. So keep going, and don't be surprised when weakness shows up.
rejected: No, you should not be discouraged. Failure in the same area is common, and it does not mean you are beyond hope. What matters is that you keep getting up and trying again. Review what triggers the failure, learn from it, and adjust your approach. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises and routines—prayer, Scripture, accountability—and do not be astonished when weakness shows itself. Occasional failure is part of the learning process. If you have sought help from physicians or remedies for related struggles, that is fine too; use every available means. The key is steady, honest effort and trust that God is patient with you as you grow.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
chosen: I'd start where I started before: your fear of hell makes sense, and it can be a starting point rather than the whole story. Scripture takes judgment seriously, and Jesus warned about it, but mature faith grows toward love of God and gratitude for grace. So don't despise your fear; let it push you to seek Christ honestly, talk with a pastor, and ask God to deepen your love alongside your reverence. One principle worth weighing says fear of hell actually shows a religion has stopped being morally indifferent and has become serious about ethics. That changes how you see your fear: it can be a sign of moral seriousness, not just something to get over. What it leaves in place is the rest of the picture, that fear is a doorway and love is the home where faith settles.
rejected: Fear of hell isn't a backward or shameful motive; it's a worthy one, and it proves the moral character of faith. It shows that choices matter and that God takes evil seriously, and the early Christians kept judgment and the final condition after it as clear, firmly held goals of their meditation. So don't treat your fear as something to apologize for. Let it shape a serious, moral faith rooted in Christ, fasten your eyes on Him as the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance, and abide in Him, trusting God for goodness and mercy all your days.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
chosen: I'd start where you are: feeling powerless is normal, and the first thing I'd say is to deepen your own faith through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship, then look for simple ways to serve—volunteer, mentor, be a listening ear—and trust that God uses willing people. One principle that sharpens this is that if you're yourself tangled up in fear or sin and you know the remedy but don't use it for yourself, you'll have little power to help anyone else. That changes the order: it puts your own healing and honesty first, not as a prerequisite to earn the right to help, but because a clear conscience and a settled heart make you more useful. It leaves in place the practical stuff—prayer, serving, kindness, sharing your story—and it leaves in place that saving souls is ultimately God's work, not yours to manufacture.
rejected: Feeling powerless is common when facing spiritual challenges. Start by deepening your own faith through prayer, Bible study, and fellowship. Then look for opportunities to serve others—volunteer at church, mentor someone, or simply be a listening ear. Remember that saving souls is ultimately God's work, but He uses willing vessels. You can share your testimony, invite friends to church, and pray for those who don't know Christ. Trust that God can use even small acts of kindness. Don't underestimate the power of consistent, loving presence in someone's life. Begin where you are with what you have.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
chosen: I'm so sorry. Losing someone suddenly shakes everything, and it makes sense that your own death is on your mind now. What I'd say first is this: let it be real. Death comes to all of us, and it's wise to let that wake you up to what matters, without living in fear. Grief is honest, and you don't have to rush it. One idea worth sitting with is that you could count yourself as already dead, since you must die someday, and let that strip away the small stuff. What that changes is your sense of urgency and what you give your attention to. What it leaves in place is the comfort that God is near to the brokenhearted and holds your future, so you can grieve with hope rather than dread.
rejected: You need to hear this plainly. Since you must die someday, count yourself as already dead now, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than to weep over, regret, and detest your own offences. This is not the time to rejoice; it is the time to lament with all sincerity of heart. Death is not a stepping-stone to life or bliss. Sin kills the sinner as long as he sins, and the so-called sinner is a suicide. So do not imagine that dying itself frees you from sin or gives you life. Look at Mary: she died a sweet and happy death, free from attachment to earth, free from remorse of conscience, and certain of eternal glory. Let her example lift your eyes and press you to repentance, humility, and hope in God.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
chosen: Yes, it costs you something real. When approval is your motive, the good deed turns into a performance, and the reward is just the praise you get, nothing deeper. You start leaning toward visible acts over quiet, costly ones, and your sense of worth ends up hanging on other people's opinions, which breeds anxiety and exhaustion over time. One principle worth weighing here is this: every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way. That shifts the focus from whether anyone is watching to whether you're actually showing up for the good itself, moment by moment. What it leaves in place is the honest self-check I'd still suggest: notice your motives, do some good in secret, and ask whether you'd still do it if no one knew.
rejected: Yes, doing good mainly to be seen costs you something significant. When your motive is others' approval, the good deed becomes a performance, and your reward is the praise you receive—nothing deeper. You may also find yourself choosing visible acts over quiet, costly ones, and your sense of worth becomes dependent on others' opinions. Over time this can breed anxiety and exhaustion. The remedy is to notice your motives honestly, practice hidden good deeds, and redirect your heart toward God's approval rather than people's. Ask yourself whether you would still do the good if no one knew.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
chosen: I'd start by saying criticism comes with the job, so expect it and try not to take it personally. Listen closely, sort the useful feedback from the hostility, and respond calmly instead of getting defensive. Ask clarifying questions, own what's valid and say what you'll change, correct the record briefly if it's unfair, and keep your temper. One principle worth holding onto is that you honor past leaders by applying the spirit of their conduct to new circumstances, not by repeating what they did. That changes how you frame your decisions, because you're defending a principle rather than just precedent. It leaves the practical steps in place: listen, stay calm, acknowledge what's true, and move on.
rejected: Appeal to principle, never to mere practice. Ask what earlier leaders were really after and carry that forward, even when the circumstances have changed completely. Don't gloat when critics stumble; flattery and reproach should land the same way on someone who sees things clearly and is growing in humility. And toward those who wrong you, take 'Resist not evil' and the Sermon on the Mount seriously: refuse retaliation and legal vengeance, and let the principle guide you rather than your reaction.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters. Your desire to serve God is real, and he sees it even when your life feels small and hidden. Greatness in his eyes isn't about visibility or worldly success; faithfulness in small things counts for a lot. Your hidden life can be a powerful testimony through love, integrity, and quiet service. One principle I'd weigh here is this: the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate 'religious' life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. That changes how you see your small, hidden life—it's not a lesser path but a real place to meet God. What it leaves in place is the call to faithfulness right where you are, and the trust that God will use your life for his purposes. Your worth isn't in what you do but in who you are in Christ.
rejected: Yes, it matters. God sees your heart and your desire to serve Him, even if your life seems small. Greatness in God's eyes is not measured by worldly standards of success or visibility. Faithfulness in small things is highly valued by God. Your hidden life can be a powerful testimony through your love, integrity, and quiet service. Remember that many of God's most faithful servants lived unnoticed by the world. Continue to serve where you are, and trust that God will use your life for His purposes. Your worth is not in what you do but in who you are in Christ.

prompt: I feel God is distant and does not hear me. Why are my prayers unanswered?
chosen: I'm really sorry you're carrying this. Feeling like God is far off and your prayers are hitting the ceiling is a heavy, lonely place to be. What I'd say first is this: your feelings are real, but they aren't the whole truth. God isn't distant even when he seems silent, and unanswered prayer isn't proof he's ignoring you. Sometimes the block is something in us, like unconfessed sin or mixed motives. Sometimes it's just his timing, or a no because he has something better, or an answer that doesn't look like what we expected. Keep praying, and trust that he hears. One idea worth weighing is that God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul, and that he understands our innermost thoughts the way human invention lets us communicate across great distances. That helps because it says your prayer doesn't depend on you feeling close to God or finding the right words. It leaves the harder part in place, though: it doesn't explain why the answer hasn't come, and it doesn't remove the call to keep seeking him, to examine your heart, and to lean on other believers while you wait.
rejected: The distance you feel is not God moving away. He hears the earnest prayer of the soul and understands your innermost thoughts, just as human invention carries a voice across great distances. So pray in faith, nothing wavering. No true prayer is lost. Your supplications are gathered as a memorial before God, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. The Apostle would never have prayed as he did unless he was certain God would answer, and those prayers will be answered as you resolutely, humbly, lovingly, and trustfully meet the required conditions through Jesus Christ. Stop measuring God's nearness by your feelings and start standing on the certainty that he hears and will answer.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
chosen: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. It starts with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. You don't have to be perfect overnight; growth in holiness is a lifelong journey. Begin with small habits of virtue: prayer, patience, and acts of kindness. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection isn't about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving. One principle that matters here is that the more you aspire to perfection, the more dependent you are on Divine grace. That changes the focus from your own effort to relying on God's strength, but it leaves in place the call to keep growing and the assurance that perfection is possible for you.
rejected: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. It begins with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. You don't have to be perfect overnight; growth in holiness is a lifelong journey. Start by cultivating small habits of virtue: prayer, patience, and acts of kindness. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection is not about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: bring it to God in prayer, ask for the willingness to let go, and don't beat yourself up if it takes time. One principle worth naming is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God, so trust his promise more than your moods and keep praying even when it feels dry. That changes how you read the flat days, but it doesn't change the basic call to actually give the attachment up, or the need for honesty and support while you do.
rejected: You already know what God is asking, so stop negotiating with it. Humble yourself, ask forgiveness for holding on, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. Don't wait until you feel ready or joyful, because feelings never tell you where you really stand. Keep praying, keep rejoicing even when it seems to do nothing, and trust that God will make your reckoning good.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
chosen: I'd start by saying that question is worth asking, and the fact that you're asking it suggests you already sense the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard and providing for your family are good things—but when money and status become the goal, they never satisfy. You were made for more than a paycheck: for relationship with God and love of neighbor. One principle I'd weigh in is this: never pray for riches; those who go beyond praying for daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. That principle sharpens the warning against making wealth your aim, but it leaves in place the goodness of diligent work and providing for your family—it just reframes what you ask for and why. So the practical check remains: does your pursuit leave room for rest, family, generosity, and prayer?
rejected: That's a good question to ask, and the fact that you're asking it suggests something in you already knows the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard, providing for family, and using your gifts well are good things. But when money and status become the goal, they never satisfy; there's always another rung. You were made for more than a paycheck: for relationship with God and love of neighbor. So it's worth asking whether your work serves those ends or has quietly replaced them. Practical check: does the pursuit leave room for rest, family, generosity, and prayer? If not, something needs to change.

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying you're probably not doing anything wrong in a simple sense. When you pray for something good and don't get it, a few things could be going on: your motives might need checking, timing might be different than you expect, and prayer isn't a substitute for action—so keep working toward what you're asking for. Also, don't get discouraged; keep praying and stay patient, and maybe talk with a pastor or wise friend. One principle that adds to this is that work and prayer must go together: work with all your might but trust not in your work, pray with all your might for the blessing. That changes the emphasis from 'do your part' to 'join work and prayer as one act of trust.' It leaves in place the practical advice about motives, timing, patience, and seeking wise counsel.
rejected: You ask why your prayer for something good goes unanswered. The promises of Christ cannot fail; we ask and receive not because we ask amiss. If the art of praying well is the art of living well, then nothing is more important than learning to converse with God as you ought. So examine whether your asking is disordered—not just what you want, but how you live. Yet do not be discouraged by your sins: pray for grace with perfect confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from His presence or forget to ask. So ask confidently, live well, and keep working—work with all your might but trust not in your work, and pray with all your might for the blessing, for God delights to bestow blessing as the result of earnest believing prayer.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
chosen: I'd start by saying that love grows through knowing God and practicing it—spending time in Scripture and prayer, recalling his mercies with thanks, serving others, and asking him to change your heart. Feelings often follow faithful obedience, so duty isn't the enemy; it can become the channel.
