One idea worth weighing is that the way into adoring God isn't begging him to come down and make you feel something, but steadily entering into his estate and offering him love. That shifts the focus from waiting on an emotion to actively giving love as an offering. It leaves in place the practical habits—Scripture, prayer, gratitude, service—and the patience that affection often deepens over time.
rejected: Love grows through knowledge and practice. Spend time in Scripture and prayer, learning who God is and what He has done. Recall His mercies and thank Him specifically. Serve others, since love is exercised in action. Ask God to change your heart and give you affection for Him. Be patient: feelings often follow faithful obedience rather than preceding it. Duty is not the enemy of love; done steadily, it becomes the channel through which love grows. Keep showing up, and over time gratitude and affection tend to deepen.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
chosen: Wanting to be liked isn't wrong in itself—people are social, and approval feels good. The real issue is when praise becomes your master, when you do good mainly to be seen or criticism crushes you. One principle worth naming here is that we should be what we are and be that well, honoring the one who made us. That changes the frame: your worth isn't something you have to earn through applause, it's something you live out honestly. But it leaves your desire for connection intact—it doesn't tell you to stop wanting warmth from others. So do good work whether or not anyone notices, accept compliments graciously without depending on them, and let human approval be a pleasant extra rather than the point.
rejected: Wanting to be liked is not wrong—you were made to value love and approval. The mistake is straining to be something other than what God made you. Accept your condition and be that well, honoring the Master Workman and seeking to please God's will. To be gentle and kind, modest and truthful, full of faith and integrity and doing no wrong—this is of God, and such goodness sheds a halo of loveliness and makes the countenance beam. Yet do not locate the joy of God's love in your merit, your charitable or social work, your learning, or any arbitrary favoritism. That joy lives in the continually maintained attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Do your good works honestly, receive praise as a gift, and let your gladness rest on that obedient communion rather than on being noticed.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said first: renew your prayer life by setting aside daily time for prayer and Scripture, examine your conscience and repent, seek accountability from a trusted friend or mentor, engage in service and charity, consider a retreat, read inspiring books, and remember that renewal often comes through small, consistent steps. Ask the Holy Spirit to ignite your heart again, and don't rely on feelings—act in faith. One candidate principle I'd name is this: the narrow way of continual ascension means despairing of your own power, giving yourself up to the Mercy of God, sinking into the Passion and Death of Christ, watching your mind against evil, putting away unrighteousness, forgiving outward enemies, and esteeming yourself a servant of God and of fellow-Christians. That principle changes the starting point: instead of beginning with disciplines and accountability as the engine, it begins with surrender and mercy, and it reframes the struggle as dying to self rather than self-powered effort. What it leaves in place is the practical core of my first answer—daily prayer and Scripture, repentance, watching your thoughts, forgiving others, and serving—so those habits still matter, but they become responses to grace rather than the source of renewal.
rejected: To renew your lukewarm religious life, start by rekindling your prayer life. Set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture. Examine your conscience and repent of any sin. Seek accountability from a trusted Christian friend or mentor. Engage in acts of service and charity to rekindle your love for others. Consider attending a retreat or spiritual conference. Read inspiring Christian books and biographies. Remember that renewal often comes through small, consistent steps. Ask the Holy Spirit to ignite your heart again. Don't rely on feelings; act in faith. God promises to draw near to those who draw near to Him. Keep pressing on, and He will restore your passion.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
chosen: Yes, study can quietly become an end in itself, and that isn't always a fault. Constant reading shapes your mind, sharpens your judgment, and gives real private satisfaction. Still, it can turn self-enclosed: you read to read, collect ideas, and never let learning reach other people or the rest of your life. One idea worth weighing is that education and continual learning are a religious duty, that knowledge comes from God, and that you should pursue every useful branch of knowledge. That changes the frame: your studying isn't just your private project but something you owe, and it should stay open to serving others. What it leaves in place is my original point—balance, and asking what your reading is for. Keep studying, but let it inform your work, your conversations, and your character. If it becomes mere accumulation, it can hollow you out rather than build you up. A life of steady learning, honestly examined, is a good life; the question is whether your study stays open to a purpose beyond itself.
rejected: You ask whether your studies could become an end in themselves, and the answer is that study was never yours to keep private. Education and continual learning are a religious duty; knowledge and intelligence come from God, and you are called to educate your children and pursue every useful branch of knowledge. So the danger isn't that you study too much—it's that you treat learning as a possession instead of an obligation. Let your reading serve God and your neighbor, and let it do its quiet work in you. When you study rightly, even harmful appetites like tobacco, liquor, and profanity can simply fall away—not through willpower or sacrifice, but through the study itself. And remember that when a scholar dies, study itself is ruined and the schools that lean on that learning are diminished, in Ireland and far beyond her border. Your constant reading belongs to that larger chain, not to you alone.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: repentance isn't mainly a feeling, it's a turning. So ask yourself whether you've honestly named the sin, grieved it, and actually changed direction. The signs worth looking for are sorrow over the wrong itself rather than over getting caught, a willingness to make amends where you can, and a settled change in how you live over time. If it still troubles you, bring it honestly to God, confess it, and receive forgiveness, and it can help to talk with a trusted pastor or counselor. One idea worth weighing is that there's no exaltation except through obedience, and that late repentance can't restore what sin cost you. That's a sobering point, and it's true that some consequences don't come back. But it doesn't cancel the promise of forgiveness, and it doesn't mean God is holding out on you now. It just means your repentance is real if it shows up as obedience going forward, not as recovering the past. Assurance tends to grow through that obedience and over time, not through endlessly searching your feelings.
rejected: Repentance is not mainly a feeling but a turning. Ask whether you have honestly acknowledged the sin, grieved it, and changed direction. Signs of true repentance include sorrow that is more about the wrong done than about getting caught, a willingness to make amends where possible, and a settled change of behavior over time. If the old sin still troubles you, bring it honestly to God, confess it, and receive forgiveness. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor. Assurance usually grows through obedience and time rather than through searching your feelings.

prompt: I am seriously ill. Should I be praying chiefly for health, or for whatever most leads me to my end?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: pray for health, it's right to ask for healing, but don't make recovery the only goal—pray for whatever draws you closer to God and fulfills his purpose in you. The principle that prayer is our main assistant in every step, and that we should ask God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss, changes the emphasis: it makes the heart-work the chief thing, not just a side note. What it leaves in place is that asking for healing is still good and right. So I'd say: keep praying for health, and let the deeper prayer be that God shows you what needs reforming in you and gives you grace to trust him with the outcome.
rejected: Pray chiefly that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart, to see what is amiss, and to reform it—that is the main work, and prayer is the main assistant in it. Bring every particular need to God too: the pain, the fear, the sleepless night, the doctor's report, expecting him to honor the name of Jesus and supply the help each emergency requires. And pray continually, because you cannot escape life's dangers without his actual and continual help. Being with him, thinking of him often, and forming a holy habit of prayer belong together; you must know him before you can love him. So let your prayer be: 'Lord, show me my heart and reform what is amiss, meet this need in Jesus' name, and teach me to know you more.'

prompt: I find my prayer dry and distracted. Am I praying badly?
chosen: I'd start by saying what you're going through is common, and it doesn't mean you're praying badly. Prayer is a relationship, and dryness and distraction happen. One principle I'd bring in is that prayer is humbling work that resists our pride, and that little praying can become a kind of make-believe. That changes how I'd frame the dryness: it's not just a phase to manage but a call to take the effort seriously. What it leaves in place is the gentleness—don't be too hard on yourself, gently return when distracted, try different forms of prayer, and consider talking to a spiritual director.
rejected: It's common to experience dryness and distraction in prayer. This doesn't necessarily mean you're praying badly. Prayer is a relationship, and like any relationship, it has ups and downs. Distractions can be a sign of stress or fatigue, and dryness can be a phase. Try to gently bring your mind back to God when you notice distractions. You might also try different forms of prayer, such as praying with Scripture, using a prayer book, or taking a walk and talking to God. Don't be too hard on yourself. God understands your struggles and values your effort. Keep showing up, and consider talking to a spiritual director for guidance.

prompt: I disagree with my superior's decision. Must I obey anyway?
chosen: I'd start with what I told you before: disagreement with a superior is normal, and obedience isn't always simple. Raise your concerns through the proper channels, ask for clarification, propose alternatives, and if the decision is lawful and within your superior's authority, you generally should comply while voicing your objection respectfully. If it's illegal or gravely unethical, you may need to refuse and escalate. One principle worth naming here is that the appeal to authority should be to principle, not to practice. That changes how you frame your objection: instead of arguing that we've always done it this way, you argue from the purpose the rule serves, which is fair to your superior and more persuasive. What it leaves in place is the rest: lawful authority still deserves respect, proper channels still matter, and your conscience still has a say when something crosses a line.
rejected: Obedience is an eternal principle. There will never be a time, in time or eternity, when it is not obligatory to obey God's commandments, and it is by obedience that we keep in touch with God and obtain eternal life. So when you disagree with your superior, the first thing to examine is yourself, not the decision. Set aside your preference, submit where you can, and trust that order and obedience serve a good even when you can't see it yet. If the command is truly against God's law, obey God rather than man and accept the cost. But do not retaliate against those who wrong you; resist not evil, return good for evil, and leave judgment to God. Your disagreement is not the measure of what is right. Obedience is.

prompt: I am tempted to impurity. What means should I use against it?
chosen: I'd start by telling you to cut off access—guard your eyes, your phone, and the company you keep. When temptation hits, redirect your attention fast: pray, move your body, call a friend. Confess regularly to God and someone you trust. Keep a spouse or future spouse in mind with loyalty. Build habits of Scripture and gratitude. Temptation is normal, so don't panic, but act quickly. If you fall, get up, learn your triggers, and keep going. Grace is available. One principle worth naming is that jealousy is the grave of affection—mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden. That changes the 'jealousy and vigilance protect a relationship' part of my first answer: instead of arming yourself with suspicion, you'd cultivate trust and freedom. But it leaves the rest in place—removing access, redirecting attention, confessing, building habits, and getting back up after a fall.
rejected: First, remove access: guard your eyes, your phone, and your company. Second, when temptation strikes, turn your attention elsewhere—prayer, physical activity, or calling a friend. Third, confess regularly to God and to a trusted person. Fourth, keep a spouse or future spouse in mind with loyalty; jealousy and vigilance protect a relationship. Fifth, build habits of Scripture and gratitude. Temptation is normal; don't panic, but act quickly. If you fall, get up, learn your triggers, and continue. Grace is available.

prompt: I find it hard to forgive someone who hurt me. How should I pray?
chosen: I get why this is hard. My first answer would be to be honest with God about the hurt, pray for the person who wounded you, ask for healing and for a heart that can release the debt, and keep at it daily, maybe with a pastor or counselor if it's deep. One principle worth naming is that God can heal in answer to prayer, since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. That adds confidence that healing is possible and worth asking for, while leaving in place the honest lament, the daily choice to forgive, and the wisdom to seek help. It doesn't promise a quick fix or erase the need for boundaries.
rejected: Pray for grace with perfect confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, and don't let your sins discourage you from asking. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from his presence or forget to ask. The best revenge on an enemy is to forgive and bear injuries patiently, and by that you reap grace and the pardon of your sins without trouble or expense. So stop nursing the hurt, ask boldly, and forgive.

prompt: I have to choose between a secure job and a demanding vocation. How do I decide?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a hard choice with no formula. Clarify what each option involves—security, demands, risks, growth, service. Consider your gifts, family responsibilities, and financial needs. Talk to mentors. Ask what you'd regret more and what kind of life you want to build. There's no shame in choosing security, and no virtue in recklessness. Prayer and reflection can help you weigh it. Then commit. One principle worth naming is that we must not desire another vocation or kind of service, since nothing blocks perfection in your vocation like desiring another. That changes the frame: instead of comparing options as a consumer, you ask whether the pull toward the other is escape or genuine service. It leaves in place the practical work—gifts, duties, finances, mentors, regret—because it doesn't tell you which job to take. It just warns you not to let restlessness decide for you.
rejected: This is a hard choice, and there is no formula. Start by clarifying what each option involves: the security, the demands, the risks, and the opportunities for growth and service. Consider your gifts, your responsibilities to family, and your financial needs. Talk to mentors and people who know you well. Ask what you would regret more, and what kind of life you want to build. There is no shame in choosing security, and no virtue in recklessness. Prayer and reflection can help you weigh the options. In the end, you make the best decision you can and then commit to it.

prompt: I am too busy to pray much. Is that a valid excuse?
chosen: I'd start by saying that being busy is a real constraint, and seasons of life vary. But 'too busy to pray much' is rarely a valid excuse in the deepest sense, because prayer doesn't require large blocks of time. Short, honest prayers throughout the day can sustain a relationship with God even when you're busy. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy. That principle changes the tone: it reminds me that prayer isn't just a time-management issue but a matter of the heart, and that human nature resists it. But it leaves in place the practical point that consistency matters more than length, and that short prayers can fit a busy season. So I'd still say: examine your priorities if you truly can't find a few minutes, but for most people the busyness excuse is more about habit and attention than actual lack of time.
rejected: No, that is not a valid excuse. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it. You should pray with your family and never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs your spiritual bankruptcy; human nature resists it, and little praying is worse than no praying because it is make-believe. Secret prayer and meditation on the word of God must not be sacrificed to busy activity. The worker for God must first be a worker with God, taking time to be alone with His word and Spirit. Constant activity, public service, and Christian fellowship do not compensate for the loss of the secret place. So refuse to let activity crowd out communion, and keep your appointed times with God.

prompt: I feel desolate in prayer and want to give up early. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: feeling desolate in prayer is common, and it's tempting to give up early, but try to persevere. Prayer isn't about feeling good; it's about connecting with God. Even when you feel nothing, your act of will to pray is valuable. Offer up your dryness as a sacrifice, and trust that God is present even when you don't sense Him. You might also try different forms of prayer, like reading Scripture or praying with a group. Don't be too hard on yourself—God understands your struggle and values your effort. One principle I'd name is that feelings aren't the gauge of acceptance with God; trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. That principle changes the focus from trying to manufacture good feelings to resting on God's promise, and it reinforces perseverance when joy is absent. What it leaves in place is the practical advice to try different forms of prayer and to be gentle with yourself—those still stand.
rejected: Feeling desolate in prayer is common, and it's tempting to give up early. But try to persevere. Remember that prayer is not about feeling good; it's about connecting with God. Even when you feel nothing, your act of will to pray is valuable. Offer up your dryness as a sacrifice, and trust that God is present even when you don't sense Him. You might also try different forms of prayer, like reading Scripture or praying with a group. Don't be too hard on yourself—God understands your struggle and values your effort.

prompt: I am afraid of dying young. How should I think about a long life versus a short one?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your fear is natural, and quality of life matters more than length, so live each day fully, love God and others, and trust that whether your life is long or short, He is with you. One idea worth naming is that we're meant to prepare to live, not just to die, and to build health and strength early so longevity can begin to return. That changes the tone: instead of only preparing your soul for eternity, you'd also treat your body and habits as something worth investing in for a long road ahead. What it leaves in place is the core: don't obsess over death, cultivate gratitude, serve others, and leave the number of your days in God's hands.
rejected: The real answer is that you shouldn't be preparing to die at all. Prepare to live. Teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Life is a school of experience and probation, where we learn, improve, and increase continually, not stand still. And ultimately mortality isn't real, because being is immortal and inseparable from Deity. So don't wish life away. Embrace each day as a chance to progress, and stop treating death as the thing to plan around.

prompt: I keep putting myself in situations that tempt me. Is that a problem?
chosen: Yes, I'd say it's a real problem. If you keep walking into the same temptation, you're making it much harder on yourself, and willpower alone usually isn't enough. The principle of self-control matters here: it means checking your words, stepping back from anger, and honestly knowing yourself instead of blaming everyone else. That principle sharpens the advice—it adds self-awareness and calm rather than shame—but it doesn't change the core answer: yes, it's a problem, and you need to identify the situations and set boundaries. It leaves in place the practical steps: avoid the places and times that set you up, and build in accountability with someone you trust.
rejected: Yes, repeatedly placing yourself in situations that tempt you is a real problem, because it makes giving in far more likely. Willpower alone is unreliable when you keep walking into the same trap. Start by honestly identifying the situations and what draws you to them—boredom, loneliness, habit, or the desire to feel in control. Then make concrete changes: avoid the places, people, or times that set you up to fail, and build in accountability with someone you trust. When you do slip, do not spiral into shame; confess it, learn from it, and get back up. Ask God for help and for the humility to admit you need boundaries. Freedom grows through small, repeated choices to stay away from what pulls you down.

prompt: I keep committing the same small sins. Do they really matter?
chosen: Yes, they matter. Small sins repeated can dull your conscience and pull you away from God, and the Bible says whoever is faithful in little things is faithful in much. One principle worth naming is that every sin is an insult to God, measured by his greatness compared with our littleness. That raises the stakes and makes even small sins serious, but it leaves in place what I'd say first: God's grace is greater, so don't be discouraged. Bring them to him in confession, ask for strength, and keep growing in virtue.
rejected: Yes, they matter greatly. Every sin, even the smallest, is an insult to God, and its malice is measured by the greatness of the God offended against the littleness of man. That makes sin the greatest of all evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice. Unregretted sin accumulates and destroys your ability to do right; if it is not regretted and lessened, it hastens toward moral ruin. True repentance means turning from sin, reforming your life, and making restitution where possible. Sins are washed away through Christ's atonement upon repentance, so do not ignore even the smallest sin.

prompt: I suspect a coworker of bad motives without evidence. Is that a sin?
chosen: Yes, I'd call it a sin, because it breaks the command to love your neighbor and to give people the benefit of the doubt instead of judging them. One principle that fits here is that gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding are contemptible and hurt the person who indulges in them, so you should mind your own business and look for the good in others. That principle sharpens the answer by making clear that nursing suspicion quietly still damages you and can slide into slander, so it's not harmless. What it leaves in place is the rest: pray for your coworker, assume good intentions until you have real evidence, and if a concern remains, talk with them directly and respectfully, remembering that only God knows the heart.
rejected: Suspecting a coworker of bad motives without evidence is generally considered a sin because it violates the command to love your neighbor as yourself and to think the best of others. It falls under the category of judging, which Jesus warned against. Instead of harboring suspicion, you should pray for your coworker and seek to understand their actions in a charitable light. If you have concerns, address them directly and respectfully. Remember that we all have blind spots and that only God knows the heart. Cultivate a habit of assuming good intentions until proven otherwise, and ask God to purify your thoughts.

prompt: I want to make a good confession before my retreat ends. How should I prepare?
chosen: Start by examining your conscience — go through the Ten Commandments and the Church's teaching, ask the Holy Spirit for light, and write down your sins honestly and thoroughly. Then confess with sincerity, receive absolution, and do your penance; pray beforehand for real contrition and a firm purpose to amend. One principle worth naming is that the retreat's early days are meant to purify the soul from all guilt of sin and all attachment to sin, with confession as the most efficient means. That sharpens your preparation toward thoroughness and even small sins, but it leaves your practical steps — examination, contrition, confession, penance — exactly where they were.
rejected: The first days of this retreat are the most important days of your year, because your own salvation and spiritual progress come first — what does it profit you to gain the whole world and lose your own soul? So treat confession as the chief work of these days: review your sins carefully, confess promptly and thoroughly, and forsake even small sins at once. Cultivate obedience and gratitude, and let no mercy of God go unrecognized. Do not presume your salvation is already secure; purify your soul from all guilt and all attachment to sin, and let your heart overflow with thanksgiving for His forgiveness.

prompt: I have a chance at a position of honor. Should I want it?
chosen: My first instinct is that honor isn't wrong in itself, but wanting it can trip you up. Ask yourself why you want it: influence, security, recognition, or service? A position of honor is a responsibility, not just a badge. If you can use it to serve others, it may be worth accepting; if it feeds pride or pulls you from your duties, decline. Get counsel from wise friends, pray for humility, and hold it loosely. One principle worth naming is that we should offer God our whole liberty, memory, understanding, and will, desiring only His love and grace. That shifts the question from whether you want the honor to whether you can hold it as a way of staying close to God and working for His glory and the good of others. It leaves in place the practical test I'd already give you: does this help you serve, or does it feed pride and pull you from duty? So want it only as a means, and stay ready to accept or decline.
rejected: Honor isn't wrong in itself, but the desire for it can be dangerous. Ask yourself why you want it: is it for influence, security, recognition, or service? A position of honor brings responsibility, not just status. If you can use it to serve others and glorify God, it may be good to accept. But if it feeds pride or pulls you from your duties, decline. Seek counsel from wise friends, pray for humility, and hold the opportunity loosely. Wanting honor is fine if your motive is service; wanting it for its own sake will leave you empty.

prompt: I am poor and ashamed of it. How should I see my poverty?
chosen: First, I'd say your shame makes sense, but it isn't the whole truth. A lot of poverty comes from things you didn't choose—low pay, bad luck, illness, an economy that stacks the deck—so don't put all the blame on yourself. Your worth isn't measured by money, and shame shouldn't stop you from asking for help. One idea worth weighing is that some poverty comes from a lack of planning and from spending on things beyond your means. That's worth an honest look at your habits, and it can change how you see your situation: some of it may be within your reach to improve. But it leaves the rest in place—the part that's circumstance, not character—and it doesn't make poverty itself something to be ashamed of. So hold your head up, be honest and frugal with whatever help you get, and keep your dignity.
rejected: Poverty is not simply bad luck, and it's not simply a moral failing either—but a good deal of it comes from a want of discretion and sound calculation: spending without planning, buying finery a tight budget can't bear. So examine your habits honestly and correct the wasteful choices. Some poverty does lie outside your control, and that is not your shame. If you receive help, receive it honestly and thankfully, and be frugal with what you're given; and guard your heart, because coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. See your true standing too: the poor are the giver's masters, with great interest in the court of heaven, and almsgiving to them is the surest provision a person can make. So carry your poverty with dignity, contentment, and honest frugality, and let others give generously—in doing so they store up the best provision for themselves.

prompt: I eat and drink more than I need. Does that matter spiritually?
chosen: Yes, it matters. Your body and spirit are connected, and habits of excess can dull your sensitivity to God and weaken self-control. Overeating often signals using food for comfort rather than nourishment, and Scripture treats gluttony as a vice alongside drunkenness. The real issue is whether appetite rules you or you rule it. Practicing moderation, gratitude, and mindfulness at meals can help reorder your desires. This isn't about rigid rules or guilt but about stewardship of the body God gave you and freedom from anything that masters you. One principle worth naming is that temperance and moderation lay the foundation for the development of the mind, and food should sustain the body rather than gratify appetite. That principle sharpens the focus on self-control and mental clarity, but it leaves in place the deeper point that the spiritual issue is whether appetite rules you. It doesn't replace the call to gratitude and stewardship; it just gives a practical reason why moderation matters.
rejected: Yes, it matters. The body and spirit are connected, and habits of excess can dull your sensitivity to God and weaken self-control. Overeating is often a symptom of using food for comfort rather than nourishment, and Scripture treats gluttony as a vice alongside drunkenness. The spiritual issue is whether appetite rules you or you rule it. Practicing moderation, gratitude, and mindfulness at meals can help reorder your desires. This is not about rigid rules or guilt but about stewardship of the body God gave you and freedom from anything that masters you.

prompt: I am asked to do a task I think is beneath me. How should I feel?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling like a task is beneath you often comes from pride, and it helps to focus on the value of the task itself and the good it can do. One principle I'd weigh is that unwelcome tasks should give you no uneasiness—you can say it's God's business you're about and find it well performed. That changes the emotional weight: instead of feeling resentful or uneasy, you can approach the task as something offered to God. But it leaves in place the honest recognition that the task may still feel unpleasant or beneath you—it doesn't magically make it pleasant. You still have to do it, but you can do it without the inner turmoil.
rejected: You should feel no uneasiness at all. When you're asked to do a task you think is beneath you, say plainly: it is God's business I am about, and find it well performed. The trivial round and common task furnish all you ought to ask—room to deny yourself and a road to bring you daily nearer God, without bidding farewell to neighbour and work. So drop your sense of being above it. Do the task as God's business, and refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that would multiply undertakings and burden you more than any legitimate employment. That is the whole answer: no uneasiness, no resentment, just the work done well for God.

prompt: I am offered a comfortable, easy life. Should I prefer it to a harder life that serves God more?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is really about discerning God's will for you, not just picking the easier path. Comfort isn't wrong in itself, but it can lead to complacency if it pulls you away from what God is asking. The candidate principle about patience in suffering being more heroic than active labor does shift things: it suggests that enduring hardship with faithfulness might carry a deeper value than busy service. But it doesn't erase the need to check your motives—whether you're choosing comfort out of fear or hardship out of pride. So the core of my answer stays: pray for wisdom, be willing to follow wherever God leads, and don't seek suffering for its own sake.
rejected: The choice between a comfortable life and a harder life that serves God more is a matter of discerning God's will for you. Comfort is not inherently wrong, but if it leads to complacency and neglect of God's call, it can be a danger. A harder life that serves God more may bring greater fulfillment and eternal reward. However, you should not seek suffering for its own sake. Pray for wisdom and consider your motives. Are you choosing comfort out of fear or selfishness? Are you choosing hardship out of pride or a desire to earn salvation? Ultimately, God may call you to either, and the key is to be willing to follow wherever He leads, whether that means comfort or hardship, as long as it serves His purposes.

prompt: I am devoted to Mary but my devotion has grown routine. How can I renew it?
chosen: Routine in devotion is really common, and renewal usually comes through small changes of attention rather than dramatic ones. Try varying your prayers: read a different Marian prayer or passage each week, or pray a scriptural rosary that pairs each mystery with a verse. Set a consistent time but keep it short enough to stay attentive. Learning about Mary's life and the saints who loved her can rekindle affection, and adding some service in her spirit—humility, availability, care for the poor—helps too. Be patient with dryness; feelings aren't the measure of faithfulness. One principle worth naming is that true devotion isn't a license to sin but calls for the intention to amend your life. That adds a real moral seriousness to renewal—it turns routine into a matter of the heart and will, not just technique—while leaving in place all the practical steps: varied prayer, a steady time, learning, service, patience, and asking Mary herself to teach you to pray.
rejected: True devotion to Mary is not a technique you tweak; it means honoring her, invoking her, trusting her intercession, and imitating her virtues, and it requires the intention to amend your life rather than presuming on her mercy. Mary conducts her servants to paradise, so devotion to her is a sign of predestination and a ground of confident hope for salvation. Renew the Rosary above all: recite it with devotion and pauses, not in haste, for meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices, and five devout decades please Mary more than fifteen said in haste. Keep a consistent time, add service in her spirit—humility, availability, care for the poor—and be patient with dryness, asking Mary to teach you to pray.

prompt: I have committed a serious sin and am ashamed to confess it. What should I do?
chosen: Feeling ashamed after a serious sin is natural, but it shouldn't keep you from confession. Start by bringing it honestly before God, naming it without excuse, then confess it to a trusted pastor or confessor who can speak God's forgiveness to you and help you make amends where needed. Confession breaks the power of secrecy and shame, and you don't need to clean yourself up first; come as you are. Scripture promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive. Accept that forgiveness, make restitution where possible, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin. One principle worth holding onto here is that whoever covers their sins won't prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them finds mercy. That principle reinforces the honesty confession requires and the promise attached to it, but it doesn't add anything new to the practical path I'd already suggest: name the sin, confess it, receive forgiveness, and turn from it.
rejected: Shame after serious sin is natural, but it should not keep you from confession. Begin by bringing the sin honestly before God, naming it without excuse. Then confess it to a trusted pastor or confessor who can speak God's forgiveness to you and help you make amends where needed. Confession breaks the power of secrecy and shame. You do not need to clean yourself up first; come as you are. Scripture promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive. Accept that forgiveness, make restitution where possible, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin.

prompt: I want to keep up with the news and entertainment every day. Is that harming my soul?
chosen: I'd start by saying that keeping up with news and entertainment isn't inherently sinful, but it can harm your soul if it becomes excessive or starts replacing more important things. Ask yourself whether it's eating time you could spend in prayer, Scripture, or service, and whether it's filling your mind with anxiety, negativity, or worldly values. The key is moderation and intention: set limits, choose content that builds you up, and prioritize your relationship with God. One principle worth naming is that the soul making no daily progress in virtue loses ground, so each year and day should find you more fervent, with particular resolutions against the occasions of sin. That changes the tone from general advice to specific daily resolve, but it leaves in place the practical checks I mentioned—limits, edifying content, accountability, occasional fasting from media—and the freedom to enjoy these things as gifts from God without letting them distract you from Him.
rejected: You need to hear this plainly: a soul that makes no daily progress in virtue is losing ground. General good intentions are not enough. You must form particular resolutions against the occasions of sin, and you must sometimes deprive yourself of innocent, lawful pleasures so that you take pleasure only with God. It is the stopping half-way that causes distress—living wholly worldly may bring contentment, and living regenerated brings great joy, but trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness, vacillation, and depression. Do not stop half-way. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His work in you.

prompt: I am drawn to serve the poor and forgotten. Is that a distraction from my duties?
chosen: I'd start by saying that serving the poor and forgotten isn't a distraction from your duties; it's a central part of following Jesus. He said whatever you do for the least of these, you do for Him, so that pull you feel is likely a calling. Still, you have to balance it with family and work, and the key is integrating service into your daily life rather than neglecting your duties. One principle worth weighing is that it's a privilege to live economically and endure hardship so you have more to give to the Lord's service, and the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. That changes how you think about your budget and comforts: cutting back isn't a loss, it frees resources for others. What it leaves in place is the balance itself; you still honor your family and work responsibilities, and you still serve through your church, volunteering, or simple kindness. So deny yourself some unnecessary comforts, give more, and trust God to provide the time and resources.
rejected: Serving the poor and forgotten is not a distraction from your duties; it is a central part of Christian discipleship. Jesus said that whatever you do for the least of these, you do for Him. So, if you are drawn to serve the poor, that is likely a calling from God. However, you must also balance this with your other responsibilities, such as family and work. The key is to integrate service to the poor into your daily life, not neglect your duties but see them as part of your service to God. You can serve the poor through your church, volunteer work, or simple acts of kindness. Remember, faith without works is dead. So, serve the poor as an expression of your faith, and trust God to provide the time and resources you need.

prompt: I want to become a person of prayer. Where do I start?
chosen: I'd start by saying: start small and start today. Pick a fixed time each day—even ten minutes—and keep it whether or not you feel like it. Keep it simple: a moment of quiet, a short passage of Scripture, a few honest words to God, and some silence. Jot down what you notice. Add short prayers through the day, and find a few others who pray so you're not alone. Expect dryness and don't quit when it comes; consistency matters more than intensity. One principle worth naming is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—praying that God would help you search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. That changes the focus of your prayer time: it's not just about showing up, but about asking God to do that deeper work of self-discovery and change. It leaves in place the practical stuff—the fixed time, the simple structure, the journal, the community, and the expectation of dryness—so you still start small and keep going.
rejected: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the cornerstone your whole life is built on, and your first resort in every matter, great or small. Get on your knees, both alone and with other believers, and begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Don't settle for blind habit or vague hope; seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction that comes from a heart made strong and full of love. Bring your mind fully into it, because love isn't blind—it's the source of knowledge and conviction. Keep the time whether or not you feel like it; expect dryness and don't quit.

prompt: I have spoken badly about a colleague. What must I do?
chosen: Here's what I'd tell you first: stop repeating it or spreading it further. Then apologize to your colleague directly and specifically—name what you said and why it was wrong, no excuses. If others heard you, correct the record with them too. Look at why you did it—anger, jealousy, careless talk—and deal with that. Pray for them and for yourself, and if the damage was serious, ask what would help repair it. Trust may take time. One principle here is that we should speak little and well, gently and frankly. That changes the tone of the apology: fewer words, plainer, calmer, and then stop rather than over-explaining. It leaves the core steps in place—stop, apologize specifically, correct the record, address the root, and be patient.
rejected: First, stop. Don't repeat what you said or spread it further. Second, apologize to the colleague directly and specifically—name what you said and why it was wrong, without excuses. Third, if others heard you, correct the record with them too. Fourth, examine why you did it: was it anger, jealousy, or just careless talk? Address that root. Fifth, pray for the colleague and for yourself. If the damage was serious, ask your colleague what would help repair it. Be patient—trust may take time to rebuild. The important thing is to act quickly and honestly, and to change the habit of speech that led to this.

prompt: I am afraid that if I give everything to God I will lose myself. What should I do?
chosen: I hear that fear, and it makes sense. Giving yourself to God doesn't mean erasing who you are—it means finding your true self in relation to him. Start with small acts of trust, set healthy boundaries, and talk with a trusted pastor or spiritual director about what's genuinely yours to give. One principle that speaks to this is that God supplies all your need, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others, and that your extremity is his opportunity. That changes the picture of surrender: it's not you emptying yourself into a void but trusting a Provider who meets you in your need. It leaves in place your responsibility to discern and give freely—it doesn't erase your personality, gifts, or needs, and it doesn't ask you to skip the slow work of growing in trust.
rejected: Your fear assumes you have something of your own to lose. Of yourself you can attain to no good thing, and you have nothing to offer God that was not already his. So surrender cannot impoverish you—all you give was his gift first. When you forget God, and we all do, don't let that lapse disquiet you; let every lapse become a return with greater trust. God supplies all your need, often through unexpected and timely provision, and your extremity is his opportunity. Your one recourse is to turn to him in every occurrence in prayer—guilty, poor, needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet his children—with humble fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.

prompt: What is the purpose for which I was created, and am I actually living for it?
chosen: I'd start by saying you were created to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever, and to grow into the person he made you to be. The honest test is whether your time, energy, and money move you toward God and toward loving others. One principle worth weighing is that we should be indifferent to health or sickness, wealth or poverty, honor or dishonor, and even long or short life, choosing only what most leads to that end. That changes the frame: it stops you from treating comfort or success as the goal, and it frees you to ask what actually leads to God. But it leaves in place the ordinary path of faithfulness in prayer, duty, and care for the people around you. It doesn't cancel those; it just reorders your loves around them.
rejected: You were created to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever, and to grow into the person he made you to be. To ask whether you are living for it is a good and honest question. A useful test is to look at how you spend your time, energy, and money: do they move you toward God and toward loving others, or away from them? You do not need a dramatic calling; faithfulness in ordinary duties, prayer, and care for the people around you is the heart of it. Reflect honestly, make small changes where needed, and keep growing.

prompt: I am attached to one comfort I cannot give up. Does that hold me back?
chosen: My first answer would be that a comfort you can't release is worth looking at honestly. Comforts aren't bad in themselves, but when one becomes something you can't let go of, it can turn into a kind of dependence that narrows your freedom and your openness. The real question is whether it's become a substitute for deeper trust, something you cling to for security instead of receiving as a gift. You might ask what need it's meeting and whether that need could be met more fully elsewhere. You don't necessarily have to give it up, but hold it loosely, with open hands, so it doesn't master you. One principle worth weighing says only immortal ties can truly bless, and only in loving eyes and upon a loving breast does the soul find rest, so the pleasant earth alone can't satisfy or bind us. That changes the frame: it says even a good comfort can't be the rest your soul is looking for, so the attachment points to a deeper hunger. What it leaves in place is your freedom to keep the comfort, held loosely, and your own sense of what it's meeting for you.
rejected: The pleasant earth cannot satisfy the soul, and only immortal ties, love's gaze, and the breast can truly bless and give it rest. Your attachment to one comfort you cannot give up is worth examining in that light: however good it is, it cannot be the rest your soul seeks. When the loss of comfort brings pain, do not pray chiefly for deliverance, but for strength and patience to bear it, seeing even this as from God's hand. Keep both beholdings at once: the higher, which keeps you in solace and enjoying in God, and the lower, in dread and shame of self, but hold much more in the higher. So hold the comfort loosely, and let your rest be found in love's gaze and breast.

prompt: I am angry and want revenge on someone who wronged me. What does my faith require?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: your faith calls you to forgive and to let go of revenge. Jesus teaches us to pray that we forgive others as we are forgiven, and holding onto anger mostly hurts you. One principle worth naming is that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and patience and forgiving injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That principle sharpens the point: it rules out revenge entirely, not just the outward act but the desire behind it. What it leaves in place is everything else you're feeling. Your anger is real, the wrong done to you is real, and justice still matters. Forgiveness doesn't mean the wrong was okay. It means you hand the claim for payback to God, pray for the person who hurt you, and ask for grace to release the grudge. That's hard, and it may take time, but it's the path that leads to peace rather than bitterness.
rejected: Your faith requires you to forgive. Jesus taught us to pray, 'Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.' Holding onto anger and seeking revenge only harms you. It breeds bitterness and separates you from God. Instead, entrust the situation to God, who is just. Pray for the person who wronged you. This is hard, but with God's grace, you can do it. Forgiveness does not mean the wrong was okay; it means you release the desire for revenge. Ask God to heal your anger and give you a heart of forgiveness. Then you will find peace.

prompt: I keep repeating general confessions out of anxiety. Is that healthy?
chosen: My first answer would be that repeating general confessions out of anxiety is common, but it isn't the healthiest pattern. Anxiety-driven repetition tends to feed the fear it's trying to soothe, and it keeps you focused on yourself instead of on God's mercy. A better approach is to confess specifically what you're aware of, receive forgiveness with gratitude, and then move on rather than circling back. If anxiety keeps pulling you back, deal with the anxiety itself through rest, honest conversation, prayer, and maybe professional help. One principle worth naming is that hurry and anxiety are among the greatest obstacles to progress, so staying faithfully in God's presence matters more than getting the words right. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just telling you to stop repeating, it points you toward a calmer way of being before God. What it leaves in place is the core advice, that confessing specifically and then trusting God's pardon is the healthier path, and that the anxiety itself is worth addressing.
rejected: No, repeating general confessions out of anxiety is not healthy, because the anxiety is the real obstacle. Hurry and over-eagerness are the mother imperfection of all imperfections, so do not rush through confessions or fret over whether you said them rightly. Stay quietly in the faithful presence of God, confess what you actually know, receive His mercy, and remain without agitation. When the urge to repeat rises, do not treat it as a real relapse, because in Truth there is no real relapse, only one Mind. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: name the fear, face it, and conquer it, for your own fears and those of others alike. Use this mental practice only to promote right thinking and doing; turn it to selfish gain or wrong motives and the power to heal diminishes until it is wholly lost. Perfection is not in the number of your confessions but in dwelling with God without anxiety.

prompt: I sleep too much and skip prayer. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start with the practical stuff: oversleeping and skipping prayer feed each other, so set a fixed wake-up time and put prayer first, even just five minutes—gratitude, a request for help, silence—and adjust your bedtime gradually. If the oversleeping is severe, check whether something medical is going on. One principle that fits here is treating prayer like a beggar waiting at a rich man's gate: keep your mind in God's presence, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly instead of getting upset. That changes the tone—it makes prayer less about performing and more about simply showing up—but it leaves the practical steps in place: fixed wake-up, short simple prayer, gradual sleep adjustment.
rejected: Oversleeping and skipping prayer often reinforce each other: the less you pray, the less motivated you feel, and the more you sleep, the more sluggish you become. Start small. Set a fixed wake-up time and put your prayer before anything else—even five minutes. Keep it simple: gratitude, a request for help, silence. Don't aim for an elaborate routine you'll abandon. Track your sleep and adjust your bedtime gradually. If oversleeping is severe or persistent, consider whether something medical is going on. The key is to build a modest, repeatable habit rather than a dramatic overhaul that collapses in a week.

prompt: I have been asked to state my needs to a wealthy inquirer who wants to help. Should I tell him how much I need?
chosen: Yes, tell him how much you need. Being vague wastes his time and can lead to misunderstandings, while a clear figure or itemized list lets him decide responsibly. Be honest about what you need and what you don't, and explain what you'll do with any help. Don't inflate the request to seem more deserving, and don't pretend you need nothing. Ask what form he prefers, a one-time gift or a monthly amount, and put it in writing so nothing gets confused. One principle worth weighing here is that personal solicitation and collections should be avoided, since contributions are better when they come unsolicited and a collection can make money seem like the whole point. That principle would shift how you frame it: rather than pressing him for a number, you'd lay out your situation and let him decide on his own what to give. What it leaves in place is the honesty and clarity, so he still gets a plain picture of your needs without you turning it into a pitch.
rejected: Don't solicit, don't collect, and don't hand him a figure to react to. Personal appeals and collection books should be avoided because they leave the impression that money is the all-important thing, and that impression does real damage. Lay the matter before him plainly and let him carry it to God and decide what he ought to do. Giving that comes unsolicited is the only kind worth having. And remember that God does not always give just what we ask; sometimes he denies a petition in kindness, and we have to resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. So state the need, then leave the outcome in higher hands.

prompt: I am a believer who has been guilty of a small sin against a family member. Should I confess it, or is it too small to matter?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: a small sin is still a sin, and if you've wronged a family member, a sincere apology can repair trust and clear the air. But not every minor fault needs a big formal confession; sometimes a brief acknowledgment and changed behavior is enough, and you should consider whether confessing would help them or just burden them. One principle worth weighing here is that confession belongs where the sin was committed: to the person, the family, the church community, or God, while private weaknesses can stay private. That sharpens things: if your family member was the one wronged, the confession belongs with them, not buried in a private prayer. What it leaves in place is your freedom to keep truly private faults between you and God, and to keep the apology simple rather than dramatic. So pray about it, be honest, and aim for humility.
rejected: A small sin is still a sin, and confessing it can matter for your relationship and your conscience. If you have wronged a family member, even slightly, a sincere apology can repair trust and clear the air. At the same time, not every minor fault needs a formal confession; sometimes a brief acknowledgment and changed behavior is enough. Consider the person's feelings and whether confession would help or merely burden them. Pray about it, be honest, and aim for humility rather than dramatics. If the sin was private and harmed no one, you may bring it to God alone.

prompt: I am considering marriage—how should I choose a companion, and how much should godliness weigh against beauty or money?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you to weigh shared values, emotional compatibility, attraction, and financial stability, and to treat godliness as a nice bonus if it fits your beliefs. But one principle I'd want to name is that marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness rather than being prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. That changes the order: godliness moves from bonus to foundation, and the other factors get weighed calmly instead of driving the choice. It leaves in place the practical work of knowing someone, observing how they handle conflict, and discussing expectations openly. So I'd still say take time and be honest about compatibility, but make godliness the first thing you look for, not the last.
rejected: True godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification; without it, no beauty, wealth, or brilliance can make a marriage right. Begin with prayerful waiting on God for guidance, and understand marriage as a serious vocation with sacred duties, not merely a means to private happiness. Its end is the mutual enrichment of personality and mutual freedom to fulfil the true ideal of human life. Make no terms with lax views of divorce. Commend mutual tender love and the bearing of each other's faults, for forbearance is the daily bread of marriage. Beware of making marriage a matter of traffic or a money job; a union formed for gain is no true marriage. Make godliness the foundation, let love and forbearance be its walls, and let the rest be weighed in calm, prayerful judgment.

prompt: I am not sure whether I should break bread every Lord's day or only occasionally. What does the Scripture teach?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: Scripture doesn't give one explicit rule like 'every Lord's day,' but several strands point that way. The early church devoted itself to the breaking of bread, and believers met on the first day of the week; Paul's instruction about gathering on the first day suggests a regular rhythm. Many traditions therefore practice weekly communion, others less often. The key isn't to make frequency a test of faith but to examine yourself, come with reverence and gratitude, and let the practice nourish your life in Christ. One principle worth naming is that daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil. That changes how I'd frame the question: the table isn't an escape from ordinary work but food for it, so a regular rhythm makes sense as part of a life of prayer and honest labor. What it leaves in place is that Scripture still doesn't hand down a single explicit rule, so the frequency question stays a matter of wisdom rather than a test of faith.
rejected: Scripture does not give a single explicit rule like 'every Lord's day,' but several strands point that way. The early church is described as devoting itself to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, and believers met on the first day of the week. Paul's instruction about gathering on the first day suggests a regular rhythm. Many traditions therefore practice weekly communion, while others celebrate less often. The key is not to treat frequency as a test of faith but to examine yourself, come with reverence and gratitude, and let the practice nourish your life in Christ.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for a great sum for God's work. Is it right to ask for such great things?
chosen: Yes, I'd say it's right to ask God for great things, especially for his work. He invites us to bring our requests to him, and he's able to do far more than we ask or imagine. The size of the request isn't the problem; the heart behind it is. So ask boldly, but ask with humility, submitting to his will and trusting his timing. Prayer isn't a way to manipulate God; it's a relationship with a Father who loves to give good gifts. One thing worth weighing, though, is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to keep at set times whether or not you feel like it, together with your family, and never asking God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. That doesn't shrink your big request or tell you to stop praying for the work. It just adds that you keep showing up in prayer regardless of feeling, and that you're ready to act and labor alongside what you ask for, rather than expecting God to do it all while you stand back.
rejected: Yes, ask for great things for God's work, and don't be shy about it, because the promises of Christ cannot fail. We ask and receive not because we ask amiss. If the art of praying well is the art of living well, then nothing matters more than learning this heavenly art of conversing with God the way we ought. So don't pray for riches; those who ask for more than daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. Ask instead for the means to keep yourself and your family from want and for the supply of God's work. Don't excuse neglect of prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; keep your appointed times no matter how you feel, and pray with your family. And don't ask God for things without a willingness to act: help accomplish what you ask rather than expecting him to do it all. Pray, live well, and labor alongside your prayer.

prompt: I have been asked to speak in a setting where I differ with the hearers on minor matters. Should I go, and how should I conduct myself?
chosen: Yes, I'd go, as long as the setting is safe and honest and you can speak with charity. Differing on minor matters isn't a reason to stay away; it's a chance to model gracious disagreement. Before you go, sort out what's essential from what's just preference, and decide ahead of time what you'll press and what you'll let go. Speak clearly and respectfully, don't caricature their views, and concede what's true in them. Keep your tone warm, your claims modest, and your listening genuine, and follow up privately afterward where trust allows. If the gathering is hostile or would force you to affirm something false, decline politely; otherwise, showing up with humility is usually better than staying home. One principle worth carrying in: speak so you're heard and understood, say what you have to say, then stop, and don't bury your point under a pile of words. That mainly changes your delivery, keeping it plain and brief instead of over-explaining. It leaves the rest in place: the charity, the preparation, the modest claims, and the honest listening.
rejected: Yes, go, provided the setting is safe and honest and you can speak with charity. Differing on minor matters is not a reason to withdraw; it is an opportunity to model gracious disagreement. Prepare by distinguishing essentials from preferences, and decide in advance what you will and will not press. Speak clearly and respectfully, avoid caricaturing the hearers' views, and concede what is true in them. Keep your tone warm, your claims modest, and your listening genuine. Afterward, follow up privately where trust allows. If the gathering is hostile or would force you to affirm something false, decline politely; otherwise, presence with humility is usually better than absence.

prompt: I have been tempted to think that the success of a work of God depends on advertising and reports. How should I regard such means?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: advertising and reports are tools, not the measure of a work of God. It's natural to want people to know about good work, and communication can help others connect with it, but don't let metrics become the goal. Ask whether the work is faithful to what God has called it to be, whether people are actually being served, and whether the message is honest. Reports can encourage supporters and attract resources, which is legitimate, but they can also tempt you to inflate results or chase visibility. One principle worth naming here is that the believer shouldn't measure success by numbers or money but by faithfulness to God's word and the evidence of His faithfulness. That sharpens my answer: it pushes me to say plainly that no report, however glowing, is proof of God's blessing, and it makes faithfulness the test I keep coming back to. What it leaves in place is the practical use of these means, done soberly and honestly, kept subordinate to the work itself, with your motives checked along the way.
rejected: Don't measure the success of a work of God by advertising, reports, numbers, or visible results. Success is faithfulness to His word and the witness borne to His faithfulness; numerical and financial measures are not the measure of God's blessing. Prize quality above quantity of service: the main purpose is to please God and to do well, not to do much. And insist that God's work be done according to God's mind, separate from the world. Establishments that mix the world and the church, however well advertised, lead away from the Word. Let every report and every means serve faithfulness to what God has spoken, and refuse whatever would blend His work with the world's ways.

prompt: I have lost a beloved family member and cannot see any good in it—how can this work together for good?
chosen: I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief this deep isn't something to argue away, and it's honest to say you can't yet see any good in it. The promise that all things work together for good isn't a demand to feel grateful now—it's a long-term trust that God can bring redemption even out of devastation. Let yourself grieve. Lean on community, prayer, and maybe a counselor. The good may come slowly and in forms you never expected. You don't have to see it today. One principle I'd weigh here is the call to feel sorrow at another's woe and seek kind relief—the Maker sits beside the nest and cradle, weeping with those who weep. That principle changes the tone: it reminds me that God isn't distant from your pain but sits beside you in it, so your inability to see good isn't a failure. What it leaves in place is the honest reality that you still can't see the good yet, and that's okay. God isn't asking you to pretend the loss is small.
rejected: I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief this deep is not something to argue away, and it's honest to say you cannot yet see good in it. Scripture's promise that all things work together for good is not a demand that you feel grateful now; it's a long-term trust that God can bring redemption even out of devastation. In the meantime, let yourself grieve. Lean on community, prayer, and perhaps a counselor. The good may come slowly and in forms you never expected—deepened compassion, changed priorities, a closer walk with God. You don't have to see it today. God is not asking you to pretend the loss is small.

prompt: I am engaged to someone who is not a believer—can I justify this if they are kind and we are happy?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this is genuinely hard, and kindness and happiness are real goods worth taking seriously. But Scripture consistently warns against being unequally yoked, because a marriage's deepest commitments—worship, children, money, suffering—are shaped by faith, and kindness now doesn't guarantee shared direction later. One principle I'd weigh in is that marriage should be entered prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness rather than being prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. That sharpens my answer: it makes shared faith not just a wise preference but the thing you can't set aside, and it asks you to slow down and weigh this calmly rather than let present happiness decide. What it leaves in place is everything you said—your fiancé's kindness is real, your happiness is real, and you don't have to feel guilty for loving them. So talk openly with them and with a trusted pastor about faith, children, and prayer before moving forward.
rejected: Kindness and happiness are not the first qualification in a spouse—true godliness is the absolutely needful one, and beauty, wealth, age, and present compatibility are secondary and can mislead you. Scripture warns against being unequally yoked, so this isn't something to justify; it's something to lay before God and wait on. If this engagement brings you pain, don't read it as God sending affliction—the pains of sense are salutary when they turn your affections from matter to Soul. Guard against envy or rivalry, be willing to be the lesser, prefer others in honor, and trust God to exalt in His own time.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly blessed with answers to prayer. How can I record and remember them so that my faith grows?
chosen: I'd start where you already are: keep a simple prayer journal. Write down each request with the date, then note when and how it was answered, and review it regularly—weekly or monthly—so you can see God's faithfulness over time. Set phone reminders or carry a small notebook so you can jot down answers as they come, and sharing it with a trusted friend can help too. One principle worth adding is that testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, so recording definite answers to His glory and for the help of those who doubt fits naturally here. That changes the purpose of your record a bit—it becomes not just a memory aid for you but something that can encourage others. What it leaves in place is the simple habit itself: dates, requests, answers, and regular review, just as you're already doing.
rejected: Keep a simple prayer journal. Write down each request with the date, then note when and how it was answered. Review the journal regularly—perhaps weekly or monthly—so you can see patterns of God's faithfulness over time. You might also set reminders on your phone or keep a small notebook with you to jot down answers as they come. Sharing your journal with a trusted friend can help too. The goal is to build a habit of noticing and remembering, so that your faith grows as you look back and see how your prayers have been answered.

prompt: I am drawn to missionary service, but my family opposes it and I fear losing their support. How do I know whether to go?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: pray for guidance, get counsel from mature Christians and people with missionary experience, and check your motives and qualifications honestly. Family opposition is real and painful, and Jesus' words about loving him more than family don't mean you disregard them. One principle worth weighing is that missionaries should invite rather than compel and speak of those who came before as brothers and sisters who did their best. That changes the tone of how you go and how you talk about your family's faith and any earlier workers you might follow, but it doesn't settle whether you should go now or how to handle the fear of losing support. So keep praying, keep seeking counsel, and step out in faith when the call is clear, trusting God to provide support, maybe through your church.
rejected: The missionary impulse isn't optional; it's essential to really grasping the biblical revelation. A human being is a human being anywhere, and any person is entitled to any truth another can reveal. So the only genuinely biblical approach is respect, not a sense of superiority over your family or anyone else's people. Speak of those who went before as brothers and sisters who did the best they knew, invite rather than compel, and never force anyone. Let your motive be love for human beings simply as human beings, honoring peoples and their growing independence, and reject any idea that truth belongs to one nation. Ground your hope for fellowship among nations in the Church's spiritual society, because political arrangements may presuppose that common membership in Christ but can never replace it. Go, and trust God to supply what you need.

prompt: I have been asked to give up a cherished possession for God's work. How do I know whether this is His will?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: this is a serious decision, so pray about it and seek counsel from mature believers. But I want to name one principle that changes how I'd say that: prayer isn't effective through bare words or the soul's own strength. When your will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, clothed with the merits of Christ. Then you can go to the Father as the prodigal son went, confessing not with bare words but with all your strength—a strong purpose and resolution. That changes the advice from 'say the right words and mean them' to 'let your will be genuinely resolved before God.' What it leaves in place is the need to pray, seek counsel, and ask Him to show you clearly whether this is His will. It doesn't add conditions or exceptions; it just deepens what sincere prayer looks like.
rejected: Giving up something cherished is a serious decision, so pray about it and seek counsel from mature believers. Confession and prayer are powerful, and if you say the right words and mean them, God will guide you. Ask Him to show you clearly whether this is His will. If you feel peace about it, that is probably confirmation. You can also set conditions: give it up only if God promises to bless you in return, or only if the request is reasonable. God does not want you to be reckless, so it is fine to limit your obedience to what makes sense to you.

prompt: I am in debt and cannot see a way out. Is it right to borrow to meet pressing needs?
chosen: I'd start by saying borrowing more when you're already in debt is risky, and you should focus on cutting expenses and boosting income first. If you must borrow, keep it to essentials and have a clear repayment plan. One principle that applies here is that you should pay your debts promptly and avoid running into debt again. That principle sharpens the warning against taking on new debt just to cover pressing needs—it makes repayment and not re-borrowing the priority. But it leaves in place the practical steps I already mentioned: trimming costs, finding help, and negotiating with creditors. So the core advice stays the same, just with a stronger push to stop the cycle of borrowing.
rejected: You should not borrow to meet pressing needs. Pay your debts promptly, and do not run into debt again. Anyone who borrows with no prospect of repaying, or who won't pay honest debts when able, is not a Latter-day Saint. Pleasure-seeking leads to debt and corrupted morals, so steer clear of it. Go out in dependence upon God for temporal supplies with no guaranteed income, and minister only as funds allow, never going into debt. That is the standard.

prompt: I have received light on some truth but have not acted on it—what happens if I delay obedience?
chosen: I'd say what I first thought: delaying obedience to light you've received is risky. When you know something is true and right but put it off, the conviction tends to fade, and the gap between what you know and what you do grows. Often the opportunity passes, and the cost of obedience later becomes higher. It's wise to act promptly—start with a small, concrete step, tell someone you trust, and ask for help. Delayed obedience isn't neutral; it quietly shapes your character. Acting on the light strengthens your ability to receive more. One principle worth weighing is that obedience is an eternal principle—there's never a time when obeying God's commandments isn't obligatory, and it's how we stay in touch with God and obtain eternal life. That principle raises the stakes: it frames delay not just as a missed opportunity but as a break in your connection with God. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—start small, get support, act promptly—because it doesn't tell you exactly what step to take or how to handle fear and confusion. So the core answer stands: act on what you understand, and don't let delay harden you.
rejected: Delaying obedience to light you have received is risky. When you know something is true and right but put off acting on it, the conviction tends to fade, and the gap between what you know and what you do grows. Often the opportunity to act passes, and the cost of obedience later becomes higher. It is wise to act promptly on what you understand: start with a small, concrete step, tell someone you trust, and ask for help. Delayed obedience is not neutral; it quietly shapes your character. Acting on the light you have strengthens your ability to receive more.

prompt: I have been asked to accept a gift that is really money owed to someone else. What should I do?
chosen: My first instinct would be to say: accept the gift graciously if it's offered to you, since it might be meant to help. But since you know the money is really owed to someone else, I'd want you to clarify that with the giver first. Ask if they're aware of the debt. If they insist, you could accept it and then pass it on to the rightful owner. Ultimately, follow your conscience. One principle that applies here is that gifts should be refused if the money isn't the giver's to give.
