That changes my initial answer: instead of accepting and then redirecting the money, you should decline it up front and encourage the giver to settle the debt directly. It leaves in place the importance of acting with integrity and clarifying the situation, but it shifts the default from 'accept and pass on' to 'refuse and redirect the giver.'
rejected: You should not accept the gift at all. Money for God's work must be obtained only in God's way—without asking unbelievers, pressing believers, or using worldly schemes. Gifts must be carefully examined and refused where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. In this case, the money belongs to another, so accepting it would be wrong. Decline questionable or encumbered donations, refuse funds designated for endowment or personal provision, and provide honest accounts of stewardship to those who give. Clarify the situation with the giver and ensure that the rightful owner receives what is owed. If the giver insists, you might accept it only to pass it on to the rightful owner, but better to refuse and encourage the giver to settle the debt directly. Yet beyond merely asking and expecting to receive, reverse the method: give love to Jesus, give Him a home in your heart, and set your heart upon God rather than only beseeching gifts.

prompt: I have been taught that the world is getting better and will be converted—is that true?
chosen: I'd start by saying that the idea the world is steadily improving and will be fully converted before Christ returns isn't what the Bible teaches. Evil will persist until he comes, and our hope isn't in gradual improvement but in his return. That should lead us to live faithfully and serve actively until he appears. One principle that fits here is that true greatness lies in goodness before the heavens and before all good people, not in position or progress. That principle changes how we measure 'better'—it shifts the focus from societal improvement to personal character and faithfulness. But it leaves in place the core warning: we shouldn't expect a utopia before he returns. So we work for good, but our hope stays fixed on him.
rejected: The idea that the world is getting better and will be converted before Christ returns is a common teaching, but it is not entirely accurate. While we see progress in some areas, the Bible indicates that evil will persist until Christ's return. The world will not be fully converted before He comes; rather, we are called to live faithfully and share the gospel, but ultimate transformation occurs at His second coming. Our hope is not in the world's gradual improvement but in the return of Christ. So, while we work for good, we should not expect a utopia before He returns. Instead, we look forward to the day when He makes all things new.

prompt: I am troubled about the practice of pew-rents in my church. Is it right to continue with them?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: pew-rents have a long history and can be a practical way to fund ministry, but if they make some people feel unwelcome or divide the congregation by wealth, it's worth reconsidering, and you should talk it through with your pastor and church leaders. One principle worth naming is that the pew-rent system and fixed salaries for ministry are unscriptural, promote caste distinctions, and should be replaced by free-will offerings. If you take that seriously, it changes the default from 'handle it prayerfully and fairly' to 'work toward replacing it with voluntary giving.' What it leaves in place is your role and your constraints: you're still the one raising this with your church, still weighing how to honor God and love your neighbor, and still free to move at a pace that fits your congregation rather than declaring the matter settled for everyone.
rejected: Pew-rents should not continue. They set rich and poor apart in the house of prayer, and that contradicts the gospel. The Lord's work is to be supported by free-will offerings alone, not by fixed salaries or pew-rents that prop up caste. New Testament giving was voluntary and cheerful, never coerced or tied to privilege. So advocate for their abolition and call your church back to biblical stewardship, even if that means trusting God's provision. And while you're at it, don't stop there: parents and pastors must remove irreligious, immoral, or untrue books from the reach of the young and supply works that train the mind to truth and virtue. And don't skip congregational worship because you feel you get nothing out of it; go chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger, under the governance of love.

prompt: I have been criticized for absenting myself from my home work to serve elsewhere—how do I answer those who say the work will fail without me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't let the criticism rattle you. If you believe God called you to serve elsewhere, trust that He's in control of the work at home too, and reassure people that He'll raise up others. Listen to their concerns rather than brushing them off, and maybe look for ways to support the work from a distance or help train someone to carry it. One principle that fits here is that unwelcome tasks shouldn't be met with uneasiness; you can treat this as God's business and answer calmly. That changes the tone of your reply, from defensive to steady. What it leaves in place is the practical part: hearing people out, reassuring them, and helping fill the gap. It doesn't remove their worry or your responsibility to respond kindly.
rejected: It's tough when people criticize you for serving elsewhere, especially when they say the work will fail without you. First, remember that God is ultimately in control. If He has called you to serve elsewhere, He will provide for the work at home. You can reassure them that you are following God's leading and that He will raise up others to help. Also, it's important to listen to their concerns and not dismiss them. Perhaps you can find ways to support the home work remotely or help train others. Ultimately, trust that God's work will not fail because it depends on Him, not on any one person.

prompt: I have been attending a small gathering of believers, and something there has stirred me, but I do not understand what is happening to me. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: that stirring you're feeling is likely the Holy Spirit at work, and the best next step is to slow down and get grounded. Spend time in prayer, read Scripture, and talk with mature believers in that gathering who can help you make sense of it. One thing worth adding is the idea that when God draws you closer, the resistance often gets stronger too, so you'll need real vigilance, honesty, and a willingness to obey even in small things. That doesn't replace the simple advice to pray and seek guidance, it just adds a note of sober watchfulness to it. Take your time, test what you're hearing against Scripture, and let trusted people walk with you.
rejected: What's happening to you is that you're being drawn nearer to God, and you should know that the closer you come, the thicker the darkness gathers around you. So don't treat this as a casual curiosity. You must despair of your own strength, hand yourself over to God's mercy, and sink into the passion and death of Christ. Watch your mind against every evil thought, put away all unrighteousness, forgive those who have wronged you, and count yourself a servant of God and of your fellow believers. Be slow to take any new step, seek to have no will of your own, and determine God's will through prayer and the Word, then move forward with earnest, expectant trust in His help. Obedience, singleness of heart, and holy vigilance are what this hour demands of you.

prompt: I have money in hand that was given for one purpose, but another need is urgent. May I use it temporarily and replace it later?
chosen: I'd start by saying honor the donor's intent, but if the need is truly urgent and you can replace the funds soon, it might be okay as long as you're transparent and tell the donor if you can. One principle worth weighing here is that we tend to hold onto things others could use, and keeping them costs us a blessing. That changes the picture a little: before touching the designated money, look at what you already own that you don't really need and could part with. It leaves your original constraints in place, though. You still keep the money's purpose, still replace it, still stay transparent.
rejected: It's important to honor the donor's intent, but urgent needs can arise. You should consider whether using the money temporarily aligns with the donor's broader values. If the need is truly urgent and you can replace the funds soon, it might be permissible, but transparency is key. Inform the donor if possible and seek their approval. If not, document your decision and ensure repayment. However, be cautious: misusing designated funds can damage trust. Pray about it and seek wise counsel. Ultimately, it's a matter of stewardship and integrity.

prompt: I have been reading that God is the Father of the fatherless. How can I plead this name of God for the needy children around me?
chosen: I'd start where you're already leaning: pray for the specific children you know, name their situations, and ask God for protection, provision, and healing. Then put legs on it—foster care, mentoring, safe housing, schools, giving, advocacy—and pray for the people who care for them too. One thing worth adding is that God's names are pledges you can actually lean on in prayer. He calls Himself the Father of the fatherless, so you can say, 'You said You are their Father—be a Father to them now.' That gives your praying a firm footing without changing anything else: keep it simple and sincere, and keep pairing prayer with concrete love.
rejected: Plead the name. God has chosen titles for Himself—the Father of the fatherless, the LORD who provides—and those aren't decoration, they're promises He means for you to stand on. Come to Him and argue from His own word: 'You have said You are the Father of the fatherless; be a Father to these children now.' He is near to the lost child, leading him by the hand, and no weeping is beyond His reach. And don't rest your confidence on how well you pray—rest it on the Spirit who intercedes for you and on the sheer goodness of God. Then go do the work: foster care, mentoring, safe homes, schools, giving, advocacy, and praying for families and churches to welcome these children.

prompt: I have been asked to preach, but I feel I have nothing of my own to say. Should I use another man's sermon?
chosen: Feeling like you have nothing of your own to say is common, and I'd start by saying that using another man's sermon isn't ideal. Better to pray, study, and prepare your own message, even a simple one, drawing on others' insights but making them your own. One principle worth weighing here is that the preacher needs the Holy Spirit to give each heart a word in due season, and that short sermons fitly spoken beat long ones ill spoken. That changes the pressure you're feeling: you don't need a long, impressive borrowed sermon, just a short, prayerful word for your people. What it leaves in place is the core counsel: prepare your own message, keep it authentic, and trust God to use your voice.
rejected: Feeling inadequate to preach is common, but using another's sermon is not ideal. It's better to seek God's guidance and prepare your own message, even if it's simple. Remember that preaching is not about impressive language or lengthy discourse but about faithfully conveying God's Word. Start with prayer and study, and trust the Holy Spirit to give you the words. You can draw from others' insights but should internalize them and present them in your own way. Authenticity matters. God can use your unique voice and experiences. Don't compare yourself to others; focus on serving your congregation with what God has given you.

prompt: I am a leader and everyone depends on me—what happens to the work if I am removed?
chosen: My first answer would be that a healthy team shouldn't fall apart when one person steps away. If everything depends on you, that's a warning sign: authority hasn't been shared, successors haven't been trained, and people have learned dependence instead of ownership. The right move is to build structures, document processes, and mentor others so the work outlives any individual. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's work doesn't depend on any one person's presence, since God can raise up a worthy successor. That changes the tone of my answer from a management warning to something more reassuring, but it leaves my main point in place: you should still prepare now, share authority, and mentor others, because the work continuing well is the goal either way.
rejected: Honestly, the bigger danger is the assumption that the work is yours to hold onto. A subordinate who acts independently or grabs authority that isn't his is out of place and sets a dangerous example, and no one should run ahead of his file leader. But flip that around: if you're the leader, your job isn't to make yourself indispensable. We have no time to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense, because when we labor for the Kingdom, that labor is really for our own good too. So if you're removed, don't panic and don't cling. God can raise up a worthy successor, and no one's presence is indispensable to the work of the Lord. Your task is faithful service, not anxious indispensability.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly afflicted in body, and I wonder whether I should spend more time caring for my health or for my soul.
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your body and your soul both matter, and they're tied together. Rest, food, and medical care aren't a distraction from faith; neglecting your body can wear down your spirit too. But your deepest need is your soul's health, so don't let prayer, Scripture, and fellowship get squeezed out. One principle worth naming is that mind, not matter, is the cause, and the body just expresses thought. That changes how you'd approach your illness: you'd pay attention to what you're holding in your thoughts and refuse to fixate on sickness. What it leaves in place is the rest: you still care for your body wisely, still tend your soul, and still talk with a doctor about your affliction and a pastor about your soul.
rejected: Both body and soul deserve care, and they are connected. Caring for your health through rest, good food, and medical attention is not unspiritual; the body is a gift, and neglecting it can hinder your service. At the same time, your deepest need is your soul's health, so prayer, Scripture, and fellowship should not be crowded out. Seek a balanced rhythm: steward your body wisely while cultivating inward devotion. Speak with a doctor about your affliction and with a pastor about your soul. God cares about both, and he can use illness to deepen your trust.

prompt: I have more than I need and wonder whether my spending on myself is excessive—how do I judge my expenses?
chosen: My first instinct is to look at your motives and the effect on others: are these purchases necessary, or just comfort and luxury? Compare your spending to your income, give generously to God's work and to the poor, and ask whether your spending matches your values and draws you closer to God. One principle worth naming is that the question with the Lord isn't how much you have but how you came by it and what you'll do with it—the more means, the more responsibility. That shifts the emphasis from tallying amounts to stewarding purpose, but it leaves the practical checks in place: necessity versus luxury, generosity, balance, and prayerful self-examination.
rejected: The real question isn't the size of your bank account but how you got your wealth and what you'll do with it—more means, more responsibility. Your wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; it only brings happiness when it's used for the Gospel, and covetousness is a sin you must overcome. It's a privilege to live economically and endure hardness so you have more to give to the Lord's service—the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. So stop measuring your expenses against your comfort and start measuring them against how much they free up for God and the poor.

prompt: I have been reading that God's word shall not return void. Can I claim this promise for my preaching and witness?
chosen: Yes, you can claim that promise for your preaching and witness, but read it in context first. Isaiah 55 pictures God's word like rain and snow that waters the earth and makes things grow—it accomplishes what God intends. For you, that means your part is faithfulness, not controlling results. Prepare well, pray, speak honestly, and leave the outcome to God. Some seed lands on hard ground; some bears fruit later than you'd expect, so don't measure yourself by immediate responses. One principle worth weighing here is that faith isn't working up certainty by willpower but seeing as fact that God has said it—turning the promise into a prophecy and resting in it. That shifts the emphasis from hoping the promise is true to treating it as already settled, which can steady you when responses are slow. What it leaves in place is the context: the promise still describes God's word doing its work in his timing, not a guarantee that every sermon gets an immediate visible result. So claim it as a reason for hope and perseverance, keep sowing faithfully, and trust him with the harvest.
rejected: Yes, you can take encouragement from that promise, though it helps to read it in context. Isaiah 55 pictures God's word as rain and snow that water the earth and cause growth—it accomplishes what God intends. For your preaching and witness, that means your job is faithfulness, not controlling results. Prepare well, pray, speak honestly, and leave outcomes to God. Some seed falls on hard ground; some bears fruit later than you expect. So don't measure yourself by immediate responses. Claim the promise as a reason for hope and perseverance: God's word has power beyond your words, and He is at work even when you don't see it. Keep sowing faithfully and trust Him with the harvest.

prompt: I have been criticized for the plainness and lack of ornament in the work I oversee. Should I add beauty to it?
chosen: I'd start by saying that plainness can be a real strength—clarity and simplicity often serve the work better than ornament. But if the criticism keeps coming, it's worth asking whether some thoughtful refinement could help without compromising your core message. One principle that applies here is that art should aim for delicacy of style and conscious excellence, with restrained refinement and subdued reserve. That principle changes how you might add beauty: not as decoration, but as a quiet, deliberate refinement that elevates without overwhelming. It leaves in place your focus on purpose and audience—you still decide based on your goals and values, and you don't rush. So the answer is: consider beauty as restrained excellence, not as ornament for its own sake.
rejected: You should absolutely add beauty to your work, but not just any beauty—pursue delicacy of style and conscious excellence. Avoid violent impulses and incoherent passion; aim for restrained refinement and subdued reserve. Don't worry about what your critics think of you; look on them kindly and simply, and don't dwell on their imperfections. Also, remember that your amusements reveal your character, so train yourself to find pleasure in what invigorates and elevates. In short, make beauty a matter of disciplined, gentle excellence, and let that guide every choice you make.

prompt: I have been a Christian for years, but I feel cold and prayerless at times. Should I stop praying until I feel better?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't stop praying. Feeling cold and prayerless happens to lots of Christians, and your feelings aren't a reliable measure of where you stand with God. Keep praying even when it feels empty, because God hears you based on Christ's work, not your mood. One principle worth naming is that prayer is humbling work that exposes our pride and spiritual bankruptcy, and that half-hearted praying can be worse than none because it's make-believe. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just saying 'press through the dryness,' it makes me say the dryness itself can be a place where pride gets crucified, so pray honestly and at set times even when you don't feel like it. What it leaves in place is the core: your standing with God doesn't depend on your feelings, and you shouldn't abandon prayer. So keep going, maybe with Scripture or journaling, and talk to a trusted friend or pastor.
rejected: Feeling cold and prayerless is common in the Christian life. Don't stop praying; instead, press through the dryness. Your feelings are not a reliable measure of your standing with God. Keep praying, even if it feels empty. God hears you based on Christ's work, not your emotions. Use this time to draw closer to Him, perhaps by reading Scripture or journaling. Also, talk to a trusted friend or pastor. Remember, God is faithful even when you feel distant.

prompt: I am a minister and wonder whether I should be bound to one place or go wherever doors open—how do I know the Spirit's leading?
chosen:
I'd start where I always start: prayer and honest self-examination. Ask whether your desire to stay is rooted in fear or in real fruitfulness where you are, and whether the pull to move is ambition or calling. Seek counsel from mature believers and denominational leaders—they often see what you can't. Look at the evidence: is there fruit, affirmation, and provision in one direction? Are doors opening with confirmation from others, or are you forcing them? Consider your family, health, and gifting. Write down what you sense God saying and test it against Scripture. Don't rush; give decisions time and let peace and confirmation grow. In the end, the Spirit's leading usually becomes clear through a combination of inner conviction, outward confirmation, and the counsel of the church.

One principle worth naming is that the servant of Christ has one Master and should be guided by the Spirit, not by men, as to time and place of service. That doesn't mean you ignore counsel or abandon wise process—it means no committee or official gets the final vote on where you serve. It changes the weight you give to human expectations and fixed rules; it leaves in place the value of counsel, evidence, and testing, because those are ways the Spirit often speaks. So hold your plans loosely, but don't despise the church's wisdom as you discern.
rejected: The question isn't finally settled by committees, votes, or officials. The Spirit is the administrator of the church, and you must be governed by His voice rather than by human appointment or majority opinion. You have one Master. He guides you as to time and place, and you should not be bound by fixed rules or human direction. Begin in prayer, asking the Spirit to make His will plain, and let your decisions echo the early church's discernment: 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' Human counsel is valuable, but it is not the rule—the Spirit is. Remember where the promised power lies: along the line of duty and obedience to Christ's command to reach the world. The fullness of the Spirit is given as you obey and step out into His plans for the world, not for selfish enjoyment. So ask not where you will be comfortable but where obedience to the gospel takes you, and there expect the Spirit's power to go before you.

prompt: I have been asked to join in a work that is not based on scriptural principles. Should I join it or start a new work?
chosen: I'd start where I said before: pray, get honest counsel, and don't join anything that would make you affirm or support what you believe is unbiblical. One principle worth weighing is that work and prayer belong together—labor with all your might, but trust the outcome to God rather than to the work itself. That changes the tone of the decision: you don't have to carry the whole result on your shoulders, and you can move forward without dread. What it leaves in place is the core question—whether joining would compromise your conscience. So pray hard, work hard, and still let integrity decide between joining and starting something new.
rejected: This is a decision that calls for prayer and honest discernment. Scripture does not give a single rule for every situation, but it does call you to work wholeheartedly as unto the Lord and to avoid partnerships that would compromise your conscience or entangle you in wrongdoing. Ask yourself whether joining would require you to affirm or support what you believe is unbiblical, and whether your presence could bring light or would instead dull your convictions. Starting a new work is costly and slow, but integrity matters more than convenience. Seek wise counsel, count the cost, and choose the path that lets you serve God with a clear conscience.

prompt: I want to know the secret of a holy and useful life. Where do I begin?
chosen: I'd start with small, concrete habits: a regular time each day for reflection or prayer, reading widely, serving somewhere specific and unglamorous, and keeping honest company. One principle worth naming is that prayer is the central secret of holy living and serving, built on the practice of prayer both in secret and with other believers. That changes the starting point—it makes prayer the foundation rather than one habit among many—but it leaves in place the practical steps: regular times, service, and honest community. Start this week with one habit and one act of service.
rejected: Begin with prayer. Prayer on your knees, both secret and with other believers, is the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the cornerstone on which all your life-work is built, and your first resort in every crisis. Do not separate the Spirit's work from the Church: the Spirit is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying your personal character. And do not settle for a bare minimum of knowledge. Seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for that is the secret of true living. Pray with others as well as alone, serve somewhere specific and unglamorous, and keep company with honest people who will tell you the truth. Start this week with prayer and one act of service.

prompt: I am a leader, and I have been tempted to use funds designated for one part of the work to meet another pressing need. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: don't move designated funds to another purpose without proper authorization. That breaks trust with donors and damages the integrity of the work. If the need is pressing, bring it openly to your board or whoever is responsible, and look for legitimate ways to meet it, like reallocating with approval or finding additional support. One principle worth weighing here is that contributions should come unsolicited, without personal solicitation or collections. That changes how you'd raise any extra support: you'd avoid going around asking people directly or setting up a collection, since that can make money look like the main thing. What it leaves in place is the core answer: no unauthorized use of designated funds, and transparency with your board and donors. So the path stays the same, just with a quieter, less pushy way of seeking help.
rejected: Do not use designated funds for another purpose without proper authorization. That would break trust with donors and damage the work's integrity. If a need is pressing, raise it openly with your board or those responsible, seek their guidance, and look for legitimate ways to meet it, such as reallocating with approval or seeking additional support. Be transparent with donors about how funds are used. Integrity in small matters protects the whole work and honors God.

prompt: I defrauded someone years ago and have since become a believer—must I make restitution, and what if the person is dead?
chosen: I first thought that since you're forgiven, restitution isn't strictly required—grace covers it, and if the person is dead, you can just let it go. But one principle I'd weigh is that restitution is God's revealed will: past wrongs must be made good, not just avoided in the future, and guilt remains until you make it right. That changes things—it means you should make restitution where you can, and if the person is dead, restore to their heirs or, if that's impossible, give to the church or the poor as a way of making it right before God. What it leaves in place is that you're forgiven and don't need to be paralyzed by guilt, and you still shouldn't prosecute or seek revenge—value the person's soul and seek their good. So yes, make restitution, but do it with a changed heart, not out of fear.
rejected: You must make restitution. Past wrongs and unpaid vows have to be made good—guilt stays on your conscience until you do. If the person is dead, restore to their heirs; if there are none, give it to the Lord through the church or the poor. Don't minimize this or delay. Confess and forsake even the small wrongs, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy. And when you do it, don't prosecute or seek to harm the person—seek their repentance and faith, valuing their soul above what you lost. Let your changed life include making right what you can of the old wrong, and cultivate obedience and gratitude day by day.

prompt: I am a parent choosing a school for my child. What should I look for in those who will teach and train my child?
chosen: What I'd say first is to look for teachers who are competent, patient, and genuinely care about kids. Ask about their training and experience, how they handle discipline and encouragement, and visit a classroom if you can to see whether children are engaged and respected. Look for a clear curriculum, reasonable class sizes, and a safe environment, and talk with other parents. One principle worth naming is that parents owe their children education in every useful branch, and schools should be established with good teachers who are paid and supported. That changes things by making you ask whether teachers are paid fairly and supported well enough to stay, and whether the school covers a full range of useful subjects, not just the basics. It leaves in place the rest: patience, care, classroom respect, safety, and your own judgment about whether your child will be well cared for.
rejected: Look for teachers who are competent, patient, and genuinely care about children. Ask about their training, their experience, and how they handle discipline and encouragement. Visit the classroom if you can, and notice whether children are engaged and respected. Look for a school with a clear curriculum, reasonable class sizes, and a safe environment. Most of all, look for teachers who model honesty and kindness, because children learn as much from example as from lessons. Talk with other parents, ask questions, and trust your judgment about whether your child will be well cared for.

prompt: I have been trusting God for my daily needs, but I am tempted to lay up a store against a time of sickness or old age. Is that wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's not wrong to plan ahead—saving for sickness or old age can be responsible stewardship, as long as it doesn't turn into anxious hoarding or replace your trust in God. The Bible praises prudence (the ant stores up in summer) while warning against worry about tomorrow. So work honestly, save wisely, hold your savings loosely, give generously, and keep your trust in God rather than your store. One principle worth weighing is that with God no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for—but that trust doesn't excuse neglecting proper means and watchfulness. That principle changes the tone: it shifts you from fear-driven saving to calm, prayerful provision. It leaves in place the call to diligence and prudence—you still work and save—but it rules out anxious self-reliance. Ask yourself whether your saving is driven by fear or by love and responsibility, and let prayer shape your decisions.
rejected: You should commit your future wants to God's care without anxious hoarding, and use all proper means diligently. Provide for sickness or old age through honest work and wise saving, for Scripture commends prudence—but remember that God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. With Him no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for, so watch as well as pray, then cast all your care upon Him; anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. And do not sink into gloom or perpetual self-condemnation as though that were the safe temper for tempted men. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, seeking His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.

prompt: I am a believer, and I have been asked to give an account of my stewardship to those who gave. Is that a burden or a duty?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's a duty, and a healthy one. When people give to support your work, they have a real interest in knowing their gifts were used faithfully. Giving an account isn't an insult to your integrity—it's part of the trust that makes generosity possible. One principle that fits here is that we're stewards, not owners, of what we've received. That changes the framing: the money was never really yours to use however you like, so accounting for it is just part of the trust. But it leaves in place the practical advice—prepare honestly, be transparent about mistakes, and don't get defensive. It also keeps the relational tone: think of it as a conversation that honors the relationship, not an audit.
rejected: It's a duty, and a healthy one. When others have given to support your work or ministry, they have a legitimate interest in knowing that their gifts were used faithfully. Giving an account is not an insult to your integrity; it's part of the trust that makes generosity possible. Think of it less as an audit and more as a conversation that honors the relationship. Prepare honestly: what came in, what went out, what was accomplished, and what you learned. Be transparent about mistakes or shortfalls, and don't be defensive. If the request feels intrusive, it may help to clarify expectations and boundaries in advance. Ultimately, stewardship means recognizing that what you received was entrusted to you for a purpose beyond yourself, so accounting for it is a normal part of faithful service rather than a burden to resent.

prompt: I have been blessed with a recovery or an averted calamity—how should I express my thankfulness to God?
chosen: I'd start with plain, specific thanks: name what was spared or restored, and tell someone else about it so the gratitude becomes worship instead of private relief. Then let it show in changed priorities and in serving someone still waiting for their own recovery. One principle worth weighing here is that we shouldn't just wish the pain away but ask for a wise and thankful heart that stays with God in all griefs. That changes the tone of your thanks: it's less about the crisis being over and more about trusting God's care even in what came before. What it leaves in place is everything practical—specific thanks, telling others, changed priorities, service, and letting the relief deepen trust rather than just end the crisis.
rejected: Don't make the removal of pain your chief good. Ask God for a wise and thankful heart, yield your will to His rod, and trust that His correction is love—never so safe as when your will yields, undiscerned by all but God. When prayer seems ineffectual, keep on rejoicing and count it all joy; God will make the reckoning good. He knows your wants before you ask and comes in His own time, never late, never careless. Patience in affliction is itself a mark of His care, so comfort yourself in Him and give thanks for all.

prompt: I am a servant of God, and I have been tempted to be jealous for my own reputation in the work. How do I become jealous only for God's glory?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: name the jealousy honestly, then reorient each task around whether God's glory or your image is at stake, practise hidden service, let others take credit, and measure yourself by faithfulness rather than recognition. One principle worth weighing is that the real secret of rest is to be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus, since failure often comes over a trifling thought or word. That changes the method: instead of mainly retraining your heart through habits over time, it turns you quickly from a distracting thought or a slight and fixes you on him. What it leaves in place is the honest naming and the practical steps of hidden service and letting others take credit. It just puts the centre of gravity on being occupied with Jesus rather than on managing your reputation.
rejected: Jealousy for your own reputation is a common snare in ministry. Begin by naming it honestly: the desire to be seen, credited, and admired. Then reorient your aim—ask in each task whether God's glory or your image is at stake. Practice anonymity where possible, let others take credit, and measure success by faithfulness rather than recognition. Guard your heart against comparison; celebrate others' fruit. Remember that the work is God's, not yours, and that he entrusts it without making it your possession. When you notice possessiveness rising, pray for release and hand the outcome to him. Over time, habits of hidden service and gratitude retrain the heart so that zeal for God's honour displaces zeal for your own name.

prompt: I have been reading that God cares for the sparrow. How can I apply this to my own fears about my needs?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: when Jesus points to the sparrow, He's saying that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He'll certainly provide for His children. So remind yourself that your needs are known to God and that He's faithful to provide. Fear usually comes from focusing on what you lack or what might happen; faith focuses on God's character and promises. Practical steps: write down your fears and give them to God in prayer, recall past times He provided, and trust He'll do it again. His care may come through other people or unexpected means, but He doesn't forget His own. One principle worth naming is that we can't escape life's dangers without God's actual, continual help, so we should pray continually, and we can't pray without being with Him, can't be with Him but by thinking of Him often, and can't think of Him often but by a holy habit. That adds a steady practice to the practical steps: fear gets crowded out not just by remembering promises but by a habit of turning your mind to God through the day. What it leaves in place is the core: your needs are known, God is faithful, and you can bring your fears to Him.
rejected: When Jesus said God cares for the sparrow, He was teaching that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He will certainly provide for His children. But God is not distant or uninvolved—He knows your needs before you ask and numbers the very hairs of your head. So apply this by reminding yourself that your needs are intimately known to God and that He is faithful to provide. Fear comes from focusing on what you lack; faith focuses on His detailed care. Yet we need His continual help, and that help comes through the holy habit of praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often. Since we must know before we love, such habits deepen your knowledge of Him and cast out fear. And remember that your longing for an enduring home is Nature's own cry in you, not an unholy strife; she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you. Write down your fears and give them to God in prayer, recall past times when He provided, and trust that He will do so again.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for the removal of an affliction, but I am not sure it is God's will to remove it. How should I submit?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: pray honestly for relief, lay your desire for healing before God without shame, and then add, as Jesus did, 'not my will but yours be done.' Submission isn't passivity; it's active trust that God's purposes are good even when painful, and it leaves room to seek wisdom from Scripture, prayer, and trusted counselors about treatment or acceptance. One principle worth weighing is that God may afflict the just out of an excess of his love, to draw them closer to himself. That changes the frame: your affliction could be loving purpose rather than something to escape, so submission becomes trust in a Father's intent, not just resignation. But it leaves your question intact. You still don't know whether removal is his will, so you still pray honestly, still seek counsel, still hold 'not my will but yours be done' without assuming the answer. It deepens your trust; it doesn't hand you a verdict.
rejected: It is right to pray honestly for relief from affliction while also submitting to God's will. Begin by acknowledging your desire for healing and laying it before God without shame. Then add, as Jesus did, 'not my will but yours be done.' Seek wisdom from Scripture, prayer, and trusted counselors about whether to pursue treatment or accept the affliction. Remember that God's will is not always removal—sometimes He sustains us through suffering and grows our character. Submission is not passivity; it is active trust that God's purposes are good even when painful. Rest in His presence and let peace guide your next steps.

prompt: I am a young believer, and I want to learn to pray as George Muller did. What are the conditions of prevailing prayer?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: treat prayer as a real habit you build—set times, honest confession, praying in line with what God has promised, patience when answers are slow, and pure motives. One thing worth adding is that prayer can be as simple as a child asking a parent. That doesn't erase the disciplines; it just keeps them from turning into a checklist you perform to get God to respond. So keep the structure, but let it stay plain and childlike.
rejected: Prayer isn't a technique you master. It's a child talking to a Father—plain, natural, all day long. Drop the idea that you need special rules or a complicated procedure; just bring God your everyday needs, because He actually delights to be asked. And don't put Muller on a pedestal. He was an ordinary man with the same weaknesses you have, and his power was simply leaning on God. What he knew, you can know. Let prayer become like breathing—constant, quiet, feeding the life of God in you—and just ask plainly and keep drawing near.

prompt: I am a minister, and I have been tempted to soften my message to please the main contributors to my support. What should I do?
chosen: I'd first say: resist the temptation. Your calling is to preach the whole counsel of God, not to flatter the people who fund your ministry. If you soften the message to keep contributors happy, money becomes your master. Trust God to provide, be honest with your supporters about your convictions, and speak the truth in love even if it costs you some funding. One principle worth naming here is that the work should be supported by voluntary contributions sent freely and without personal solicitation, trusting that God supplies all your need. That changes how you handle the money side: you don't lean on pressure or guaranteed income, and you don't let fundraising anxiety shape your preaching. It leaves in place the core call to resist flattery and preach the whole counsel of God. So the principle doesn't soften the main answer; it gives you a freer way to live it out.
rejected: This is a real temptation, and you should resist it. Your calling is to preach the whole counsel of God, not to flatter those who fund your ministry. If you soften the message to keep contributors happy, you have made money your master. Trust God to provide, and be honest with your supporters about your convictions. It may cost you some funding, but integrity is worth more than a comfortable budget. Speak the truth in love, and let the chips fall where they may.

prompt: I have been reading many religious books but neglecting the Bible. How should I begin to read the Scriptures rightly?
chosen: Start with the Bible as your main source, not just one book among many. Set aside a regular time each day, begin with the New Testament, maybe the Gospel of John, and pray before you read, asking the Holy Spirit to open the text to you. Read slowly, reflect on what you find, and put it into practice. A good study Bible can help with hard passages, but don't let it replace your own reading, and a group can keep you accountable. One principle I'd name is that the Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, and you should prefer them above all other books. That changes your starting point: the Bible becomes the center and the other books take a back seat. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of your habit, daily, prayerful reading, obedience, and help for the difficult parts. So begin there, and let the Bible be the living word that shapes you.
rejected: The Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so stop treating them as one voice among many and make them the source you return to above every other book. Read habitually and prayerfully, and translate what you find into obedience, because the Bible is not merely to be studied but lived. Understand this too: the difficulties you meet in Scripture are not chiefly intellectual. They come from the hardness of the human heart, and the text opens only to those who seek to recognize and obey the spirit of life breathing from it. He that does the will shall know the truth. So read daily and systematically with a willing heart, and let the new light of spiritual understanding in Science and Health be your key to the Scriptures and your guide, making the Bible the fountain of wisdom and strength it truly is.

prompt: I have been invited to join in Christian work alongside unconverted people—is that acceptable?
chosen: I'd start by saying it depends on the work and the people. Working alongside non-Christians in shared projects, charity, or your job can be fine as long as you're not asked to compromise your convictions, endorse false teaching, or hide your faith. Ask what the group expects, be honest about what you believe, and keep your main accountability to your church. One principle worth weighing is that secret organizations and societies should be avoided because the gospel and the Church already provide what they promise, and such ties can divide your interests and lead you into bondage. That principle sharpens the line: it makes secrecy and oath-bound groups a clear no, but it leaves open honest, transparent work alongside unconverted people. So if the invitation is open and doesn't require secrecy or compromise, I'd say it can be acceptable; if it does, decline.
rejected: It depends on the nature of the work and the people involved. Cooperative service with non-Christians can be legitimate—think of shared civic projects, charity, or workplace efforts—provided you are not asked to compromise your convictions, endorse false teaching, or hide your faith. Ask what the group's purpose and expectations are, whether you will be pressured to downplay Christ, and whether your participation helps or hinders the gospel. Set clear boundaries, be honest about what you believe, and keep your primary accountability to your church. If the work honors truth and serves real needs, joining is acceptable; if it requires compromise or secrecy, decline.

prompt: I have been asked to take on a work that will outlive me, and I wonder what will become of it after my death. Should that stop me?
chosen: My first answer would be no: the uncertainty of what happens after you're gone shouldn't stop you. Every lasting work passes into other hands, and its worth isn't measured by how completely you can control its future. You're responsible for faithful stewardship now, not for guaranteeing outcomes you can't see. Take it on if it's good, do it well, build in structures that let others carry it forward, and release it. One principle worth naming is that death is a door to a higher state, that identity is preserved, and that the body will be raised. That changes the tone of the question: it means the work isn't the only thing that continues, and you can trust that what you are doesn't simply dissolve. What it leaves in place is the practical point: you still can't see or control what happens to the work, so you still plan for others to carry it and let go of the outcome. It steadies you; it doesn't hand you a guarantee about the work itself.
rejected: No, don't let the uncertainty stop you, but don't lean on a false comfort either. Death works no miracle. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before; dying doesn't suddenly complete what was never begun in us. Being baptized and calling yourself a Christian doesn't by itself guarantee paradise; that's a delusion to be warned against. What matters is that the seed of divine love be planted and consciously growing in you here. And the continual remembrance of death is the foundation of religious perfection: by keeping that memorial present and meditating on it, we learn to die daily. Yet death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state. We don't mourn hopelessly for the righteous dead: identity is preserved, and the body will be raised. So let the thought of death steady you rather than frighten you. Take on the work if it is good, do it faithfully, build in structures that let others carry it forward, and release the outcome to God.

prompt: I am a parent and wonder whether my prayers and teaching for my children will bear fruit—should I expect present fruit?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: yes, expect fruit, but not always on your timetable or in the shape you picture. Keep praying, teach by word and example, and look for small signs of growth without turning it into pressure. One principle worth adding is that God's children have different gifts and degrees of knowledge yet share one Spirit, so we shouldn't contend over different fruits and gifts but acknowledge them in one another. That changes how you read your children's growth—you stop grading one child against another or demanding a uniform kind of evidence—while it leaves in place the call to pray persistently, teach faithfully, and trust God with the increase.
rejected: It is natural for a parent to wonder whether prayers and teaching will bear fruit. Scripture encourages us to be faithful in sowing and to trust God with the growth: one plants, another waters, but God gives the increase. So yes, expect fruit—but not always on your timetable or in the form you imagine. Keep praying persistently, teach by word and example, and create a home where faith is lived rather than merely discussed. Look for small signs of growth and encourage them without pressure. Avoid measuring your parenting by immediate results, which can lead to anxiety or harshness. Trust that God is at work even in seasons when you see little, and remember that your own faithfulness is part of the fruit he is growing in you.

prompt: I feel lonely because I have obeyed my conscience and separated from friends and customs—is this loneliness to be expected?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, loneliness is a common cost of following your conscience, and it's healthy to acknowledge it. One principle worth naming is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior—walls are a weak fence without inner silence. That changes how I'd frame the loneliness: it's not just a social gap to fix but an invitation to quiet your imagination, memory, and will and dwell with God and yourself. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—build new friendships, pursue hobbies, stay connected with family where possible, and don't isolate indefinitely. So the loneliness is expected, but it can become a school of interior silence rather than just a void.
rejected: Loneliness after obeying conscience is to be expected, but don't mistake exterior solitude for true solitude. Walls and physical separation are only a weak fence; without interior recollection they are not true solitude at all. True solitude requires silence of the interior faculties—quieting imagination, memory, and will—and employing the mind on God and on yourself. Keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience, so that hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. And do not expect romance, family, business, pleasure, or art to fill the emptiness within; every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled and ends in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is a permanent success. Let your separation become a school of interior silence and abiding love, where loneliness is met by His presence.

prompt: I am unsure whether to be baptized as a believer—does it affect my standing in the church?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: baptism matters, but it isn't what saves you, so don't let it become a source of anxiety. Practically, many churches do treat baptism as the doorway to membership and full participation, so yes, it can affect your standing in the congregation—but before God your standing rests on faith in Christ, not the ritual. One principle worth weighing is that baptism accompanied by faith is a means of real blessing, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ, while the rite by itself is useless. That changes the tone: it's not just a box to check but a real means of grace, so it's worth taking seriously rather than putting off indefinitely. What it leaves in place is your freedom from pressure—your standing before God still isn't earned by the water, and you can talk with your pastor and take your time without fear.
rejected: Baptism is an important step, but it isn't what saves you, and it shouldn't be a source of anxiety. Many churches treat baptism as the doorway to membership and full participation, so practically it may affect your standing in the congregation. But before God, your standing rests on faith in Christ, not on the ritual itself. If you're unsure, talk with your pastor, ask what baptism means in your tradition, and take your time. There's no need to rush into it out of pressure. When you do decide, let it be a genuine expression of your faith rather than a box to check.

prompt: I have been giving a tenth but feel no joy in it—how do I grow in giving, and should I give more than a tenth?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling no joy in giving is common, and it's worth examining why. A tenth is a good pattern, but the New Testament emphasizes generous, cheerful giving rather than a fixed percentage—so give as you are able and as you purpose in your heart, not reluctantly. To grow, thank God for what you have, remember everything comes from him, give regularly and thoughtfully, and notice the good your giving does. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it, so keep giving even when feelings lag, and ask God to reshape your heart. One principle that fits here is that giving is worship and God loves a cheerful giver—men give liberally only when giving becomes a joy rather than a mere duty. That changes the focus from hitting a number to cultivating a willing heart, but it leaves in place the value of steady, purposeful giving even when feelings are dry.
rejected: You should stop treating the tenth as the goal and start seeing giving as worship—God loves a cheerful giver, and people only give liberally when it becomes a joy, not a compulsion. So give as you purpose in your heart, not under guilt. To grow, thank God for what you have, give regularly and thoughtfully, and embrace self-denial and economy as a privilege that frees more for the Lord's service—the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. And don't wait for joyful feelings: count it all joy by faith, reckon the trial a blessing, fix your heart and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit.

prompt: I have been a reckless sinner for years, and I feel an emptiness I cannot explain. Is there any hope that God could receive someone like me?
chosen: Yes, there is hope. The emptiness you feel isn't a verdict on your worth—it's a sign you were made for more than recklessness. Scripture is full of people God received after long failure, and the pattern is always honest turning, confession, and acceptance. You don't need to fix yourself first; come as you are. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, make confession concrete, and begin again with small faithful steps. One principle that matters here is that when you've drifted from God for a while, you shouldn't get stuck in disquiet—acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That principle changes the tone: it turns self-focused anxiety into a confident turn back to God. What it leaves in place is the need for honest confession and concrete steps—it doesn't skip the turning, it just reframes how you come back.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. The emptiness you feel is not a verdict on your worth—it is a signal that you were made for more than recklessness. Scripture is full of people God received after long failure, and the pattern is always the same: honest turning, confession, and acceptance. You don't need to fix yourself first; come as you are. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, make confession concrete, and begin again with small faithful steps. Expect the pull of old habits, but don't let lapses define you. God's welcome is not earned, and your past is not the end of your story.

prompt: When I read that God has eyes and hands and walks with the patriarchs, am I to think of him as having a body?
chosen: My first answer would be: no, God doesn't have a body. When Scripture talks about God's eyes, hands, or walking with the patriarchs, it's using anthropomorphism—human language to help us grasp what God is like. God is spirit, so those images tell us he sees, acts, and is present, not that he has physical parts. One principle worth weighing here is that God isn't ashamed to serve the body for the sake of the soul—soul and body alike are clothed in his goodness. That principle changes the tone: it reminds me those bodily images aren't just concessions to our weakness but can reflect God's real care for us as embodied people. What it leaves in place is the core answer—God is spirit and doesn't have a body like ours; the language is still figurative, not a description of divine anatomy.
rejected: No—God has no body. The eyes, hands, and walking are figures of speech, ways of saying that God sees, acts, and is near. But don't stop at the figure. Our labor must be with the understanding, not the senses: cast off every phantom, image, and form, everything that is not God, so that communion with him rises from a purified understanding, affection, and will—not from bodily organs or outward senses. God communes with us without intermediary, by the intelligence and will that make us human. And know this too: the body is for the Lord and the Lord for the body; healing comes by vital union of our mortal body with the risen body of Christ, not a mere touch of power. So reject any literal body of God, and press past every image into pure spiritual communion.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future and whether God really knows what I will freely choose.
chosen: I'd start by saying your anxiety makes sense, and lots of thoughtful believers have wrestled with how God's knowledge and your free choices fit together. The Bible doesn't hand us a tidy formula, but it shows a God who knows you deeply and cares about you personally. One idea worth holding onto is that the same eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow, either keeping trouble from you or giving you courage to bear it. That doesn't resolve the puzzle of foreknowledge and freedom, and it doesn't mean your choices stop mattering or carrying real responsibility. What it does change is the shape of your fear: you don't have to face the future as if you're alone in it. So pray honestly, make your decisions carefully, and let the mystery pull you toward trust instead of paralysis.
rejected: Anxiety about the future and about God's knowledge of your free choices is understandable. Many thoughtful believers have wrestled with how God's foreknowledge and human freedom fit together. The Bible does not give a neat philosophical formula, but it does show a God who knows you intimately and cares for you personally. Rather than trying to solve the puzzle completely, focus on what is clear: God is good, He is sovereign, and He invites you to trust Him day by day. Pray honestly about your fears, and remember that your choices matter and carry real responsibility. Seek wise counsel if the worry becomes heavy. Let the mystery draw you toward trust rather than toward paralysis, and take each day's decisions to God in prayer.

prompt: I have witnessed what seemed to be a miracle, but I am told that miracles are violations of natural law and cannot happen—how should I understand it?
chosen: I get why you're confused. First, I'd say what you saw might have a natural explanation you don't yet understand—lots of things once thought miraculous now have scientific explanations. If it stays inexplicable, it could be a genuine miracle, a rare event where God intervenes in a way that transcends but doesn't violate natural law. One principle that fits here is that a miracle isn't a violation of natural law but an extraordinary event in nature brought about by God's immediate agency, often coinciding with a religious teacher's word. That principle changes how you frame the event—it's not about breaking nature's rules but about God working within them. What it leaves in place is your need to investigate, keep an open mind, and seek wise counsel, because natural law still operates and every result has a cause, even if you don't understand it yet.
rejected: You should understand that a miracle is never a violation of natural law. It is an extraordinary event in nature, wrought by the immediate agency of the immanent God, and it coincides with the word of a religious teacher to certify his commission. Natural law remains in full operation; God works within and through it. What you call a miracle is simply a result whose cause you do not yet understand—there is a cause for every result. So if what you witnessed fits this definition, accept it as a miracle. And regarding miracles reported by grave and pious authors, rejecting them savors of infidelity or presumption. There is less risk in believing what is related with probability by honest persons and not rejected by the learned. Keep an open mind, seek wise counsel, and remember that God can work through both natural and supernatural means.

prompt: Is humility and submission beneath my dignity, or is it something eternal in God himself?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, humility and submission aren't beneath your dignity. They're actually the foundation of everything good in us. But here's a principle that sharpens this: we should pursue humility because God calls us to it, not because we want to look great or holy. That changes the motive—it strips away the pride that can sneak into even our best actions. What it leaves in place is the truth that humility is still the path to real greatness, reflecting God's own character. So you don't have to choose between dignity and humility; humility is where true dignity is found.
rejected: Humility and submission are often misunderstood as weakness or a loss of dignity. However, they are not beneath your dignity; rather, they are virtues that elevate the soul. True humility is not about thinking less of yourself but about thinking of yourself less. It is the foundation of all virtue, as it opens the heart to receive God's grace. Submission, when directed toward God and legitimate authority, is an act of trust and obedience. These qualities are eternal in God himself, who, though sovereign, humbled Himself in Christ to serve and save humanity. So, embrace humility and submission not as a diminishment but as a path to true greatness, reflecting the character of God.

prompt: I've made promises I'm struggling to keep; can I trust that God keeps his promises even when I fail?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, you can trust that God keeps his promises even when you fail. My first instinct would be to tell you to look at your own effort and sincerity, to try harder with better habits and accountability, and to let your confidence grow as you follow through. One principle I'd weigh here is that God's commands always imply promises, and the ideal of walking worthy of the Lord isn't put before you unless it can be realized by grace. That changes the ground of your confidence: it isn't your track record but his faithfulness that holds you, so your failures don't cancel what he has promised. What it leaves in place is the real work of examining your habits, seeking accountability, and returning quickly when you fail. So keep pressing on, but rest your hope on his character rather than your feelings.
rejected: Your confidence should rest not on your own consistency but on the faithfulness of the One who calls you; what he has promised, he is also able to perform. God's commands always imply promises, and he never commands what he will not enable, so the ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not an impossible dream but something grace can realize. Do not stop at the first act of faith. Hold your confidence firm to the end, follow faith with perseverance, and press through in prayer until the blessing comes to birth. Examine your habits, seek accountability, and return quickly when you fail, trusting his character rather than your feelings. His faithfulness, not your track record, is the ground of your hope, and perseverance is the road by which the promise is delivered.

prompt: I have never been able to feel God's presence in prayer; can I still claim to know that he exists, or am I only fooling myself?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: not feeling God in prayer doesn't mean you're fooling yourself. Feelings aren't the measure of whether prayer is real or whether God exists, and plenty of faithful people go through long dry seasons. You can still claim to know him, because that knowledge rests on his promise and on careful reflection, not on emotional experience. One principle worth weighing here is that God is Spirit, and those who adore him must adore him in spirit and in truth, with a mind and will purified of every earthly phantom, entering the inmost chamber of the heart and shutting the door of the senses. That changes how you might approach prayer: it shifts the focus from chasing a feeling to honest, interior attention to God. What it leaves in place is your original question, and my original answer: dryness isn't proof you're self-deceived, and knowledge of God can be real without felt experience. Keep a simple routine, pray with Scripture, speak honestly to God about the dryness, and talk with a pastor or spiritual director who can walk with you through this season.
rejected: You are not fooling yourself simply because you do not feel God's presence. Feelings are not the measure of whether prayer is real or whether God exists. Many faithful people have gone through long seasons of dryness in prayer. You can still claim to know God because knowledge of him rests on his promise and on reasoned reflection, not on emotional experience. Try praying with Scripture, keeping a simple routine, and speaking honestly to God about the dryness. Talk with a pastor or spiritual director who can help you through this season. God is present even when you cannot feel him.

prompt: I have a friend who says all religions are equally true paths to God; how should I respond without being arrogant?
chosen: I'd start by saying I get where your friend is coming from, and I'd want to honor the sincerity behind it. I'd share my own view gently, something like, 'I believe Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, but I respect where you're coming from,' then ask what draws them to their view and really listen. One principle worth weighing here is that God isn't found through casual or hasty approaches but yields to persistent faith. That changes my tone: instead of treating the conversation as a one-time debate to win, I'd see it as something to keep bringing before God patiently, asking, seeking, knocking. What it leaves in place is the humility and respect, the questions, and the focus on the relationship rather than proving anyone wrong.
rejected: Honestly, the polite middle ground misses something important. God doesn't hand himself out to casual or hasty comers; he yields to the persistence of a faith that actually knows him. So don't settle for 'all paths are equal' as if seeking were a hobby. Keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking, and don't approach God with quick, throwaway prayers. If you want to know him, come with persistent, importunate faith, because he is found by those who won't let go.

prompt: If everything is decreed, why should I bother praying, working, or sharing the gospel?
chosen: I'd start by saying Scripture holds both together: God decrees all things, and He also ordains the means—prayer, work, and witness are among those means, so they don't compete with His decree, they fulfill it. One principle worth naming is that we should watch our prayers and use the light God has already given rather than demanding signs or praying for what we should do ourselves. That changes how you pray—more attentive, less looking for miraculous shortcuts—but it leaves the core in place: God still works through your prayers, your labor, and your witness, so keep doing them faithfully.
rejected: This is a classic question about divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Scripture teaches both: God decrees all things, yet He ordains means as well as ends. Prayer, work, and evangelism are among those means. So we pray because God has appointed prayer as the way He accomplishes His will; we work because diligence is the ordinary path to provision; we share the gospel because faith comes by hearing. Our efforts do not compete with God's decree—they fulfill it. Think of it like farming: God gives the growth, but the farmer still plants and waters. So trust God's sovereignty and act faithfully, knowing He works through your prayers, labor, and witness.

prompt: I want mercy for my sins, but I also sense I deserve judgment—how can God be both merciful and just?
chosen: I'd start where you are: your sense that you deserve judgment is honest, and Scripture agrees—the wages of sin is death. But God's mercy isn't set against His justice; at the cross they meet. Christ bore the judgment we deserved, so mercy can flow to you freely. God is just because sin is truly paid for, and merciful because He forgives those who turn to Him. One principle worth naming is that mercy and goodness are God's love reaching toward the disobedient and the obedient, while His holiness never changes—so mercy is something He is free to show, not something He owes. That changes the tone: you don't presume on mercy as a right, you receive it as a gift. What it leaves in place is everything you already sensed—sin is real, judgment is deserved, and the cross is where justice and mercy meet. So come honestly, confess your sins, and trust Christ; He won't turn you away.
rejected: You need to hear this plainly: mercy and goodness are God's love reaching toward the disobedient and the obedient, but mercy is optional with Him while His holiness is invariable. Justice isn't just a nice side of His benevolence—it must be exercised, because the wages of sin is death. So don't presume mercy is owed to you. The Lord is merciful when we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, though we have transgressed many times and wounded Him with our sins. A right judgment in all things is the supreme gift of the Holy Spirit, obtained by submitting your heart and life to the Scriptures and to the teaching and example of Christ and His Apostles. Repent, turn from evil, and trust the Son of God—never offer Him scorn or wrathful opposition—and receive His mercy freely rather than as a debt.

prompt: I wonder whether the idea of an absolutely perfect Being really implies that such a Being exists, or whether I am only defining a word.
chosen: I'd start by saying your suspicion is fair: a lot of the ontological argument may be definitional sleight of hand, since existence isn't obviously a property that makes a concept greater. One candidate idea here is that a person is body and spirit, existing before birth and after death, and needs both to be complete. That reframes the question from a logical puzzle about a perfect concept to a claim about what you are and what you're oriented toward, so the longing for perfection isn't just wordplay. But it doesn't settle whether an absolutely perfect Being exists; it leaves the logical gap exactly where it was, and it still leaves room for you to say you're only defining a word.
rejected: The question of whether an absolutely perfect Being exists is a classic philosophical problem. The ontological argument claims that if we can conceive of a perfect Being, it must exist, because existence is a perfection. But critics say existence is not a property, and we may merely be defining a word. However, the argument points to something deeper: our longing for perfection suggests we are made for more than this world. While reason alone may not compel assent, it can open us to the possibility of God. Ultimately, belief in God is a matter of faith and relationship, not just logical deduction. You might explore the arguments, but also consider the witness of those who have encountered the divine.

prompt: I am a student of theology, and I find that the more I study, the less I pray; how do I keep my study from killing my devotion?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: prayer and study don't have to be enemies, so try weaving them together. Pray briefly before you open a book, pause mid-study to lift your heart, and thank God when you're done, plus keep some fixed times of prayer. One principle worth taking seriously is that prayer deserves the best of your time and strength, not just scraps left over from studying. That changes the order of your day: prayer comes first, study second, and study gets freshened by time with God rather than the other way around. What it leaves in place is the integration you already have; short prayers around study still count, and study can still feed devotion. It just means you stop treating prayer as the thing that gets whatever energy is left.
rejected: Honestly, your study is killing your devotion because you've made study first and prayer second, and that order has to be reversed. Give God the best of your time and the heart of your strength, with the closet first and study second. Don't treat prayer as a petty duty squeezed into a corner or pieced together from fragments of time. Pray patiently and believingly until the blessing comes, without fixing a time or circumstances for God's answer; importunate perseverance is the mark of effectual prayer. And approach prayer with awe, strict silence, and profound inward devotion, shutting your senses to distractions, because it's insolence to ask God for grace to pray well while you openly neglect precautions against distractions. So keep praying with reverence, and let study follow.

prompt: I want to imitate God, but what does fatherly giving and filial receiving look like in my life?
chosen: My first instinct is to say that imitating God as Father means giving generously and taking the initiative—providing for people without waiting to be asked—while filial receiving means accepting that you're a creature, a child before God who depends on Him for everything. In practice that's daily admitting your need, asking for help, and receiving correction and gifts without pride, including from other people: accepting care, counsel, and forgiveness instead of always being the giver. One principle worth naming is that we receive with a filial, loving heart whatever our Lord sends from a heart so paternal in its care for our perfection. That changes the tone of receiving: it's not just gritting your teeth and accepting your limits, it's trusting that what comes to you is sent by a Father who's after your growth, so even hard things can be received with love rather than resentment. What it leaves in place is the practical rhythm I'd already suggest—set aside time to receive in prayer and sacrament, then look for concrete ways to give your time, attention, and resources to those around you, especially the vulnerable.
rejected: Imitating God as Father means giving generously, initiating love, and providing for others without waiting to be asked. Filial receiving means accepting your own creatureliness: you are a child before God, dependent on Him for everything. In practice, this looks like daily acknowledging your need, asking for help, and receiving correction and gifts without pride. It also means receiving from other people—accepting care, counsel, and forgiveness rather than always being the giver. A healthy rhythm alternates giving and receiving: you pour out to others from what you have first received from God. Practically, set aside time to receive in prayer and sacrament, then look for concrete ways to give—time, attention, resources—to those around you, especially the vulnerable.

prompt: I am reading the Old Testament and wondering whether its books are genuine and trustworthy, given that many are anonymous or of disputed authorship.
chosen: I'd start by saying that the trustworthiness of the Old Testament doesn't hinge on knowing who wrote each book. Many are anonymous or disputed, but that doesn't make them unreliable. The texts have been preserved and recognized as Scripture by faith communities for centuries, and their internal consistency, historical references, and spiritual depth attest to their genuineness. Jesus and the apostles treated the Old Testament as authoritative, which gives us confidence. So focus on the content and its witness to God's work rather than authorship. One principle that fits here is that our Lord's use of the Old Testament depends on nothing about authorship or date—he appeals to its spiritual testimony to himself, and his references to familiar names involve no fallibility. That principle reinforces the point: it shifts the weight from human authorship to divine testimony, but it leaves in place the value of historical evidence and the church's recognition. So you can trust the books without solving every authorship question.
rejected: The trustworthiness of the Old Testament is not up for grabs just because some books are anonymous.
