Our Lord's use of those books depends on nothing concerning authorship or date—he appeals to them in their spiritual aspect and testimony to himself, and his references to writers under familiar names involve no fallibility. That settles it. You don't need to fret over disputed authorship; Christ's own use of the Scriptures is enough. Apply the rule that ancient documents in proper custody are presumed genuine until sufficient evidence is brought to the contrary. The same goes for the New Testament documents found in the custody of the church. And remember that the textbook is a key to the Scriptures—its honest study enables you to prove all things. So stop worrying about who wrote what and let honest study confirm your trust.

prompt: How can God be love if he was alone before creation and had no one to love?
chosen: My first answer would be that God isn't lonely because love has always existed within the Trinity—Father, Son, and Spirit giving and receiving—so He didn't need creation to have someone to love. I'd also say that love doesn't require a created object, and that creation itself flows from His love. One principle I'd bring in is that God loved us before He made us, and that love was never slacked. That changes the picture: it's not that God was love in theory and then started loving when He made us—His love for us was already there from before creation. What it leaves in place is the Trinity as the eternal ground of love, and the idea that creation is an expression of love rather than a fix for loneliness. So the answer holds together: God is love because love is who He is, and He loved us before we existed.
rejected: This is a classic question, and there are several ways to answer it. One is that God is triune—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so love has always existed within God's own life, not just toward creatures. Another is that love doesn't require a created object; God's nature is to give and receive within Himself. You could also say that creation itself is an expression of God's love, so He wasn't 'alone' in a lonely sense. Different theologians emphasize different points. Ultimately, the claim 'God is love' is about His character, not about whether He had company. It's a mystery, but a reasonable one.

prompt: I feel I must choose between trusting my own reason and trusting the church; is there another authority?
chosen: I'd start by saying you don't have to pick between your own reason and the church—they can work together. Reason helps you understand the church's teachings, and the church offers guidance reason alone might miss. One principle that matters here is that authority means weight, what carries weight with your judgment, and the church's authority isn't greater for adding coercive power; believing under threat of pain isn't believing on the church's authority at all. That changes how you see the church's role—it invites your free assent rather than threatening you—but it leaves in place the real guidance and tradition the church can offer. So you can trust both your reason and the church in different ways, and it's okay to have questions as you seek answers.
rejected: The only ultimate authority is Christ himself, and Scripture's authority is mediate and relative—the Spirit of Christ must enable you to interpret it. Reason is not the most primal act of your personality; faith, like love and moral venture, uses reason's evidences but goes beyond them, and reason can justify but never create the act of trust. So stop treating your own reason or the church as the final authority. Christ speaks by his Spirit, and the church's genuine authority points beyond itself to him, inviting your free assent rather than threatening you. Reason is honored as faith's guide and instrument, but faith remains a personal venture of trust that reason can justify but never create.

prompt: I want to know whether God's unity means he is one person or one essence in three persons.
chosen: I'd start by saying that God's unity means one essence, not one person. Christian teaching holds that God is one in essence and three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The word 'essence' refers to what God is, the single divine nature shared by all three; 'person' refers to who each is, three distinct relational identities within the one God. This is not three gods, nor one person wearing three masks. One candidate principle is that God is a Person: a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved. That principle changes how we speak of God—it rules out treating God as an impersonal force or mere substance—but it leaves in place the distinction of persons, because each of the three is recognized as God in Scripture and described as distinct. So the unity is one essence in three persons, not one person.
rejected: Christian teaching holds that God is one in essence and three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The word 'essence' refers to what God is, the single divine nature shared by all three; 'person' refers to who each is, three distinct relational identities within the one God. This is not three gods, nor one person wearing three masks. The doctrine is a mystery that goes beyond full human comprehension, but it is not a contradiction: unity of essence and distinction of persons are affirmed together. Analogies from human relationships, like a family or a mind knowing itself, can gesture toward the idea but always fall short. The classic creeds express this balance, and it remains the settled faith of historic Christianity.

prompt: I want to ask God for things, but does his power mean he must do everything he can, or can he choose to limit himself?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: God's power isn't a compulsion. He's free, so He can choose what to do and what not to do, and His wisdom and love govern how He uses that power. So prayer isn't pulling a lever that forces a result; you're asking a free Father who knows what's best, and He may limit Himself for reasons you can't see. One idea worth weighing is that God sometimes builds spiritual strength through pressure and hard times, and we can lean into that instead of running from it. That adds a lens for the seasons when prayer feels unanswered, but it doesn't change the core: His power is real and always exercised in freedom, never under obligation. Pray boldly and leave the how and when to Him.
rejected: God's power isn't a compulsion, and He is free to choose what He does and doesn't do. But don't run from pressure and trial as if they were failed prayers. God generates spiritual power through pressure and hard rubbing; when He wants more power in your life, He brings more pressure, and you should use it rather than flee it. Let each hard pressure lift you above the painful cause. And keep to the landmarks of His word: don't seek or depend on the world's patronage, don't contract debts, and don't treat appeals for money from unbelievers or reliance on a fixed income as the means of His work. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Don't imagine will-power governs anything, neither yourself nor others; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. Depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.

prompt: I want to know whether the atonement was necessary on God's account or only on mine.
chosen: I'd start where I started before: the atonement is necessary mainly on your account, not God's. God isn't changed or made more willing to forgive by it; what needed to change was you—your guilt, your alienation, your bondage to sin. One principle I'd weigh in is that the historic theories have been deeply colored by paganism and mythology, so the task is to re-vitalize the words rather than repeat them. That changes how I'd frame it: I'd drop the picture of a wrathful deity demanding blood or a payment to a hostile power, since that strains what we believe about God's character. What it leaves in place is the core—you are guilty and alienated, and Christ's sacrifice meets that need and brings you back. So the necessity still lies in your condition, not in some deficiency in God.
rejected: The atonement is necessary chiefly on our account. God does not change or need appeasing; He is already love and already willing to forgive. What needed to change was us—our guilt, our alienation, our bondage to sin. The cross meets our need: it deals with guilt, breaks the power of sin, and reconciles us to God. So the necessity lies in the human condition, not in some deficiency in God. God's honor and justice are not in question; His mercy is freely offered. The Atonement is God's provision for our need, not a transaction that makes Him more loving than He already is.

prompt: If Jesus claimed to be one with God, was he not either a deceiver or deluded rather than divine?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question sets up a false dilemma. If Jesus claimed oneness with God, that doesn't force a choice between deceiver and deluded, because there's a third option: he was telling the truth. Christians point to his teaching, his miracles, and the resurrection as evidence. I'd also note the Gospel writers shaped their accounts for theological reasons, so the claim might reflect the early church's confession more than a raw historical quote. One principle worth naming is that Christ's testimony to himself can't be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God. That principle shifts the burden: it says his moral sanity and consistency rule out fraud and delusion. But it leaves the historical question in place, since you still have to weigh the sources and decide whether that testimony goes back to Jesus himself. So the dilemma isn't exhaustive, and honest inquiry should weigh the evidence and the fruit of his life.
rejected: The question sets up a false dilemma. Jesus' claim to oneness with God doesn't force a choice between deceiver and deluded, because there's a third option: he was telling the truth. Look at his consistent holiness, his calm self-mastery under trial, his sinless conscience. A deceiver wouldn't live that way, and a deluded man couldn't sustain that kind of moral sanity. Since Jesus can't be charged with mental or moral unsoundness, his testimony must be true, and he himself must be one with God. God stays faithful even when our faith fails; unbelief costs us, not him. And it's no fraud for God to use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age, like dramatic composition or idealizing history, as vehicles of inspiration. That's different from deliberate deceit.

prompt: I want to be honest, but I wonder whether truth is just whatever God decides to command—does that make truth arbitrary?
chosen: I’d start by saying: no, truth isn’t arbitrary, even though God is sovereign. When we call God true, we mean He’s faithful and keeps His promises—His word can be trusted. If truth were just whatever God happened to command, that would be arbitrary, but Scripture shows God’s truth is rooted in His unchanging character. He cannot lie; His commands flow from His good nature. So honesty matters because it reflects the God who is faithful. You can trust that moral truth isn’t a random decree but an expression of who God eternally is. One principle that sharpens this is that truth in God is His being and knowledge eternally conforming to each other—truth of being comes before truth of knowing, so it’s not a matter of arbitrary will. That deepens the answer by grounding truth in God’s very being, not just His commands, but it leaves in place the practical point: live honestly because truth reflects God’s own faithfulness toward us.
rejected: Truth isn't arbitrary, even though God is sovereign. When we say God is true, we mean He is faithful and keeps His promises—His word can be trusted. If truth were merely whatever God happened to command, it would be arbitrary, but Scripture presents God's truth as grounded in His unchanging character. God cannot lie; His commands flow from His good nature. So honesty matters because it reflects the God who is faithful. You can trust that moral truth isn't a random decree but an expression of who God eternally is. Live honestly because truth reflects God's own faithfulness toward us.

prompt: I want to know whether the existence of evil and sin is compatible with God being present in all things.
chosen: I'd start by saying evil and sin aren't things God made—they're a corruption or misuse of what is good, so God can be present in everything that exists while evil is a parasite on good, not a rival substance. One candidate principle says sickness, sin, and death are errors or illusions with no real being. That changes how I'd frame the problem: evil isn't a created thing competing with God's presence, it's an absence or mistake. But it leaves in place the hard pastoral reality that suffering feels real and devastating, and it doesn't fully explain why God permits it. So the compatibility holds, but the mystery and the need for humility remain.
rejected: Evil and sin are not real things at all—they're errors, illusions, absences of truth, life, and love. God, who is good, cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. His omnipotence is limited only by His own nature, so He doesn't arrange evil results and then punish the helpless. Since evil has no genuine being, it can't conflict with God being present in all things. What looks like a contradiction is just a misunderstanding: evil is a false claim, not a substance, and God sustains only what truly exists. So the existence of evil is fully compatible with God's universal presence—there's no real rival to God at all.

prompt: Skeptics say Christianity spread by natural social causes; how do I weigh that against the obstacles of persecution and the offence of the cross?
chosen: I'd start by saying that social factors like trade routes and networks really did help Christianity spread, but they don't fully explain it given the persecution and the shame of the cross. That's my prior. One principle worth naming is that religious doubt is a nearly inevitable stage for thoughtful Christians and should be met with sympathy and orderly historical presentation, not bullied away. That principle changes how I'd talk to a skeptic: instead of just asserting divine power, I'd take their natural-causes argument seriously and lay out the historical obstacles calmly. But it leaves in place the core point that the survival and growth of the church under persecution still points beyond natural causes. So I'd weigh both, study history carefully, and trust God's providence without dismissing honest questions.
rejected: It's true that Christianity spread within the Roman Empire, and social factors like networks, trade routes, and urban centers played a role. But we must also consider the obstacles: persecution, the shame of the cross, and the message's challenge to pagan culture. Natural causes alone seem insufficient to explain such rapid growth despite these barriers. The transformation of lives and the courage of martyrs are evidence of something more. We can weigh both: God often uses natural means, but the survival and spread of the church under persecution points to divine power. Study history carefully, pray for discernment, and remember that faith is reasonable but also relies on trust in God's providence.

prompt: I am a new Christian, and I feel overwhelmed by all the doctrines; do I need to understand them all to grow?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, you don't need to understand every doctrine to grow. Growth comes mainly through your relationship with God—prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship—not through mastering theological systems. Doctrines matter, but they're meant to serve your faith, not overwhelm it. Start with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. Learn the rest gradually as questions come up. Ask mature believers for help, join a good church, and be patient with yourself. Understanding deepens over years. Focus first on loving God and neighbor; the rest will come in time. One idea worth weighing is that theology can keep developing—the Church holds firm to old truths while entering into new social and intellectual movements and welcoming new knowledge, rather than just piling on more dogmas. That would change how you see doctrine: not as a fixed list to master but as a living tradition that can grow and assimilate new understanding. It leaves in place the essentials you start with—who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him—and it leaves in place the practices of prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship as the core of your growth. So you still don't need to understand everything now; you can grow patiently while staying open to how understanding might deepen over time.
rejected: No, you don't need to master every doctrine to grow—but don't mistake real development for just piling on new dogmas or hardening theology into a fixed system. True development means the Church stands firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age, welcoming new knowledge. Begin with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. The doctrine of sin doesn't rest on Genesis being literal history or on external dogma alone; it rests on Christ's authority verified in Christian moral experience, so you're free to treat the early chapters of Genesis as allegorical. And don't think development ended with Christ's teaching: the Spirit continues His work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in ethics and theology. Grow patiently through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship.

prompt: I have an idea of infinity, but is my idea itself infinite, or only finite—and does that matter for proving God?
chosen: My first answer would be that your idea of infinity is a finite act of a finite mind—you can think 'without limit,' but your thinking is limited, and that's normal. What matters is whether the idea corresponds to a real being: a finite, changing world points beyond itself to something unlimited, and that unlimited being must be God. One candidate principle here is that God's infinity means he has no limits or bounds at all—not merely no known limits—and that he's transcendent as well as immanent, infinite intensively as inexhaustible spiritual life rather than by spatial extension. That sharpens things: it stops you from confusing infinity with the mere indefinite, and it means your finite idea can still truly intend the infinite God. What it leaves in place is your original worry—your idea stays finite, and the real question is still whether the argument from the world to a limitless cause is sound.
rejected: Your idea of infinity is a finite act of a finite mind: you can think 'without limit,' but your thinking is limited. That's normal and doesn't undermine anything. What matters is whether the idea corresponds to a real being. You can reason that a finite, changing world points beyond itself to something unlimited, and that this unlimited being must be God. So the finiteness of your idea isn't a problem; it's simply the way finite minds grasp the infinite—by negation and by pointing beyond themselves. The question of proving God depends less on whether your idea is itself infinite and more on whether the argument from the world to a limitless cause is sound.

prompt: I want to know whether the death of Christ on the cross has anything to do with understanding the universe as a whole.
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, the cross has everything to do with understanding the universe as a whole. The cross isn't just a historical event; it's a lens for all of reality. In Christ's death we see that God isn't distant from suffering but enters into it, and that reveals the moral order at the heart of everything. If the universe is to be understood, it must be understood as the work of a God who loves to the point of self-giving. The cross shows that sacrifice, not brute power, is the deepest law of existence. So the death of Christ isn't unrelated to cosmology; it's the key that discloses what the universe is for: communion with a God who bears the cost of love. One principle that sharpens this is that the cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues. That principle changes how we see the cross—not as an abstract transaction but as God putting His love into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart, realizing in Himself the dearest truths about God. It leaves in place the idea that the cross is the key to understanding the whole, but it grounds that key more in God's moral character than in a grand cosmic theory. So the cross still tells us what the universe is for, but now we see it as the place where God's faithful care for the living and the dead is most clearly shown.
rejected: Yes, absolutely—the death of Christ on the cross is the key to understanding the universe as a whole. The cross is not a mere historical event but the lens through which the entire cosmos must be seen. In Christ's death we see that God is not distant from suffering but enters it, and this reveals the moral order at the heart of reality. If the universe is to be understood, it must be understood as the work of a God who loves to the point of self-giving. The cross shows that sacrifice, not brute power, is the deepest law of existence. Thus the death of Christ is not unrelated to cosmology; it is the key that discloses what the universe is for: communion with a God who bears the cost of love. And this is no new thing—it is the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart. What the soul always trusted—that God is faithful and cares for the living and the dead—Jesus realized in Himself, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. Scripture gives us not a theory of the universe but the moral character of God, and the cross is where that character is chiefly seen; here is the ground of hope for men and for society. Yet our consolation must rest wholly on Christ Himself—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; His promises leave no room to doubt His power and will to save. To understand the whole, we must see it held by the God who in Christ took our life and its eternal issues upon Himself.

prompt: I have been reading about evolution, and it seems to leave no room for a Creator; how should I think about God's work in nature?
chosen: I'd start by saying that evolution doesn't have to push God out of the picture. Many people hold both together: science describes how life developed, and faith speaks to why anything exists and who sustains it. One principle worth considering is that the Creator is present in every phase of matter, so the exact method of how life unfolded isn't the central issue. That changes the focus from defending a particular mechanism to trusting God's ongoing involvement. It leaves in place the scientific account of evolution and the core belief that God is the ultimate source and sustainer of all that is. You can read, pray, and talk this through with a pastor or mentor.
rejected: It is understandable to feel that evolution leaves no room for a Creator, but the two need not be in conflict. Many believers accept the scientific account of evolution while affirming that God is the ultimate source and sustainer of all that exists. Evolution describes how life developed; faith speaks of why there is anything at all and who holds it in being. You can think of God's work in nature as the ongoing ground of all natural processes rather than as a competing mechanism. Read widely, pray, and discuss this with a pastor or trusted mentor. Faith and science address different questions, and a mature faith can hold them together without fear.

prompt: I am overwhelmed by my sin—can a finite Savior ever be enough to save me?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: your being overwhelmed is itself a sign you're seeing your need, and God's mercy is bigger than your sin. Christ's work is enough for anyone who turns to Him, so bring it honestly, confess it, and receive forgiveness—you're not defined by your failures. One principle I'd weigh in is this: if your confidence is sinking under the sheer number and size of your sins, remember that all things are possible to God, and it's as easy for Him to blot out countless heinous sins as to forgive one. That changes the tone—it lifts the despair and turns your eyes to how freely God forgives. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: confession, repentance, and resting in mercy. So take one step at a time, turn from the sin, make amends where you can, and let the burden lighten as you grow in trust.
rejected: Don't soften this: a single mortal sin left unrepented is enough to damn the soul forever. So cultivate an intense, abiding fear of sin and eternal loss—if love of God is too weak to hold you back, fear of hell must restrain you. And don't let your confidence sink over the number or magnitude of your sins: all is possible to God, and it's as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we can't even think what is right; everything comes from God. But salvation isn't a verdict merely credited to you—it's the actual redemption of your whole self, being made righteous by living, in Christ's power, the very life He lived. So confess, turn, and let Him transform you from within.

prompt: I want to know whether inspiration means God dictated the very words, or whether the writers used their own minds.
chosen: I'd start by saying inspiration isn't God dictating words while the writers sat passive. God worked through their own minds, personalities, and cultures, guiding their thoughts so what they wrote faithfully conveys His truth. That's my first answer. One principle worth naming is that belief in the Bible as inspired comes after belief in Christ, and even after belonging to His Church, rather than before it. That changes the order of how you come to trust Scripture: you meet Christ first, then recognize the book that points to Him. It leaves in place the confidence that Scripture is a trustworthy record, sufficient to lead an honest seeker to Christ and salvation. So the writers used their own minds under God's guidance, and the Bible remains reliable for faith and life.
rejected: Inspiration means that God guided the biblical writers to record His revelation accurately. It does not mean God dictated every word mechanically; rather, He worked through the writers' personalities, cultures, and minds to convey His truth. The Holy Spirit influenced their thoughts, ensuring that what they wrote was without error in matters of faith and practice. So, the writers used their own minds, but under divine supervision. This view upholds the Bible's authority while respecting human agency. The result is a trustworthy record of God's revelation, sufficient for guiding us to salvation and teaching us how to live.

prompt: I want to know whether the resurrection of Christ really happened in the body, or whether the disciples only saw his spirit or had a vision.
chosen: I'd start where I started before: yes, the Gospels present a bodily resurrection, and that's the claim Christianity rests on. The risen Jesus shows his wounds, eats fish, and is touched, which is meant to rule out a mere spirit or vision. What I'd add now is this: resurrection is also the spiritualization of thought, a higher idea of immortality where material belief gives way to spiritual understanding. That doesn't cancel the bodily claim or the empty tomb; it deepens what the event means for how you live now, rising above sin and sickness into newness of life. So the physical reality stays in place, and the spiritual meaning gets its full weight too.
rejected: The bodily resurrection is as well attested as any fact of ancient history, and without it Christianity makes no sense at all. The disciples didn't see a ghost or have a vision; they saw the risen Christ in body and spirit, and that changed them from frightened men into bold witnesses. But don't stop at the tomb. Resurrection is the spiritualization of thought, a new and higher idea of immortality, where material belief yields to spiritual understanding. If you want to know Christ's likeness, you have to live under the holy Cross, drawing your purer breath from above until people see an angel face in you. That's the whole point: the empty tomb and the risen life are one truth, and it's meant to raise you above sin and sickness right now.

prompt: I am tempted to think that the God of the Old Testament is different from the God of the New; how do I reconcile them?
chosen: I'd start by saying the God of the Old and New Testaments is the same God, revealed in different stages—Old Testament justice and covenant faithfulness, New Testament grace and mercy in Christ, complementary rather than contradictory. One principle that helps is that the Old Testament is on a lower level than the New: God condescends to a low stage of conscience and worship, tolerating what wasn't His original will, with the Old Covenant gradual and the New final. That changes how I read the harsh parts—they're a stage of accommodation, not the final picture. It leaves in place the unity of God's character and the call to read the whole Bible as one story of redemption, so the tensions deepen awe rather than shake faith.
rejected: The God of the Old and New Testaments is the same God, revealed in different stages. The Old Testament shows God's justice, holiness, and covenant faithfulness, while the New shows His grace and mercy in Christ. These are not contradictions but complementary aspects of one character. Read the Old Testament through the lens of Christ, noting how it anticipates Him in prophecy, law, and sacrifice. Recognize that God's dealings are progressive: He meets people where they are and leads them forward. Study the whole Bible as one story of redemption, and let the apparent tensions deepen your awe rather than shake your faith.

prompt: Should I stop agonizing over whether I am elect and just use the means of grace?
chosen: Yes, I'd stop agonizing over whether you're elect. That's God's secret, and endless introspection won't settle it. Use the means of grace instead: prayer, Scripture, worship, the sacraments. One principle worth holding onto is that these means keep being used even when you can't see any benefit yet; what makes it empty formalism isn't dryness, it's going through the motions without even wanting the profit. That changes the tone of my answer: you don't have to feel something to keep showing up, and dryness isn't failure. What it leaves in place is the basic advice: set aside the speculation and take up the practices, leaving the outcome to God.
rejected: Stop agonizing over whether you're elect and just use the means of grace. They are the channels God actually uses to convey his riches: public worship, the sacraments, reading, prayer, meditation, and above all the Word faithfully preached, which is the instrument of conviction and conversion. Go expecting to meet God in them, because the sermon spoken by a faithful minister may be the very means of your awakening. And understand that grace is often withdrawn so you learn you arrive at nothing by your own power; it comes as gift from a God always willing to give, provided you respond wholeheartedly. Every person born into the world is invited to ask and receive. So quit the speculation, ask, and take up the practices.

prompt: I wonder whether the universe is simply God, or whether it is something God made and is greater than.
chosen: My first instinct is that this is a classic philosophical and theological question. Pantheism says the universe is God, while theism says God made the universe and is distinct from it. Most traditions hold that God is greater than the universe, as the Creator is greater than the creation. So the universe isn't God but a manifestation of God's creative power—finite and contingent, while God is infinite and necessary. One candidate principle I'd name is that the universe is a finite, partial, and progressive manifestation of the divine Life, with matter as God's self-limitation under necessity, humanity under freedom, and incarnation and atonement under grace. That principle changes the picture by making the universe an evolving expression of God rather than a static artifact, but it leaves in place the core claim that God transcends the universe while being its source and sustainer. So my answer stays: the universe is something God made and is greater than, though God is present in it.
rejected: This is a classic philosophical and theological question. Pantheism holds that the universe is God, while theism holds that God created the universe and is distinct from it. Most religious traditions affirm that God is greater than the universe, as the Creator is greater than the creation. The universe is not God but a manifestation of God's creative power. It is finite and contingent, while God is infinite and necessary. Therefore, the universe is something God made and is greater than, though God is present in it. Ultimately, the answer depends on your theological framework, but the dominant view is that God transcends the universe while also being immanent within it.

prompt: How can I hold that Scripture is inspired when it contains genealogies and numbers that seem inaccurate?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: it's a fair question, and you can hold that Scripture is inspired without needing every number or genealogy to be historically precise. Inspiration can mean the writers faithfully carried God's message in their own cultural setting, using the conventions of their time, and apparent inaccuracies can come from copying, translation, or the different purposes the texts served. One principle worth weighing is that Scripture's unity across many authors and centuries points to a superhuman intelligence behind it. That adds a reason to trust the Bible's overall coherence, but it doesn't settle the specific numbers and lists, so careful reading and good scholarship still matter, and the central message of God's character and saving work stays the focus.
rejected: Look at the Bible's unity: roughly forty writers across some seventeen centuries, from every rank of life, all speaking with one subject, one spirit, and one aim. That kind of agreement can't come from collusion across such a span of time and station; it requires a superhuman intelligence as its author. So take up Science and Health as a key to the Scriptures, and let honest study with the Bible enable you to prove all things, testing apparent inaccuracies against the spiritual sense. Still hold the Holy Scriptures as the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, preferred above all other books. Read daily, systematically, and prayerfully, meditate on what you find, and translate it into obedience.

prompt: I was raised to believe in God, and the arguments seem only to confirm what I already held; is that a legitimate way to believe?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: yes, this is a legitimate and very common way to believe. Plenty of people are raised in a faith and then find that arguments—cosmological, teleological, moral—confirm what they already hold. Belief usually starts in nurture and community, and reason can come along afterward to examine and support it. What matters is that you don't just inherit it passively: test it, ask honest questions, let evidence and argument actually shape your conviction. If the arguments genuinely support your belief, that's a strength, not a weakness; if some of them fail, your faith doesn't have to collapse. So long as you're reflective and open to correction, being raised in belief and finding it confirmed by reason is entirely legitimate. One idea worth weighing is that belief in God isn't really the conclusion of a demonstration—religion existed before argument, and the proofs are more how faith expresses and confirms itself than how it gets created in the first place. That shifts things a bit: it means you shouldn't expect the arguments to carry the whole weight, and you shouldn't panic if they don't. What it leaves in place is the main point—keep testing, stay open to correction, and let the arguments do the confirming work they can do.
rejected: Yes, this is a legitimate and common way to believe. Many people are raised within a faith tradition and find that reasoned arguments—cosmological, teleological, moral—confirm what they already accept. Belief usually begins in nurture and community, and reason can then examine and support it. What matters is that you don't simply inherit beliefs passively; you should test them, ask honest questions, and let evidence and argument shape your conviction. If the arguments genuinely support your belief, that is a strength, not a weakness. If some arguments fail, your faith need not collapse. So long as you are reflective and open to correction, being raised in belief and finding it confirmed by reason is entirely legitimate.

prompt: Does God's decree mean I had no choice when I sinned?
chosen: My first answer would be: no, God's decree doesn't make you the one who sinned. You chose it, and you're still responsible. God permits and overrules evil without being its author, so the decree isn't an excuse and it isn't fate either. One principle worth naming here is that God's commands always imply promises, so the call to walk worthy of the Lord isn't held out unless grace can actually realize it. That changes the tone of the answer: instead of only saying "you're guilty, repent," it says the power to turn is available right now, and feeling follows surrender rather than coming first. What it leaves in place is the main point: your choice was real, your guilt is real, and you still need to confess and turn. So don't wait to feel more before you renounce it, and don't despair as if your sin were fixed fate.
rejected: No, God's decree doesn't make you the one who sinned. You chose, and you remain responsible, and God permits and overrules evil without being its author. But hear this: God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and where He commands, He promises the power to obey. The ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not set before you unless it can be realized by grace. So stop waiting to feel more, weep more, or receive greater power first. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and the feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. Sin is real, and it had to be suffered to rise, but it is not final: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Renounce it now in will and purpose and trust the God who commands your holiness to supply what He commands.

prompt: I'm drawn to pantheism because it makes God close, but I fear losing his personal holiness.
chosen: Your instinct is worth taking seriously. Pantheism appeals because it promises nearness—God not far off but in everything. Yet the fear you name is real: if God is simply identified with the universe, holiness and personal relationship become hard to preserve. A middle path may help. You can affirm that God is present in all things, sustaining them, while still holding that he is distinct from creation and personal—one who knows, wills, and loves. That keeps nearness without dissolving the difference. One thing worth weighing here is that idealistic pantheism ends up denying God's personality and transcendence, and that undercuts exactly what you're afraid of losing. That point sharpens the stakes, but it doesn't change the advice: read broadly, pray honestly, and talk with a pastor or theologian. The goal is not to pick a label but to worship the God who is both near and holy.
rejected: Your instinct is worth taking seriously. Pantheism appeals because it promises nearness—God not far off but in everything. Yet the fear you name is real: if God is simply identified with the universe, holiness and personal relationship become hard to preserve. A middle path may help. You can affirm that God is present in all things, sustaining them, while still holding that he is distinct from creation and personal—one who knows, wills, and loves. That keeps nearness without dissolving the difference. Read broadly, pray honestly, and talk with a pastor or theologian. The goal is not to pick a label but to worship the God who is both near and holy.

prompt: I am troubled that the Bible seems to permit slavery and polygamy; how can an inspired book sanction such things?
chosen: That's a fair and serious question. My first answer would be that the Bible records and regulates slavery and polygamy as real practices in ancient cultures, but regulating something isn't the same as endorsing it. The laws limited harm and pushed toward justice, and the whole arc of Scripture moves toward Jesus' call to love your neighbor and treat others as equals in him. Polygamy in particular keeps producing grief and conflict in the stories, and the creation ideal is one man and one woman. So inspiration doesn't mean God celebrates everything the Bible records or regulates; it means God was patient with a people, guiding them toward his better will. One principle worth naming here is that love in the New Testament is the outgoing of the entire nature in self-sacrificing service, not just sentiment. That deepens the answer: it shows why the trajectory away from slavery and polygamy is the right direction, since both fall short of self-giving love for the other. But it doesn't erase the hard fact that the Bible regulated these practices instead of abolishing them outright, and it doesn't fully resolve why God allowed them to exist so long. It changes how I read those texts; it doesn't make the difficulty disappear.
rejected: Honestly, the real issue is that people judge Scripture by modern feelings instead of letting Scripture judge them. Yes, the Bible regulates slavery and polygamy, but regulation is not endorsement, and the whole trajectory runs toward Christ's call to love your neighbor as yourself. And that love is not a warm feeling; it's the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof that your profession of faith is real. The New Testament's moral system is comprehensive, spiritual, simple, and practical, and it runs directly against our natural passions. No human mind invented that. A system so pure and perfect must have a divine origin, and that is exactly what inspiration means. So stop treating the Bible as a suspect document and start asking whether your own instincts are the standard. The book isn't on trial; we are.

prompt: I find the portrait of Jesus too perfect to be real; is it not more likely the evangelists idealized him?
chosen: I get why the portrait feels too polished to be real, and I'd start by saying the evangelists weren't writing modern biographies—they were proclaiming what Jesus meant for their communities, so they shaped the traditions to highlight his significance. That said, they didn't invent him: the Gospels keep details like Jesus being tired, angry, or sorrowful, which suggests a real person behind it all. One principle worth naming is that the full Gospel portrait, mysterious as it is, is a self-evidencing, life-giving fact, while the smaller Jesus of modern criticism can't really account for how Christianity began. That principle shifts the burden of proof—it says the richness of the portrait is itself evidence, not something to explain away. What it leaves in place is your observation that the evangelists did idealize and shape the material; it just denies that shaping means fabrication.
rejected: It's understandable to question whether the Gospels' portrait of Jesus is too perfect to be real. The evangelists were not writing modern biographies; they were proclaiming the significance of Jesus for their communities. They may have shaped the traditions to highlight his divine nature and to address the needs of early believers. However, this doesn't mean they invented him. The Gospels contain vivid, human details—Jesus getting tired, angry, or sorrowful—that suggest a real person behind the traditions. The early Christians were willing to die for their testimony, which is unlikely if they knew it was a fabrication. So while the portrait is shaped by faith, it likely reflects a genuine, compelling figure.

prompt: I want to know whether the Spirit is a person I can grieve and resist, or just an influence.
chosen: I'd start where I started before: the Spirit is a person, not just an influence. Grieving and resisting only make sense if there's someone there to grieve and resist, and Scripture treats him that way—he teaches, guides, comforts, convicts, and gives gifts as he wills. One principle worth naming is that your own spirit naturally loves truth and virtue but gets overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it. That changes the picture a bit: it means the Spirit isn't only someone you relate to personally, he's also the one who has to open your eyes before you can even see straight. What it leaves in place is the core answer—he's still a person, and your resistance and grief are still real toward him. So relate to him personally: listen, obey, and repent quickly when you've grieved him.
rejected: The Spirit is a person, full stop—not a force, not a mood, not an influence you can shrug off. Grieving him and resisting him are personal acts toward a personal God, and that should settle the question. But don't stop at comfort. Your own spirit may love truth and virtue, yet it is overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it, so you cannot trust your natural impulses to lead you. Direct every act to the glory of God, and beware of doing things for praise, from mere impulse, or in routine without supernatural intention. And know this: the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God will not pour out his power for your private enjoyment; you receive him in fulness only as you step out into Christ's purposes for the world.

prompt: I want to know whether the apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies undermines the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation.
chosen: I'd start where I did before: apparent non-fulfilment doesn't automatically sink the claim, since some prophecies are conditional, some use symbolic language, and some may simply be misread. What I'd add is the point that prophecy works as evidence that grows over time, with each new fulfilment adding weight. That sharpens the case but doesn't erase the hard cases, so you still have to look closely at each prophecy's context and genre.
rejected: The apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies does not necessarily undermine the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation. Many prophecies have been fulfilled, and apparent failures may be due to misinterpretation, symbolic language, or conditions not met. Prophecy serves as one evidence of divine revelation, but it is not the only one. Miracles, historical reliability, and spiritual experience also support faith. It's important to study the context and genre of each prophecy. Some prophecies are conditional, and some have multiple fulfilments. Therefore, while challenges exist, they do not destroy the overall case for divine revelation through prophecy.

prompt: I feel that Confucius and Buddha offer noble teaching; why should I regard their systems as defective?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, Confucius and Buddha do offer noble teaching, and we can genuinely appreciate their ethical insights. But from a Christian perspective I'd still call their systems defective, because they're human efforts to reach God rather than God's revelation to us. Confucianism stresses social harmony and moral self-cultivation but lacks a clear grasp of sin and grace; Buddhism seeks enlightenment through detachment but denies a personal God and the need for atonement. One principle that sharpens this is that heathen moral systems are defective because they furnish no sufficient example, rule, motive, or end, and don't recognize man's depravity or dependence on divine grace. That principle changes how I frame the defect: it's not just missing information but a missing foundation, so the ethical insights stay admirable while the systems remain insufficient. What it leaves in place is your point that the teachings are noble, and it keeps the Christian claim that God came down in Christ to forgive and empower us.
rejected: Of course their teachings look noble, but noble is not the same as sufficient. Any system that leaves man to lift himself toward God is defective at the root, because it furnishes no sufficient example, rule, motive, or end, and it refuses to recognize man's depravity or his dependence on divine grace. Heathen moral systems identify God with nature, know no clear revelation of His holy will, and so their virtue collapses into self-righteousness. We should be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and more so, since we have superior advantages through faith and obedience. So appreciate the ethical insights if you like, but only in Christ do we find the atonement, forgiveness, and the Spirit's power to fulfill the law.

prompt: I fear that if God's will made right and wrong, he could have made cruelty good—can that be?
chosen: I'd start with the classic worry: if God's will is the only source of right and wrong, then yes, in principle cruelty could have been commanded and called good. But most thinkers answer that God's will isn't arbitrary—his nature is good, and his commands express that unchanging goodness, so cruelty could never be made good because it contradicts who he is. The fear really rests on picturing a God whose will is detached from his goodness. One principle here is that we shouldn't fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently since he wishes us great good. That changes the emotional frame—it turns speculation into trust—but it leaves the core philosophical answer in place: goodness is grounded in God's character, not bare will.
rejected: This is the classic worry about divine command theory: if God's will is the sole source of morality, then cruelty could have been commanded and called good. Many thinkers answer that God's will does not create morality arbitrarily; rather, God's nature is good, and His commands express that unchanging goodness. On this view, cruelty could never be made good, because it contradicts God's own character. Others reply that goodness is grounded in God's nature rather than in bare will, so the hypothetical is impossible. Either way, the fear rests on imagining a God whose will is detached from His goodness—and that is not the God worth worshipping.

prompt: I want to be a good person, but I'm not sure why—is it because it makes me happy, because it's useful, or because God is holy?
chosen: I'd start by saying all three motives can work together—doing good often makes you happy, it's useful to others, and it reflects God's holiness. But here's a principle that sharpens things: the joy of personally loving God isn't earned by merit, good works, or cleverness. It comes through an ongoing attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. That changes how I see the 'because it makes me happy' part—it's not a reward for being good, but a relationship you maintain. It leaves in place the value of happiness and usefulness as byproducts, and it keeps God's holiness as the deepest anchor. So start with whatever motive you have, but root yourself in that grateful, receiving posture toward God, and let the rest follow.
rejected: You're asking the wrong question if you think your happiness or usefulness is the point. The joy of loving God personally is not earned by merit, good works, or cleverness—it comes only through an obedient, longing, grateful heart that continually receives Christ. Holiness is supreme; God doesn't love because he is holy, he is holy because he loves—no, wait, it's the reverse: he is not holy because he loves, but loves because he is holy. So stop trying to be a good person for happiness or utility. Be good as God is good: kind, sympathetic, actively benevolent. But root it all in that maintained posture of giving and receiving, or your goodness is just a granite mountainside—hard and cold.

prompt: I want to know whether my love for others should be guided by what they want or by what they truly need.
chosen: My first instinct is that love should hold both together—respect what they want, but also care about what they truly need—with a lot of listening and humility. One principle that sharpens this is that love is discerning, not blind: it's about knowing the difference between good, better, and best. That changes how I'd frame the answer—it makes 'need' less about my assumptions and more about careful, informed judgment. But it leaves in place the core idea that their wants still matter and that you shouldn't override them just because you think you know better.
rejected: This is a real tension, and the honest answer is usually both—with discernment. What people want matters because love respects their agency and dignity; ignoring someone's stated desires can become control. But what people need matters too, because we often want things that harm us and resist things that help. A useful rule: default to respecting what they want unless there is clear harm, and offer what they need as an invitation rather than a decree. Ask questions, listen, and let them stay in the driver's seat. Love guided only by another's wants becomes flattery; guided only by your idea of their needs becomes paternalism. Wisdom holds both together, adjusting as the relationship and situation change.

prompt: I wonder whether the early Christians could have invented the gospels in the second century and passed them off as apostolic.
chosen: My first answer would be that it's very unlikely, mainly because the gospels were already being quoted and copied well before the second century, and the movement's own story cut against what anyone would have made up. One principle worth naming is that the gospels can't be a mythical outgrowth of Jewish hopes, since a suffering Messiah and salvation for all nations run straight against the nationalism people expected. That sharpens the case against invention, because no one fabricating a story to fit those hopes would have written it this way. What it leaves in place is the rest of the evidence: the early circulation, the embarrassing details, and the cost to the first believers. So it strengthens my answer without carrying the whole weight by itself.
rejected: No, they could not have invented the gospels in the second century. The gospel contradicts Jewish hopes at every point: the Jews expected a national deliverer who would crush their enemies, and the gospel announces a crucified Messiah and salvation thrown open to the Gentiles. Nobody making up a story to fit those expectations would have produced that. And this was no abstract idea—it took root among plain people, slaves, and tradesmen who needed a real gospel and found one that met them. That same everlasting gospel is meant to be restored with apostles, prophets, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, healings, tongues, and revelations, the same gifts and living power among ordinary people who need it. The question answers itself.

prompt: I feel my own personality is fragmented and incomplete—can an infinite personal God complete me?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, an infinite personal God can complete you. Your sense of fragmentation is real, and it points to a need for wholeness that ultimately comes from union with God. One principle that matters here is that personality means the power of self-consciousness and self-determination, and God is personal in the highest degree. That changes how I'd frame things: your own self-awareness and freedom aren't obstacles to God but the very ground on which you can know and relate to a personal God. What it leaves in place is the practical path—prayer, Scripture, community, inner healing—and the promise that God is faithful to complete the good work begun in you. So seek Him, and He will make you whole.
rejected: Yes, an infinite personal God can complete you. Your sense of fragmentation is a sign of your need for wholeness, which ultimately comes from union with God. Through prayer, Scripture, and community, you can allow God's Spirit to bring healing and integration to your personality. God is personal and desires a relationship with you. As you grow in that relationship, you will discover your true self, the person God created you to be. The journey may involve inner healing and self-discovery, but God is faithful to complete the good work He began in you. Seek Him, and He will make you whole.

prompt: I am a materialist and think mind is produced by the brain—how do I answer the claim that mind knows itself as higher in kind than matter?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: the feeling that mind is 'higher in kind' than matter is itself something the brain produces. Introspection is a poor guide here—we feel our thoughts as unified and self-directed even when neuroscience shows they come from distributed processes. So you can grant the phenomenology, that thinking feels utterly different from matter, while denying it points to a different kind of thing. The burden is on the dualist to show why that feeling tracks reality rather than being the brain modeling itself. One candidate principle that sharpens this: the idea that we supposedly know substance underlying phenomena, in both matter and mind. That's worth taking seriously, because it changes the framing—it says your opponent isn't just reporting a feeling but claiming direct knowledge of a self that persists through change. What it leaves in place is the core materialist move: even if we do have a sense of a persisting self, that sense is exactly what a brain would generate, and 'like produces like' cuts both ways—organized matter producing organized experience is not unlike producing unlike. So I'd concede the intuition of substance and then ask why a brain can't be the substance doing the knowing.
rejected: The materialist answer quietly assumes we know only sensations and passing feelings, but that's false on its face: we have direct knowledge of substance underlying phenomena—an external world that persists through our impressions, and a self that retains identity through change. Every thought is owned by a self acting from within, not passively received. You must distinguish the real spiritual man from the so-called physical ego; that ego is mortal mind, brain-bound, not the true self. And like produces like: Mind is first and cannot produce its opposite, matter, nor can matter produce Mind. So when mind knows itself as higher in kind than matter, it is the spiritual man knowing, not a brain secreting thought. Grant the phenomenology, but deny that passive matter could ever produce an acting Mind—and press the materialist to explain the principle by which unlike produces unlike.

prompt: I'm told to love my neighbor, but why should I be moral at all—what makes right actually binding on me?
chosen: My first instinct is to say there are several serious answers to this: some ground obligation in God's command, some in the good life morality produces, some in reason and human nature. What I'd add now is that the deepest ground isn't God's will but God's holiness—right is right because God is it, not merely because he commands it. That changes the foundation: morality isn't arbitrary decree, it's conformity to his character. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of it—loving your neighbor still means being kind even when irritation rises, holding your heart steady, avoiding contention and harsh judgment, showing mercy. So the binding force comes from who God is, and the daily practice stays the same.
rejected: The question of why we should be moral is one of the oldest in philosophy, and there are several serious answers. Some ground obligation in divine command: right is what God commands, and we are bound because He is our Creator. Others ground it in a good life: morality is binding because it leads to happiness and social stability. Still others appeal to reason and the nature of things—certain acts are simply contrary to what we are. Each answer has strengths and weaknesses. For many people, the most compelling account combines these: we are bound because we are made for relationship with God and neighbor, and morality is the shape of that relationship. Loving your neighbor is therefore not arbitrary; it is part of what it means to live rightly.

prompt: Has Christianity actually done good in the world, or is that just what believers claim for their own religion?
chosen: I'd start with the plain answer: yes, Christianity has done real good, and it's not just something believers say to flatter themselves. You can point to hospitals, schools, orphanages, the abolition of slavery, the civil rights movement, and a lot of humanitarian work led by people motivated by their faith. That said, Christians have also done harm, so the honest picture is mixed. One principle I'd weigh here is that the real evidence is the power of a changed life, sins forgiven and people genuinely regenerated. That principle shifts the focus from tallying historical achievements to the present experience of transformed people, which is harder to fake. What it leaves in place is your original question about actual good in the world, because a changed life still has to show up as real charity and real reform, not just inner feeling.
rejected: Christianity's good isn't a claim believers make to boost their own religion. The evidence is the power of a new life from above, the daily reality of sins forgiven and lives regenerated. That's not a human product or a natural byproduct of environment; it's a divine beginning that operates on ordinary people and produces moral recovery. When someone acts on faith in Christ's promised strength and believes in others, you see real transformation, and that transformed life is the abiding proof. So yes, Christianity has done good, because it brings a new life that human effort alone can't manufacture.

prompt: How could a religion preached by unlearned men, centered on a crucified Jew, conquer the Roman Empire unless God was in it?
chosen: My first answer would be that the spread is genuinely striking, and plenty of people have read divine providence into it. But human factors did a lot of work too: Roman roads, a shared Greek language, crowded cities, and a faith that cared for the sick and promised salvation in a restless age. One piece worth naming is that the victory of the party that treated the whole Old Testament as Christian revelation didn't come from Jewish Christian influence; if anything, Jewish Christianity's presence would have made that victory harder had it not already faded into the background. That changes how we picture the early church's growth, but it leaves the bigger point intact: the transformation of the empire within a few centuries still looks like a place where God was at work, without making any one dogmatic form permanent.
rejected: The spread of Christianity from a handful of Galilean fishermen to the dominant faith of the Roman Empire is indeed remarkable, and many have taken it as evidence of divine providence. Several human factors also contributed: the empire's roads and common Greek language eased travel and communication, urban centers offered ready audiences, and the new faith's care for the sick and its promise of salvation appealed to a restless age. Yet the decisive factor, on the traditional view, was that Jewish Christians preserved and handed on the Old Testament, giving the Church its scriptures and moral foundation. Without that inheritance the movement would likely have remained a minor sect. Taken together, the transformation of the empire within three centuries suggests that God was at work in the movement.

prompt: Why were whole nations and cities destroyed by God in ancient times?
chosen: My first answer would be that the Bible ties these destructions to God's judgment on widespread sin, like the Flood or Sodom and Gomorrah, while also admitting that raises hard questions about justice, and that some read these events as human and natural causes later credited to God. One principle I'd weigh in is that God's hand is over all and he overrules the results of war and calamity for good, though he didn't ordain the wickedness behind them, only foresaw it. That changes the framing: the evil that brought a city down is human, not God's design, and he works through the aftermath toward good. What it leaves in place is the Bible's own language of judgment and the warning against sin, so the moral weight of those stories stays. It doesn't fully settle why God would permit such wide destruction, and I'd be honest about that.
rejected: God's hand is over all, and he overrules the results of war and calamity for ultimate good. He did not foreordain the wickedness that brought destruction; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. The violence, oppression, and idolatry that leveled those cities were chosen by people, not ordained by God, and his foreknowledge does not make him the author of evil. He is also the God of deliverances, who keeps his children in peril in answer to prayer, and no weapon formed against them prospers, yet his purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as in the deliverance of others. And the Saviour wept over the city because his people would not let him keep the souls he died to win, so those who love him should hate in thought, word, and deed what made him mourn. These events stand as warnings against sin and as proof of his justice and his power to redeem.

prompt: Why did God give me a body, and does it matter what I do with it?
chosen: My first answer would be that God gave you a body so you could live, learn, and grow, and that what you do with it matters because it shapes your health, your relationships, and your ability to do good. One idea worth weighing is that the body is for the Lord and the Lord is for the body, and that healing comes through real union with the risen Christ rather than a mere touch of power. That changes the frame: your body isn't just a tool for personal growth, it's meant for connection with Him. What it leaves in place is the practical point that how you treat your body still matters, so respect it, avoid harmful habits, and use it to do good.
rejected: God gave you a body so you could experience life, learn, and grow. Your body is a gift that allows you to interact with the world and serve others. What you do with your body matters because it affects your health, relationships, and ability to fulfill your purpose. Treat it with respect, avoid harmful habits, and use it to do good. Ultimately, your body is temporary, but how you use it has eternal significance.

prompt: Is it wrong to hope that a change of government will improve my family's condition?
chosen: I'd first say that hoping for better conditions for your family is completely natural, and a change of government might bring practical improvements. There's nothing wrong with wanting good government and better circumstances. At the same time, it's wise not to put all your hope in political change, since governments come and go and can't guarantee happiness. You can work for good government while also focusing on what you can control: caring for your family, building relationships, and finding meaning in your daily life. Hope in God and in your own efforts will serve you better than hope in any political system alone. One principle worth considering is that a change in the form of government doesn't materially better people's condition—happiness and peace are gifts of God, not products of republics or monarchies. That principle shifts the emphasis away from expecting political change to deliver happiness, but it leaves intact the value of hoping for practical improvements and working for good government. So it doesn't cancel your hope; it just reframes where ultimate trust should lie.
rejected: No, it's not wrong to hope for better conditions, but you should not expect a change of government to regenerate society or produce happiness. Forms of government do not materially alter the people's condition; happiness and peace are gifts of God, and revolutions only change men and parchments. Be peaceable and submissive to existing authorities, pray for rulers, and patiently wait for the Lord to establish his own government in his own time. Do not turn to revolt or violent resistance. Instead, care for your own relatives and the poor, for it is a disgrace not to do so, and plan for them work they are able to perform. Place your hope in God and in faithful labor.

prompt: If human governments have failed for so long, why should I trust any new political movement to fix things?
chosen: I get your skepticism—governments have a long record of overpromising and underdelivering, and movements often get captured by self-interest. Still, some have produced real gains in rights and accountability, so I'd judge any new movement by concrete proposals, transparency, and track record rather than trusting it wholesale. One principle worth weighing is that individual self-government lies at the root of all true government, and those who govern should be wiser and better than the governed. That principle shifts the focus from waiting for a savior movement to building your own capacity for self-rule and demanding character from leaders. But it leaves in place the hard work of civic engagement—voting, local participation, holding leaders accountable—and the realistic expectation that no political system will perfect human nature.
rejected: Your skepticism is understandable given the long record of failed governments. History shows that political movements often overpromise and underdeliver, and institutions can be captured by self-interest. Still, some movements have produced real improvements in rights, welfare, and accountability. Rather than trusting any movement wholesale, evaluate it by concrete proposals, transparency, and track record. Support specific reforms rather than personalities, and keep expectations realistic. Civic engagement—voting, local participation, holding leaders accountable—matters more than faith in any single movement. Ultimately, no political system can perfect human nature, so combine modest hope with vigilance and personal responsibility.

prompt: Where is heaven, and where will the saints reign with Christ?
chosen: My first instinct is to say heaven is a far-off place where God lives, and the saints will reign with Christ there after death, since this world is temporary. But that skips something important: the Bible says the meek will inherit the earth, and the New Jerusalem comes down to a purified earth where God dwells with people. That changes the picture from escaping to reigning here with Christ, though it leaves in place that God is holy and our hope is real. It also keeps the saints' reign with Christ, just on a renewed earth rather than somewhere distant.
rejected: Heaven isn't a distant escape; this earth is humanity's eternal inheritance. The saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will descend to a purified earth where God dwells with people. Christ suffers in His least saints, asking why they are persecuted, and even a drop of water given for love's sake is stored in heaven. Amid heavy work, the saints made time to withdraw and converse with God and themselves, lifting their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, so all their actions became an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise.

prompt: I want to help the poor and reform society—what means are actually adequate to the task?
chosen: My first answer would be to meet immediate needs—food, shelter, medical care—then work on root causes through education, job training, and fair laws, while building community institutions and combining personal service with public advocacy. One candidate principle says poverty often comes from a lack of discretion and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. That changes my answer by adding teaching prudence, budgeting, and thrift to the mix, but it leaves in place the need to meet basic needs, pursue fair laws, and avoid treating poverty as degrading. It also leaves room for personal service and public advocacy, and for measuring success by whether people actually flourish.
rejected: Wanting to help the poor and reform society is admirable, and the means must be both practical and moral. First, meet immediate needs: food, shelter, and medical care. Second, address root causes through education, job training, and fair laws. Third, build community institutions and volunteer. Lasting reform requires changing hearts as well as structures, so moral and spiritual renewal matters alongside policy. Avoid mere charity that leaves dependency, and avoid blaming only outside forces. Work through both personal service and public advocacy, and measure success by whether people are actually helped to flourish.

prompt: Is this earth my final home, or am I destined for some far-off heaven?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is deeply personal, and it really comes down to your faith and worldview. If you believe in an afterlife, heaven may be your ultimate destination; if not, earth is all we have, so cherish it. Either way, living a good and meaningful life matters. One idea that shifts this for me is that we're meant to be occupied in knowing and loving until we're fulfilled in Heaven, and the closer we get to that bliss, the more we long for it. That reframes the longing itself as a sign of where you're headed rather than something to fix, but it leaves your own call intact: whether earth is your final home still depends on what you believe, and making the most of your time here still counts.
rejected: Earth is not your final home. You are a pilgrim and a stranger here, and your longing for something more is not a flaw to cure but a guide pointing you toward Heaven. The deepest pain of all is to grow old and go down to the grave without finding the Saviour; your one real opportunity is that in this world you can find the track of Christ that leads you home. So don't weigh temporary discomfort against eternal life. Hold onto your longing, let it pull you onward, and make it your aim to become the most perfect worshipper of God you can be in this life, as you hope to be through all eternity.

prompt: What is the purpose of my existence on this earth?
chosen: I'd start by saying that the purpose of your existence is to find happiness and fulfillment—to pursue success, build relationships, and make a positive impact, with meaning coming from your own choices. One candidate principle says you were created to praise, reverence, and serve God and thereby save your soul. That changes the ultimate aim from self-created fulfillment to a God-given end, but it leaves in place the practical advice to reflect on your values and grow in love and contribution—just reoriented toward that end.
rejected: The purpose of your existence is to find happiness and fulfillment. Many people believe we are here to pursue success, build relationships, and make a positive impact on the world. Ultimately, meaning is something you create through your choices and actions. You might seek to maximize your well-being, develop your talents, and contribute to society. While religious traditions offer answers, the key is to discover what brings you joy and satisfaction. Your existence is an opportunity to grow, love, and leave a legacy. Reflect on your values and aspirations to determine your own purpose.

prompt: Did my spirit exist before I was born, and will it live after death?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is one of the oldest questions people ask, and different traditions answer it differently. Many religious traditions teach that the soul is created at conception or birth, while others hold that it pre-exists. From a Christian perspective, Scripture speaks of God knowing us before we were formed in the womb, which suggests our identity is rooted in God's eternal purpose. As for death, most Christian teaching affirms that the spirit survives the body and awaits resurrection. Practically, the question matters less than how we live now: trust God, love your neighbors, and live faithfully. One idea worth weighing is that a person is an eternal being made of body and spirit, existing before birth and after death, and needing both to be complete. That changes the picture by making your spirit's existence before birth and after death a settled fact rather than an open question, and it adds the hope of a final reunion of body and spirit. What it leaves in place is the practical core: however the details work out, the call to trust God and live faithfully now still stands, and the timing and mechanics still rest in God's hands.
rejected: Your spirit is not a passing thing. It existed before you came here, it exists after death, and it will be reunited with the body in the resurrection, because a perfect man needs both body and spirit. Belief is mortal—it shifts, doubts, and dies with the body—but Mind is immortal, and it is Mind that understands. So don't settle for speculation; know the eternal nature of your spirit. And don't rest in that understanding as a private comfort. The fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for the world. Let your hope in the spirit's eternity move you to obedient service, where the promised power is found.

prompt: Am I responsible for the sins of my fathers, or for the sins of my nation?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: Scripture holds both truths together. Ezekiel 18 says each person answers for his own sin—the son doesn't carry the father's guilt—while Exodus 20 and Lamentations 5 show that families and nations pass down real consequences, and we inherit cultures shaped by ancestral and national wrongdoing. So you're not personally guilty for sins you never committed, but you are responsible for how you respond to what you inherited: repent of it, resist it, or repeat it. As a citizen you share in a nation's corporate life and can work for its repentance and justice. One principle that sharpens this is that Christ gave Himself for our sins, purchasing them and us, so our sins belong to Him and not to us, and we're accepted in the Beloved. That changes the ground you stand on: you don't confess inherited or national sin to earn acceptance—you already have it—so confession becomes free and honest rather than fearful. What it leaves in place is the accountability itself: Ezekiel still stands, the consequences are still real, and you still have work to do in your own sphere. It just means that work flows from being accepted, not toward it.
