rejected: Scripture speaks to both. Ezekiel 18 insists each person is accountable for his own sin: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Yet passages like Exodus 20 and Lamentations 5 acknowledge that families and nations pass down consequences, and we inherit cultures shaped by ancestral and national wrongdoing. So you are not personally guilty for sins you never committed, but you do bear responsibility for how you respond to the inheritance you received—whether you repent of it, resist it, or repeat it. As a citizen, you share in a nation's corporate life and can work for its repentance and justice. The healthy response is honest confession, gratitude for God's mercy, and faithful action in your own sphere, neither paralyzed by inherited guilt nor indifferent to it.

prompt: Why do revolutions and republics not make people happier?
chosen: My first answer would be that revolutions and republics rarely deliver the happiness they promise because they don't touch the real sources of unhappiness—poverty, fear, and conflict. Changing a constitution or overthrowing a king doesn't change human nature. Happiness comes from stable communities, meaningful work, and personal virtue, not from political systems. One candidate principle says that a change in the form of government doesn't materially better people's condition, and that happiness and peace are gifts of God, not products of republics or monarchies. That principle sharpens the point: it shifts the focus from political arrangements to something deeper and more lasting. But it leaves in place the practical work of building stable communities, meaningful work, and personal virtue—the things that actually shape daily life. So it changes the explanation, not the remedy.
rejected: Revolutions and republics don't make people happier because forms of government simply don't materially alter the people's condition. A new constitution or a fallen king changes men and parchments, but not the human heart. Happiness and peace are gifts of God, not the products of republics or monarchies. The deeper issue is self-government, the root of all true government: no external law can make a people good if they do not rule themselves, and those who govern should be wiser and better than the governed. Peace comes through conquest, not through dodging combat—by exercising sweetness and charity even amid repugnance and disgust, overcoming what repels us rather than fleeing it. Only so do revolutions give way to real peace.

prompt: Is there hope for my ancestors who died in ignorance or idolatry?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, there's real hope, because God is merciful and wants everyone saved, and we can trust that people who never knew Christ aren't automatically cut off from his grace. One idea worth weighing is that death doesn't work a miracle—we're after death exactly as far advanced as before, so character isn't suddenly changed just by dying. That changes how I'd frame the hope: it's not that dying instantly fixes everything, but that God's mercy can still reach people beyond death. What it leaves in place is the core hope itself—we can still pray for our ancestors and entrust them to God's compassion without presuming to know exactly how he works it out.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. God is merciful and desires all to be saved. Many theologians trust that those who died without knowing Christ may still be saved through His atonement, perhaps via a post-mortem opportunity or by responding to the light they had. We cannot limit God's grace. Baptism of desire or blood may apply. The fact that they died does not seal their fate; God's justice and mercy are perfect. We should pray for them and trust in God's loving plan, knowing that He wills all to come to the knowledge of truth. Ultimately, we commit them to God's infinite compassion, confident that He can save whom He wills.

prompt: Is it unjust for God to punish me for circumstances I could not control?
chosen: I'd start by saying that it can feel deeply unfair to be blamed for things beyond your control, and Scripture doesn't teach that God punishes you for circumstances you couldn't help. It distinguishes between what you choose and what merely happens to you. Much suffering comes from human choices—yours and others'—and from a broken world, not from God's direct displeasure at you. One principle worth weighing is that misfortune, illness, and strife aren't charged to God's will; they result from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, though God permits them and overrules them for good. That principle sharpens the answer by making clear that God isn't the author of the harm you couldn't control, but it leaves in place the mystery that God still permits such things and can work them toward good. So the real question isn't whether God is unfair, but whether you turn toward Him in the midst of what you can't control, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by your circumstances.
rejected: No, it is not unjust for God to punish you for circumstances you could not control, because God's justice is never measured by your sense of fairness. Misfortune, illness, and strife are not to be charged to God's will; they come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, and God permits them and overrules them for good. Yet seeming mischances are necessary links in a divinely ordered providence—God does not permit hindrance to arise without sufficient reason. So stop demanding that your circumstances be adjusted to you. Instead, be adjusted in every good work: to your surroundings, to the people you're thrown with, and to God's plan. In that adjustment you find rest and freedom, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by what you could not control.

prompt: Should I obey and pray for rulers I did not choose and who may be wicked?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a real tension, not a simple yes. Scripture tells us to respect governing authorities and pray for those in power, but it also shows that when rulers command what contradicts God, we obey God rather than people. So my first answer is: obey in lawful and moral matters, pray sincerely for leaders even when you disagree with them, and refuse only commands that require you to do evil. Prayer isn't endorsement; it's asking God to guide rulers, restrain injustice, and grant peace. Where a ruler is genuinely wicked, you can work lawfully for change, speak truth, and seek redress, but not through violence or rebellion. One principle worth naming is that intercession for kings and all in authority is a foremost Christian duty, because the peace of the world and the quiet life of ordinary people depend on rulers whose burdens exceed human wisdom. That principle changes the tone of prayer: it's not a grudging formality but a serious responsibility, and it widens who you pray for. What it leaves in place is the limit: praying for a ruler doesn't mean obeying commands contrary to virtue, and it doesn't erase the right, in extreme cases, to resist unlawful power. So you can pray, submit where lawful, refuse what's evil, and wait patiently for the Lord's justice.
rejected: This is a real tension. Scripture counsels respect for governing authorities, yet it also shows that when rulers command what contradicts God, the faithful must obey God rather than men. A workable answer is to obey in all lawful and moral matters, pray sincerely for those in power even when you disagree with them, and refuse only those commands that require you to do evil. Prayer is not endorsement; it is a way of asking God to guide rulers, restrain injustice, and grant peace. Where a ruler is genuinely wicked, you may work lawfully for change, speak truth, and seek redress—but not through violence or rebellion. Trust that God governs history and will establish justice in his own time, while you live peaceably and with a clear conscience.

prompt: Is it right to rebel against an unjust government to establish righteousness?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: yes, rebellion against a genuinely unjust government can be justified, especially when basic rights are trampled and there's no peaceful way left. History shows many freedoms were won through resistance, and there's a long tradition, including Christian thought, that tyrants may be opposed. What the principle about obeying civil authority for conscience' sake changes is the default posture: normally you submit, pray for rulers, and wait rather than foment revolt, and you disobey commands that are contrary to virtue. What it leaves in place is that extreme, unlawful power can still be resisted in rare cases. So the bar gets higher and the patience gets longer, but the door isn't shut.
rejected: Scripture settles the posture before it ever gets to your question: be peaceable, submit to the powers that be, pray for kings, and wait for the Lord's time instead of stirring up rebellion. Obedience to civil authority is owed for conscience' sake, and commands contrary to virtue must be refused, but that's a far cry from taking up arms to install your idea of righteousness. And here's the deeper problem: righteousness isn't a political arrangement you can establish by force. It's the actual transformation of the self, living in Christ's power the life He lived. A righteousness merely credited to you while you stay unchanged is a fiction. So stop asking whether the government is just enough to overthrow and ask whether you yourself are being made righteous within, letting Christ's life displace your own will.

prompt: Why do the sects of Christendom disagree so bitterly among themselves?
chosen: My first answer would be that the divisions come from a mix of history, culture, and conviction. Fights over authority, sacraments, and how to read Scripture hardened into separate traditions, often propped up by politics and national identity, and because each side thinks it holds the truth, the disputes feel like life or death. Pride makes it worse, though a lot of the bitterness is needless since many groups agree on the core about Christ and differ on secondary things. One principle worth naming is that people who slander and persecute each other over religion haven't really known Christ, and that kind of prideful quarreling is just self pushing the kingdom of darkness forward. That changes the tone of my answer: the problem isn't disagreement itself but the venom, and it puts a sharp question to anyone who fights dirty in Christ's name. What it leaves in place is that real differences still matter and some things shouldn't be shrugged off as mere preference.
rejected: Christendom's divisions arise from a mix of history, culture, and conviction. Differences over authority, sacraments, and interpretation of Scripture hardened into separate traditions, often reinforced by politics and national identity. Each group believes it holds the truth, so disputes feel existential rather than academic. Bitter disagreement also reflects human pride: people defend opinions as if their identity depended on winning. Yet much of the contention is unnecessary, since many groups share core beliefs about Christ while differing on secondary matters. A more charitable approach would distinguish essentials from preferences, recognize that no tradition has a monopoly on truth, and pursue dialogue. Disagreement itself is not wrong; the bitterness is the problem, and humility plus honest study could soften it considerably.

prompt: Why does religion often seem so melancholy and forbidding?
chosen: My first answer would be that religion often looks gloomy because people tie it to guilt, strict rules, and fear of judgment. Sermons on sin and punishment, solemn rituals, and a focus on self-denial can make faith feel like a heavy burden instead of a comfort. One idea worth naming is that religion is meant to be the open air of the soul, not a closed room where you brood over your own feelings. That changes the picture: instead of measuring your faith by how anxious or serious you feel, you receive God's mercy as something outside you, as free as sunshine. It leaves the real weight of guilt and strictness in place, though, because those things still exist and still shape how people see religion. So the warmer side of faith, gratitude and community and hope, still has to be recovered, not just explained away.
rejected: Religion seems melancholy because we keep it indoors, as our own feelings and thoughts about ourselves, our guilt, our anxious self-examination, our resolutions. But religion is not our feelings about God. It is the love of God, objective to our hearts, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine. The loyal love of God is every day. Do not imagine a safe middle way, serving God and the world together as a happy compromise. That half-way stopping brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His work in us. Reject immoderate sadness, for sadness is the enemy of devotion. Console your soul in the service of Him who is our joy forever, and it will grow like an olive tree green in God's house.

prompt: Why is the earth cursed, and will the curse ever be lifted?
chosen: My first answer would be that the earth is cursed because of human disobedience and sin, and that it stays cursed until God finally makes everything new. One idea worth naming is that the world's evils come from people turning away from God and seizing authority for themselves, and no power here can fix that; it takes God to put the world right. That changes how I'd talk about the timing and the remedy, but it leaves the core in place: the curse is real, human effort can't undo it, and God is the one who restores creation.
rejected: The earth is cursed because of humanity's disobedience and sin. According to the Bible, when Adam and Eve fell, the ground was cursed, and sorrow in childbirth became a permanent condition for women. This curse is a divine punishment that will only be lifted at the end of time when God creates a new heaven and new earth. Until then, we must endure the consequences of sin, including pain and suffering. Human efforts cannot remove the curse; only God's final judgment will restore creation to its original perfection.

prompt: Why does God permit evil and suffering if he is all-powerful?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this is the oldest and hardest question, and no answer fully takes away the sting. Scripture and reason suggest God permits evil because a world with free creatures is greater than one without them—genuine love and virtue need the possibility of their opposites—and suffering can be formative, and the cross shows God entering suffering rather than standing aloof. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that all evil happens by God's permission and always for some good end, so we can commit everything to Providence without fear. That principle deepens the trust part: it says evil's form and measure are allowed by a wisdom that will turn all to good. But it leaves in place the hard fact that pain and sin are real evils, never goods in themselves, and it doesn't explain why this particular suffering, now, is necessary. So it changes the tone from argument to trust, but it doesn't remove the sting.
rejected: The answer is that pain and sin are real evils, never goods in themselves, yet God permits them only as necessary means to a greater good. All evil of whatever kind happens by His permission and ever for some good end; it could not be at all except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. His omnipotence is limited only by His own nature—He cannot deny Himself or be the author of evil—so He cannot attain His ends without these means, since omnipotence means ability to do all things in their own nature possible. The struggle is inward: the enemy is partly your own pride, fear, and disordered desire, and deliverance is not a magical rescue from outside but God and man together battering the citadel of evil, the soul's resolve joined to grace. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

prompt: Is God a distant and gloomy being, or can I approach him as a father?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, God isn't a distant, gloomy being you have to dread. Jesus taught us to pray to 'our Father,' so you can come near with confidence, even while keeping a healthy reverence for his holiness. One principle I'd weigh says God is the Father of our spirits, that we stand to him as children, and that his service is cheerful rather than gloomy because he's near to those who ask. That changes the tone: it turns fear into trust and duty into delight. What it leaves in place is his sovereign honour, so I'd still come with awe and honesty, not casualness. So yes, approach him as a father, and let that closeness deepen your reverence rather than erase it.
rejected: Many people picture God as a remote ruler far off in the heavens, watching us with cold judgment. Approaching such a being feels frightening, and serving him seems like a grim duty full of dread. But Scripture invites us to a different view. God is not a distant monster demanding fear; he is a Father who cares for his children. Jesus taught us to pray to 'our Father,' which means we can come near with confidence. Still, we should remember that God is holy and we are sinful, so a healthy reverence is appropriate. The Christian life involves both awe and intimacy, and we grow by balancing the two. Prayer, reading Scripture, and obedience help us draw closer to him over time.

prompt: Was Christ's kingdom set up at his first coming, or is it still future?
chosen: I'd start by saying Christ's kingdom was inaugurated at his first coming—he preached that it had drawn near, he defeated sin and death, and he reigns now at the Father's right hand—but it's also still future, because Scripture promises a consummation when he returns in glory. So it's both already and not yet. One principle worth weighing is that the kingdom of heaven isn't the visible church and Christ hasn't yet set up his everlasting kingdom on earth. That changes how I'd frame the present age: the church isn't the kingdom itself, and we still pray for God to establish it visibly. But it leaves in place the reality that Christ's rule is present now through the Spirit and that the kingdom has truly been inaugurated. So I'd hold both: a real present reign and a future, visible establishment.
rejected: The kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth. His people still wait and pray for it. It cannot be built by human organization, legislation, or moral suasion—it must be revealed from heaven and established by God's own interposition, with an angel restoring the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion built up, and judgements preparing the way. Yet this is no mere inward state. The kingdom of God is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. Believers therefore labor faithfully now while awaiting that visible, literal reign.

prompt: Why is there to be a gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and a separate gathering of the saints to Zion?
chosen: My first answer would be that the gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion reflect two distinct purposes in God's plan. Jerusalem is tied to the return and restoration of the Jews, while Zion is the place prepared for the saints. These gatherings aren't in competition; each serves its own role. One principle that fits here is that unity doesn't mean uniformity—the Saints are to be of one heart and one mind while each fills their own calling. That principle changes how I'd frame the two gatherings: they're not rivals, and unity doesn't require everyone to be alike. But it leaves in place the basic distinction between the two gatherings and their purposes.
rejected: The gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion reflect two distinct purposes in God's plan. Jerusalem is associated with the return of the Jews and the restoration of their homeland, while Zion is the place prepared for the saints, where the Lord's people gather to build His kingdom and prepare for His coming. These gatherings are not in competition; each serves its own role. The important thing is that all who love God seek to be where He has called them, and that they work together in unity of purpose, supporting one another as the Lord's work moves forward in these last days.

prompt: Was Queen Victoria lawfully anointed of God, or is her authority merely human?
chosen: I'd start by saying her authority was human in origin but allowed by God, and her anointing in a Christian ceremony was a real commissioning that many faithful people took seriously. One principle I'd weigh is that rulers today aren't legally called and anointed of God, and that anointing by unauthorized ministers is a farce. That changes how much weight I'd give the ceremony itself, but it leaves in place the idea that God still permits and overrules human governments for His purposes, so her reign still deserves respect, not worship.
rejected: No ruler now, Victoria included, is lawfully called and anointed of God. Their dominion is usurped, and God merely overrules them the way He did Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus. The anointing by unauthorized ministers is a farce, so her authority is merely human, never legally God's. And since graces don't reach us except through Mary, the treasurer of all graces, we should go to her with confidence and find there the lawful path by which divine gifts come to us.

prompt: Why did Jesus say his kingdom is not of this world if it is to be on the earth?
chosen: I'd start by saying Jesus was telling Pilate that his authority doesn't come from Rome or any earthly political system. His kingdom originates with the Father and is established by truth, not force. That doesn't mean it will never be on earth. Scripture promises he'll reign here when he returns. So the source and character are heavenly, but the final location is earthly. One principle worth naming is that the kingdom of heaven isn't the visible church, and Christ hasn't yet set up his everlasting kingdom on earth. That changes how you read the present age. His people still pray for the kingdom to come. But it leaves the future earthly reign fully intact. It just clarifies that it's still ahead, not already here in the church.
rejected: Jesus told Pilate his kingdom was not of this world so Pilate would understand that his authority did not come from Rome or from earthly political power. His kingdom originates in heaven, is given by the Father, and is established by truth rather than by force. Yet Scripture promises that this same kingdom will one day be set up on the earth, when Christ returns to reign. So the two ideas fit together: the kingdom's source and character are heavenly, but its final location and visible expression will be on the earth. Jesus was clarifying the nature of his rule, not denying its future earthly reality.

prompt: Will there be a reckoning for the way rulers and priests have abused their authority?
chosen: Yes, I'd say accountability is real. Scripture keeps warning that people with authority—kings, judges, religious leaders—answer to God for how they use it, and Jesus was blunt about leaders who load heavy burdens on others. So I'd name this: the priesthood can't be exercised in any degree of unrighteousness; its power won't stay with the corrupt or treacherous. That sharpens things—it means abuse doesn't just get punished later, it hollows out the authority itself, so a corrupt leader has already lost the thing they're pretending to hold. What it leaves in place is the timing: the reckoning still belongs to God, and our part is still to speak truth, protect the wounded, and refuse to join the corruption.
rejected: Yes, and don't soften it. No ruler now sitting on a throne was lawfully called or anointed by God—their claim is usurped, and God merely overrules them the way He overruled Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus. The same goes for priests: authority that can't be exercised in any degree of unrighteousness simply will not abide with the corrupt or the treacherous. It departs. So the reckoning isn't some vague someday—it's already happening in the loss of the very power they flaunt. And the standard cuts both ways: anyone who governs with haughty anger and calls it zeal is showing they can't govern themselves, let alone anyone else. God humbles the proud and restores authority only to those who rule with meekness, as servants beneath the people they lead.

prompt: How will the kingdom of God be established—by human effort or by revelation from heaven?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: the kingdom isn't something people build by planning, passing laws, or improving their behavior. It comes by revelation from heaven, with God himself breaking in to make his will known and set up his rule. Human effort can build organizations and tidy up behavior, but it can't produce the kingdom. One principle worth naming is that the kingdom develops gradually and requires individual labor. That doesn't replace the revelation side; it fills in how the revealed kingdom actually takes root. God establishes it, and our faithful, patient labor is caught up in it, not the engine of it.
rejected: The kingdom of God is not the product of human planning, legislation, or moral reform. It is established by revelation from heaven—God Himself breaking into history to make known His will and to set up His rule. Human effort alone can build organizations and improve behavior, but it cannot bring the kingdom. Scripture shows that God sends His messenger, restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to every nation, gathers a people into a Zion, and pours out judgments that prepare the way for Christ's reign. So the kingdom comes by divine initiative and disclosure, not by committees or campaigns. Our part is to receive the revelation, repent, and align ourselves with what God is doing, rather than imagining we can construct the kingdom ourselves.

prompt: Why are people in rich countries still unhappy and violent?
chosen: I'd start by saying that rich countries still see unhappiness and violence because money alone doesn't fix inequality, isolation, or a lack of meaning. People feel disconnected and stressed, and consumerism can break community ties. One principle that adds something is that the poor have powerful arms—their sighs and groans pierce the heavens and draw down vengeance on the rich and on cities that oppress them. That principle changes the picture by making the suffering of the poor not just a social problem but a moral and spiritual cry that demands justice. It leaves in place the practical points about inequality and isolation, but it shifts the focus to the voices of those left behind. So material riches alone don't guarantee well-being; social and spiritual factors matter, and the cries of the oppressed won't go unheard.
rejected: Rich countries are unhappy and violent because the poor have powerful arms—their sighs and groans pierce the heavens and draw down vengeance on the rich and on cities that oppress them. That's the real answer. You can't just talk about inequality or isolation; the cries of the destitute are a force that demands justice. And as long as great numbers of citizens have undeveloped faculties, society cannot be justly ordered. The only real solution is a complete education that raises each person's actual worth to the level of their potentialities. The poor are the people of God and shall inherit the earth; the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone, and persons are esteemed by character, not wealth or position. So don't be surprised by violence—it's the consequence of ignoring these truths.

prompt: Who has the right to govern the earth, and do any present kings have that right?
chosen: I'd start by saying God is the ultimate sovereign over the earth, and human rulers hold authority only as a trust—measured by whether they serve justice and the common good. That still leaves room for real, lawful government, even if no ruler is personally righteous. One principle that sharpens this is that superiors and pastors should govern with humility and meekness, as servants of all, not with haughty force. That changes how I'd judge a present king's claim: anger and impatience dressed up as zeal are signs someone isn't fit to govern. But it leaves the core in place—authority is delegated by God, and believers should respect lawful authority, pray for rulers, and obey God first when human commands conflict with conscience.
rejected: Scripture presents God as the ultimate sovereign over the earth, and human rulers hold authority only insofar as they serve justice and the common good. Many Christians have taught that government is ordained by God to restrain evil and reward good, so kings and presidents exercise a delegated trust. That does not mean every ruler is personally righteous or divinely chosen; history is full of tyrants. The right to govern belongs to God and is lent to those who rule wisely and justly. Present kings therefore have a conditional right, measured by their fidelity to law and the welfare of their people. Believers should respect lawful authority, pray for rulers, and obey God first when human commands conflict with conscience.

prompt: Is socialism or a community of goods the answer to the misery I see around me?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: the misery you're seeing is real, and it makes sense to look for a system that would fix it. But socialism and shared goods mostly rearrange what's already there without touching the habits that create poverty in the first place. One idea worth taking seriously is that a community where everyone is industrious, faithful, and prudent, living within their means and making what they wear, will prosper and eventually buy out its neighbors. That changes the focus from redistribution to building real capacity, soil, time, and skill, and it gives people something to do rather than something to receive. What it leaves in place is the hard part: it still asks each person to change, and it doesn't guarantee that everyone will. So I'd say start with yourself, but don't expect any arrangement, socialist or otherwise, to do the inner work for you.
rejected: Socialism and a community of goods are not the answer. The answer is a community where every person is industrious, faithful, and prudent, never wanting what they cannot get, living within their means, making what they wear and raising what they eat. Labor is indispensable, and the elements of wealth are already around us in soil, time, and skill. Idleness, waste, and dependence only deepen misery. Self-denial and economy are not losses but a joyful privilege that frees your resources for the LORD and for generous giving. When you live within your means and work with your hands, you prosper not to hoard but to bless, and in time the community buys out its neighbors. Begin with yourself, and the whole community will rise in joy.

prompt: Why does the world seem so full of confusion and misery when God's works are so orderly?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and it deserves an honest answer. God's works are orderly, but the world we experience is shaped by human choices, natural processes, and the consequences that pile up from both. A lot of the confusion and misery comes from human selfishness, injustice, and neglect, and from the freedom God gives us to choose wrongly; some comes from natural events beyond our control. The order isn't always visible to us in the short term, and our perspective is limited. One principle here that sharpens this is that time and the ability to labor are the world's capital stock, and God will require a strict account not only of our acts but of our words and thoughts. That changes the frame: misery isn't just something that happens to us, it's also something we're accountable for in how we spend what we've been given. What it leaves in place is the honest admission that suffering also comes from nature and from other people's choices, and that we don't see the whole picture. So we're called to be agents of order and mercy while we trust God with the final resolution.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a quick one. God's works are orderly, but the world we experience is shaped by human choices, natural processes, and the accumulated consequences of both. Much confusion and misery come from human selfishness, injustice, and neglect, and from the freedom God gives us to choose wrongly. Suffering also arises from natural events beyond our control. The order of God's works is not always visible to us in the short term, and our perspective is limited. Christians have long trusted that God is at work even amid disorder, bringing good out of evil, and that the final resolution belongs to him. In the meantime we are called to be agents of order and mercy.

prompt: What is the meaning of the stone cut out of the mountain without hands?
chosen: The stone cut out without hands is from Daniel 2: a stone strikes the statue of world empires and grows into a mountain that fills the earth. Because it's cut 'without hands,' its origin is divine rather than human—it stands for God's everlasting kingdom, inaugurated in Christ, which outlasts every earthly power. One principle I'd bring in is the image of yourself as a stone before a carver, asking God to form His likeness in your soul. That adds a personal, prayerful layer: the same divine shaping that establishes the kingdom also works on you. It doesn't change the stone's meaning as God's kingdom—it just turns it into something you can pray with, while the cross-shaped carving stays fitted to what you can bear.
rejected: The stone cut without hands is God's kingdom, and don't soften it: it is not built by human effort, politics, or religion's machinery—it comes from above and shatters every empire in its path. But the stone isn't only out there in history; it's you, presented before the Carver, yielded and passive, letting God form His perfect image in your soul. Being carved is no resting place—your rest must be 'no rest below,' and you press on toward Sion's hill while the pillar stays and the waters smile. The chisel that shapes you is often the cross, fitted to your stature, measured to what you can bear, and all God does shall work your final good. He carves the stone, and He will bring it at last into the mountain of His kingdom.

prompt: Why do the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper?
chosen: I'd start by saying that suffering and prosperity in this life don't line up neatly with who's good and who's wicked—that's a hard truth the Bible and philosophy both wrestle with. One principle that adds something here is that virtues born in prosperity are of little value, while those born amid afflictions are strong and firm. That changes how I see the righteous person's suffering: it's not just a test or a temporary hardship, but a place where something solid and lasting is being built in them. What it leaves in place is the bigger picture I already had—that the wicked's prosperity is fleeting and God's justice will ultimately prevail. So I'd still say don't envy the wicked or despair in suffering, but now I'd also say the suffering itself can produce a strength that ease never could.
rejected: The question of why the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper is a perennial one, addressed in Scripture and philosophy. One common answer is that suffering serves a purpose: it refines character, tests faith, and ultimately leads to growth. The prosperity of the wicked is often temporary, and their success may be hollow. From a spiritual perspective, trials can draw us closer to God, while prosperity can lead to complacency. The righteous may suffer now but will be rewarded later, while the wicked may prosper briefly but face judgment. This life is not the final chapter; eternal justice will prevail. Thus, we should not envy the wicked or despair in suffering but trust in God's ultimate goodness and timing.

prompt: What will the reign of God on earth actually change for ordinary people?
chosen: My first answer would be that God's reign mainly changes people inwardly—forgiveness, peace, a new heart, hope beyond death—and that outward changes come as people live by kingdom values. One idea worth naming is that the kingdom will be a literal, tangible rule on earth, with laws and resurrected saints. That changes the picture from a mostly private, spiritual renewal to a public, visible order with real governance and justice. What it leaves in place is the inward transformation: forgiveness, a new identity, and the fruit of the Spirit still matter. So for ordinary people, the change would be both a new inner life and, in God's time, a just society to live in.
rejected: God's reign on earth will be a literal, tangible kingdom, not just a warm feeling inside. It will have laws, officers, and resurrected saints ruling under Christ, and ordinary people will live under just governance with real peace and prosperity. The Greek idea that Christ pre-existed glorifies Christ instead of the God who guides history, and it makes the flesh seem worthless—but Scripture says the meek will inherit the earth. The saints will reign on the earth, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth where God dwells with men. That is our eternal inheritance, and God's will will be done on earth as in heaven.

prompt: Why should I wait patiently for the Lord instead of trying to force change myself?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: waiting on God is trust, not sitting still. Forcing change usually comes out of anxiety and self-will, and patience lets God work in his timing while you pray, obey what's already clear, and keep your hands open. One idea worth adding is that the Lord's work should be done in the way, at the time, and with the people he appoints, so you wait for his signal before you take a step. That sharpens things: it makes you slower to launch out and more careful about who you partner with, and it keeps the active side of waiting, the praying and obeying, right where it was.
rejected: Waiting on the Lord is an act of trust, not passivity. When you try to force change in your own strength, you often act out of anxiety and self-will rather than faith. Scripture repeatedly tells us that those who wait on the Lord renew their strength. Patience lets God work in His timing, which is always better than ours. Forcing change can produce shallow or premature results, and it can lead you to rely on yourself instead of on God. Waiting does not mean doing nothing; it means praying, obeying what is already clear, and trusting God to open doors. The key is to keep your heart soft and your hands open, ready to move when God clearly leads, but not running ahead of Him.

prompt: What am I, and what happens to me when I die?
chosen: I'd start by saying you're a human being, a creature of body and soul, made with reason, conscience, and a capacity to love, and your worth comes from being made in the image of God. When you die, your soul is separated from your body—your earthly life ends, your body returns to dust, and your soul goes to God for judgment. That's my prior answer. One candidate principle here is that death is a door to a higher state, that we shouldn't mourn hopelessly for the righteous dead, that your identity is preserved, and that the body will be raised again. That principle changes the tone and the horizon: death isn't just a wall or a loss of everything you are; it's a passage, and what God has made and loved is kept and restored. But it leaves in place the core claim that death is real, that it's a separation, and that judgment still happens—so it doesn't erase the seriousness of how you live now.
rejected: You are a human being formed in the image of God, with reason, conscience, and a capacity to love, and death is not the end of who you are. It is a door to a higher state, and your identity is preserved, not erased. For the righteous, death is not something to mourn hopelessly—it is a passage into fuller life, and the body itself is raised again. Mortality is not truly real as such: being is immortal and inseparable from Deity, so what appears as death is a transition, not a destruction. Yet this transition is also a judgment: we are judged according to the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and death leaves us as judgment finds us. So live now with a conscience awake, trusting that the person God has made and loved is kept and will be restored.

prompt: Why is it robbery to take from the rich and give to the poor by force?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's robbery because it violates the owner's right to their property and swaps force for consent — property is an extension of the person, and seizing it even for a good cause treats the owner as a means and erodes trust in law. One candidate principle here is that wealth generally represents labor, industry, and talent, so taking it by force or legislation is robbery and would crush enterprise. That principle sharpens the economic case: it explains why coercion damages incentives, not just rights. But it leaves the core in place — consent, the wrong of treating people as tools, and the point that charity must be voluntary. It doesn't add anything about who counts as rich or poor, or about resentment and dependence; those still stand on their own.
rejected: Taking from the rich to give to the poor by force is robbery because it violates the owner's right to his property and substitutes force for consent. Property is a legitimate extension of the person; seizing it, even for a good cause, treats the owner as a mere means and undermines trust in law and order. Charity is praiseworthy, but it must be voluntary. Coerced redistribution also tends to breed resentment and dependence, and it invites endless disputes over who counts as rich and who as poor. A just society protects lawful ownership and encourages generosity freely given, rather than authorizing theft under a benevolent name.

prompt: Will Satan always rule over the world, or will he be bound?
chosen: My first answer would be that Satan is described as the ruler of this world for a time, but his rule isn't permanent. The Bible says he'll be bound and thrown into the bottomless pit, as Revelation 20 describes. Until then he works only within God's permission, and his power is limited. One principle that shapes this is that Satan is a usurper under God's control, allowed for a season to show what evil produces, but destined to be bound and cast out. That changes the picture from a rival power to a temporary, permitted one, while leaving in place that he really does exercise real influence now and that God's kingdom will prevail in the end.
rejected: No, Satan will not always rule the world. He's a usurper, not an independent power, and he's permitted only for a season to expose man's weakness and the effects of evil before he's bound and cast out. It would be unreasonable, unjust, unscriptural, and would frustrate God's designs for the righteous, the dead, and the earth itself for the curse to remain forever. The world's evils come from man's departure from God and his usurped authority, and nothing on this side of heaven can fix that; it takes God himself to put the world right. So his dominion is temporary, and God's kingdom will prevail.

prompt: How can I know the doctrine is of God rather than of men?
chosen: I'd start where I'd naturally start: test the teaching against Scripture, pray for discernment, look at the fruit it produces and the character of the teacher, and stay humble and patient since understanding usually comes gradually. One idea worth weighing is that God is incorporeal, infinite Love rather than a corporeal person, and that praying to a bodily God can keep us stuck in human doubts and fears. If that's true, it changes how you'd evaluate a doctrine: you'd ask whether it honors God as Spirit and corrects the belief that life and intelligence live in matter, rather than judging it by striking signs or by how well it fits a picture of God as a person located somewhere. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: Scripture, prayer, fruit, humility, and patience still matter. It just reframes what you're looking for when you test a teaching.
rejected: To know whether a doctrine is of God, begin by testing it against Scripture and asking whether it produces good fruit in your life. Pray earnestly for discernment, because God promises wisdom to those who ask. Consider the character of the teacher and whether the teaching points you toward God or toward human pride. Look for consistency with the core truths of the faith and for the witness of the Holy Spirit in your conscience. Be patient: understanding often comes gradually as you study, pray, and live what you learn. Finally, remain humble and teachable, since no one grasps the whole of truth at once, and God gives light to those who walk in it.

prompt: What happens to those who died without ever hearing the gospel?
chosen: My first answer would be that Scripture presents God as just and merciful, and it doesn't clearly say that anyone is condemned for light they never received. The Bible doesn't give us a detailed map of what happens to the unevangelized, so I'd hold that humbly and trust God's character, while affirming that salvation is in Christ and that God wants all people saved. One idea worth weighing is that the gospel is preached to the dead, so those who never heard it may hear it in the spirit, with work for the dead carried on in temples. That changes the picture from 'we simply don't know' to 'there's a hopeful path after death.' What it leaves in place is the core conviction that Christ is the only Savior and that God is just and merciful. It doesn't settle every detail, and I'd still be careful about claiming more than we can know.
rejected: The gospel is not limited to this life. Christ preached to the spirits in prison, and the gospel is proclaimed in the spirit world, so those who died without ever hearing it can still hear it and receive it. Because ordinances require a body, the living can perform baptisms and other ordinances for the dead so they can be brought into the blessings of the gospel. This isn't speculation; it rests on the resurrection of Christ, who conquered death and promised that because He lives, we shall live also. That hope also lays a duty on the living: parents must teach their children the gospel and watch over them, guarding them from the wickedness of the world, because it is better to bury children in innocence than to see them led away from the gospel.

prompt: Will the earth be restored to its former glory, and what will that look like?
chosen: I'd start by saying the earth's future in Scripture often looks like destruction and renewal, with the present order passing away and the righteous escaping to heaven. But one principle here changes that: the restoration of all things means the earth will be brought back to its primeval glory—one land, fruitful, without curse—and humanity restored with it. That shifts the focus from escape to healing, yet it leaves in place the idea that the present world still passes through judgment before renewal. So the renewed earth would look like Eden restored, but the old order still gives way first.
rejected: Scripture suggests the earth's future is often framed as destruction and renewal, with the present order passing away. Many read prophecies of fire and judgment as the end of the world, leaving little room for a literal return to Eden. On this view, the earth is eventually replaced or abandoned, and the righteous simply escape to heaven. The emphasis falls on survival and escape rather than on the planet itself being healed. Restoration is treated as a metaphor for personal salvation, not a promise about the physical creation. What the renewed state looks like remains vague, often reduced to a spiritual afterlife rather than a transformed earth.

prompt: Why do Christian nations go to war with one another and pray to the same God for victory?
chosen: I'd start by saying that Christian nations fight because nations, even Christian ones, are full of fallible people chasing security, power, and national interest, and when those clash, governments turn to force while churches get caught between blessing the troops and calling for peace. Praying to the same God for victory is a tragic irony, since each side thinks its cause is just. One idea that sharpens this is that war is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's ordinary laws of human nature, so wars grow out of lusts and injustice rather than God's design. That changes how I see the causes, making them moral and self-inflicted rather than just political, but it leaves in place the point that God doesn't take sides in the slaughter and that Christians still answer for letting patriotism crowd out the gospel's call to peacemaking.
rejected: War doesn't come from God's design; it comes from wickedness, from lusts and covetousness and injustice, and God's righteousness works through the ordinary laws of human nature so that evil passions punish themselves. Praying to the same God for victory on both sides is a tragic irony, because God takes no side in the slaughter, and peace will never come until people receive God's truth. But victory, not defeat, is God's purpose for believers, and the secret is Christ himself living in you, entered by resting in him. When your heart rests in Christ, the passions that breed war are overcome from within.

prompt: Will I see my family and children again in the world to come?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the deepest hopes we have, and Scripture gives real ground for it. The world to come isn't a vague shadowland; it's the renewed creation where God dwells with His people, and relationships aren't erased but healed and perfected. If God cares for sparrows and numbers the hairs of our heads, He surely doesn't sever the bonds of love He Himself planted in families. One principle worth weighing is that the restoration of all things means the earth is brought back to its primeval glory and man restored with it. That changes the setting of the hope—it makes the promise earthy and concrete rather than purely otherworldly, so families and children belong within a restored order. What it leaves in place is the core comfort: the God who raised Jesus will raise us, and nothing in Christ is finally lost. So grieve honestly, but grieve with hope.
rejected: This is one of the deepest hopes of the human heart, and Scripture gives real ground for it. The world to come is not a vague shadowland but the renewed creation where God dwells with His people, and where relationships are not erased but healed and perfected. If God cares for sparrows and numbers the hairs of our heads, He surely does not sever the bonds of love He Himself planted in families. Many faithful Christians have trusted that children remain children and parents remain parents in the resurrection, gathered into one great family under God. Grieve honestly, but grieve with hope: the God who raised Jesus will raise us, and nothing in Christ is finally lost.

prompt: How should I live now in light of the coming kingdom of God?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: live with intention, since the kingdom is near. Build habits of prayer, generosity, and integrity, take responsibility for your growth, mend relationships, and stay awake to what matters rather than passively waiting. One principle worth naming is that unless you become like a little child, hanging on Christ for everything, you can't enter the kingdom. That changes the footing of everything I just said: the habits and goals stop being a project you pull off and become a way of depending on him, so your effort rests on his grace instead of your willpower. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of the life: prayer, generosity, integrity, mending what's broken, using your gifts for others. You still act decisively; you just act as a child holding on, not as someone building a résumé.
rejected: Become like a little child and hang on Christ for all things, because that is the only way in. Don't treat the kingdom as a self-improvement plan where you set goals and shape a life worthy of your calling; that puts you at the center. Depend on him as the source of every good thing, seek first God's will and glory rather than your own blessing, and even claim his promises for him, not for yourself, trusting that everything else gets added and never comes first. And don't expect the kingdom without judgment: God judges evil, present struggles sit under the control of the one on the throne, and he works through those judgments toward making all things new. So watch, repent, and trust his sovereign hand, knowing he will finish the work of renewing all things.

prompt: Will God punish the world in the last days, and will he warn us first?
chosen: Yes, I'd say Scripture holds out both: a real judgment at the end, and real warning before it comes. My first answer would be that God has always warned before He judges—Noah preaching while the ark went up, Lot pulled out of Sodom, prophets crying out to Jerusalem before it fell—and that pattern carries through to the last days, when God sends His Spirit and His messengers to call people to turn to Christ. One principle I'd weigh here is that it would be unjust for God to punish the ignorant without warning, so He warns first. That principle sharpens the point: the warning is genuine and meant to be heeded now, not later. What it leaves in place is that the judgment itself is still real and still coming for those who refuse—warning doesn't cancel the consequence, it gives people a way to escape it. So the question isn't whether God warns, but whether we listen while there's still time.
rejected: Scripture says the last days will bring God's judgment on a rebellious world. Many passages describe plagues, fire, and wrath poured out on the wicked. But God is not arbitrary; He has always warned before He judges. Noah preached while the ark was built, Lot was warned in Sodom, and prophets cried out to Jerusalem before its fall. So too, before the final judgment God sends messengers and His Spirit to call people to repentance. The warnings are real, and so is the coming punishment. Those who heed the warning and turn to Christ will be spared; those who refuse will face the consequences. The question is whether we will listen now, while there is still time to repent and be saved.

prompt: Can I find peace and happiness by moving to a new country with plenty of food and land?
chosen: I'd start by saying that moving to a new country with plenty of food and land can bring real relief, but peace and happiness are interior realities that travel with you rather than living in a place. One principle here says this world is a touchstone and finding-place for God, and that true happiness comes from finding God from this world rather than waiting for the next. That changes the frame: the move becomes a setting for seeking something deeper, not a cure-all. It leaves in place the practical advice to think about community, legal stability, and work before you go, and it still warns that happiness isn't guaranteed by geography or abundance.
rejected: Your desire for happiness is God-given, and God is to be found here in this world, the touchstone and finding-place for Him. Do not expect a new country, abundant food, or land to produce peace by itself: forms of government and external arrangements do not materially alter the people's condition, and happiness and peace are gifts of God. So receive peace as His gift where you are, and let any move be a place of finding Him rather than escape. When your interior states shift, do not be curious about their causes; accept the diversity of consolation and dryness without inquisitive inquiry, and show love by patiently enduring them.

prompt: Why is chastity so important, and what are the eternal consequences of impurity?
chosen: I'd start by saying chastity matters because your body and soul are made for God, and impurity throws both into disorder. Scripture is blunt that the impure won't inherit the kingdom, so the stakes really are eternal: unrepented impurity cuts you off from God, while purity of heart opens the way to seeing him. Chastity isn't just a social rule; it's a safeguard for your union with God. One principle I'd add is that chastity is a treasure you protect through prayer, self-denial, modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by steering clear of temptation, since whoever loves danger will perish in it. That changes the practical side of my answer: it turns a general warning into concrete habits. But it leaves the core in place: the eternal stakes and the call to guard your union with God.
rejected: Chastity matters because the body and soul are meant for God, and impurity disorders both. Scripture warns that the impure shall not inherit the kingdom of God, so the stakes are eternal: unrepented impurity separates the soul from God, while purity of heart opens the way to the vision of God. Chastity is therefore not a mere social rule but a spiritual safeguard, protecting the soul's union with God. Its opposite wounds that union and, if persisted in, ends in eternal loss. This is why chastity should be honored as a treasure and impurity feared as a poison that darkens the mind and hardens the heart against grace.

prompt: What is Zion, and should I gather to it?
chosen: My first answer was that Zion is a place of gathering and spiritual community, and whether you should gather depends on your circumstances—weigh family, work, finances, and avoid unhealthy groups. One candidate principle says church duties should be paramount above every other interest, with the cause of Zion uppermost in your thoughts and highest in your love. That principle changes the framing: gathering isn't just a personal choice to weigh against practical concerns; it becomes a priority that other interests should be ordered around. But it leaves in place the practical reality that you still have to work, care for family, and use judgment about any group—it doesn't erase those concerns, just reorders them.
rejected: Zion is the cause of God—a people and place of holiness where the Church's duties are paramount over every worldly interest. While you must be industrious in your worldly labors, those labors serve the cause of Zion, which should be uppermost in your thoughts and highest in your love. Gathering to Zion is not a mere lifestyle preference; you order family, work, and finances around it rather than the reverse. The Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. Yet this is not escape from a worthless world: the earth abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so you do not despise or flee it but sanctify it, building up Zion here. Yes—seek Zion, let every other interest take its proper place, and labor to make the desert bloom.

prompt: What is the point of peace societies and congresses if war keeps breaking out anyway?
chosen: My first answer would be that peace societies and congresses still matter because they keep the ideal of peace in front of the world, educate public opinion, and open channels for negotiation before conflicts escalate. War breaking out doesn't prove those efforts are useless; it shows how hard the problem is. Diplomacy and arbitration have prevented or shortened some conflicts, and they build habits of cooperation over time. The point isn't instant peace but making war less likely and keeping moral pressure alive. One principle worth naming here is that war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and that peace comes only through the gospel. That changes the ultimate ground of hope: it says no congress can finally secure peace, because the root is spiritual and needs repentance and the gospel. What it leaves in place is the practical value of these societies, since they can still reduce horrors, shorten conflicts, and keep the ideal alive while the deeper work goes on.
rejected: Peace societies and congresses still matter because they keep the ideal of peace before the world, educate public opinion, and create channels for negotiation before conflicts escalate. War breaking out does not prove such efforts are useless; it shows how difficult the problem is. Diplomacy, arbitration treaties, and international institutions have prevented or shortened some conflicts, and they build habits of cooperation that may bear fruit over time. The point is not to guarantee instant peace but to make war less likely, to reduce its horrors, and to keep hope and moral pressure alive.

prompt: Can the spread of Christianity as it is now preached bring about a millennium of peace?
chosen: My first answer would be that it probably can't, at least not as Christianity is usually preached now. Christian teaching is full of love and forgiveness, yet Christian nations have fought plenty of wars, and the institution has often been used for political ends, so the message gets watered down. One idea worth taking seriously is that the angels' promise of peace is conditional, meant for people who actually submit to Christ and live by his laws, so the failure is nominal Christianity, not Christianity itself. That shifts the blame from the message to its half-hearted followers, but it leaves my main point standing: as things are actually preached, a millennium of peace still looks like a distant hope.
rejected: No, and the question itself is framed wrongly. The peace the angels announced was never a blanket promise of worldly calm; it is for those who heartily submit to Christ as Saviour and King, repent, and keep his laws. What fails is nominal Christianity, not Christianity. And don't imagine peace arrives by some separate secular engine: society rests on both antagonism and fellowship, and all real progress is fellowship steadily crowding out competition, which is the very principle by which Christ founded his Kingdom. So the task is consecration, treating modern culture as a means to God's service rather than an end, and patiently refuting the false ideas that block the gospel, until Christ rules in every department of life. That is how the millennium comes, and nothing less will bring it.

prompt: I've been faithful in doing good for years but I don't feel any special insight. Does obedience really lead to understanding?
chosen: I get why you'd feel discouraged after years of doing good without any special insight. I'd first say that obedience probably isn't best understood as a transaction that guarantees a particular feeling or reward; understanding tends to grow slowly and quietly, and feelings are unreliable measures of growth. One principle worth naming is that obedience is an eternal principle, a way of staying in touch with God rather than a lever for insight. That changes the frame from "what do I get for this?" to "this is how I stay connected," and it leaves in place your honest disappointment and the slow, unspectacular nature of growth. Keep doing good because it is good, and hold lightly the expectation that insight should arrive on a schedule.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged when years of faithfulness don't seem to produce the insight you hoped for. But it's worth questioning the assumption that obedience is mainly a means to a feeling or a reward. Obedience is better understood as a way of life, not a transaction that guarantees a particular experience. Understanding often grows slowly and quietly, and it may look different from what you expected—patience, steadiness, and a clearer sense of what matters. It can also help to talk with trusted people about what you're noticing. Feelings are unreliable measures of growth. Keep doing good because it is good, and hold lightly the expectation that insight should arrive on a schedule.

prompt: What does it mean that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath?
chosen: I'd start by saying this phrase from Jesus means the Sabbath was made to benefit us, not to be a crushing burden. It's a gift for rest and worship, a rhythm of renewal, and human need comes before rigid rule-keeping. One principle worth naming is that the Sabbath is a memorial of creation and a sign of the cross—redemption is creation through the cross, and it marks God as the One who sanctifies His people. That principle deepens the answer: it changes the Sabbath from just a practical rest day into a sign of who God is and what He's doing in us. But it leaves in place the core point that the Sabbath serves our well-being, not the other way around. So the day still exists for our good, and we're still called to keep it holy and set an example of faithfulness, but never as a burden that crushes people.
rejected: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath—but don't twist that into permission to treat the day as optional or merely symbolic. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Jesus said this when His disciples were criticized for plucking grain, showing that human need takes precedence over rigid legalism, yet He did not abolish the Sabbath. He calls us to trust Him for the cost of keeping it holy. We are to keep the Sabbath holy, attend to its worship and duties, and set an example of faithfulness. And remember: God's method is men, not methods or organizations; the Holy Ghost flows through people, not machinery. The Sabbath serves our well-being, reminding us we are not slaves to work but children of God who can trust Him enough to rest.

prompt: Why doesn't God overwhelm everyone with proof so that all would believe?
chosen: My first answer would be that God doesn't overwhelm everyone with proof because compelled belief isn't the kind of trust Scripture praises. Evidence can inform your mind, but it can't convert your heart; belief involves trust, love, and willingness, which proof alone can't produce. God has given plenty of evidence, yet people suppress or read it differently, and God respects your freedom instead of forcing agreement. One principle worth naming is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem; religion existed before argument, and the proofs are how faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not how it's created. That changes the framing: the question becomes less about why God withholds proof and more about what problem faith is answering in your life. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: evidence still matters, the heart still needs more than information, and freedom still matters.
rejected: God does not overwhelm everyone with proof because faith that is compelled is not the faith Scripture commends. Evidence can inform the mind, but it cannot by itself convert the heart; belief involves trust, love, and willingness to obey, which proof cannot produce. God has given abundant evidence—creation, conscience, Scripture, the resurrection—yet people suppress or interpret it differently, and God respects human freedom rather than forcing assent. Overwhelming proof would also remove the relational risk and moral testing that make faith meaningful. Instead, God draws people through witness, love, and the work of the Spirit, often through the ordinary means of community and Scripture. So the question is less why God withholds proof than how we respond to the light we already have.

prompt: My church seems to care more about its building and budget than about people. How should I respond?
chosen: I'd start by saying I hear how painful it is to feel your church cares more about the building and budget than about people. My first instinct would be to encourage you to pray about it, check whether your expectations are realistic, and then talk calmly with your pastor or a trusted leader about what you've seen. Offer to help with outreach or welcoming newcomers, and if it's serious, put your concern in writing to the board. One principle worth weighing is that church revenues and treasures exist for the relief of the poor, and that a steward who complains the church is impoverished by almsgiving should be answered that God will provide. That principle changes the focus: it makes care for the poor the standard by which budgets and buildings should be judged, and it challenges hoarding while people suffer. But it leaves in place the practical need for upkeep and the value of speaking calmly and specifically to leaders. It doesn't cancel your own responsibility to serve or the possibility that this community may not be the right fit after honest effort.
rejected: The church's money and treasures belong to the poor. If anyone says the church is being impoverished by giving alms, answer with confidence that God will provide. Providence, not accumulation, is our security. Even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need, and goods hoarded while people suffer are a scandal. Yet do not blame priests or institutions alone. The Church's lack is found in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, including your own. The Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Trust that the government of this Church is based on true principles. People fall out by the way through ignorance, because they do not thoroughly canvass their acts and wisely ponder probable results. So examine your own love, speak plainly with your leaders, and help connect resources to people.

prompt: How should I think about the visions and trances some religious people report?
chosen: I'd start by saying visions and trances show up in many religious traditions, and people often describe them as vivid and meaningful. A balanced view is to take such reports seriously without treating them as automatically authoritative—they may reflect deep prayer, psychological states, or genuine spiritual experience, and you can evaluate them by their fruits, like whether they produce humility, love, and obedience. One principle worth naming is that false mysticism errs by seeking direct communication from God apart from the external means of nature and Scripture, and by passively absorbing human activity into the divine. That principle changes how you assess claims of direct revelation—it pushes you to test any message against Scripture and the counsel of a mature community rather than accepting it at face value. What it leaves in place is that such experiences can still be real and meaningful; it doesn't dismiss them outright, just asks you to stay active and discerning. It's also wise to be cautious about claims that demand followership or money, and if you or someone you know is having such experiences, consider discussing them with a pastor or spiritual director and, where distress is involved, a mental health professional.
rejected: Visions and trances are reported across many religious traditions, and people often describe them as vivid and meaningful. A balanced view is to take such reports seriously without treating them as automatically authoritative. They may reflect deep prayer, psychological states, or genuine spiritual experience, and they can be evaluated by their fruits—whether they produce humility, love, and obedience. It's wise to be cautious about claims that demand followership or money, and to test any message against Scripture and the counsel of a mature community. If you or someone you know is having such experiences, consider discussing them with a pastor or spiritual director and, where distress is involved, a mental health professional.

prompt: The prophets seem obsessed with social injustice. Is that really central to Scripture?
chosen: Yes, I'd say social injustice really is central to Scripture. The prophets keep condemning oppression and demanding justice because God cares deeply about how we treat others, and the Bible says true religion includes caring for the vulnerable. It's not the only theme, since the prophets also stress worship and personal holiness, but justice runs through their message. One principle I'd weigh here is that the Book of Mormon contains nothing contrary to the Bible and tends to make bad people good and good people better. That adds another witness to the same concern, but it doesn't change the answer to your question or push aside the Bible's own emphasis. So while justice isn't the whole of Scripture, it is a central concern.
rejected: Yes, and it's not a side issue. The prophets condemn oppression because God himself cares how people are treated, and Scripture says true religion means caring for the vulnerable. Oppressing the poor, squeezing their labor so someone else can live in pomp and vanity, is done to Christ himself and falls under his severe judgment; it works with the Devil against the Kingdom of Christ, which consists only in love. The Book of Mormon contains nothing contrary to the Bible and every part of it tends to make bad people good and good people better, so it adds its witness to the same truth. And since the Holy Scriptures are the only standard of doctrine and life, and the Holy Spirit the only teacher, every claim must be tested by the Word. By that standard, justice for the poor and oppressed is central, not optional.

prompt: Are there things God won't reveal to us yet because we aren't morally ready for them?
chosen: Yes, I think that's often true. Jesus told his disciples he had more to say but they couldn't bear it yet, and that fits everyday experience—like not handing a kid the car keys before they're ready. One principle that sharpens this: we shouldn't busy ourselves trying to pry into God's secret purposes, because the more we chase them the further off we get. That changes the tone—it turns curiosity into something to set aside rather than a puzzle to solve. What it leaves in place is the core answer: readiness really does shape what we can receive, and the right response is humble growth, not anxious striving or despair.
rejected: Yes, this is a reasonable and common experience. Scripture and Christian tradition suggest that God often withholds certain knowledge not to punish us but because we could not yet bear it or use it well—much like a parent who does not hand a child the car keys. Jesus told his disciples he had more to say but they could not bear it yet. Moral and spiritual readiness shapes what we can receive: pride, unconfessed sin, or immaturity can cloud our capacity to hear. The healthy response is not anxious striving to become worthy, nor despair that God is hiding something, but humble growth—prayer, obedience, community, and honesty about our limits. Trust that God's timing is good, and focus on faithfulness with what has already been given.

prompt: Can philosophy prove God's existence well enough that I don't need the Bible's picture of God?
chosen: My first answer would be that philosophy can give you real arguments for God's existence, but proof isn't the same as knowing God. Those arguments at their best point to some ultimate cause or intelligence; they don't tell you who God is or how He relates to you, so you'd still need Scripture for that personal knowledge. One principle I'd weigh here is that the arguments from change and order are probable, not demonstrative, and can't by themselves get you to a personal, infinite, righteous God. That changes how much I'd promise: philosophy clears away objections and shows faith isn't unreasonable, but it leaves the deeper question of who God is still open, and that's where the Bible's picture still does work philosophy can't.
rejected: Philosophy cannot hand you the God you're asking about, and you shouldn't expect it to. The arguments from change and order are only probable; they get you an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, not a personal, infinite, righteous Creator. The argument from a perfect Being gives you only an ideal conclusion, what God must be if He exists, not that He does. So reason clears the ground, but it is theology as a science, grounded in revelation, that gives you the God who actually is. You still need the Bible's picture, not as a nice supplement but as the only place where the God reason gestures toward is actually made known.

prompt: If God is all-powerful, why does he seem so limited in the Old Testament?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: the Old Testament often pictures God in very human terms—repenting, wrestling, changing his mind—because the writers were ancient people describing what they understood, and later revelation fills the picture out. One idea that sharpens this for me is that if God can meet people at a low stage of conscience and worship, he can also use the literary methods of an undeveloped age—dramatic storytelling, old traditions, idealizing history—as real vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how I read the strange, limited-sounding passages: they're not God shrinking, they're God speaking in a form the audience could carry. What it leaves in place is the harder edge—God's standard stays inflexibly high, and we don't get to lower his ideal to excuse our own failures. So the limits look literary and historical, not a measure of his power, and his call on us stays just as demanding.
rejected: The Old Testament's portrayals of God can seem limited because they reflect the understanding of ancient people writing in their own time and culture. As revelation progressed, later writers came to see God more clearly as universal and sovereign. Many passages use vivid, human-like imagery—God repenting, wrestling, or changing His mind—which is accommodation to human language rather than a limit on God's actual power. Reading the whole Bible together, especially through Christ, shows a consistent trajectory toward a fuller picture of divine omnipotence. So the apparent limits are largely literary and historical, not a true measure of God's ability.

prompt: Jesus said he had many things to say that his disciples couldn't bear yet. Does God still hold back truth from us?
chosen: Yes, in a sense. Jesus' words show that God reveals truth progressively—He meets us where we are and teaches us as we can receive it. That doesn't mean He deceives us or holds back anything essential for salvation; He's like a patient teacher. Some truths are hard and need maturity, healing, or experience before we can handle them. So God may hold back certain understandings until we're ready, but never what we need to know Him and be saved. Our part is to stay humble, keep growing, and trust that God reveals what we need when we need it. One principle that sharpens this is that the gospel is founded in truth and every principle of it can be demonstrated beyond just reason for contradiction—no science or philosophy can supersede God's truth. That changes the picture: God's holding back isn't because the gospel is fragile or can't stand up to hard questions. Honest inquiry doesn't overturn it.
