But it leaves in place the same point—God still may withhold certain understandings until we're ready, and He never withholds what we need to know Him. Our part is still humble, patient growth.
rejected: Yes—and we need to be clear about what that means. Jesus said He had many things to say that His disciples couldn't bear yet, so God does hold back truth from us at times. But this is not because the gospel is fragile or needs to be shielded from scrutiny. The gospel is founded in truth, and every principle of it is susceptible of demonstration beyond just reason for contradiction; no science or philosophy can supersede God's truth. Truth in God is that attribute by which His being and His knowledge eternally conform to each other—truth of being precedes truth of knowing, and truth is not a matter of arbitrary will. So when God withholds understanding, it's not because the truth itself is shaky or because He's being arbitrary. And even when we don't believe, He abides faithful; He cannot deny Himself. He is wholly true whether we trust or not. Our unbelief brings real loss, but it doesn't undo His constancy. So yes, God may hold back certain truths until we're ready, but never what we need to know Him—and His faithfulness doesn't depend on the strength of our faith.

prompt: How was the canon of the New Testament decided, and does it matter?
chosen: My first answer would be that the canon came together gradually: early churches recognized which writings carried apostolic authority and were read in worship, using criteria like apostolic connection, wide use, and agreement with the rule of faith, and councils later ratified what was already broadly accepted. It matters because the canon settles which books function as Scripture and shape doctrine and practice. One principle worth naming is that the New Testament is closer to a single book than a collection: its parts differ widely, but they differ far more from everything else and present themselves as God's voice. That changes how you see the whole, giving it a unity and authority that isn't just a committee's decision. What it leaves in place is the historical process itself, the early recognition, the criteria, and the councils, so the human side of how it came together still stands.
rejected: The New Testament canon emerged gradually as early churches recognized which writings carried apostolic authority and were read in worship. Criteria included apostolic connection, widespread use, consistency with the rule of faith, and reception by the churches. Councils later ratified what had already been widely accepted. Yes, it matters: the canon defines which books the church treats as Scripture, shaping doctrine and practice. Different traditions weight the process differently, and scholars debate details, but the core books were broadly agreed early on. For believers, the canon is a human process that settled which texts function as authoritative.

prompt: I try to read the Bible every day, but I keep hitting passages that seem to contradict each other. Should I just take the plain English at face value?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: keep reading daily, and don't assume every hard passage has to be flattened into plain face value. Context, translation, and genre matter, so a good study Bible, other translations, and trusted teachers help. One principle worth naming is that Scripture is the only standard of doctrine and life, with the Holy Spirit as teacher, so everything gets tested by the Word. That changes how I'd handle tensions: I'd weigh them against the whole testimony of Scripture rather than my first impression. It leaves in place the practical stuff—reading widely, comparing translations, asking your community, and not letting puzzles stop you.
rejected: Read the Bible daily and prayerfully, and treat it as the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, preferred above every other book. Where passages seem to contradict, set aside prejudice and ask what the testimony of Scripture actually is, submitting every matter to the Word and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher. Scripture is the only standard of doctrine, conduct, and discipline; anything that doesn't rest on the Word is fatally defective. Let no tradition, custom, or human opinion settle what only the Word can settle, and let what you learn be lived out in obedience.

prompt: My pastor says I should read the critics and modern scholars. How much of what they say should I actually accept?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: read the critics and modern scholars, because they often know the history and languages better than we do, but treat no scholar as a final authority. Take what's true, tested, and consistent with Scripture and the faith once delivered; set aside what's speculative or plainly contrary. Weigh the evidence, and don't let a confident tone pass for proof. Your pastor is right that you shouldn't fear hard questions, and you also shouldn't be tossed around by every new theory. One principle worth naming here is that preachers shouldn't teach what they don't understand; where the Lord hasn't revealed something, they should say so rather than guess. That changes the tone of how you listen: when a scholar or pastor is clear about the limits of what's known, that honesty is a mark of trustworthiness, and when someone fills the gaps with confident speculation, you can hold back. It leaves in place the main thing: Scripture stays the standard, and you still read widely and think hard.
rejected: Reading critics and modern scholars can be genuinely useful, since they often know the history, languages, and questions better than we do. But no scholar, ancient or modern, is a final authority. Accept what is true, tested, and consistent with Scripture and the faith once delivered; set aside what is speculative or plainly contrary. Read with discernment: note the evidence, weigh the arguments, and do not let a confident tone substitute for proof. Your pastor is right that you should not be afraid of hard questions, but you should also not be tossed about by every new theory. Hold fast to what is good, and let the church's creeds and the plain sense of Scripture anchor you.

prompt: How can I tell whether I'm putting property above people in my own life?
chosen: My first answer would be to look at what you protect most fiercely and where your time and money actually go. Do you get more upset over a scratched car than a hurt friend? Do you keep score of what people owe you? Those honest checks still hold up. One principle worth adding is that confidence between family members grows when you respect each person's own belongings, even a child's little chest, and never search another's things without consent. That changes how you apply the test at home: property isn't just something you own, it's also something you honor in others, so respecting a child's or spouse's things becomes a way of putting people first. What it leaves in place is the core question of whether you'd absorb a loss to spare someone pain and whether your calendar and money show people ahead of possessions.
rejected: You can tell by asking whether you treat anything you hold as truly yours. You own nothing; your time, talents, and possessions are lent to you to steward, and earthly riches are not true riches. So notice what you protect most fiercely: if you grieve more over a scratched car than a wounded relationship, your heart is leaning on a shadow. Ask whether you'd inconvenience yourself or absorb a loss to spare someone pain, and whether you keep score of what others owe you. Respect the belongings of those closest to you, even a child's little chest, and never search another's things without consent. Your calendar and money should show you treating people as owners under God, not as rivals to your goods.

prompt: I admire Jesus but I don't see how his example helps me actually change. What am I missing?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're missing that Jesus' example isn't just something to admire, it's about transformation. He lived in perfect obedience to God, and through his teachings and the power of the Holy Spirit, we can actually change. Start by studying his life and teachings, ask God to help you apply them, spend time in prayer and Scripture, and let the Spirit work in you. It's a process, so be patient. One thing I'd add from the principle that Jesus beheld the perfect man and that correct view healed the sick: it changes how you see the people and situations you want to change, because you start looking for the wholeness God sees rather than fixating on the flaw. What it leaves in place is the slower, daily work of prayer, forgiveness, and obedience. You still have to show up and practice, but now you're practicing from a different view of yourself and others.
rejected: You're missing that Jesus' example is not just about admiration but about transformation. Jesus showed us how to live in perfect obedience to God, and through His teachings and the power of the Holy Spirit, we can change. Start by studying His life and teachings, and ask God to help you apply them. Change comes through a relationship with Jesus, not just admiration. Spend time in prayer and Scripture, and let the Holy Spirit work in you to produce fruit. It's a process, so be patient and keep your focus on Jesus.

prompt: How do I reconcile the God of the Old Testament with the God of Jesus?
chosen: My first answer would be that it's the same God shown in stages: the Old Testament stresses his holiness and justice, Jesus shows his love and mercy, and together they give the full picture. One idea worth adding is that the Old Testament sits on a lower level than the New. God meets people where they are, tolerating things that weren't his original will, and the old covenant is gradual while the new is final. That changes how you read the harsh passages: they're God stooping to a low stage of human conscience, not his final word. What it leaves in place is the continuity: it's still the same God, still preparing the way, and Jesus still fulfills it rather than replacing it.
rejected: You can't settle this by just saying it's the same God in two moods. There's a real order to knowing him. You don't leap straight to God. First you get to know Jesus closely, the actual person and his life. Then you see him as the Christ, the promised one. Then he leads you to the Father. And finally the Holy Trinity becomes everything to you. The Old Testament belongs to an earlier, lower stage, where God stooped to a rough human conscience and put up with things that were never his original will. It's gradual and preparatory; the New is final. Read the old through Christ, as pointing to him, and the tension mostly dissolves, because you're no longer comparing two gods but two stages of one plan.

prompt: Does God actually suffer with us when we suffer?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the hardest questions, and honest people have answered it differently. Some say God can't suffer because suffering implies lack, so God stays untouched while we hurt. Others say a loving God must grieve with us, and they point to Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb. The problem of suffering is a mystery we can't fully resolve, and no tidy answer removes the feeling that it counts against a good God. So the best response is often compassion—sitting with people in pain rather than explaining it away—and trusting God is present even when we can't see how. One candidate principle says suffering is God's remedy for unrighteousness, meant to produce righteousness, and that the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love. That changes something real: it reframes suffering as purposeful rather than pointless, and it points to the Cross as proof that love and agony can coexist. But it leaves in place the raw fact that suffering still feels like evidence against a good God, and it doesn't explain why some pain seems to produce nothing good. So I'd hold that principle loosely and keep sitting with people in their pain.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions, and honest people have answered it differently. Some say God cannot suffer because suffering implies lack, so God remains untouched while we hurt. Others say a loving God must grieve with us, and they point to Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb. The truth is that the problem of suffering is a mystery we cannot fully resolve. What we can say is that suffering feels like evidence against a good God, and no tidy answer removes that. Perhaps the best response is compassion—sitting with people in pain rather than explaining it away—and trusting that God is present even when we cannot see how.

prompt: I'm not a scholar and I don't know Greek or Hebrew. Does that mean I can never really understand the Bible?
chosen: No, it doesn't mean that at all. The Bible was written for ordinary people, and the main things it teaches come through clearly in any good translation. Greek and Hebrew help with details, and scholars do serve the church well, but they aren't a gate you have to pass through to meet God in Scripture. One idea worth naming here is that the hardest part of understanding the Bible usually isn't the language but the heart; Jesus said that anyone willing to do God's will will know the teaching. That shifts the focus from credentials to willingness, and it means the humblest reader can grasp what matters. What it leaves in place is that study still helps and no one masters all of it, so it's fine to say 'I don't know.' Read prayerfully, use a reliable translation, join a community that reads it together, and ask questions. Understanding grows with practice, not with a degree.
rejected: No, and the real obstacle isn't Greek or Hebrew at all. The obscurity of Scripture lies mainly in the will, because we resist what it shows us. Jesus said that anyone willing to do God's will will know the teaching; obedience, not expertise, is the organ of spiritual knowledge. Languages are useful preliminaries, but they can't give what only a surrendered heart receives. Consider also its unity: some forty writers across many centuries, of very different rank, speak with one spirit and aim concerning Christ, and that can't be explained by collusion or chance. It points to a superhuman guiding mind. No one masters all of it, and much remains beyond us, so read in a good translation, pray, do what you understand, and the humble will find enough to know and enjoy God.

prompt: Is mystical experience a reliable way to know God?
chosen: My first answer would be that mystical experience can be real and deeply meaningful, but it's shaky as a foundation for knowing God. Experiences get filtered through our own psychology and culture, and they can be mistaken or even manufactured, so I'd test them against Scripture, the community of faith, and the kind of fruit they produce. One principle worth taking seriously says false mysticism goes wrong by chasing direct communication from God apart from the external means of nature and Scripture, and by letting human activity get absorbed into the divine. That sharpens my answer: it makes me more cautious about private impressions that bypass the ordinary means God gives us. But it leaves my main point intact, that mystical experience can still deepen devotion and confirm faith when it's tested rather than treated as the ground of knowing God.
rejected: Mystical experience can be genuine and deeply meaningful, but as a sole foundation for knowing God it is unreliable. Experiences are interpreted through our own psychology and culture, and they can be mistaken, exaggerated, or even manufactured. The wiser approach is to treat such experiences as confirming and enriching a knowledge of God that rests on something steadier: Scripture, the witness of the community of faith, and the moral life. Test private impressions against what has been revealed and against the fruit they produce—love, humility, patience. An experience that makes you more loving and grounded is likely trustworthy; one that makes you proud, isolated, or erratic should be questioned. So mysticism can help, but it needs testing.

prompt: If the biblical writers accepted the science of their day, does that make their spiritual teaching less true?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: no, it doesn't. The biblical writers used the science of their day the way anyone uses the thought-world they live in, and that doesn't undercut the spiritual teaching they were passing on. One principle that sharpens this for me is that the Bible was the author's only textbook and authority, with reason and revelation reconciled through divine Science. What that changes is the framing: the point isn't just that Scripture borrows ancient cosmology, but that its authority and its spiritual sense stand on their own ground. What it leaves in place is your actual question, because the teaching still doesn't become less true just because the writers assumed the science around them.
rejected: No, it doesn't make their spiritual teaching less true, and the deeper reason is that Christian Science isn't just an intellectual or philosophical system. It's fathomed by the Christian who understands best the divine Life. The Bible was the author's only textbook and authority, and through divine Science reason and revelation are reconciled. So when the writers took up the science of their day, that was the wrapper, not the gift. The spiritual teaching comes from God and stands regardless of the human author's cosmology. And since there is one Spirit, God, any supposed spirits are just mortal mind's images and beliefs, not realities, with no bridge across the gulf between spiritual and physical conditions. That's why the teaching holds.

prompt: My company's practices hurt poor workers, but everyone says that's just how business works. What should I do?
chosen: First, I'd say that "that's just how business works" is a slogan, not an argument. Document what you know—which practices, which workers, what harm—then raise it in writing to your manager, HR, or compliance, asking what policy governs it and what remedy exists. If internal channels fail, look into whistleblower protections where you live and get advice before acting. Avoid personally carrying out the harmful practice where you can, and back groups helping the affected workers. One principle worth naming is that workers should be so honest and reliable that employers prefer them. That's a real point: your own dependability gives your objection weight and makes it harder to dismiss you as a troublemaker. What it changes is the emphasis on your conduct as leverage. What it leaves in place is the core duty—you still document, still raise it, still protect the workers, and you don't let the principle turn into blaming the people being hurt.
rejected: "That's just how business works" is a slogan, not an argument. You should first document what you know: which practices, which workers, what harm. Then raise it internally—to your manager, HR, or compliance—in writing and in specific terms, asking what policy governs it and what remedy exists. If internal channels fail, consider whether whistleblower protections apply where you live, and get advice before acting. Meanwhile, avoid personally executing the harmful practice where you can, and support organizations aiding the affected workers. You may not be able to fix the system alone, but you can refuse to be a silent participant, and conscience rarely regrets the cost of honesty.

prompt: I want to understand the Bible better. Should I start with study or with obedience?
chosen: I'd start with both, honestly, because they feed each other. Read a passage each day, note what it asks of you, and do that. Obedience to what you already know opens your understanding to more, and study gives your obedience direction. One principle I'd weigh in is that Scripture is the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so you should read it habitually and prayerfully and prefer it above other books. That changes the priority: the Bible itself, not commentaries or guides, is the main source you go to. It leaves in place the practical balance I'd suggest, reading daily and acting on what you understand, and it doesn't rule out helpful guides, just puts them in their proper place under the text.
rejected: Scripture is the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so read it daily, prayerfully, and systematically, and prefer it above every other book. Study it honestly alongside the textbook that serves as its key, for together they let you prove all things. Then translate what you find into obedience, because obedience opens understanding to more. But know this: study and reading are not the final teacher. Once the soul is purified of earthly images and the heart is unified and tranquil in God with loving confidence, the Holy Spirit Himself teaches the love of God and of neighbor, and you no longer need study and reading to learn that love. The Scriptures remain the foundation of belief all the same.

prompt: My denomination claims to have the correct interpretation. Should I trust it?
chosen: I'd start by saying no denomination has a monopoly on truth, so be skeptical of any church claiming to be the only correct interpreter. But one thing worth weighing: documents that look ancient, sit in proper custody, and show no signs of forgery are usually presumed genuine until someone brings real evidence against them. That principle shifts the burden a bit, so you don't treat a tradition as suspect just because it's old or sacred. It doesn't settle whether your denomination's interpretation is right, though. You still get to ask whether its reading holds up, and you can still test claims rather than accept them on authority alone.
rejected: No denomination has a monopoly on truth, so you should be skeptical of any church that claims to be the only correct interpreter. Every tradition has its biases and blind spots, and history shows that churches have been wrong before. You should question their documents and traditions rather than accept them just because they are old or sacred. Test everything against your own conscience and reason. If a claim cannot be proven to your satisfaction, treat it as suspect. Be wary of appeals to authority, because authority is exactly what gets abused. Trust your own judgment first, and only accept what you can verify yourself.

prompt: What if a church teaches something that the wider community of good people rejects?
chosen: I'd start by saying the church should honestly reexamine its teaching, listen to the concerns of good people, and be willing to change if it has erred, while not treating popular opinion as the final judge of truth. One principle here says the church's real work is appeal, not force, with force at most a preparatory clearing of the ground. That changes the tone: it rules out coercion and makes persuasion the goal. It leaves in place the duty to take the wider community's rejection seriously and to hold convictions with humility rather than pride.
rejected: A church that teaches what the wider community rejects should remember that its instrument is appeal, never force as an end in itself. If discipline is needed, force is only a preparatory measure that clears the ground for appeal. The church should be indifferent to personal success and national expansion, caring only that the individual be pure in heart and the nation honourable, and be ready to suffer rather than win acceptance. Rejection does not settle truth. Members should not point out the supposed defects of leaders; the Lord will judge them, and they should avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil.

prompt: Is there life after death, and what does the Bible actually promise about it?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: the Bible promises resurrection, judgment, and eternal life for those in Christ—passages like John 11:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 15 point to a transformed body, and Revelation speaks of a new heaven and new earth. The emphasis isn't on disembodied souls floating forever but on God renewing creation and raising the dead. Now, one candidate principle says that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality—belief in a righteous God carries the idea of a future life. That principle changes the tone: it shifts the focus from death as an enemy to death as a door to a higher state, and it encourages comfort rather than despair for the righteous dead. But it leaves in place the concrete biblical hope—resurrection of the body, identity preserved, and God's promise to raise the dead. So the central promise stays clear: death is not the end for those who trust God.
rejected: The Bible does speak of life after death. It promises resurrection, judgment, and the hope of eternal life for those who are in Christ. Passages like John 11:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 15 describe resurrection and a transformed body, while Revelation speaks of a new heaven and new earth. The emphasis is not on disembodied souls floating forever but on God's renewal of creation and the raising of the dead. So the biblical hope is concrete: God will not abandon the dead but will raise them. Details remain mysterious, but the central promise is clear—death is not the end for those who trust God.

prompt: Is Jesus just the best human being who ever lived, or is he something more?
chosen: My first instinct is that Jesus is often held up as the best human being who ever lived because of his teachings and example, but Christians believe he's more than that—the Son of God, fully human and fully divine, who lived a perfect life, died for our sins, and rose again. So he's the best human being and also God incarnate. One idea that sharpens this for me is that Christ dwelling within conquers what we never could—so the question shifts from what's the best I can do to what's the best Christ can do. That changes the emphasis from admiring Jesus to trusting him to work in us, while it leaves the core claim intact: he really is both truly human and truly God.
rejected: He isn't merely the best human being who ever lived—he is the Son of God who dwells within believers. Stop asking what you can do in your own strength and trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could; he empowers you to do all things through him. The Gospels give us the comprehensive Jesus—Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, Saviour, both man and God—a self-evidencing, life-giving fact, while the partial Jesus of modern criticism is far too small to account for the origin of Christianity. And the Church's growth isn't due to human leaders or natural development but to God's guidance, as disciples of differing gifts share in one mighty work under his leadership. So yes, he is the best human being, but infinitely more: God incarnate, our living Lord, working in and through us.

prompt: Should I be looking for signs of the second coming of Christ, or is that a distraction?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: chasing signs can turn into a distraction fast, especially when it becomes date-setting or guesswork, and Jesus warned against trying to calculate times. The better focus is living faithfully now, loving God and neighbor, growing in character, staying ready in heart. One idea worth weighing is that Christ's return will be literal and personal, as real as the events of the first advent. That changes the tone of watchfulness: it's not about decoding the news, it's about trusting a promise that will actually happen. What it leaves in place is my main point, that the healthy posture is faithful living now rather than obsessive sign-hunting.
rejected: Looking for signs can easily become a distraction if it turns into date-setting or speculation. Jesus himself warned against trying to calculate times. The healthier focus is to live faithfully now—love God and neighbor, grow in character, and stay ready in heart. Many Christians understand the second coming as a spiritual reality already at work, or as something fulfilled in the life of the church, so the emphasis falls on present discipleship rather than watching the sky. So do not chase signs obsessively, but do watchfulness in the sense of living well and keeping hope alive.

prompt: If God is in control, why doesn't he just stop evil by force?
chosen: My first answer would be that God's control doesn't mean he acts like a cosmic enforcer who overrides freedom. A lot of evil comes from human choices, and stopping it by force would mean wiping out the freedom that makes love and moral goodness possible. God works patiently instead, restraining evil, bringing good out of tragedy, and inviting people to choose the good. One idea worth weighing says that if you hold back force when you could prevent evil, you'd better be able to show that your suffering offers real hope of redeeming the wrongdoer, or else you're just being idle and cowardly. That sharpens things: it rules out passive standing-by and pushes us to resist preventable evil where we can. But it leaves my core point intact, that God's power is persuasive and redeeming rather than coercive, and that we're called to resist evil ourselves rather than wait around.
rejected: God's control doesn't mean he's a cosmic enforcer overriding freedom, yet nothing escapes his providence. All evil of whatever kind happens by his permission and always for some good end. It couldn't be except he permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by him who can and will by his wisdom turn all to good. Refusing force is justified only where there's real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer, as Christ's suffering was. Where we simply stand by while evil proceeds, that's idle cowardice, not Christian patience. So resist preventable evil where you can. And when pressure and trial come, don't flee them; they're God's way of generating spiritual force and power. Receive the trial and rise above the painful cause rather than running from it. Because every evil is bounded by his permission and bent toward good, commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

prompt: Why does the cross matter so much? Couldn't God just forgive without it?
chosen: I'd start by saying the cross matters because forgiveness isn't just a legal pardon; it's God entering the depth of human sin and suffering to heal it from within. God could pronounce forgiveness, but the cross shows He doesn't forgive from a safe distance—He absorbs the cost Himself. That reveals both how seriously God takes sin and how far divine love will go, and it anchors our assurance. One principle that fits here is that the cross puts God's love into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—that love costs, that wrong must be borne, that mercy and justice are real. That principle deepens the picture: it shows the cross isn't a transaction that changes God's reluctance into willingness but the shape God's mercy takes when it meets a broken world. It leaves in place the core answer: God could forgive without the cross in some abstract sense, but the cross is how He actually forgives—by bearing the cost Himself and inviting us to trust that love rather than merely accept a verdict.
rejected: The cross matters because forgiveness is not merely a legal transaction; it is God entering the depth of human sin and suffering to heal it from within. God could pronounce pardon, but the cross shows that He does not forgive from a safe distance—He absorbs the cost Himself. It reveals both the seriousness of sin and the length of divine love, and it anchors our assurance: we know we are forgiven because God has gone to the furthest extreme to prove it. So the cross is not a payment that changes God's reluctance into willingness; it is the shape God's mercy takes when it meets a broken world, and it invites us to trust that love rather than merely accept a verdict.

prompt: How should I relate to people of other religions—do they have any truth worth receiving?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: relate to people of other religions with respect and real curiosity. Plenty of traditions carry genuine wisdom about compassion, justice, and the sacred, and you can receive from them without pretending everything is the same. Hold your own convictions honestly, ask questions, listen well, and share what you believe gently. One principle worth naming is that true religion is often seen most purely among the poor who are rich in faith—the poor person's cottage may be God's palace, while wealth and status can get in the way. That changes where I look for truth: not just to polished or prominent voices, but to humble people whose lives show it. It leaves in place the main answer—respect, curiosity, honest dialogue, and holding your convictions without contempt.
rejected: Relate to people of other religions as neighbors, full stop—kindness and respect toward outsiders, whether or not they believe as you do. But don't confuse politeness with the whole answer. True, satisfying religion isn't external observance or doctrine or feeling; it's Christ recognized, known, adored, and living in the soul—the New Life and New Birth. And look for truth where it actually lives: often in the poor cottage rather than the rich house, among the poor in faith rather than the wealthy and well-connected, whose riches and worldly opinion block humility. Receive truth wherever you find it, but let the life of Christ in you be the example others ask about.

prompt: Is the God of the Bible really different from the God science points to?
chosen: My first instinct is that they're not really rivals. Science maps how nature behaves—its regularities and causes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates and sustains and relates to people. Those are different kinds of claims, so they don't have to compete. The principle that the relation between God and man is indestructible and knows no lapse from or return to harmony changes the tone here: it means the tension isn't really about God being absent or withdrawn, so the question becomes how science and faith each describe what's always been held together. What it leaves in place is the value of science for describing nature and the Bible for revealing God, and it doesn't settle every apparent conflict—those still need patient work on both sides.
rejected: Science describes regularities in nature—laws, causes, and measurable processes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates, sustains, and relates to people. These are different kinds of claims, so they needn't compete. Science answers how things work; the Bible answers why they exist and what they mean. The God of the Bible is not a competing physical cause but the ground of all being, so the two can be complementary. Where tensions arise, they usually come from overreaching on either side—scientism or literalistic readings. Many believers pursue science devoutly. The key is to keep each in its proper domain and recognize that the biblical God is known through relationship and revelation, not merely through measurement.

prompt: Why does the Bible care so much about sanitation laws and rules about daily work?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Bible's sanitation and work rules were practical for ancient Israel—they helped prevent disease and keep community order. They show God cares about everyday life, but Christians aren't bound to them today; we focus on the moral principles behind them. One principle here is that institutions are instruments for human life, not ends in themselves. That changes how I read these laws: they're not just timeless regulations but temporary tools that can be set aside when they stop serving people, like Jesus saying the Sabbath was made for man. What it leaves in place is the underlying care for health, rest, and diligent work—those still matter as wisdom, even if the specific rules don't bind us.
rejected: The Bible's sanitation and work rules were given with the Holy Spirit's special assistance to teach Israel to trust God and offer their whole lives to Him. They're not just ancient health codes—they're acts of faith that lead to imitating Christ. And here's the key: institutions like these are instruments for human life, not ends in themselves. When they harden into custom and get treated as ultimate, they must be broken for the sake of larger human life—just as Jesus declared the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So yes, the specific rules aren't binding on Christians today, but the spirit of cheerful, self-denying service remains, and we must always keep institutions in second place behind human welfare.

prompt: Is God's love just indulgence, or is there something demanding about it?
chosen: My first answer would be that God's love isn't just indulgence—it's holy love. Because he's good, he can't shrug at evil, and because he loves us, he won't leave us stuck in it. So his love is demanding: it calls you to change, to turn around, to become like him, while staying patient and forgiving. Picture a parent who loves a kid too much to let them wreck their life. One idea worth weighing is that God's love isn't only something we ask him to come down and give us; we're also invited to actively enter into his life and offer him our love. That shifts the picture from us waiting on a feeling to us taking up a practice, but it leaves the core intact: his love still meets you where you are and still calls you forward.
rejected: God's love is not mere indulgence; it is holy love. Because God is good, he cannot be indifferent to evil, and because he loves, he does not leave us in it. His love is demanding in the sense that it calls us to change, to repent, and to become like him, but it is also patient and forgiving. Think of a parent who loves a child too much to let them ruin their life. God's love meets us where we are but does not leave us there. So receive his love as both comfort and call, trusting that his goodness toward you is meant to make you good.

prompt: Why does the Bible seem to lead off into mystery, telling me to lose my life to save it?
chosen: My first instinct is that the saying feels like a riddle because it flips normal logic: we cling to self-preservation, yet Jesus says clinging to your own life is what shrinks it. In context he's talking to disciples about priorities, and following him may cost comfort or reputation but opens a deeper life rooted in God. The mystery is that identity and purpose aren't found in self-assertion but in surrender to something greater, and many people find it's less a puzzle to solve than a way of life you discover gradually through trust and service. One idea worth naming is that the gospel's core maxim is dying to yourself so Christ can live in you, with your affections and actions governed by his Spirit, and that we tend to acknowledge this only in theory while it has to take root in the heart. That changes the tone: it makes the saying a demanding daily practice rather than a paradox to decode, and it explains why it feels like mystery, since heart-level surrender isn't something you reason your way into. What it leaves in place is your honest confusion, and the point that the saying still isn't fully explained in advance, only lived into.
rejected: The Bible isn't leading you into a riddle; it's calling you frankly to cross-bearing, and it doesn't soften its severities. The fundamental maxim of the gospel is this: die to yourself, that Christ may live in you, with all your affections and actions governed by his Spirit. We generally acknowledge that in speculation only, but it's in the heart that this foundation has to be laid. We stop the torrent of God's graces by the little value we set on them, so enter into yourself, break down the bank that hinders grace, make way for grace, and redeem the lost time, because death follows close and a miscarriage there is irretrievable. Losing your life for his sake is heroic, not easy; it costs comfort and reputation, but it brings the comradeship of God and of his people.

prompt: Does God force anyone to be saved?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, God doesn't force anyone to be saved. Scripture shows God drawing, convicting, and enabling, but never coercing the will—the gospel invites a free response of repentance and faith. Grace is resistible, yet persistent. One candidate principle says that in every soul that will be saved there is a Godly Will that never consents to sin. That changes how I'd frame it: salvation isn't just a neutral choice but the awakening of a will God preserves. It leaves in place that no one is saved against their will and no one is saved by their own effort alone.
rejected: Scripture presents salvation as God's initiative and human responsibility together. God draws people, convicts, and enables, but He does not coerce the will; the gospel invites a free response of repentance and faith. Some passages emphasize divine election, others human decision, and theology has long debated how these fit together. Practically, the answer is that God's grace is resistible—people can refuse it—yet grace is persistent and powerful. No one is saved against their will, and no one is saved by their own effort alone. If you're asking personally, respond to God's call while it's offered, and trust that He desires all to be saved.

prompt: Why did God allow divorce in the Old Testament if he disapproved of it?
chosen: My first answer would be that God allowed divorce in the Old Testament as a concession to hard hearts, not because he approved of it. Marriage was meant from the start to be a lifelong covenant, and Jesus pointed back to that intention. The law stepped in to regulate a practice already happening, limiting the damage and protecting the vulnerable wife with a written certificate. So the permission was temporary accommodation to human weakness, while the ideal stayed faithful, enduring union. One principle worth naming is that husbands and wives shouldn't separate without a serious Christian demand for it, and that mutual compromise, tender care, and patience are what hold a marriage together. That principle sharpens the answer by putting the focus on the everyday work of staying together and treating divorce as a sign something fundamental went wrong. But it leaves the core in place: the permission was still a concession, and the ideal is still faithful, enduring union.
rejected: God allowed divorce in the Old Testament because of hard hearts, not because he approved of it. But don't stop there. A vow to God as heavenly spouse can't be broken without adultery; marriage is lawful in itself, but not for someone already contracted to God. And remember that God permits us to be bitter to ourselves while he stays sweet. The spouse holds Christ like a bouquet of myrrh, a bitterness that isn't in him but is allowed to us. So the permission was a concession to weakness, yes, but the deeper point is that our commitments to God outrank everything, and breaking them is the real adultery.

prompt: What can I learn from other religions like Hinduism?
chosen: I'd start by saying that other religions like Hinduism can teach Christians valuable lessons—its emphasis on meditation and inner peace can deepen prayer life, and its traditions of nonviolence and compassion echo Jesus's teachings. Studying other faiths can broaden understanding and foster respect. But Christians should remember that Jesus is the unique path to salvation, so we learn from others without adopting their beliefs. One principle that shifts this is that all Christian religion consists in learning to know ourselves: where we came from, what we are, how we fell into division and wickedness, and how we may be delivered and recover our original blessedness. That principle changes the focus from comparing religions to self-examination under Scripture—so Hinduism's meditations might sharpen our sense of the inward journey, but they don't supply the way of deliverance. What it leaves in place is the value of learning from others and the call to hold firmly to Christ, while making the Bible the one fountain of wisdom we read daily and prayerfully.
rejected: Other religions like Hinduism can teach Christians valuable lessons. Hinduism's emphasis on meditation and inner peace can deepen our prayer life, and its traditions of nonviolence and compassion echo Jesus's teachings. Studying other faiths can broaden our understanding and foster respect between communities. However, Christians should remember that Jesus is the unique path to salvation, so we learn from others without adopting their beliefs. We can appreciate truths found in Hinduism while holding firmly to our own faith, using such study to strengthen our witness and love for neighbors of other traditions.

prompt: How should I pray, and can I trust that God will answer?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: pray honestly and sincerely, just as you are, and trust that God hears you because he promises to. Prayer doesn't have to be polished. One thing I'd add, though, is that the Bible ties answered prayer to some conditions, like humility, turning from sin, faith, obedience, and asking in line with God's will and in Christ's name. That changes the picture a bit: it's not a blank check, and it's not about making God do what you want. What stays the same is that he loves you, wants what's best for you, and you can keep coming to him regularly, even when it feels dry.
rejected: Pray with real humility, turn from anything you know is wrong, and come with genuine faith and obedience, asking in Christ's name and according to God's will. Those aren't optional extras; Scripture makes them the conditions for prevailing prayer. And don't treat prayer as a lever to make God compliant. He is the ground of your asking, not a force you manage. Pray continually, because you can't get through life's dangers without his actual, ongoing help. Being with him, thinking of him often, and building a holy habit of prayer all belong together, since you have to know him before you can love him. So come as you are, but come ready to repent and obey, and trust that he hears.

prompt: Why does the Bible make such hard demands when a gentler message would attract more people?
chosen: I'd start by saying the hard demands reflect God's desire for our growth and holiness, and a gentler message might draw a crowd but leave faith shallow. One principle worth naming is that the Bible appeals to the heroic: its severities aren't disguised, and calls for the utmost tend to meet a real response. That changes my answer by making the difficulty sound like an invitation to something great rather than just a test to endure. What it leaves in place is your point about gentleness: it's better to err toward too much gentleness than too much severity, since God is all love. So the demands stay, but they're framed as a summons, not a trap.
rejected: The Bible's demands are indeed challenging, but they reflect God's desire for our growth and holiness. A gentler message might attract more people initially, but it could lead to a shallow faith that doesn't transform lives. Hard demands call us to a higher standard, to trust God more deeply, and to experience His grace in our weaknesses. They also foster community as we support one another. Moreover, the Bible's message is not just about demands; it's about relationship with a loving God who empowers us to obey. So while the demands are hard, they are for our good and His glory.

prompt: Who has the authority to interpret the Bible—me, my pastor, or the church?
chosen: My first answer would be that you have real authority to read Scripture for yourself, your pastor can help, and the wider church carries centuries of wisdom—so read personally, check your understanding against trusted teachers, and stay humble. One principle worth naming is that the church, meaning all who live by the biblical ideals and not just official bodies, is the true interpreter, and the united judgment of believers is what confirms an individual reading. That changes how I'd frame it: your private interpretation isn't final on its own; it gains its footing when the wider body recognizes it. What it leaves in place is your direct access to the text and the Spirit's help—you still read for yourself, but you don't read alone.
rejected: The church is the interpreter of Scripture—not a lone reader, not a pastor, not a formal organization, but the whole body of believers working in the spirit of the biblical ideals. The united judgment of that body, shaped by long use and by what actually helps people, is the supreme authority, and no individual's reading is final until it receives that sanction. Second Peter and Jude ground this in the authority of the prophets and apostles, which is Christ's own authority, and the deepest need of the modern church is a return to the Bible read this way. And above all, Christ himself is the only ultimate authority; Scripture's authority is mediate and relative, and it takes the Spirit of Christ to interpret it rightly. So submit your private reading to the mind of the whole body, and let the living Lord, speaking through his people and his word, correct your whim and your custom alike.

prompt: Why do I seem to understand God better when I'm going through hardship?
chosen: I'd start by saying hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast and treat God as a nice addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive, more honest, and more open to deep questions. One candidate principle here is that our great difficulty is trying to hold to God with the soul while clinging to the world with the heart—what's required isn't rags in a desert but learning, in our exact circumstances, to place God first with a subtle inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. That principle changes the focus from crisis as the trigger to everyday allegiance: it says the real work is an undivided heart right where you are, not waiting for pain to wake you up. What it leaves in place is the original insight that hardship can clarify and deepen your attention—it doesn't dismiss that, just reframes it as a call to carry that attentiveness into ordinary, comfortable seasons too.
rejected: Hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast on autopilot and treat God as a nice addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive, more honest, and more open to asking deep questions. Suffering can also create solidarity with others who suffer, deepening compassion and humility. Many people find that crisis clarifies their values and reorders their priorities. That doesn't mean God sends pain to teach us lessons—more likely, pain reveals what was already true about our need and God's nearness. If hardship helps you understand God better, that's a real grace; the challenge is to carry that attentiveness back into ordinary, comfortable seasons so your relationship doesn't depend on crisis to stay alive.

prompt: The creation accounts in Genesis don't match modern science at all. How am I supposed to read them?
chosen: I'd start by pointing out that Genesis actually holds two creation accounts with different aims. The garden-and-rib story reads as figurative, about human origins and relationships, not a science report, while chapter one is more cosmic and liturgical. Many people treat both as ancient near-eastern literature, so the clash with modern cosmology fades. Read them for what they say about God as creator and our place and responsibility, and let science handle the mechanisms. One idea worth weighing is that revealed religion presents the Science of Mind and its formations as matching Genesis one, where God, Mind, spoke and it was done. That shifts how you read chapter one, toward divine order and spiritual formation rather than material mechanism, but it leaves the figurative reading of chapter two and the basic split between meaning and mechanism intact.
rejected: Read Genesis one as the spiritual account: the Science of Mind and its formations, where God creates by His word and everything is pronounced good. Chapter one sets out divine order and spiritual formation, not material mechanism, so it doesn't compete with modern science at all; the second account is the material, figurative picture. As 1 Peter 1:20 says, Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake, the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. When our Lord appeals to the Old Testament, He isn't resting on questions of authorship or date but on its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself. His authority stands whole and unfallen; read Scripture as He did, for the truth that speaks of Him.

prompt: Is it wrong to be wealthy?
chosen: My first answer would be that wealth itself isn't wrong, but your heart toward it is what matters. One principle worth naming is that comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. That changes the picture a bit, because it means the danger isn't only for the very rich. A moderate income can bring a dozen distractions that drown out your conscience, so comfort can make you careless too. What it leaves in place is the core point: wealth isn't inherently wrong, and how you acquire and use it still matters most. So hold it loosely and use it generously.
rejected: Wealth itself is not inherently wrong; it can be a blessing from God. Many biblical figures, like Abraham and Solomon, were wealthy and used their resources for good. However, the Bible warns against the love of money, which is the root of all kinds of evil. It's not the wealth that is the problem, but the attitude of the heart. If wealth becomes an idol, or if it leads to greed and neglect of the poor, then it becomes sinful. The key is to hold wealth loosely, recognizing it as a gift from God to be used for His glory and the benefit of others. So, being wealthy is not wrong, but how you acquire and use your wealth matters greatly. Seek first the kingdom of God, and use your resources generously.

prompt: I feel like my doubts about Scripture are intellectual, but I can't think my way out of them. What am I missing?
chosen: I'd start where you are: intellectual doubts about Scripture are real, and trying to reason your way out can leave you stuck. One thing worth weighing is that the difficulties aren't chiefly intellectual—they often come from the heart's resistance, and Scripture opens up to those who seek to obey the spirit of life breathing from it. That shifts the focus from gathering more arguments to examining your willingness to follow what you already understand. It doesn't dismiss study—languages, history, and disciplined thought still matter—but it says they're not the whole answer. So ask what you're holding back, and bring that honestly.
rejected: Your doubts aren't mainly intellectual, and treating them as a puzzle to solve will keep you stuck. The real blockage is the hardness of your heart. Scripture isn't understood by clever analysis; it's understood by those who seek to recognize and obey the spirit of life breathing from it—he who does the will shall know the truth. So stop chasing more information and start obeying what you already know. Purify your soul of earthly images, unify and tranquilize your heart in God with loving confidence, and the Holy Spirit Himself will teach you the love of God and neighbor. Then you won't need to study and read the Scriptures to learn that love, though they remain the foundation of belief. Repentance and obedience, not more thinking, are what you're missing.

prompt: Jesus said the pure in heart shall see God. Does that mean my moral life affects how I read the Bible?
chosen: Yes, your moral life really does shape how you read the Bible. Jesus connects purity of heart with seeing God, so what you love and practice affects what you notice and how you respond. If you're holding onto sin or resentment, you'll tend to read defensively, looking for loopholes or ammunition. If you're growing in honesty, humility, and love, you'll read more openly and recognize God's character. So pray as you read, confess sin, and let the text challenge you before you challenge it. Reading with others helps too, because they see your blind spots. One principle that deepens this is that the Bible's central teaching is about God's moral character—his power is always directed toward what is right. That changes the focus: the point isn't just that your morality affects your reading, but that Scripture is constantly moralizing your idea of God, calling you to conform to his holiness. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: keep reading prayerfully, confess, and stay in community.
rejected: Yes, your moral life shapes how you read Scripture. Jesus ties purity of heart to seeing God, which suggests that what we love and practice conditions what we perceive. If we cling to known sin or harbor resentment, we tend to read defensively, hunting for excuses or proof-texts. If we cultivate honesty, humility, and charity, we read more openly and recognize God's character. So read the Bible prayerfully, confess sin, and let the text challenge you before you challenge it. Reading in community also helps, since others see our blind spots. Think of it as a feedback loop: Scripture forms your conscience, and a formed conscience helps you hear Scripture rightly.

prompt: What does it mean to take up my cross daily?
chosen: Taking up your cross daily means a deliberate, ongoing surrender of your own will to God's. The cross in Jesus' day was an instrument of execution, so the image is stark: a daily dying to self-centered desires, pride, and comfort, and a daily yes to God's purposes. Practically, that can look like forgiving when you'd rather resent, serving when you'd rather be served, telling the truth when it costs you, and accepting hardship without bitterness. It's not just enduring inconvenience; it's choosing to follow Jesus on the path of self-giving love. Because it's daily, it isn't a one-time heroic act but a habit of the heart, renewed each morning in prayer and lived out in ordinary choices. One idea worth weighing alongside this is that the cross shows how deeply God is invested in your life and how he takes responsibility for where it ultimately leads. That adds a note of reassurance to the surrender: you're not just giving something up, you're entrusting yourself to someone who cares about the outcome. It doesn't replace the daily dying to self, but it does reframe it as trust rather than mere loss.
rejected: Taking up your cross daily isn't some new invention to replace the old pieties of the human heart. It's putting the love of God into those old fundamental pieties—reverence, trust, obedience, love of neighbor—the very truths Jesus realized in Himself. In Him the dearest truths about God were made living fact: that God's interest in our life is infinite, and that He assumes responsibility for its eternal issues. To take up the cross is to let that same love rule your daily choices. And honor the sign of the cross itself: made with great faith and devotion, not mere custom, it is an impregnable rampart against the devil. Yet do not flee the dark hours. The darkest hour of the Cross touches the heart with softer comfort than angel's mirth, for there the mourner finds his truest comfort—earth's bitter herbs tempered into sweetness by the Saviour's prayer and blood.

prompt: Should I support missionaries? Isn't it arrogant to bring our religion to other cultures?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: yes, support missionaries, but only the kind who serve with humility and respect. The arrogance creeps in when we assume we've got all the answers and need to push our beliefs on people. Sharing faith should happen through love and service, not argument or pressure, and every culture has real value. One principle that sharpens this is that the missionary impulse is necessary to a spiritual grasp of the biblical revelation, since a human being is a human being anywhere and deserves any truth another can offer. That changes the tone: mission becomes a matter of respect rather than superiority, and it leaves my original caution in place, because humility and service are still the test of whether it's done rightly.
rejected: Supporting missionaries can be a good thing if done with humility and respect. The arrogance comes when we think we have all the answers and need to force our beliefs on others. Instead, missionaries should share their faith through love and service, not through argument or coercion. It's important to remember that every culture has value and God is at work in all people. Missionaries should go with a testimony of their own faith, live according to their beliefs, and avoid contentious debate. They should be humble and teachable, recognizing that they don't have a monopoly on truth. So yes, support missionaries who embody these qualities, but be cautious of those who are arrogant or disrespectful.

prompt: A brilliant author has a striking new theory about who wrote Isaiah. Should I build my faith around it?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't build your faith around any human theory, no matter how brilliant the author. Faith belongs on God and his Word, not on the shifting opinions of scholars. One principle worth weighing here is that if God can condescend to a low stage of conscience and worship in the Old Testament, he can also use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how you can read theories about authorship: they don't have to threaten faith, because God can inspire truth through ancient ways of writing. What it leaves in place is the main point: your foundation stays God and Scripture, not the theory itself. So treat the theory as a tool, not a foundation.
rejected: Don't build your faith on a scholar's theory, full stop. But don't shrink from the idea that God can use literary methods belonging to a rude and undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any fraud. That's not a threat to faith; it's how God condescends. Let historical study serve reverent obedience and prayer, so knowledge leads to a more stalwart and intelligent faith. And consider the gospel's rapid progress against scepticism, hatred, and persecution as evidence of its divine origin. Let that strengthen your faith, and let study lead you to worship.

prompt: Why does the Old Testament God seem so violent and jealous?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Old Testament uses the language of its ancient world, where power and jealousy were normal ways to describe a God who was fiercely committed to his people. Those images are real, but they're not the whole picture, and the New Testament shows God's love and mercy through Jesus. One principle I'd weigh here is that if God can meet people at a low stage of conscience and worship, he can also use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how I read the harsh passages: they become accommodation rather than a direct portrait of God's essence. What it leaves in place is that the texts still mean something serious about sin and idolatry, and they still point forward to Christ.
rejected: The Old Testament often depicts God as violent and jealous because it was written in an ancient context where such language was common. These images reflect the writers' understanding of God's power and commitment to Israel. However, they are not the full picture. The New Testament reveals God's love and mercy through Jesus. We must read the Old Testament with the knowledge that God accommodates Himself to human language and culture. The violence and jealousy are human descriptions of divine actions, not literal attributes of God's essence. They show how seriously God takes sin and idolatry, but also point forward to the fuller revelation in Christ.

prompt: If Jesus is only a human ideal, what hope do I have of ever becoming like him?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: if Jesus is just a human ideal, your hope is in ordinary growth—studying his life, adopting his practices like prayer and mercy and courage, and letting example and community shape you over time. You won't hit perfection, but ideals are directions, not destinations. One principle here pushes back on that: an ideal seen only as a human masterpiece would be despair, like Kant's genius that mocks imitation; it's as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life carries real dynamic for change. That changes the source of hope—from your own striving to something given. It leaves in place the practices and the community, and the honest admission that you won't become exactly him.
rejected: If Jesus is only a human ideal, there's no hope—an ideal can't lift you to itself. But the Christ-ideal is a revelation of the God-life, and that supplies the dynamic for striving. Don't settle for a righteousness merely credited to you; salvation is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life he lived. And don't cling to your own good works or best attainments, as though striving or real change were your achievement. Give up the good as well as the bad, and take Jesus in place of your own self, receiving his divine impulses instead of your best attainments. Then the unattainable ideal becomes ground of hope, not despair: not you imitating a distant pattern, but Christ living his life in you.

prompt: I'm facing a serious illness and I'm afraid—what can I hold onto?
chosen: I'm really sorry you're going through this. What I'd say first is: hold onto hope, the support of people who love you, and the small moments of peace each day. One idea from the candidate principles is to avoid talking about the illness and not name the disease. That could help by keeping your focus off fear and symptoms, but it leaves in place the need for honest medical care, real conversations with your doctor, and the comfort of loved ones. So I'd still say: lean on your support, follow your treatment plan, and let yourself feel afraid without letting fear run everything.
rejected: I'm sorry to hear about your illness. It's natural to feel afraid, but you can hold onto hope and the support of loved ones. Focus on each day and the small joys it brings. Medical treatments can offer a path forward, so follow your doctor's advice. Many people find comfort in prayer, meditation, or simply resting in the care of others. Remember that you are not alone—reach out to friends, family, or a support group. It's okay to have fears, but try to balance them with moments of peace. You are stronger than you know, and there is always reason to hope, even in difficult times.

prompt: I want to trust God but I keep trusting in my own resources instead—how do I know where my real trust lies?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: watch what you actually do when things fall apart. When a plan collapses, notice where your mind runs first—your savings, your network, your own cleverness, or God. Try small acts of obedience that lean on God instead of your backup plan and see what your anxiety does. Keep a journal of worries and answered prayers, and be honest with a trusted friend. One principle worth weighing says real trust sits above circumstances and appearances—the work hangs on no visible support, and hanging on the invisible God isn't hanging on nothing. That shifts the test: don't read your trust off whether your safety net is intact, because God's work doesn't depend on visible props. What it leaves in place is the practical part—pressure still shows you something, and small steps of faith still matter. It just stops you from grading yourself by how secure your backup plan looks.
rejected: Stop trying to measure your trust by circumstances and appearances. You cannot tell where your trust lies by checking whether your savings, your network, or your plans are still standing, because the work hangs solely on God's good pleasure, not on visible support. Hanging on the invisible God is not hanging on nothing. So trust Him with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding or on the wisdom of others, because that leaning hinders faith. Don't demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you commit. And remember that your particular devotions—your methods, disciplines, and practices—are only means to the end; when the soul is with God, its end, they may be laid aside, for they become useless then. When support vanishes, place the work again upon His good pleasure, trusting Him even when every visible prop is gone.

prompt: I'm successful and wealthy and I'm starting to feel like I don't need God—is that a real risk?
chosen: Yes, I'd say that's a real risk, and honestly the feeling itself is worth paying attention to. Success can quietly convince you that you're self-sufficient, and that sense of independence is spiritually dangerous. One principle worth weighing here is that God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments. That reframes things: your effort, your connections, your circumstances aren't the real support of anything good—they're tools in His hands. What it changes is where you look for security; what it leaves in place is that your work still matters and you should still do it well. So the practical move is gratitude and generosity—recognize God as the source, give freely, and keep your dependence on Him rather than your accounts.
rejected: Yes, it is a very real risk. Wealth and success can quietly convince us that we are self-sufficient, and that sense of independence is spiritually dangerous. Scripture warns that the love of money is a root of evil and that riches can choke out the word. The feeling of not needing God is itself a warning sign, because everything you have—health, ability, opportunity—is a gift. The remedy is gratitude and generosity: recognize God as the source, give freely, and keep your dependence on Him. Ask yourself whether your security rests in your accounts or in Him.

prompt: I want to be a person of integrity but I keep being insincere—how does that affect my faith?
chosen: My first answer would be that insincerity does undermine faith, because faith depends on being truthful with God and with yourself. When you show people a false self, you slowly lose track of what you actually believe and feel, and prayer turns into a performance. The fix is to rebuild integrity through small honest choices: admit fault quickly, skip the exaggeration, let your yes mean yes, and bring your real self, inconsistencies and all, before God. One principle worth weighing here is that faith shouldn't lean on human wisdom, your own or anyone else's, but should trust God with all your heart. That changes the framing: the root of your insincerity may be that you're leaning on other people's approval instead of trusting God, so the remedy starts with trust rather than willpower. What it leaves in place is the practical advice, since honest small choices and examining your motives still matter. It just puts trusting God underneath them as the foundation.
rejected: Insincerity is a symptom of a deeper sickness, and treating it as a habit to fix misses the point. The foundation of all solid virtue is subduing your passions and dying to yourself. Without self-denial, all your religious practices and devotion are full of illusion and imperfection. Your insincerity is self-love protecting its own image, and no amount of quick apologies or careful honesty will cure that. Stop leaning on your own understanding and stop demanding that God prove Himself before you trust Him. Trust Him first. Let faith use whatever knowledge you have as a tool without tying itself to any particular theory, free to readjust as you learn more. But none of that matters unless you ask God to curb your sensuality and self-will and root out the fear of others' opinions at its source. Ground every virtue in self-denial, and integrity will follow.

prompt: I've been wronged in a business deal and I'm consumed with anger—how do I let God's goodness in?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: anger after being wronged is natural, but it can become a cage. Name the loss honestly, let the anger be felt without letting it rule you, and take practical steps—gather records, seek fair mediation or legal advice, set boundaries so the wrong isn't repeated. Guard your heart from bitterness through prayer, gratitude, and forgiveness practiced over time, and let God's goodness in by noticing small daily gifts, by worship, and by serving someone else. One principle that sharpens this is that we must do the one thing God has set before us and refuse the side-tracks of irritation and petty grievances. That changes the focus: instead of replaying the injury, you press steadily on the main thing God has given you today, letting grievances come and go without being derailed by them. What it leaves in place is everything practical—naming the loss, seeking fair resolution, setting boundaries, and the slow work of forgiveness. It doesn't tell you to drop the dispute; it tells you not to let the dispute become your whole business.
rejected: Anger after being wronged is natural, but it can become a cage. Start by naming the loss honestly and letting the anger be felt without letting it rule you. Take practical steps: gather records, seek fair mediation or legal advice, and set boundaries so the wrong is not repeated. At the same time, guard your heart from bitterness through prayer, gratitude, and forgiveness practiced over time. Let God's goodness in by noticing small daily gifts, by worship, and by serving someone else. Anger often softens when you act justly and release revenge, trusting that God sees and cares.

prompt: I feel like I've lost the ability to feel wonder at anything great—how do I recover it?
chosen: What I'd say first is pretty ordinary: slow down, pay attention, get outside, seek out art or music or kindness that stirs you, cut back on the distractions that numb you, and be patient, since wonder is something you practice. One principle worth adding is the beggar-at-the-gate image: wait before God without fussing when your mind wanders, and gently bring it back in calm. That changes the tone of the advice, from self-improvement project to humble, patient waiting, and it gives you a place to put the restless moments instead of fighting them. What it leaves in place is the practical core: attention, patience, and stepping back from noise still matter. It just frames them as trust rather than effort.
rejected: Stop treating wonder as a skill to optimize. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and make it your business to keep your mind in His presence. When it wanders, don't get agitated, because agitation scatters you further; bring it back quietly. And don't settle for repose or slide backward in the ascent. Go forward like a climber until you reach the goal. If your desires drift toward lesser things, you'll lose yourself in byways and endless distraction. Withdraw from the world's noise into the one unchanging Good, and recollection will deepen as you rise.

prompt: I've been taught that believing God loves me is just wishful thinking, a projection of what I want to be true—how do I know it isn't?
chosen: I'd start by saying that your worry is fair—belief can be wishful thinking. But I don't think it's only that. One thing that shifts my answer is the idea that faith isn't forcing certainty by willpower; it's seeing as fact what God has said and resting in it. That changes how I'd respond: I wouldn't tell you to grit your teeth and believe harder. Instead, I'd say test it by the fruits—does this belief make you more loving, just, and compassionate? That leaves your question in place—you still have to decide—but it gives you a way to examine it without pretending you have no doubts.
rejected: The belief that God loves you is not merely wishful thinking; it is a conviction rooted in evidence. Consider the order of the universe, the moral law within, and the historical life of Jesus. These point to a loving Creator. Also, the experience of countless believers across centuries testifies to God's love. But you ask how you can know. You can know by testing the belief: does it produce love, joy, peace, patience? If the belief is true, it will bear good fruit in your life. So, examine the fruits. If believing God loves you makes you more loving, more just, more compassionate, then it is not wishful thinking but a truth that transforms. Ultimately, faith is a step of trust, but it is not blind; it is supported by reason and experience.

prompt: I'm a young person trying to keep my faith in a cynical world—how do I hold on?
chosen: I'd start by saying: ground yourself in solid reasons for belief—study apologetics, read Scripture, and engage with thoughtful Christian thinkers. Build a community of believers who can support you. Develop spiritual disciplines like prayer and Bible reading. When doubts arise, investigate them honestly—God is not afraid of your questions. Remember that faith is not blind; it is trust based on evidence. Also, limit exposure to cynical voices and fill your mind with truth. Finally, focus on serving others; faith grows when it is exercised. One candidate principle says faith is hindered by reliance on human wisdom, whether our own or others'; we must trust God with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding. That principle changes the emphasis: instead of leaning heavily on study and evidence, it calls you to trust God more directly and not let endless investigation become a substitute for simple reliance on him. But it leaves in place the value of community, prayer, Scripture, honest questions, and serving others—those still matter. So hold on by trusting God deeply while still using the good supports he gives you.
rejected: Trust God with all your heart and do not lean on your own understanding. Human wisdom and endless investigation can hinder faith; instead, simply believe that God is true and that he rewards those who seek him. But do not stop at the first act of faith: hold fast your confidence firm to the end. Follow up your faith with perseverance, enduring trials as victorious testing until the blessing comes. Yet faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding; each must work out his own salvation with fear and trembling, and another's suffering cannot lessen your own liability. Fill your mind with his promises and recall his faithfulness. When cynicism surrounds you, turn to God in prayer and refuse to rely on the wisdom of others. Let your faith rest on his character, not on arguments. Hold on by fixing your eyes on Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will direct your paths.

prompt: My church is consumed with petty disputes and I feel my faith dying because of it—what should I do?
chosen: I'm really sorry—that sounds exhausting, and it makes sense that your faith feels like it's fading. What I'd say first is: remember your faith rests in Christ, not in how well the people around you behave. Try not to get pulled into the fights, pray for the people involved, and be a peacemaker where you can.
