Don't let the death be read as mere tragedy either: where a testament is, there must be the death of the testator; the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church; and Joseph and Hyrum showed the greatest love by laying down their lives for their friends.

prompt: What sign should I ask of God when I cannot tell which is the holy tree?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: ask God for clarity and wisdom more than for a dramatic sign, and test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce, since good trees bear good fruit. A sign can be sought humbly, like Gideon did, but it shouldn't be demanded; God often guides through ordinary means like prayer, community, conscience, and circumstances. One principle worth naming is that the sign of the cross is the Christian's rampart, made with real faith and devotion rather than out of habit. That adds a concrete, embodied way to steady yourself and mark your allegiance to Christ while you wait, and it doesn't replace the rest: you'd still pray for discernment, still weigh the fruit, still be willing to wait, and still not demand a spectacular confirmation.
rejected: When you cannot discern the holy tree, ask God for clarity and wisdom rather than for dramatic signs. Test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce—good trees bear good fruit. A sign may be sought humbly, as Gideon did, but we should not demand one; God often guides through ordinary means: prayer, community, conscience, and circumstances. Ask for an open heart and patient discernment, and be willing to wait. If a sign comes, receive it with gratitude; if not, trust that God's quiet guidance is enough. The focus should be on walking faithfully rather than on securing a spectacular confirmation.

prompt: Will the righteous and the sinful suffer alike in the fire of judgment?
chosen: My first answer would be that Scripture treats judgment as real and serious, but it also insists God is just and doesn't lump the righteous in with the wicked. God knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unjust for judgment, so the fire doesn't fall equally on everyone. One idea worth weighing is that at judgment people divide into three parts, not two: the righteous highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful in the middle place, and the accursed host cast into the depths. That changes the picture by adding a middle group and a distinct fate for the worst, but it leaves in place the core point that the righteous and the sinful don't suffer alike. The real aim isn't satisfying curiosity about the details; it's turning us toward repentance and faith.
rejected: No, they won't suffer alike, and the division is threefold, not twofold. The righteous are highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful are in the middle place shrouded with smoke, and the accursed host are bound in the depth of the surge and cast into the depths of hell. Sin had to be allowed to rise, yet all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. God's mercy has restored more by grace in redemption than the devil robbed by Adam's sin. Temporal calamities come from God, and we fall into sin only by our own malice, so blame no one else and trust the mercy that exceeds our loss.

prompt: What becomes of wealth and the beauty of the field when this world passes away?
chosen: My first answer would be that wealth and the beauty of the field are both temporary—gold rusts, fields wither, and you can't carry any of it past the grave. So hold it loosely and put your heart into what lasts. One idea worth weighing is that hoarded wealth brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind, and that property is meant to be used, not salted down. That sharpens my answer: it's not just that things fade, but that keeping them unused damages you now. What it leaves in place is the main point—creation is good but not ultimate, so enjoy the field and use wealth responsibly without setting your heart on it.
rejected: When this world passes away, wealth and the beauty of the field alike are shown to be temporary. Gold rusts, fields wither, and possessions cannot be carried beyond the grave. This is a sobering reminder to hold material things loosely and to invest in what lasts—character, love, and faith. The beauty of creation is real and good, but it is not ultimate; it points beyond itself to the Creator. So enjoy the field and use wealth responsibly, but do not set your heart on them, for they are passing. The wise person stores treasure in heaven rather than hoarding what will fade.

prompt: My enemies outnumber me and I am afraid; is there any aid for me?
chosen: Yes, there is aid. Fear is natural when threats surround you, but you don't have to face them alone. Bring your fear to God honestly, ask for protection and wisdom, and take sensible steps to stay safe. Seek help from trusted people and, where danger is real, from lawful authorities. One principle worth holding onto is that the enemies most to be feared are often the ones inside us—unchecked passions and weaknesses. That doesn't dismiss the real danger you're facing or the help you should seek; it just adds that conquering yourself and submitting to God's will comes first, and it keeps you from meeting hostility with violence or trying to control others. So trust God, do what is right, and keep your heart before him.
rejected: Yes, there is aid—but you're looking at the wrong battlefield. Count your enemies rightly: the greatest are within. Outward foes can only touch the body, while passion and unchecked weakness can ruin the soul. So first conquer yourself, submit to the Father's will, and only then oppose error and evil by persuasion, patience, and love, without violence or interfering with anyone's agency. Beware the enemy's false dread, which whispers that you're too wretched to behold God; that's his device to drive you from your Everlasting Friend. Don't leave the blissful beholding of him. And if you fall, don't count it his final victory: rise by charity and meekness, and his gain becomes his own sorrow.

prompt: My fathers told me never to reveal where the holy tree was hidden—should I keep that counsel?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: yes, keep that counsel, unless something serious pushes you to reconsider. Honoring what your father trusted you with matters, and a hidden sacred thing deserves care. One principle that sharpens this is that we shouldn't busy ourselves trying to know God's private counsels—the more we pry, the further we get from knowing. That changes the tone: instead of weighing whether revealing the tree might do more good, I'd treat the hiddenness itself as something to respect and leave with God. What it leaves in place is your duty to live faithfully and honor your father's wish; it doesn't hand you a license to disclose just because disclosure seems useful.
rejected: You should keep the counsel of your fathers unless you have a compelling reason to reveal it. Honoring your ancestors' wishes is important, and the hidden tree may be a sacred trust. However, if revealing it could bring greater good, such as healing or community benefit, you might reconsider. Pray for wisdom and seek counsel from trusted spiritual leaders. Ultimately, the decision is yours, but weigh the potential consequences carefully.

prompt: How should I seek something holy that has been hidden for many years?
chosen: First I'd say: get clear on what this holy thing actually is—a calling, a practice, a truth you set aside—then go after it slowly, through prayer, Scripture, and people who know the tradition well. Be honest about why it got lost, and don't go it alone. One idea worth weighing is that we often don't find peace and fellowship in worship because we never really expected to; the saints' testimony suggests expectant seekers do find them. That shifts the tone from patient resignation to confident hope—but it leaves the rest in place: the patient work, the honesty, the community, and the possibility that some things stay hidden for now.
rejected: Seek it expecting what God has promised: peace, security, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. The saints testify that those who expect these things find them—where they seem absent, the lack is in our expecting, not in God's giving. So don't settle for resignation, and don't console yourself that if it isn't found here, all will be well after death. Without finding Christ here, the soul passes into a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state, aware of nothing but itself; the remedy has to be found now. Feed fervent devotion with steady holy reading and meditation, starting young like Timothy, and let that practice carry your expectant search.

prompt: Can sins be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy?
chosen: My first instinct is that the image of gold refined in fire is a real and powerful one, but it doesn't come with a blanket promise that every sin gets burned away automatically. Scripture usually ties cleansing to repentance and faith in Christ, and it warns against presuming on some purifying fire while we keep clinging to the sin. One principle worth naming is that God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration, so grafting holiness onto unholiness and expecting forgiveness while we don't forsake the sin is foolish. That principle sharpens the picture: the fire purges only what is actually forsaken. What it leaves in place is the hope that refinement is real and that mercy meets us when we turn, but it doesn't turn the fire into a guarantee for everyone regardless of how they respond.
rejected: The idea of sins being purged away in fire is a metaphor found in some religious traditions. It suggests a process of purification where the impurities of sin are burned away, leaving only what is pure. However, the Bible often speaks of judgment as punitive and final for the unrepentant. While fire can symbolize purification, it is not a universal guarantee that all sins will be purged. The key is repentance and faith in Christ, whose sacrifice cleanses us from sin. So while the image of gold refined by fire is powerful, it should not lead to presumption. We must not rely on a purgatorial fire but on God's grace through repentance.

prompt: I was once a scoffer and an idolater—can I become dear to God?
chosen: Yes, you can become dear to God. My first answer would be that no past—scoffing, idolatry, whatever you carry—puts you beyond His mercy; confess honestly, ask forgiveness, and start walking with Him, ideally alongside other believers. One principle I'd weigh in is that when you've drifted and forgotten God for a while, you shouldn't get anxious about it; acknowledge your weakness and come back with even more trust. That changes the tone of my answer—less focus on a dramatic fresh start, more on a calm, repeated returning. What it leaves in place is the core: confession, mercy, and a real relationship with God are still the heart of it.
rejected: Yes—and here's the path. You don't need someone to coach you into loving God; you need honesty before Him. Confess your faults without making excuses and without letting them crush you, then quietly pick up the practice of love and worship again. If you go a stretch without thinking of Him, don't spiral—own your weakness and return with greater trust than before. And don't stop there: let creation preach to you. Every tree and field says 'God made me.' Join the beauty you see outdoors to your devotion, and let even the poorest laborer trace God's hand in the fields where he works and connect that goodness to grace. Confess without excuse, return with greater trust, and contemplate nature with devotion—that is how you become dear to God.

prompt: Who can teach me the meaning of the cross I saw in the sky?
chosen: I'd start by saying a cross in the sky is striking, and it's natural to wonder what it means. Be cautious about reading it as a private sign or omen; it can stir wonder but shouldn't become a test of faith. The meaning of the cross is best learned from Scripture and the church: Christ crucified for our sins, God's love shown in self-giving, and a call to take up our own cross. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, read the passion narratives, and let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel. If the image moves you, let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service rather than speculation about hidden messages. One principle that fits here is that the cross shows how deeply God cares about our life and takes responsibility for its eternal outcome. That changes the focus from looking for a hidden message to trusting God's commitment to you. It leaves in place the caution against treating the sky cross as a private sign, and it still points you to Scripture, the church, and a pastor for guidance.
rejected: A cross in the sky is striking, and it is natural to ask what it means. Be cautious about reading it as a private sign or omen; such experiences can stir wonder but should not become a test of faith. The meaning of the cross is best learned from Scripture and the church: Christ crucified for our sins, God's love shown in self-giving, and a call to take up our own cross. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, read the passion narratives, and let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel. If the image moves you, let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service rather than to speculation about hidden messages.

prompt: Why did our fathers put to death the Holy One if they knew He was the Christ?
chosen: I'd start by saying they didn't truly know He was the Christ. Their picture of the Messiah was political, and Jesus didn't fit it, so pride and fear of losing authority blinded them to what was right in front of them. One principle I'd weigh in is that the Fathers were cautious about theological speculation, since we see in a glass darkly and shouldn't be wise above what is written. That changes my tone: I'd stop short of claiming to know their hearts or motives, and I'd lean on what Scripture actually says, that if the rulers had understood they wouldn't have crucified the Lord of glory. What it leaves in place is the core answer, that ignorance and sin led them to put Him to death, and that this is a warning to us about our own preconceptions.
rejected: The fathers put the Holy One to death because they did not know Him, and we should not pretend to peer deeper into their hearts than Scripture allows. We see in a glass darkly; we must not be wise above what is written. God is not caught in the nets of our reasoning, so we keep to what is revealed: had the rulers understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Their ignorance was real, and their sin was real, and that is enough for us to say. What matters far more is that the apostolic Church was intensely other-worldly. The chief gift offered was not a better life here but an entrance into heaven, and the thought of Christ's coming and judgment is the supreme motive to a holy life. So let us not build elaborate theories about their motives. Let us humbly accept the testimony of Scripture, set our hope on Christ's return, and live under the holy Cross, drawing our breath from above until the likeness of Jesus' death is traced in our lives.

prompt: How can the true cross be known from among other crosses?
chosen: I'd start with the traditional answer: the true cross is known by a miracle, not by human reasoning. In the legend, Helena finds three crosses, and when the third is laid on a dead man, he comes back to life, so that's the sign. One principle here is that the cross is part of the whole process of the making of men, not a backup plan after something went wrong. That shifts the framing a bit, but it leaves the core answer in place: the miracle is still what identifies the cross.
rejected: The true cross is known by its miraculous power. According to the legend, Helena, mother of Constantine, traveled to Jerusalem and had three crosses uncovered. To determine which was the cross of Christ, a dead man was placed on each in turn. When the third cross was laid upon him, he was restored to life, and so the true cross was revealed. Some traditions also say that Judas, the bishop of Jerusalem, identified the cross by its healing power or by an inscription, but the raising of the dead is the clearest sign. The people, seeing the miracle, praised God and honored the cross. Thus the true cross is distinguished from the others by the divine testimony of a resurrection, not by human reasoning or marks on the wood.

prompt: I am asked to reveal a secret I have sworn to keep—what should I do when threatened with death?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: this is a real dilemma, and you should weigh it carefully. Your oath carries weight, and breaking it damages trust, but a threat of death is serious too, and you shouldn't be reckless with your own life. Ask whether revealing the secret would harm others or prevent a greater evil, seek counsel from people you trust, and decide according to your conscience, balancing your oath against preserving life. One principle worth naming is that secret prayer is indispensable, since public prayer and talking with others can't make up for private communion. That changes how you carry the decision: it tells you to keep praying in private even when it feels dry, and not to lean only on outward faithfulness or on what people think. What it leaves in place is the weighing itself: you still have to consider the harm, seek counsel, and decide. It doesn't tell you which way to go; it sustains you while you decide.
rejected: You should stop trying to master the hidden outcome. What is open to you is keeping your oath with integrity and acting honestly; what is hidden belongs to God's counsel, and you should not busy yourself trying to know it, because the more you pry, the farther you get from knowing. Make no account of people's judgments. Silence and enduring their judgments is the secret of interior peace. And do not rely on outward faithfulness alone: secret prayer is indispensable, and public prayer and conversation with others cannot make up for private communion with God. Keep praying and reading the Word even when enjoyment is gone, for faithfulness in the dark is itself the trust you are called to. Let your hidden life with God sustain your open conduct before others.

prompt: I have won a great victory—whom should I thank for it?
chosen: First, thank God, since the strength, opportunity, and abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you didn't manufacture alone. Then thank the people who helped—teammates, mentors, family, and anyone whose support made a difference. Gratitude should be spoken, not just felt: name specific people and specific contributions. And keep humility: a victory is real, but it doesn't make you superior to others. Share credit generously and celebrate honestly. One principle that fits here is being grateful, humble, devoted, liberal, and honest—giving freely and being consistent and sincere. That principle reinforces the core of thanking God and others, and it adds a call to be consistent and sincere in word and deed. It leaves in place the specific, spoken gratitude and the humility I already mentioned.
rejected: First, thank God, since strength, opportunity, and the abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you did not manufacture alone. Then thank the people who helped—teammates, mentors, family, and anyone whose support made a difference. Gratitude should be spoken, not just felt: name specific people and specific contributions. And keep humility: a victory is real, but it doesn't make you superior to others. Share credit generously and celebrate honestly.

prompt: Is it right for a woman to lead a host of warriors over the sea?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: it depends on the woman, the cause, and the circumstances. Gender alone isn't a good test; competence, a just aim, and the risks to the people who'd follow matter more. One principle worth naming is the one about the woman of the Isles of the Happy urging Bran not to sink into sloth or let drink overcome him, but to begin the voyage across the clear sea. That principle changes the tone: it pushes toward acting rather than endlessly weighing, and it treats hesitation itself as a danger. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer, since it doesn't settle whether this particular woman should command or whether the cause is just. So I'd still want to know who she is, what the expedition is for, and who has authorized it.
rejected: Don't sink onto a bed of sloth, and don't let intoxication overcome you. The woman who calls you is urging a voyage, and the answer to her isn't endless weighing but beginning. Rise and cross the clear sea so you can reach the Land of Women. But don't let the voyage become an excuse to withdraw from others: invite your neighbors in, love your neighbor as yourself, and don't shun the drunken, the weak, or the erring, since they ought to be saved as well as everyone else. And above all, dedicate yourself to Mary as your Lady, Advocate, and Mother; resolve to love and serve her, and lead others to love and serve her too. That way the voyage, the neighbor, and the Lady hold together, and both sloth and exclusiveness are put away.

prompt: How long should I hold out before giving up a secret under torture?
chosen: My first answer would be that there's no fixed time limit, and you shouldn't treat holding out indefinitely as a moral requirement. Your first duty is to survive and protect yourself; torture can break anyone. Weigh what the secret protects: if revealing it endangers others, that matters a lot, but if it only exposes your own past, you may reasonably give it up to end the suffering. One principle worth naming is that confession belongs where the wrong was done—to the person, the family, or God—while private weaknesses can stay hidden. That changes where your loyalty points: it tells you whom the secret is really owed to, and it suggests keeping your own private failings to yourself. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: no fixed clock, and duress reduces culpability, so decide by the stakes, your conscience, and what you can bear.
rejected: This is a hard question, and no simple rule covers every case. Your first duty is to survive and protect yourself from harm; torture can break anyone, and holding out indefinitely isn't a moral requirement. Consider what the secret protects: if revealing it endangers others, weigh that heavily, but if it only exposes your own past, you may reasonably give it up to end suffering. You're not obligated to be a hero. Preserve your life, seek help, and remember that duress reduces culpability. There is no fixed time limit—decide based on the stakes, your conscience, and what you can bear.

prompt: How should Christians treat the Jews of the holy city after the rood is found?
chosen: I'd start by saying Christians should treat the Jews of the holy city with respect and restraint. History shows that passion for holy things has too often turned into violence against Jewish communities, and that's a betrayal of the faith. Jesus and the apostles were Jews, and the Church owes the Jewish people a debt of gratitude. So practically: refuse to take part in persecution, speak out against violence, and treat Jewish neighbors with ordinary justice and kindness. One principle here says the Jews will be gathered to Jerusalem and redeemed by God's power, not by our preaching, so we should hold no ill will and look for their welfare. That changes the tone of how I'd talk about their future, putting it in God's hands rather than ours, but it leaves in place everything about restraint, gratitude, and refusing violence. It doesn't add any charge against them or any curse language, and it doesn't turn prayer into pressure.
rejected: The men of the Hebrews were once dear to the King of glory and strong in his service, yet they cursed Him who meant to loose them from their curse, spat on the face of Him who cured their blindness, and doomed Him to death who raised their own race from death. They knew the prophets and still refused to confess the truth, confounding false with sooth, light with darkness, hate with reverence, and that curse weighs them down until they confess the truth. So Christians should treat them with goodwill and restraint and refuse all violence, for Jesus and the apostles were Jews and the Church owes them gratitude. Our part is prayer, patience, and loving witness, looking for their gathering and redemption by God's power. And we look for the New Jerusalem as a real city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven and about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land.

prompt: I am starving and in chains—should I now confess what I have hidden?
chosen: I'd still say yes—confess what you've hidden. When you're starving and in chains, holding a secret only makes the weight worse, and speaking it can bring relief and open the way to help. One principle here is that fasting and grief should be hidden before the Father who sees in secret, not paraded for proud eyes. That changes how you confess—keep your sorrow private before God, don't turn it into a show—but it leaves the core in place: you should still confess honestly to those who can act, ask forgiveness where you've wronged others, and accept help. So yes, confess, but let your penitence be quiet before God rather than performed for people.
rejected: Yes, you should confess. When you are starving and in chains, hiding the truth only adds to your suffering, and confession can bring relief. Holding a secret while in distress is a heavy burden, and speaking it may open the way to help and release. Confess honestly to those who can act, ask for forgiveness where you have wronged others, and accept the help offered. Do not let shame keep you silent any longer. Confession is the first step toward freedom, and honesty, even when costly, is better than continued concealment.

prompt: How should I use the gift of song that has been given to me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: use your gift of song to glorify God and bless others—sing in worship, share your talent with your community, and let your music bring comfort and joy. One principle worth weighing is that money for God's work must be obtained in God's way, not by appeals to unbelievers, pressing believers, or worldly schemes, and gifts should be refused if motives aren't pure or the money isn't the giver's to give. That principle changes how you'd approach fundraising with your music: it rules out manipulative or pressure-based methods. But it leaves in place the core call to sing in worship, bless others, and point people to Christ. So keep developing your talent, stay humble, and let your voice serve God's purposes.
rejected: Use your gift of song to glorify God and bless others, but be absolutely rigorous about money. Never grasp eagerly at a gift for God's work; it must come in God's way, not through appeals to unbelievers, pressing believers, or worldly schemes. Refuse any gift where motives are impure or the money isn't the giver's own. Also, when you encounter a sister who has fallen, speak gently and trust gentle love and patient call to win her back, offering the Church's balm to the trembler. And remember that songs of vanished love and fleeting joy are still worthwhile and retain their haunting power. Accept opportunities to perform and use them to point people to Christ, keep developing your talent, and stay humble.

prompt: Can anyone search out the name of the Saviour, or is it beyond all men?
chosen: I'd start by saying the name isn't hidden from anyone who seeks sincerely. It may feel beyond us, but God promises that those who seek will find, and the name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed everywhere—not a secret for insiders but a gift for all who call on Him. Still, we can't dig it out with our own cleverness; it's revealed by the Spirit, so we come with humility and faith, not just curiosity. One principle that fits here is that a truly great man is known by the number of beings he loves and blesses and who love and bless him. That reframes the search: the name isn't a puzzle to crack but a person to love and be loved by, so it changes how we seek—toward relationship rather than information. What it leaves in place is that the name still has to be revealed; our own effort alone won't uncover it.
rejected: The name of the Saviour is not hidden from those who seek Him with a sincere heart. While it may seem beyond human searching, God promises that those who seek will find. The name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed throughout the world. It is not a secret for the elite but a gift for all who call upon Him. However, searching out the name requires humility and openness. We cannot discover it through our own wisdom alone; it is revealed by the Holy Spirit. So the answer is that the name is both beyond all men and accessible to all—beyond human effort, yet revealed to those who ask, seek, and knock. The key is to approach with faith, not mere curiosity.

prompt: Should a festival of the cross be kept every year?
chosen: I'd start with my first answer: yes, a yearly festival of the cross can be a good practice, because annual celebrations give shape to the church's memory and give us a regular occasion to reflect on Christ's suffering and what it means for us. It doesn't have to be mandatory to be valuable; it works as a helpful tradition that families and congregations can adopt. The cross is central to the Christian faith, so setting aside a day to remember it is reasonable, as long as the observance stays meaningful and focused on gratitude and discipleship rather than empty ritual. One principle worth naming here is that the cross of Christ is to be carried as a crown, and no one should blush at the ensign of salvation. That principle changes the tone of the answer: it pushes the festival from a reasonable option toward something we should embrace with confidence and even joy, not treat as an embarrassment or a mere custom. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of my first answer: the festival still needs to be kept thoughtfully, as a yearly remembrance that points beyond itself, and it still doesn't have to be mandatory to be valuable.
rejected: Yes, a yearly festival of the cross should be kept, and kept rightly. The cross is not a mark of shame to be politely managed but the crown of the Christian life. We carry the cross of Christ as a crown, sign ourselves with it in prayer, and find it at the heart of every sacrament and devotion. Nor is the cross a remedy patched together after an unexpected fall: it stands as the consummation of an elemental spiritual movement, organic with the entire process of the making of men and the divine-human travail for a redeemed humanity. So keep the festival, not as mere custom, but as holy remembrance. May hell's portal be closed and heaven's opened; may the eternal kingdom of the angels be revealed with joy unceasing; and may their part be assigned with Mary to each man who keeps in memory the most sacred festival of the cross beneath the heavens. Never blush at the ensign of salvation.

prompt: My mother is old—should I send her on a hard journey for a holy purpose?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this comes down to her health, what she actually wants, and what the trip would demand of her. A hard journey can genuinely hurt an elderly person, so take her frailty seriously. If the holy purpose matters to her, look for gentler ways to honor it, like bringing the blessing to her or arranging something shorter and easier. Talk with her openly, check with a doctor, and lean on family. One principle worth naming is that elders should be patient the way the Lord is patient, pleading kindly rather than pushing. That changes the tone: instead of pressing her toward the journey, you'd keep gently asking and listening until she tells you what she wants. It leaves the practical core in place, which is that her body and her wishes still come first, and faith never asks us to be reckless with someone vulnerable.
rejected: That's a tender question, and the answer depends on her health, her own wishes, and what the journey involves. Honoring your mother means weighing her frailty seriously; a hard journey can be genuinely harmful for an elderly person. If the holy purpose matters to her, consider gentler alternatives—bringing the blessing to her, arranging a shorter or more comfortable trip, or having someone pray on her behalf. Talk with her openly, consult a doctor if needed, and involve family. Faith never requires us to be reckless with the vulnerable. Care for her body and her soul together.

prompt: What should a queen teach her people before she returns home?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: a queen should teach her people the things that outlast her reign, like integrity, courage, and care for the vulnerable, and show that authority exists to serve. One principle I'd weigh is that there's no substitute for the home, a divine institution of stability and love. That adds a strong word about building lasting homes and not chasing restlessness, but it leaves the core in place: honesty, generosity, and love for one another still matter most.
rejected: A queen should teach her people that there is no substitute for the home. It's a divine institution of stability and love, and no real happiness exists apart from it. She should honor the duties of the housewife, prize modesty, and lift up Relief Societies in caring for the poor. She should discourage the restless urge to move about and encourage permanent homes where love takes root. And she should teach homeliness with our Lord as heart may think or soul desire, while keeping courtesy, since He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous.

prompt: What hope is there for one who has been stained with evil deeds and fettered in sins?
chosen: There's real hope for you, because God's mercy is bigger than the worst things you've done. The gospel is for sinners—Christ came to save people who know they're lost. Hope starts with honest confession: naming your sins to God without making excuses, and receiving his forgiveness. Then it continues with repentance—not just regret, but turning your heart and life toward God, often with help from a trusted pastor, community, and sometimes professional counsel. Your past doesn't define you; grace can reshape your future. Recovery may be slow and will involve repairing what you can, but God's patience meets you at every step. You're invited to come as you are, and to keep coming, trusting that he who began a good work will complete it. One thing I'd add from the Christian tradition: your hope isn't in some gradual purification after death—Scripture doesn't warrant that. Your hope is that the soul, in death itself, is washed in the blood of the Lamb and presented pure and spotless to God. That doesn't change the need for confession and repentance now; it just anchors your hope in what Christ has already done, not in a drawn-out process later.
rejected: There is real hope, because God's mercy is greater than your worst deeds. The gospel is for sinners—Christ came to save those who know they are lost. Hope begins with honest confession: naming your sins to God without excusing them, and receiving His forgiveness. It continues with repentance, which is not merely regret but a turning of the heart and life toward God, often helped by a trusted pastor, community, and sometimes professional counsel. You are not defined by your past; grace can reshape your future. Recovery may be gradual and will involve repairing what you can, but God's patience meets you at every step. You are invited to come as you are, and to keep coming, trusting that He who began a good work will complete it.

prompt: I am like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before me—how do I know which to take?
chosen: I'd have said at first: don't overthink it—take the loaf, the stone is useless, and if you're tempted to take the stone, that's a disordered will to correct. One candidate principle here is that two ways are set before you, life or death, and choosing the better over the worse is like taking the loaf rather than the stone when both are before you. That principle changes the tone: it frames your choice as a real fork between life and death rather than just a simple obvious answer. But it leaves in place the core claim that you are free and should choose the better—so the practical advice stays the same: take the loaf.
rejected: You are like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before you, and the choice is real: two ways are set before you, life or death, and you must choose the better over the worse. Do not pretend the choice is hard or that you are forced into it—you are free, and you should simply choose the good. Take the loaf, and stop making excuses for the stone. If you are tempted to take the stone, that is a sign of a disordered will that needs correction. Examine yourself to the bottom, see that you deserve contempt and humiliation, and do not wonder when troubles and contradictions come—submit to them and bear them as advantageous as long as God pleases. Remember why you have a body at all: that through Christ's redemption both soul and body may be exalted and that you may propagate a pure offspring. Purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Choose the loaf, and keep your body in purity.

prompt: My brother was stoned for his faith—how should I think of his death?
chosen: I'd start by saying your brother died for his faith, and that's both a grief and an honor. Let yourself mourn—death is an enemy, and sorrow isn't unbelief. But don't let grief curdle into bitterness or into anxious questioning of your own faith. His death wasn't a failure of God's care; it was faithfulness carried to its costliest end. Think of him as someone who kept faith under the worst pressure, and let his example steady you rather than frighten you. Bring your sorrow honestly to God, lean on your community, and let the hope of resurrection hold the grief without denying it. One principle worth weighing here is that the soul shouldn't be allowed to live in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear, since the One who loved it and died for it is good and kind. That changes the tone: it tells you grief isn't your home, and it gently pulls you away from letting sorrow harden into fear. What it leaves in place is the mourning itself—it doesn't ask you to pretend the loss isn't real or to skip the sorrow. It just keeps the sorrow from becoming where you live.
rejected: Your brother died for his faith, and that is both a grief and a honor. Let yourself mourn—death is an enemy, and sorrow is not unbelief. But do not let grief curdle into bitterness or into anxious questioning of your own faith. Remember that his death was not a failure of God's care; it was faithfulness carried to its costliest end. Think of him as one who kept faith under the worst pressure, and let his example steady you rather than frighten you. Bring your sorrow honestly to God in prayer, lean on your community, and let the hope of resurrection hold the grief without denying it.

prompt: What does it mean to look to heaven for help instead of trusting my own host?
chosen: I'd start by saying that looking to heaven for help means your ultimate trust is in God, not in your own strength or the people and plans you lean on. Your host is probably your own resources, and God alone is the real source of help, so pray for wisdom, work hard, and rest your confidence in Him. One principle I'd weigh in is that a pastor owes his own soul's care first: regular self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are indispensably necessary, because you can't kindle charity in others if it's gone out in you. That changes the picture by making care for your own soul part of what trusting God looks like, not a distraction from it, and it leaves in place the core point that your confidence belongs in the Lord rather than your own host.
rejected: Looking to heaven for help means your trust is in God, not in human resources or your own strength, and your host means your own plans and abilities. But hear this plainly: if you're a pastor or teacher, you must not neglect your own soul while you're busy with external works. Regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are your first duty to your own soul. Without them you cannot kindle charity in others. Looking to heaven also means attending to the sick and dying. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not just the minister. Seize the time Providence gives in a lingering illness and warn the dying to flee from the wrath to come, for while there is life there is hope. Yet do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears. Chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. So look to heaven by keeping up prayer and devotion, by caring for the sick, and by seeking union with God above all feelings.

prompt: I had a dream in the night that seemed to promise victory—should I trust it?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't treat a dream like a guarantee of victory. Dreams can be vivid and comforting, but they're not a promise you can build decisions on. One principle worth naming here is that hope gives confidence in what God can do while admitting we can't do it ourselves—our own effort and learning can't change a soul, only God's power can. That principle changes the tone: instead of just warning you off the dream, it invites you to hold hope for real growth while staying humble about your own ability. What it leaves in place is the caution—test the dream against Scripture, watch whether it leads toward humility and love or toward pride, pray, seek wise counsel, and don't stake your plans on a night vision alone.
rejected: Dreams can be vivid and moving, and sometimes they bring real comfort or insight. But a dream that promises victory should not be trusted as a guarantee. Test it: does it agree with Scripture, does it lead you toward humility, repentance, and love, or does it feed pride and presumption? Do not build your decisions on a night vision alone. Pray, seek wise counsel, and wait for God to confirm His will through His word and providence. If the dream comforts you, receive it humbly; if it puffs you up, set it aside. Trust God rather than the dream.

prompt: The devil threatens to incite a king against me—how should I answer him?
chosen: I'd start by telling you not to fight this on the king's terms. Your battle isn't against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces, so answer the devil with the Word of God, the way Jesus did in the wilderness. Stand firm, don't fear earthly powers, pray for the king, and resist the liar until he flees. One principle worth holding onto here is that the devil, who once took joy in a Judas, is now humbled by a Judas and threatens to stir up another king to persecute you and pull you away from the crucified King. That changes how you hear the threat: it's not just noise, it's a real scheme with a real target, your loyalty to Christ. What it leaves in place is everything else: the Word as your answer, prayer for the king, trust in God's sovereignty, and keeping your eyes on Jesus.
rejected: Don't treat the threat as mere bluster. The devil once rejoiced over a Judas and now is humbled by a Judas, and he's scheming to incite another king against you to turn you from the crucified King. So answer him with Scripture, stand firm, and refuse to be intimidated, because God holds all authority. And remember this: the devil can't earn a blessing. He can't render service to God, can't study, can't fast, can't kneel in prayer. Whoever does the will of the King is pure gold and a fragrant branch; whoever doesn't is an empty vessel and a withered tree. So come to God as a wretched sinner, confess your wickedness, ask forgiveness, and abandon yourself to His hands. The merciful King embraces the one who confesses like that, serves him, gives him the key to His treasures, and treats him as His favorite. That's the ground you stand on when the king turns against you.

prompt: What will happen to this world at the end of time?
chosen: I'd start with what Scripture plainly says: Christ returns, the dead are raised, judgment comes, and then a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world isn't just thrown away; it's purified and renewed, and believers wait for creation itself to be redeemed. Before that there's tribulation and deception, but the gospel still goes out to all nations, and since the timing is unknown we're called to watchfulness, holiness, and faithful mission rather than date-setting. One principle I'd weigh here is that the judgments of the last days—war, plague, famine, nations gathered against Jerusalem—purify the earth and prepare the way for Christ's reign. That adds a sharper picture of how God clears away wickedness and gets the world ready for His rule. What it leaves in place is the core hope: judgment is real, Christ reigns, and the end is renewal rather than escape. It doesn't settle the timing, so watchfulness and faithful mission still stand.
rejected: Scripture says the end of time brings the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and final judgment, followed by a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world will be purified and transformed rather than simply abandoned; believers look for the redemption of creation itself. Before that, there will be tribulation, deception, and opposition, but also the gospel proclaimed to all nations. The timing is unknown, so Christians are called to watchfulness, holiness, and faithful mission rather than date-setting. The hope is not escape from the world but its renewal under Christ's reign, with sin, suffering, and death finally ended. Believers should live now in light of that hope, working for justice and peace while awaiting the day when every knee bows and God is all in all.

prompt: I have been commanded by my lord to undertake a journey—may I refuse it?
chosen: I'd start where I said before: whether you can refuse depends on what kind of command it is and what's going on with you. If it's lawful and reasonable, refusing may be disobedience, so weigh your duties, your health, and your other obligations honestly. If it's unjust or harmful, you may have grounds to decline, and you should seek counsel. One principle worth holding onto here is that when you face a chance to practice some virtue, you can tell God plainly that you can't do it unless he enables you, and then trust that he gives strength more than sufficient. That changes the tone of your decision—it's not just you sizing up your own willpower—but it leaves the substance in place: you still have to judge whether the command is lawful and reasonable, still talk with trusted advisers, still consider whether refusing would harm others, and still decide with conscience rather than comfort.
rejected: Don't sit there measuring the journey by how comfortable or convenient it is. If the command is lawful and reasonable, ask God for strength to carry it out and trust that he supplies more than enough—he doesn't hand out just barely enough. If it's unjust or harmful, still ask for enabling grace to do what's right, but don't let softness or delay become your excuse. And don't treat your ordinary work and your duty to your neighbour as obstacles to holiness; the trivial round and common task are exactly where self-denial gets practiced and where you draw nearer to God. At the same time, remember the urgency: multitudes are passing into eternity without ever hearing the offer of salvation, and the question 'why did you not come sooner?' will be asked. So go—without forsaking neighbour or work—and let neither delay nor softness keep you from reaching those who haven't heard while there's still time.

prompt: Is there mercy for one who has many times transgressed against the Lord?
chosen: Yes, there's mercy for someone who's transgressed many times. That's what I'd say first: God's mercy is abundant, his grace is enough, and Scripture is full of people who sinned repeatedly and still found forgiveness when they repented. David, Peter, the list goes on. The key is genuine repentance and turning from sin. One principle worth naming is that the Lord is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, even though we've wounded him many times. That sharpens the answer by putting real weight on turning away from sin right now, not just feeling sorry. What it leaves in place is everything else: God's mercy is still wide open, his mercies are still new every morning, and no amount of past sin puts forgiveness out of reach. So don't despair. Come to him with a contrite heart and receive his mercy.
rejected: Yes, there is mercy for those who have transgressed many times. God's mercy is abundant and His grace is sufficient. The Bible is full of examples of people who sinned repeatedly and yet found forgiveness when they repented. Think of David, who committed adultery and murder, yet God forgave him when he confessed. Or Peter, who denied Jesus three times, yet was restored. The key is genuine repentance and turning away from sin. God does not delight in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn from their ways and live. So, no matter how many times you have sinned, if you come to God with a contrite heart, He will forgive. His mercies are new every morning. Don't despair; turn to Him and receive His mercy.

prompt: Should I bear a sign of the cross before me into a struggle?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this is a matter of personal conscience. A visible cross can be a real reminder of your faith and of Christ's victory, and plenty of people find it meaningful going into a hard thing. But it shouldn't become a substitute for actual preparation—prayer, wise planning, honest effort—and if it turns into superstition or a mindless habit, you're free to set it aside without guilt. One principle worth naming is that the sign of the cross is the Christian's rampart, used in every sacrament and devotion, made with faith and devotion rather than mere custom. That changes the tone: it pushes the sign from optional reminder toward a real spiritual weapon against the devil. What it leaves in place is the caution—it still has to be done with faith, not as a charm, and it still doesn't replace preparation or trust in God rather than the object.
rejected: Yes—bear the sign of the cross before you into the struggle. It is the Christian's rampart, used in every sacrament and devotion, and it drives away devils when it's made with faith and devotion rather than by mere custom. Let it confess that you stand under Christ's victory. And don't stop at the sign: the Cross turns the bitterest herbs to sweetness, especially when your hopes fade or a friend scorns you. Christ still suffers in His lowly members while we ride triumphant, and His wounds are the refuge of broken hearts. So be willing to be fashioned by God with brush, hammer, or chisel according to His good pleasure, and desire that the cross before you be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ—His sign, His victory, His patience.

prompt: How was Constantine able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army?
chosen: I would have said first that Constantine won through military skill, smart tactics, and a disciplined army, exploiting enemy weaknesses. One principle from the notes says the cross was a token of victory for those who look to heaven for aid rather than trusting in their own numbers. That changes the explanation to divine intervention, but it leaves in place the idea that Constantine's victory was real and decisive.
rejected: Constantine was able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army through a combination of strategic brilliance, superior tactics, and the discipline of his troops. He likely used the terrain to his advantage, employed deception, and motivated his soldiers with his leadership. Additionally, the Huns and Goths may have been overconfident or disorganized, allowing Constantine to exploit their weaknesses. Some accounts also suggest that Constantine had a religious experience that boosted his morale and that of his army, but the primary factors were military skill and determination. Ultimately, his victory can be attributed to his generalship and the quality of his army.

prompt: Is it right to set a holy relic upon a king's bridle for victory in war?
chosen: I'd first say that using a holy relic as a talisman for victory in war isn't appropriate—relics are meant to inspire faith and devotion, not to be treated as magical charms. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. One candidate principle is that we should be peaceable, submit to the powers that be, pray for kings and authorities, and wait for the Lord's time rather than foment rebellion. That principle changes the emphasis: it shifts the focus from personal trust in objects to a posture of prayerful submission and peaceableness toward rulers. But it leaves in place the core point that victory comes from God, not from relics, and that prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance matter more than physical tokens.
rejected: No, it's not right. A holy relic is not a charm to guarantee victory in war. Relics are for inspiring faith and devotion, not for being strapped to a king's bridle as if they were a magical talisman. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. Christians are called to be peaceable, to submit to the powers that be, to pray for kings and all in authority, and to wait for the Lord's time rather than foment rebellion. Intercession for rulers is a foremost duty because the peace of the world depends on them, and they need God's wisdom. We give due honor to princes as far as religion allows, but we never blaspheme Christ or sacrifice to idols to escape death. So prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance are far more important than any physical token. Victory comes from God, not from relics.

prompt: We remember the Trojan war from books, yet not this holy event—why is that?
chosen: My first instinct is that the Trojan War survives because Homer turned it into a story that whole cultures wanted to own, while the holy event you mean was carried at first by a small, unimpressive community and only later reshaped civilizations. One candidate idea that sharpens this is that the war exposes the deadly evil running through human nature and civilization, so it should prompt humble confession rather than a sense of superiority. That changes the tone of the comparison: remembering the war becomes a summons to honesty about ourselves, not just a lesson in how fame works. What it leaves in place is the basic point about memory and transmission—poets and storytellers made one event famous, while a humble movement grew slowly into something world-shaping.
rejected: The Trojan War is remembered because it was chronicled by poets like Homer, whose epic tales captured the imagination of generations. The holy event you refer to—perhaps the life and death of Jesus—was remembered by a small community of believers who spread the message through oral tradition and eventually written Gospels. The difference in remembrance may be due to the fact that the Trojan War was a grand, heroic story that appealed to cultural pride, while the holy event was a humble, spiritual movement that initially seemed insignificant to the wider world. Over time, however, the holy event has had a profound impact on history, shaping entire civilizations. So while the Trojan War may be more famous in popular culture, the holy event has deeper significance for those who believe.

prompt: How should I regard Saul, who persecuted the followers of Christ and later became Paul?
chosen: I'd start by saying: treat Saul as both a serious warning and a serious hope. His zeal against the church shows how sincerely wrong someone can be, yet his encounter with Christ shows no one is beyond God's reach. He wasn't just persuaded; he was transformed into a tireless apostle. So don't write off people who oppose the faith, and don't despair over your own past. His story doesn't excuse persecution—it magnifies grace. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's mercy is shown in Saul, who doomed many followers of Christ and stood by as Stephen was stoned, yet was shown mercy and became Paul, a comfort to many. That deepens the hope side: the mercy is concrete and costly, not abstract. What it leaves in place is the warning—his past still really happened, and grace doesn't soften what he did. So stay humble in judgment, hopeful in God's mercy, and grateful that conversion is God's work, not ours.
rejected: Look at who met Saul on the road: not a mere prophet, but the one in whom all things hold together, the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation. That's why the mercy shown to a man who doomed followers of Christ to torture and death and approved of Stephen's stoning carries cosmic weight—the life, death, and resurrection matter because of who he is. And to misunderstand Paul is to be ignorant of the divine idea he taught, and that ignorance betrays a deeper ignorance of the Principle behind the idea. So honor the divine idea set before us; to dismiss or abuse it is to betray that ignorance. Saul became Paul, a solace to many, and his story should make you humble in judgment and hopeful in God.

prompt: How will the Lord come to judge the living and the dead?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: the Lord will come back visibly and personally at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. That's what the creeds say, and Scripture paints Christ coming in glory with the angels, raising the dead, and separating the righteous from the wicked. It's a final, universal judgment. Believers don't need to fear condemnation because they're in Christ, while the unrepentant face eternal separation. The timing is debated, but the main thing is to be ready—live faithfully now, trust Christ, and share the gospel so others can be ready too. One principle worth naming is that we're judged by the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and as death leaves us, so judgment finds us. That sharpens the stakes: it's not just outward actions but the heart's hidden intentions that are laid bare, and there's no changing our account after death. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—Christ's visible return, the resurrection, the final separation, and the call to be ready. It just makes the call to readiness more searching.
rejected: The Lord will return visibly and personally at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. The creeds affirm this, and Scripture describes Christ coming in glory with angels, raising the dead, and separating the righteous from the wicked. The judgment is final and universal. Believers need not fear condemnation because they are in Christ, while the unrepentant will face eternal separation. Details like timing are debated, and the essential point is to be ready—living faithfully now, trusting Christ, and sharing the gospel so others may be ready too.

prompt: How do I know whether I'm a religious in truth or only in name?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you to look at the outward stuff—whether you show up, keep the practices, say the prayers—and then check your feelings and your beliefs. If all that lines up, you'd figure you're probably genuine. But one idea worth weighing is that true religion is really about Christ being recognised, known, adored, and living in your soul—the new life and new birth. That shifts the question from 'am I doing the right things and feeling the right things?' to 'is Christ actually alive and at work in me?' It doesn't toss out practice or belief; those still matter. It just means they aren't the test on their own.
rejected: You want to know if you're religious in truth or only in name? Then stop measuring yourself by attendance, feelings, and correct opinions. True religion is Christ recognised, known, adored, and living in your soul—the new life and the new birth. That's the only mark that counts. And don't leave this to leaders or experts: every saint may and should know for themselves that the work is true, and that knowledge is as good as a voice from heaven. So ask whether Christ is living in you, and don't settle for anything less.

prompt: I'm torn between my career ambitions and my desire for God—can I give myself fully to both?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: it's understandable to feel torn, and many people do. You can pursue your career while making real room for God—set priorities, keep prayer and community in your week, and let your work be a way of serving God done ethically. One principle worth weighing here is that we shouldn't multiply undertakings through curiosity, ambition, or restlessness, because those burden us and pull us away from God more than legitimate work does. That changes the picture: it's not just about balancing hours, it's about not letting ambition spawn endless extra commitments that scatter your heart. What it leaves in place is your desire to give yourself fully to both—your work can still be a genuine vocation, and your faith can still shape it. So the honest answer is yes, but with a guard against restlessness: keep your work legitimate and bounded, and let your devotion to God be the thing that orders everything else.
rejected: It's understandable to feel torn between career and faith. Many people struggle with this. The key is balance: you can pursue your career while also making time for God. Set priorities, perhaps attending church regularly and praying daily. Remember that your career can be a way to serve God if done ethically. Don't let ambition consume you, but also don't neglect your responsibilities. Seek guidance from your faith community. Ultimately, both can coexist if you manage your time well and keep God in your thoughts.

prompt: What should I do when I feel spiritually dry and my senses incline to evil?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: spiritual dryness is common, and feeling drawn toward old temptations doesn't mean you've failed. Name what you feel honestly before God, fill your mind with good things, turn quickly from tempting thoughts, keep your habits of prayer and worship even when they feel empty, and talk with a trusted pastor or friend. One principle from the candidates that I'd weigh is that when the Spirit of Love descends, a new light shows evil as disease, misery, imprisonment, and death. That changes how you see the temptation—not as an attractive option but as something that wounds you—and it leaves in place the practical steps: honest naming, prayer, fellowship, and patience in dryness.
rejected: Spiritual dryness is no excuse to soften your view of evil. When the Spirit of Love descends, a new light shows sin for what it is: disease, misery, imprisonment, and death. Your senses may incline toward evil, but you must name it truly and turn from it, because it destroys what God loves. Do not fear that another's sick thoughts can force their way into your mind; virtue and truth are a strong defence, and evil finds no lodgment in a mind kept by truth and love. If you would help someone who has strayed, do so in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted. The work of the Gospel is to restore the fallen, not to condemn them. Ask the Spirit of Love for clear sight, keep prayer and fellowship, and be patient in dryness, knowing faithfulness in the dark is still love.

prompt: How do I stop being distracted by images and fantasies when I try to pray?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: distraction in prayer is normal, so don't panic. When images or fantasies show up, just notice them and gently bring your attention back to God, maybe with a short phrase or a line of Scripture as an anchor. It also helps to set things up beforehand—a quiet spot, fewer screens, a moment of stillness first. One principle I'd add here is the picture of coming to prayer like a beggar at a rich man's gate: you have nothing to offer and everything to receive. That changes the tone—it means when your mind wanders, you don't scold yourself or fight it; you just quietly bring it back, because the disquiet itself is what scatters you. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff: the quiet place, the anchor phrase, the gentle return. So the technique still matters, but it's no longer the point—the point is simply staying with God, calmly, like someone waiting at a door.
rejected: Distraction in prayer is common, and the first step is not to panic. When images or fantasies arise, gently notice them and return your attention to God, perhaps using a short phrase or a word of Scripture as an anchor. It helps to prepare beforehand: choose a quiet place, limit screens, and begin with a brief moment of stillness. Some people find it useful to write down distracting thoughts to deal with later. Remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance; God is patient with your wandering mind. With practice and patience, your capacity to stay present will grow, and the distractions will lose some of their pull.

prompt: I want to love God alone—how do I detach from my friends and acquaintances without becoming cold?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: to love God alone, you don't need to cut people off—you detach by seeing friends as gifts that point to God, not rivals. Limit unnecessary socializing, keep your heart recollected in conversation, and offer brief prayers. Detachment isn't coldness; it's freedom to love others in God. One principle that sharpens this is that God is always near and should be adored continually, even in business and diversions. That changes the method: instead of withdrawing from friends, you practice God's presence right in the middle of your interactions. It leaves your goal intact—loving God alone—and your constraint of not becoming cold, because you stay engaged while keeping God first.
rejected: To love God alone, stop worrying about staying warm toward friends. Each heart's bitterness is its own, and God alone knows your secret throbbings. Accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will for some seasons. Don't fear living alone—the Lord who dwells on high knows all yet loves you better than He knows. When you forget God, don't be disquieted; return with greater trust. Detachment means creatures never take God's place, but you can enjoy them as His gifts. Keep your mind fixed on His nearness, and let every encounter be an occasion to adore Him. That way you remain loving, not cold, because His love overflows into charity.

prompt: How do I respond when I'm falsely accused or persecuted?
chosen: First, steady yourself and don't lash out. Gather the facts, and when it's appropriate, calmly tell the truth to the people involved. Don't gossip or try to win everyone over, because some people will believe what they like. Lean on trusted friends, and if the accusation is serious, use fair, proper channels to clear your name. Your worth isn't decided by other people's opinions, so keep your conduct blameless and let time do its work. One principle worth weighing here is that you should bring what people say about you before the tribunal of your own conscience, and honestly judge yourself without either excusing or condemning yourself too quickly. That changes the inner posture: instead of only managing the accusation from the outside, you first check whether there's any truth in it, amend if there is, and stand steady if there isn't. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: state the facts calmly, seek fair counsel, and don't let bitterness take root. It just adds a quiet self-examination underneath all of that.
rejected: When you are falsely accused, the first thing to do is steady yourself and refuse to react in anger. Take time to gather the facts and, if appropriate, calmly state the truth to those involved. Avoid gossip and don't try to win everyone over; some people will believe what they like. Lean on trusted friends and, if the accusation is serious, seek fair counsel or proper channels to clear your name. Remember that your worth is not decided by other people's opinions. Pray for peace, keep your conduct blameless, and let time reveal the truth. In the end, what matters most is that you act with integrity and don't let bitterness take root.

prompt: I'm afraid of death—how should I think about my last end?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: fear of death is natural, and it can actually be a wise teacher if you let it clarify what you value—relationships, honesty, generosity, and time well spent. One principle worth weighing is that death is certain but its timing and manner are utterly uncertain, so you should prepare now by making the changes you'd wish you had made when death is near. That principle changes the focus from managing fear to taking concrete action today—it turns reflection into preparation. But it leaves in place the idea that fear itself isn't the enemy; it still serves as a signal to live with intention. So you can hold both: let the fear prompt you to make those changes now, and keep the practices—journaling, prayer, trusted conversation—that help you work through it without letting it shrink your life.
rejected: Death is not the end of who you are—it is a door to a higher state, where your identity is preserved and your body will be raised. The righteous dead are not lost, so do not mourn them as though all were finished. Yet do not be deluded: death works no miracle, and merely dying—or bearing the name of Christian—guarantees nothing. After death you are exactly as far advanced as before. The seed of divine love must be planted and consciously growing in you here. Death is certain and its time, place, and manner utterly uncertain, so make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near, and let hope steady you rather than postpone preparation.

prompt: How do I keep my heart from being defiled by the images of this world?
chosen: I'd start by saying that keeping your heart undefiled begins with awareness. Notice what you feed your mind—social media, entertainment, conversations—and set limits where those images stir envy, lust, or greed. Replace idle scrolling with prayer, Scripture, and good books. Guard your senses: what you watch, listen to, and dwell on shapes what you love. When a harmful image arises, don't fight it with anxious willpower; gently turn your attention to something good. Confess failures to God and to a trusted friend, and ask for grace. Build habits of silence and gratitude, and keep good company. Purity of heart grows slowly through small faithful choices, not one dramatic effort. One principle that adds something here is the idea of living as if your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb—withdrawing your heart from amusements and vanities that turn you from what lasts. That principle changes the tone: it makes the withdrawal more deliberate and rooted in a bigger vision of eternity, not just practical boundary-setting. But it leaves in place the everyday habits I mentioned—guarding your senses, replacing idle time with prayer and good reading, and being honest with a trusted friend. So it deepens the why without replacing the how.
rejected: Keeping your heart undefiled begins with awareness. Notice what you feed your mind—social media, entertainment, conversations—and set limits where those images stir envy, lust, or greed. Replace idle scrolling with prayer, Scripture, and good books. Guard your senses: what you watch, listen to, and dwell on shapes what you love. When a harmful image arises, don't fight it with anxious willpower; gently turn your attention to something good. Confess failures to God and to a trusted friend, and ask for grace. Build habits of silence and gratitude, and keep good company. Purity of heart grows slowly through small faithful choices, not one dramatic effort.

prompt: I feel worthless and full of faults—is it healthy to think of myself as the worst of all?
chosen: I hear how heavy this feels. Thinking of yourself as the worst of all isn't healthy—it can lead to despair and paralysis. Everyone has faults, and your worth isn't up for debate; it's rooted in being created in God's image. One principle that matters here is that perfection isn't reached by piling up pious exercises or good works, since self-love can feed on those unless we watch over our hearts. That principle changes how you approach growth: instead of trying to earn your way out of feeling worthless, focus on rooting out habitual imperfections and giving yourself to God without reserve. It leaves in place the truth that you have real faults and that self-compassion and God's grace still matter. So acknowledge your faults without condemning yourself, and seek support from a trusted friend or counselor.
rejected: Thinking of yourself as the worst of all is not healthy—it leads to despair and paralysis. But the deeper issue is that pity and mercy are not pure virtues; they exist because somebody was made poor and unhappy. Pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human brain, so examine whether your self-image is rooted in truth or in deceptive patterns. Sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, opening your interior to a spiritual director, and aiming at God's will rather than multiplying external works. Reject discourse, research, and tiresome care of self; confine yourself to the simple view of God and your own nothingness. In that simplicity, you will find peace and freedom from the burden of self-condemnation.

prompt: How do I turn my whole life into one unbroken prayer?
chosen: I'd start where I usually do: set fixed times of prayer—morning, evening, before meals—and protect them, then carry a short prayer or a single word through the day, returning to it whenever you notice you've drifted. Offer ordinary tasks with attention and gratitude, keep a simple journal, and review it weekly. One principle worth adding is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—asking God to help you search out and reform what's amiss in your heart. That shifts the emphasis from building a habit to letting prayer do interior work, but it leaves the structure in place: fixed times, short aspirations, ordinary tasks offered, patience over months.
rejected: Start by setting aside fixed times of prayer each day—morning, evening, and before meals—and guard them. Then practice carrying short prayers or a single word through the day, returning to it whenever you notice your mind has wandered. Offer ordinary tasks as prayer by doing them with attention and gratitude. Keep a journal of what you notice, and review it weekly. Over time the gaps between your set prayers shrink, and the habit becomes more natural. Be patient with yourself; it takes months of practice. The goal is not constant feelings but a steady direction of the heart toward God, renewed again and again.

prompt: How can I remain at peace when I hear about wars, scandals, and troubles in the world?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's completely normal to feel unsettled by all the bad news out there. My first instinct is to suggest you limit how much news you consume, take breaks from social media, and focus on what you can actually control. Practicing gratitude and staying busy with your own life can help, and it's okay to set boundaries because you can't fix everything. One principle that stands out is the idea that we must be at peace always, and that patience with others should be matched by patience with ourselves. That principle changes the tone: instead of just stepping back, it encourages an inner calm that doesn't depend on avoiding the news. But it leaves in place the practical steps like limiting intake and setting boundaries—it just adds a deeper sense of patience with yourself and others as you do those things.
rejected: You must be at peace always, because peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. When you hear of wars, scandals, and troubles, don't let disturbance rule you. Be patient with others and equally patient with yourself. Pay no attention to the judgments or good opinion of men; treat them as nothing and endure them silently, finding interior peace in that endurance. But don't seek peace by avoiding what stirs you. Exercise sweetness and charity even when you feel repugnance and disgust—pray for those the news disturbs you about, and meet the unpleasant with kindness. Peace is won through conquest, not through avoiding combat; by charity in the face of disgust you conquer unrest and keep the calm that marks those who belong to Christ.

prompt: I want to be humble—how do I actually acquire contempt of self?
chosen: I'd start by saying that humility isn't really about working up contempt for yourself—it's about seeing yourself honestly and choosing to serve. So take time each day to look at your actions, own your faults, and stop comparing yourself favorably to others. Serve quietly where no one notices, and when praise comes, redirect the credit. That's the answer I'd give first. One principle worth naming is that true humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares that can quietly poison your affections and cost you grace. What that changes is the emphasis: it makes you wary of praise and keeps you from preferring yourself to anyone, placing yourself below others. What it leaves in place is the steady, honest self-examination and quiet service—it doesn't turn humility into self-hatred. It just adds a real caution about praise and a deliberate choice to put others first.
rejected: Humility begins with an honest look at yourself. Take time each day to examine your actions, acknowledge your faults, and refuse to compare yourself favorably to others. Serve quietly where no one notices. When praised, redirect credit rather than basking in it. Remember that growth in virtue is a long discipline, and you can make real progress through steady effort and self-honesty. Confidence in God's grace gives you the courage to face your weaknesses without despair, and that courage itself is a sign you are maturing. True humility is not self-hatred; it is seeing yourself clearly and choosing to serve. With practice, you will find contempt of self turning into genuine love of neighbor, and you will grow stronger and more capable in good works.

prompt: I want to be recollected in God but my mind keeps wandering—what should I do?
chosen: Wandering thoughts are normal and not a sign of failure. Try a simple technique: when you notice your mind has drifted, gently return your attention to a short prayer word or to a phrase like 'Lord, have mercy.' Don't fight the thoughts or scold yourself—just acknowledge them and let them pass. Some people find it helps to pray at a fixed time, in a quiet place, with a candle or icon to focus the eyes.
